chunks.title: What is Wazwan?
chunks.text:
Wazwan is the formal multi-course feast of Kashmir. Its dishes, mostly mutton, are cooked by professional cooks called wazas under a head cook, the vasta waza, and served on a copper trami that four guests share. It is best known from Kashmiri Muslim weddings, and it is a different thing from everyday Kashmiri home cooking. The name joins waz, cook, and wan, usually given as shop.
Dishes: 7 to 36, depending on the occasion (Rather).
Cooked by: Wazas, led by a vasta waza (Jammu & Kashmir Tourism Development Corporation. “Cuisines of Kashmir.”).
Served: Four diners to one copper trami (Wikipedia. “Wazwan”; “Sikandar Shah Miri”; “Zayn al-Abidin the Great”; “Kashmiri Pandits.”).
Ends with: Gushtaba (Wikipedia. “Wazwan”; “Sikandar Shah Miri”; “Zayn al-Abidin the Great”; “Kashmiri Pandits.”).
Best known at: Weddings (Raja Muzaffar Bhat. “Wazwan: A Culinary Legacy.” Sahapedia).
Origin: Undocumented; the wazas’ own account points to Central Asia (Arka Chakraborty. “Kashmiri Wazwan: Celebration of Food).

chunks.title: Wazwan: The wazas (who cooks it)
chunks.text:
A Wazwan is cooked by wazas, professional cooks whom a family books for the occasion. The head cook, the vasta waza, supervises while his team does the heavy work (JK Arts Foundation).
How big the team is depends on the order. In 2015 The Tribune reported that a wedding Wazwan takes at least six to eight wazas, and one waza said his bookings had started six months ahead (The Tribune). Sahapedia describes three or four wazas with assistants for 200 to 300 kg of meat (Sahapedia).
The craft runs in families. Ghulam Nabi Baba, a 74-year-old waza, told Reuters in 2026 that his forefathers settled in Srinagar's old city as part of the community of cooks known as Wazpora, and that he joined his father at 15; his own son opened a restaurant instead (Reuters via Al Jazeera). Recipes pass mostly by apprenticeship, though one waza family has published its recipes as a cookbook (Roli Books).

chunks.title: Wazwan: What’s documented, and what’s told (where it comes from)
chunks.text: No document records when or how Wazwan began; the accounts that circulate rest largely on word of mouth (JK Arts Foundation). Kashmir Life, working from medieval Persian sources, argues that it has no single starting point and took roughly its present form by the late Afghan period (Kashmir Life).

chunks.title: Wazwan: How many dishes (the size of the feast)
chunks.text:
There is no fixed number. A 2016 review in the Journal of Ethnic Foods puts a Wazwan at seven to 36 dishes (Rather, Masoodi and Akhter). Thirty-six is the traditional figure for the grandest feasts (JKTDC), but most menus are smaller.
Sahapedia describes the feast growing from a seven-dish meal to 12 to 24 dishes (Sahapedia), and Ghulam Nabi Baba told Reuters there were seven mutton dishes in his forefathers' time and about 20 now (Reuters). A funeral Wazwan usually has at least seven dishes, according to Asia Media Centre (Asia Media Centre). Restaurants serve smaller set menus or single dishes.
The dishes on this page are the Wazwan dishes in our catalogue, in the order they're served. Seven of them are commonly listed as essential, and they're marked.

chunks.title: Wazwan: Wazwan in Kashmiri life (weddings and gatherings)
chunks.text:
Weddings are where the biggest menus are cooked. Ghulam Nabi Baba told Reuters an average wedding takes about 200 kg, and the largest he ever cooked took 4,500 kg (Reuters). The cooking happens in a temporary kitchen set up at the host's home, over fires of fruit-tree wood such as apple, walnut or plum (Sahapedia), and the meat is still pounded by hand (Reuters).
Wazwan is cooked for other gatherings too, including funerals (Asia Media Centre). Guests are usually given bags to take leftovers home; one restaurateur says the custom became accepted only in recent decades and was once thought shameful (Asia Media Centre). Many people describe the shared trami as setting aside differences of status among the four who eat from it (JK Arts Foundation).

chunks.title: Wazwan: Communities and variations (who eats it, and how it varies)
chunks.text:
Wazwan as most people know it is a Kashmiri Muslim banquet (JKTDC). Kashmiri Pandits have their own festive cooking: they eat mutton and fish but not beef (Wikipedia), and traditional Pandit kitchens use asafoetida rather than onion and garlic (JKTDC). Our guide to Kashmiri Pandit food covers how it differs.
The menu also changes over time. Chicken and vegetarian dishes, mushrooms among them, have been added in recent years (Asia Media Centre); see vegetarian Wazwan. And Wazwan isn't the same as the everyday food of Kashmiri homes, which Kashmiri cuisine explained covers, or as Mughlai cooking (Wazwan vs Mughlai).

chunks.title: Wazwan: How to experience it (if you’re visiting)
chunks.text:
Weddings are private, so most visitors eat Wazwan in a restaurant, as a set menu or dish by dish. Our guide to eating in Srinagar lists places that serve it, the cost guide covers prices, and restaurant vs wedding vs home explains what changes between them.
Weddings cluster in the warmer months. In 2015 The Tribune reported a season from mid-April to the end of October, with a break during Ramadan and generally no weddings in winter (The Tribune).
At the trami, wash your hands when the tash-t-naer comes round, eat from your own quarter, and expect gushtaba to close the meal; how Wazwan is served explains the order and the etiquette. Planning a trip around it? See the Wazwan food trail itinerary.

chunks.title: What is Wazwan?
chunks.text:
What is Wazwan?
Wazwan is the formal multi-course feast of Kashmir. Its dishes, mostly mutton, are cooked by professional cooks called wazas under a head cook, the vasta waza, and served on a copper trami that four guests share. It is best known from Kashmiri Muslim weddings, and it is a different thing from everyday Kashmiri home cooking.

chunks.title: What does “Wazwan” mean?
chunks.text:
What does “Wazwan” mean?
Waz means cook, and wan is usually given as shop (Budgam district administration; Sahapedia), so the name points to the cooks rather than to a menu. Outlook India renders wan as “to spread”.

chunks.title: How many dishes are in a Wazwan?
chunks.text:
How many dishes are in a Wazwan?
Seven to 36, according to a 2016 review in the Journal of Ethnic Foods. Thirty-six is the traditional figure for the grandest feasts; wedding menus today usually run to about 12 to 24 dishes (Sahapedia), and restaurants serve smaller sets.

chunks.title: Who cooks Wazwan?
chunks.text:
Who cooks Wazwan?
Professional cooks called wazas, led by a head cook, the vasta waza, who supervises the team. Most are based in Srinagar's old city, and the craft often passes from father to son.

chunks.title: Which dish comes last?
chunks.text:
Which dish comes last?
Gushtaba, large balls of pounded mutton in a yogurt gravy, ends the main meal. A dessert such as phirni and a cup of kahwa usually follow.

chunks.title: Is Wazwan always meat?
chunks.text:
Is Wazwan always meat?
It is built mostly on mutton, with chicken, but vegetarian dishes such as dum aloo and mushrooms are served alongside, and more have been added in recent years. See vegetarian Wazwan.

chunks.title: Did Timur bring Wazwan to Kashmir?
chunks.text:
Did Timur bring Wazwan to Kashmir?
That is the wazas' traditional account, but Timur never entered Kashmir: in 1398 he demanded tribute from Sultan Sikandar from a camp on the Indus. No document records how the feast began. See the history of Wazwan.

chunks.title: Does Wazwan have a GI tag?
chunks.text:
Does Wazwan have a GI tag?
Not as a whole. In August 2024 The Kashmir Wazwan Cooperative Limited applied for geographical indications for two dishes, Goshtaba (application 1337) and Tabakmaaz (application 1336). Both were still at pre-examination on the registry when we checked in October 2026.

chunks.title: Can visitors eat Wazwan?
chunks.text:
Can visitors eat Wazwan?
Yes. Weddings are private, but restaurants in Srinagar serve Wazwan dishes and set menus; see our directory of Srinagar restaurants that serve Wazwan and our guide to eating in Srinagar.

chunks.title: What are the seven essential dishes of a Wazwan?
chunks.page: The 7 Essential Dishes of Kashmiri Wazwan
chunks.text:
What are the seven essential dishes of a Wazwan?
Tabak maaz, rista, rogan josh, aab gosht, daniwal korma, marchwangan korma and gushtaba. Three different sources name the same seven: Wikipedia, citing The Hindu; the Waza family's cookbook, published by Roli Books; and the former tourism director M. Saleem Beg in the Daily Excelsior.

chunks.title: Were these the original seven dishes of the Wazwan?
chunks.page: The 7 Essential Dishes of Kashmiri Wazwan
chunks.text:
Were these the original seven dishes of the Wazwan?
No one can show that. The feast is often said to have begun as a seven-dish meal, and a 74-year-old waza told Reuters in 2026 that there were only seven mutton dishes in his forefathers' time, but no document names which seven. The stories treat the claim as a tradition, not a record.

chunks.title: In what order are the seven served?
chunks.page: The 7 Essential Dishes of Kashmiri Wazwan
chunks.text:
In what order are the seven served?
Tabak maaz is on the trami when it arrives; rista opens the gravies; rogan josh, daniwal korma and marchwangan korma follow in the middle of the meal; aab gosht comes among the pale dishes; gushtaba is last. Kitchens vary in the middle of the feast, and the stories say where the accounts differ.

chunks.title: How were the stories researched?
chunks.page: The 7 Essential Dishes of Kashmiri Wazwan
chunks.text:
How were the stories researched?
From sources that could be read and checked: Grierson's Dictionary of the Kashmiri Language, Walter Lawrence's The Valley of Kashmir (1895), Kashmiri cookbooks including the Waza family's own, a 2012 study by researchers at the Sher-i-Kashmir Institute of Medical Sciences that counted the calories in a wedding feast, food-science papers from Srinagar's universities, government figures, the Geographical Indications Registry and reporting from Kashmir. Each story lists its sources, and sources that could not be read are not cited as if they had been.

chunks.title: Tabak maaz at a glance
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text:
Tabak maaz is lamb ribs cooked twice: simmered with spices until the bones loosen, then fried in ghee until reddish brown. It is served dry, on the rice, as one of the first dishes of a Wazwan.
Name: Plate-meat: tabakh is a large dish, plate or tray and māz is meat, in Grierson's dictionary of Kashmiri
In the feast: First: on the trami when it arrives, with seekh kebabs, methi maaz and chicken, before any gravy
Meat: The rib cage, cut into rectangles with the fat left on
Cooking: Boiled (in water in the wazas' published recipe; milk or yogurt in other accounts), then fried in ghee until reddish brown
Portion: Two to four pieces to a trami of four
Calories: About 1,470 per trami, 367 per diner, at one Srinagar wedding (SKIMS, 2012)
Pandit name: Kabargah
GI status: Application 1336, "Tabakmaaz (Meat Products) of Kashmir", filed 8 August 2024; at pre-examination when we checked on 17 October 2026 (GI Registry)

chunks.title: Rista at a glance
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text:
Rista is a ball of mutton pounded with fat, about 80 to 100 g, boiled and then cooked in a red gravy of Kashmiri chilli, mawal, saffron and fennel. It is the first gravy served at a Wazwan.
In the feast: First of the gravies, after the dishes that arrive on the trami
Meat: Leg meat, pounded on a stone within the hour of slaughter, with fresh fat
Fat: 20% lamb fat was the optimum in a 1994 study of rista (Meat Science90052-3))
Colour: Kashmiri chilli, mawal (the dried cockscomb flower) and saffron; alkanet in some accounts; no tomato
Heat: Usually mild: Kashmiri chilli rates about 1,000 to 2,000 Scoville units (Wikipedia)
Portion: One per diner, four to a trami; about 80 to 100 g each
Calories: About 1,814 per trami, 454 per diner, the most of any dish served in a gravy at one Srinagar wedding (SKIMS, 2012)

chunks.title: Rogan josh at a glance
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text:
Rogan josh is mutton or goat, usually on the bone, braised in a red gravy coloured with Kashmiri chilli and mawal, the dried cockscomb flower, or with ratan jot in some Kashmiri Pandit kitchens. Rogan josh cooked in Kashmir has no tomato.
Name: Uncertain: roghan is ghee or oil in Persian, and Grierson's dictionary glosses Kashmiri rōgan as clarified butter; another reading takes it as "red"
In the feast: Early among the gravies, after rista
Meat: On the bone, from the lower ribs, lower back, chest, neck and shoulder, in pieces of about 70 to 80 g
Colour: Kashmiri chilli and mawal (the dried cockscomb flower); ratan jot (alkanet root) in some Pandit kitchens; saffron in some; never tomato
Heat: Usually medium: Kashmiri chilli rates about 1,000 to 2,000 Scoville units (Wikipedia)
Portion: Four pieces to a trami of four
Calories: About 1,322 per trami, 331 per diner, at one Srinagar wedding (SKIMS, 2012)
Two versions: Kashmiri Muslim, with praan, garlic, mawal and ghee; Kashmiri Pandit, with no onion or garlic, and asafoetida, curd, dry ginger, fennel and mustard oil

chunks.title: Aab gosht at a glance
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text:
Aab gosht is mutton, usually a large piece, boiled and then cooked in milk reduced with fennel, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, ginger, shallot and garlic. It is mild and pale, and comes late in a Wazwan.
Name: Persian for meat broth (āb, water, and gūsht, meat); in Kashmiri, dodhe maaz, milk-meat
In the feast: Late, among the pale dishes, before yakhni and gushtaba
Meat: A large piece: tail, shoulder, shank, lower back or ribs, depending on the account
Milk: Ten litres of cow's milk reduced to one, in a waza's account; home recipes use full-cream milk powder
Portion: One large piece to a trami of four, at the wedding a medical team recorded in 2012
Calories: About 934 per trami, 234 per diner; only the single piece of dani was lighter at one Srinagar wedding (SKIMS, 2012)
Heat: None: no chilli, tomato or turmeric in any account we have read
Not to be confused with: Iran's abgoosht, or dizi, a stew of lamb, chickpeas and beans

chunks.title: Daniwal korma at a glance
chunks.text:
Daniwal korma is mutton on the bone braised in a yogurt gravy with praan and garlic and finished with a great deal of fresh coriander. It is mild, and it is served in the middle of a Wazwan.
Name: Dāñĕwal is the coriander leaf in Grierson's dictionary of Kashmiri; korma is a braise
In the feast: In the middle: after rogan josh and before marchwangan korma, in one account
Meat: On the bone, from the bony portions of the carcass
Base: Yogurt and stock, with praan (the Kashmiri shallot) and garlic roasted golden
Herb: Fresh coriander leaf, not the seed, added at the end
Heat: None: no chilli in any account; the one that names a colour calls the gravy white
Calories: No published figure: it was not among the dishes counted in the one study (SKIMS, 2012)

chunks.title: Marchwangan korma at a glance
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text:
Marchwangan korma is mutton, in smaller pieces than rogan josh, braised in a thick gravy built on Kashmiri red chilli. It is the hottest dish of a Wazwan, by the quantity of chilli rather than its strength.
Name: Chilli-braise: marʦ is the red chilli in Grierson's dictionary of Kashmiri, and korma a braise
In the feast: In the middle of the meat courses; the last hot dish before the pale ones
Meat: Mutton in smaller pieces than rogan josh, from the bony portions
Heat: The hottest on the trami: Kashmiri chilli is mild, about 1,000 to 2,000 Scoville units (Wikipedia), but the dish uses a great deal of it, by one estimate three-quarters of the feast's chilli
Portion: Four to six pieces to a trami of four
Calories: About 1,059 per trami, 265 per diner, at one Srinagar wedding (SKIMS, 2012)
Served with: Muji chetin, the radish-and-curd chutney, in the same run of courses
The chilli's GI: Application 1295, "Kashmiri Long Chilli", filed 26 June 2024; at pre-examination when we checked on 17 October 2026 (GI Registry)

chunks.title: Gushtaba at a glance
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text:
Gushtaba is a large ball of mutton pounded with fat, boiled, and cooked in yakhni, a white gravy of yogurt and mutton broth scented with cardamom, fennel, dry ginger and dried mint. It is served last.
Name: Gusht-āba, "a rich soup of pounded or minced meat", in Grierson's dictionary of Kashmiri; also called the Dish of Kings
In the feast: Last of the meat dishes; dessert and kahwa follow
Meat: Leg meat, pounded on a stone within the hour of slaughter, with fresh fat
Gravy: Yakhni: yogurt and mutton broth with cardamom, cinnamon, fennel, dry ginger, cloves and dried mint; no chilli or turmeric
Portion: One to a trami of four, divided by the eldest: 200 to 400 g in one account, 500 to 750 g weighed at one wedding
Calories: About 1,787 per trami, 447 per diner, at one Srinagar wedding (SKIMS, 2012)
GI status: Application 1337, "Goshtaba (Meat Products) of Kashmir", filed 8 August 2024; at pre-examination when we checked on 17 October 2026 (GI Registry)

chunks.title: The order a Wazwan is served in
chunks.text:
How Wazwan Way's Traditional Wazwan page sets out the meal, from the trami's arrival to the last course. Kitchens differ on the order of the gravies between the first dishes and gushtaba, which always comes last.
On the trami: Tabak Maaz, Seekh Kebab, Methi Maaz, Plain Steamed Rice, Muji Chetin, Shami Kabab. The first dishes arrive with the trami itself, laid on a mound of rice for four diners to share.
The gravies: Rista, Rogan Josh, Aab Gosht, Dhaniwal Korma, Marchhwangan Korma, Daeni Phoul, Waza Kokur, Yakhni. Then the wazas bring the meat courses to the trami one by one: pale, milky aab gosht and deep red rista among them.
Alongside: Waza Palak, Ruwangan Chaman, Wazwan Mushroom. Vegetarian dishes of spinach, paneer and mushrooms have joined the feast in recent years; potatoes in yogurt gravy appear only rarely.
The last course: Gushtaba. Gushtaba always comes last.
The seven dishes commonly listed as essential: Aab Gosht, Dhaniwal Korma, Gushtaba, Marchhwangan Korma, Rista, Rogan Josh, Tabak Maaz.

chunks.title: How to experience a Wazwan: the essentials
chunks.text:
Book in Advance: A full Wazwan is often prepared overnight, so call ahead if you want the ceremonial feast experience rather than a standard menu order. Most kitchens need a headcount, not a card number — booking is really about giving the kitchen lead time.
Come Hungry, Come Many: Wazwan is best enjoyed in a group. The shared trami experience makes the meal feel cultural, social, and complete. Four to a trami is traditional — fewer guests means more courses go untouched.
Start with the Classics: If you are new to Kashmiri food, begin with Rogan Josh, Gushtaba, Rista, and Tabak Maaz before branching into rarer specialties. These four give you the full range of Wazwan's textures before anything more adventurous.
Respect the Finale: Dishes like Gushtaba are traditionally served at the end of a Wazwan, so knowing the order makes the experience far more immersive. Save room — Gushtaba closing the feast is, quite literally, the whole point.
Ask About Authenticity: Some restaurants are polished for tourists, while others preserve older cooking styles. Use the authenticity notes in the app. A place proud of its history will usually tell you, unprompted — it's worth asking if it doesn't.
Pair Food with the Place: A Dal Lake setting, an old city dining hall, and a heritage restaurant each create a very different mood around the same dish. Same recipe, different room — the setting changes what the dish means.

chunks.title: Manners at the trami
chunks.text:
Seated at the trami: Guests traditionally sit cross-legged on a dastarkhwan, a long white cloth spread over carpets. They are grouped in fours, and each four shares one trami. Eat from your own quarter.
The order of serving: The trami usually arrives under its copper cover, the sarposh, with seekh kebabs and tabak maaz on the rice. The wazas serve the other courses in turn, usually four pieces at a time. Yakhni comes near the end; gushtaba is the last course.
Eating respectfully: The tash-t-naer, a copper basin and ewer, comes round first: water is poured over each guest's hands. Wait until all four are seated; the eldest usually says the opening prayer and begins. Wazwan is eaten by hand, by custom the right hand.
What to expect: A full Wazwan runs anywhere from seven to 36 dishes; restaurant sets are much smaller. The eldest shares out the gushtaba. Hosts often urge extra helpings, and leftovers usually go home with the guests.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht
chunks.text:
Aab Gosht is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim. It is one of the seven dishes commonly listed as essential to a Wazwan. In the feast: the gravies.
Lamb cooked in a mild milk-based curry with fennel and cardamom notes.
Aab gosht is a graceful Wazwan lamb dish known for its pale gravy and softer profile. It relies on milk, fennel, and cardamom rather than the fiery red gravies more tourists usually expect.
Counted by Wikipedia's Wazwan entry among the seven mandatory dishes of the feast, Aab Gosht (home name Doodh Maaz, 'milk meat') is the milk-white counterpoint to the reds of Rogan Josh and Marchwangan Korma in the trami's colour sequence. A note on names is essential: Persian abgoosht (also called dizi) — a rustic Iranian stew of lamb, chickpeas, potatoes and tomato eaten mashed with bread — shares only the literal meaning 'meat in water/broth' and is a completely different dish, and various other South and Central Asian kitchens carry their own aab gosht renditions. The Kashmiri dish is defined by reduced milk and fennel and should not be confused with any of these namesakes. Whether the name travelled to Kashmir with broader Persianate culinary vocabulary is plausible but not documented in the sources we consulted.
Aab gosht, also called dodhe maaz (Wikipedia), is mutton cooked in milk, or in the words of Wikipedia's Wazwan article, "lamb cooked in sweet milk curry". It is one of the seven dishes Wikipedia lists as a must at a Wazwan. The name matches the Persian abgoosht, literally "meat broth" (Wikipedia), but the two dishes share only the name: Iranian abgoosht is a stew of lamb, chickpeas, beans, onions, potatoes, tomatoes, turmeric and dried lime, with no milk (Wikipedia). How the name reached Kashmir isn't documented. It is also written aab gosh.
Tip: Perfect for diners who want to try a Kashmiri meat dish that is aromatic and rich without leaning heavily on chili heat.

chunks.title: Recipe: Aab Gosht
chunks.text:
Recipe for Aab Gosht, as written on Wazwan Way.
Aab gosht as a waza cooks it: mutton boiled and washed, cooked in its own stock with ghee, fried-shallot paste, fennel, cardamom and cloves until the stock has reduced, then simmered in milk until the gravy is thick and creamy. It has no chilli and no turmeric.
Serves 4–5. Prep 18 min. Cook 1 h 28 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 750 g mutton
- 750 ml to 1 litre of the stock from boiling the mutton
- 5–6 green cardamom pods
- 5–6 cloves
- 1 tbsp fennel powder
- 3 tbsp ghee
- ½ cup fried shallots, ground to a paste
- Salt, to taste
- For the milk: 200 g full-fat milk powder whisked into 1.5 litres of water
Method:
1. Boil the mutton until it is partly cooked. Drain it, wash it well and keep the stock.
2. Put the washed mutton in a heavy pot with the stock, cardamom, cloves, fennel powder, ghee and fried-shallot paste.
3. Cook until the mutton is tender, the stock has reduced and the ghee has separated.
4. Whisk the milk powder into the water until it is smooth, with no lumps.
5. Add the milk to the mutton, season with salt and stir gently.
6. Simmer on a low heat until the milk thickens to a creamy gravy.
Waza tips:
- Cook the mutton in its stock with the ghee and fried-shallot paste until the stock has reduced; only then add the milk.
- Whisk the milk powder into the water until there are no lumps.
- Keep the heat low once the milk is in.
Common mistakes:
- Adding the milk before the stock has reduced.
- Boiling hard once the milk is in; it is simmered on a low heat.
At home: A home version pressure-cooks the mutton with whole spices, ginger-garlic paste and fennel, makes the milk from milk powder in the same way, and finishes with a little sugar and ghee.
Serving: Serve over plain rice. At a Wazwan it comes late: in Outlook India's account of the order it follows marchwangan korma and comes before yakhni and gushtaba.
About this recipe: The waza whose method this is makes the milk from milk powder. Our story on aab gosht covers the older practice of reducing fresh milk.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: How it's made
chunks.text: Sahapedia describes meat from the lamb's tail, shoulder or shank, boiled until tender, then cooked with shallot, garlic paste, ginger powder, fennel powder, cloves, green and black cardamom, cinnamon and salt, with full-cream dry milk added to the stock and ghee to finish (Sahapedia). Others use sheep ribs and flavour the milk with green cardamom and saffron (Outlook India; Onmanorama), and Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes describes ten litres of cow's milk reduced to one (Wikipedia). None of these accounts adds chilli, tomato or turmeric.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: Its place in the feast
chunks.text: Aab gosht comes late in a Wazwan. In Outlook India's account of the order it follows marchwangan korma and comes before yakhni and gushtaba (Outlook India); in Asia Media Centre's it follows rista, rogan josh and daniphol (Asia Media Centre). It is served on the trami with rice (Sahapedia).

chunks.title: Aloo Monji (Aloo Monji / Olav Monje)
chunks.text:
Aloo Monji (Aloo Monji / Olav Monje) is on Wazwan Way under Street Food. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Medium. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim.
Crispy golden fried potato slices dipped in a spiced rice-flour batter.
Aloo Monji is a popular Kashmiri street food snack, consisting of thick potato roundels dipped in a light rice-flour and chickpea batter spiced with cumin, ajwain, and Kashmiri red chili, then deep-fried until extra crispy.
The monje family of fritters is a fixture of Kashmiri street life: crisp, spice-crusted batons sold at carts near markets and Sufi shrines, with nader monje — the lotus-stem original — carrying an aura of blessing for shrine visitors. Aloo monji is the everyday, all-season member of the family, made when lotus stem is expensive or out of season, and a standard of home frying on rainy afternoons. The rice-flour batter is the family signature, frying up glassier and crunchier than the besan coat of a plains pakora. Documentation of aloo monji specifically is thin compared to nader monje; its method is the same batter and fry applied to potato, and this entry reflects that honestly.
Sold by local street vendors (dharas) near schools, shrines, and local bazaars in Srinagar. Along with Nadur Monji, it is a staple evening snack for locals.
Tip: Always eat it piping hot straight from the deep fryer, served with spicy radish-yogurt chutney.

chunks.title: Recipe: Aloo Monji
chunks.text:
Recipe for Aloo Monji, as written on Wazwan Way.
Aloo monji are Kashmir's potato fritters — batons of potato dragged through a thin, chilli-red rice-flour batter and fried until the shell shatters. They are the potato cousin of the famous nader monje (lotus-stem fritters), sold from the same carts and paper cones on Srinagar's streets, and eaten scalding hot with a dusting of extra chilli.
Serves 4. Prep 18 min. Cook 18 min. Level: Easy.
Ingredients:
- 4 medium potatoes (about 500 g), peeled and cut into thick batons or 1 cm rounds
- 100 g rice flour
- 2 tbsp gram flour (besan) — optional, helps the batter cling; some vendors use rice flour alone
- 1–1.5 tbsp Kashmiri red chilli powder (the batter should look boldly red)
- 1/2 tsp carom seeds (ajwain) or cumin seeds
- 1/4 tsp turmeric (optional)
- 1 tsp salt, or to taste
- 120–150 ml cold water, to make a thin coating batter
- Oil, for deep frying (mustard oil for the street-authentic edge, or any neutral oil)
- Extra chilli powder and salt, for dusting
Method:
1. Soak the cut potatoes in cold water 10 minutes to rinse off surface starch, then drain and pat thoroughly dry.
2. Whisk the rice flour, besan (if using), chilli powder, carom, turmeric and salt with enough cold water to make a thin batter — it should coat a piece of potato in a translucent red film, not a thick jacket.
3. Heat oil in a kadhai to a medium-hot 170–180°C (a drop of batter should rise steadily, not instantly brown). If using mustard oil, let it smoke once and settle first.
4. Drag the potato pieces through the batter one at a time and slide them into the oil in small batches.
5. Fry at a steady medium heat, turning occasionally, until the coating is deeply crisp and the potato inside is tender — 6–8 minutes per batch; a skewer should slide through easily. High heat browns the shell before the potato cooks.
6. Drain on paper, dust immediately with a pinch of salt and chilli powder, and serve hot — monje lose their crackle as they sit.
Waza tips:
- Thin batter, twice the crunch: rice-flour batter should barely veil the potato — thick batter fries to a bready coat.
- Steady medium oil is the street cart's secret; vendors fry low and long so the inside steams tender under a hard shell.
- Dry potatoes are non-negotiable — wet pieces shed their batter into the oil.
- For cart-level crunch, double-fry: once until pale and cooked, then 1–2 minutes in hotter oil just before serving.
Common mistakes:
- A thick, pakora-style batter — the defining Kashmiri crunch comes from a thin rice-flour film.
- Frying too hot, leaving a raw, squeaky centre inside a dark shell.
- Cutting the potato thin like chips, which overcooks to hollow shells; monje are thick batons with substance.
- Letting them sit — serve within minutes of the fryer.
At home: Nothing here needs special equipment — a kadhai or any deep pan and a slotted spoon do the job. If mustard oil's pungency is unfamiliar, use a neutral oil and add 1 tsp of mustard oil to the batter for the flavour without the frying learning curve. An air fryer will cook the potato but cannot reproduce the shattering rice-flour shell; this is a dish worth actually deep-frying.
Serving: Serve in a paper cone, street-style, with a fierce dusting of chilli — or with walnut chutney (doon chetin) or radish-curd chutney on the side. They make a natural companion to noon chai on a cold afternoon.

chunks.title: Babribyol (Babri Byol)
chunks.text:
Babribyol (Babri Byol) is on Wazwan Way under Beverages. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim.
Babribyol is Kashmir's iftar drink: sweet basil seeds soaked until each dark seed blooms into a translucent, gel-haloed pearl, then stirred into chilled sweetened milk or water. In the Valley, Ramadan is almost unthinkable without it.
Breaking the fast with a basil-seed drink is described by Kashmiri publications as a centuries-old practice in the Valley — Brighter Kashmir calls babri treash (the basil-seed drink) a fixture of iftar tables, and Kashmir Vision writes that the drink and Ramadan are so closely associated 'it is almost impossible to think of Ramzan without this special drink.' The seeds — babri byol in Kashmiri, sabja or tukmaria elsewhere in India — swell to many times their size when soaked, and the drink is valued during fasting for hydration and for settling the stomach after a long day without food; Kashmiri writers also credit it as a summer coolant taken outside Ramadan. Local accounts (Kashmir Life, Rising Kashmir) frame it as both tradition and folk remedy, recommending it at iftar with a short pause before the main meal. It is a humble preparation — seeds, liquid, sugar — whose significance lies entirely in its ritual timing.

chunks.title: Recipe: Babribyol
chunks.text:
Recipe for Babribyol, as written on Wazwan Way.
Babribyol is Kashmir's iftar drink: sweet basil seeds soaked until each dark seed blooms into a translucent, gel-haloed pearl, then stirred into chilled sweetened milk or water. In the Valley, Ramadan is almost unthinkable without it.
Serves 2. Prep 8 min. Level: Easy.
Ingredients:
- 2 tbsp (about 20 g) sweet basil seeds (babri byol / sabja / tukmaria)
- 150 ml water, for soaking
- 500 ml chilled full-fat milk (or plain cold water, or half milk and half water — all three bases are traditional)
- 2–3 tsp sugar, to taste
- Small pinch of saffron strands, soaked in 1 tbsp warm milk (optional, traditional garnish)
- 1 tbsp fresh or dried coconut scrapings (optional, traditional garnish)
- Crushed ice, optional
Method:
1. Pick over and rinse the basil seeds briefly in a fine sieve to remove any dust.
2. Soak the seeds in 150 ml water for 30–60 minutes before serving time (traditionally begun half an hour to an hour before iftar), until each seed is surrounded by a plump translucent gel coat — they swell to many times their dry size.
3. Stir the sugar into the chilled milk (or water) until fully dissolved.
4. Add the bloomed seeds along with any unabsorbed soaking water and stir well so they hang evenly through the drink rather than settling.
5. Stir in the saffron milk and scatter over the coconut scrapings, if using.
6. Rest 5 minutes, stir once more, and serve cold — traditionally as the first thing taken at iftar, with a 15–20 minute pause before the meal.
Waza tips:
- Never skip the pre-soak or add dry seeds straight to milk — under-bloomed seeds are gritty and keep swelling in the glass, turning the drink stodgy.
- Soak in water even when serving in milk; seeds bloom faster and more evenly in plain water.
- Judge readiness by the gel halo: each seed should look like a tiny black pupil in a clear iris. If the halo is thin, give it another 15 minutes.
- Make it pourable, not spoonable — the seeds should drift, not pack. Thin with extra chilled milk or water if it tightens on standing.
Common mistakes:
- Confusing basil seeds with chia seeds — they look similar dry, but chia is not babri byol.
- Soaking too briefly (a few minutes is not enough for full bloom, despite what quick recipes claim).
- Over-sweetening — this is a light, restorative drink, not a dessert syrup.
- Adding so many seeds that the drink sets into a gel; 1 tbsp of dry seeds per large glass is plenty.
At home: Sabja/tukmaria seeds from any Indian grocer are the same seed; do not substitute chia, which blooms differently, tastes nuttier and is not traditional. Any milk works, including plant milks, though full-fat dairy is the Valley norm. The whole drink can be assembled in one jug and held in the refrigerator for a few hours — stir before pouring.
Serving: Served chilled at iftar to break the fast, traditionally followed by a short pause before the meal. Outside Ramadan it is drunk as a summer cooler through Kashmir's warm months.

chunks.title: Badam Phirni
chunks.text:
Badam Phirni is on Wazwan Way under Desserts. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
A chilled pudding of ground rice and almonds cooked slowly in milk until it thickens to silk, set in shallow bowls and scattered with slivered nuts. Badam phirni is the almond-rich dress of the classic phirni.
Phirni came to Kashmir with Mughal-era kitchens and settled into festive menus — Eid tables, wedding dessert rounds and the better cafes of Srinagar. The almond version outranks the plain one at celebrations, the ground badam giving body and a marzipan depth. Its markers are patience and texture: the rice must be soaked and ground coarse like fine semolina, and the milk stirred until the spoon leaves a trail. Setting it in earthenware, which drinks a little moisture, gives the classic firm surface.

chunks.title: Recipe: Badam Phirni
chunks.text:
Recipe for Badam Phirni, as written on Wazwan Way.
A chilled pudding of ground rice and almonds cooked slowly in milk until it thickens to silk, set in shallow bowls and scattered with slivered nuts. Badam phirni is the almond-rich dress of the classic phirni.
Serves 6. Prep 20 min. Cook 35 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 60 g short-grain rice, soaked 2 hours
- 50 g almonds, blanched and peeled, plus more slivered to finish
- 1 litre full-fat milk
- 120 g sugar
- 5-6 green cardamoms, seeds ground
- 1 small pinch saffron threads (optional)
- 1 tsp kewra or rose water (optional)
Method:
1. Drain the soaked rice and grind it with the blanched almonds and a splash of milk to a coarse, grainy paste.
2. Bring the milk to a boil in a heavy pan, then lower the heat.
3. Loosen the rice-almond paste with a ladle of warm milk and stir it back into the pan.
4. Cook on low heat, stirring constantly and scraping the base, until the mixture thickens and the raw rice smell disappears, 20-25 minutes.
5. Add the sugar, ground cardamom and saffron if using, and cook 5 minutes more until glossy.
6. Stir in the kewra or rose water, pour into shallow bowls — earthenware if you have it — and cool.
7. Chill for at least 3 hours; scatter with slivered almonds before serving.
Waza tips:
- Grind the rice coarse, not to flour — phirni's grain on the tongue is what separates it from custard.
- Stir without stopping once the paste goes in; the base catches in seconds.
Common mistakes:
- Under-cooking the rice paste, which leaves a raw, chalky finish.
- Setting it deep in one large bowl — phirni sets and chills properly only in shallow layers.
At home: Ground rice from a packet plus almond meal shortcut the soaking and grinding without much loss.
Serving: Serve cold, ideally in the clay bowl it set in, after a rich meal.

chunks.title: Bakerkhani
chunks.text:
Bakerkhani is on Wazwan Way under Bakery. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim.
Flaky, layered baked flatbread.
Bakerkhani is a thick, round, flaky flatbread with a golden crust, baked in a clay tandoor.
Bakerkhani belongs to a family of breads found across South Asia — Dhaka and Old Delhi have their own thick, sweetened versions — but the Kashmiri bakerkhani is distinct: thinner, crisp, layered and finished with sesame. In the Valley it is a ceremonial bread as much as a breakfast one: trays of large bakerkhanis are traditionally sent to in-laws after engagements, weddings and childbirths, and kandur-culture accounts tie it to marriage customs specifically. The name is widely said to derive from a Mughal-era figure (Aga Baker Khan) in the Bengal tradition, but that origin story attaches to the eastern bread and is contested; sources on the Kashmiri loaf do not document a founding claim, and none is asserted here.
Originating during Mughal times, the Bakerkhani has evolved in Kashmir into a popular afternoon snack, usually enjoyed with salted pink tea.
Tip: Buy it fresh from a local neighborhood kandur (baker) in the afternoon.

chunks.title: Recipe: Bakerkhani
chunks.text:
Recipe for Bakerkhani, as written on Wazwan Way.
Bakerkhani is the aristocrat of the kandur's tandoor: a round, sesame-crusted bread built from many ghee-brushed layers that bake up crisp and shatter like rough puff pastry. It looks like a naan and eats like a biscuit — more pastry than bread, made for slow mornings and long conversations over noon chai.
Serves 4 large breads. Prep 53 min. Cook 23 min. Level: Involved.
Ingredients:
- 300 g all-purpose flour (maida), plus extra for dusting
- 1/2 tsp instant yeast
- 2 tsp sugar
- 3/4 tsp salt
- 2 tbsp ghee, for the dough
- 150–170 ml warm milk (or half milk, half water), as needed
- 60–80 g ghee, softened, for laminating the layers
- 2 tbsp milk, for brushing the tops
- 3 tbsp white sesame seeds
Method:
1. Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt, rub in 2 tbsp ghee, then knead with warm milk to a smooth, medium-firm dough, about 8 minutes. Cover and rest 45–60 minutes until relaxed and slightly risen.
2. Divide into 4. Working with one piece, roll it out as thin as you can — a rough sheet 2 mm thick or less; the kandur stretches the sheet repeatedly by hand.
3. Brush the whole sheet generously with softened ghee and dust with a fine veil of flour (the flour keeps the layers separate as they bake).
4. Roll the sheet up into a tight rope, then coil the rope into a snail-shell spiral, tucking the end underneath. Rest the coils 15 minutes — this rest is what lets you flatten them without tearing the layers.
5. Press and roll each coil gently back into a round about 12–14 cm across and 1 cm thick, keeping the spiral structure intact rather than rolling it thin again.
6. Dock the surface lightly with a fork or knife point, brush with milk, and press sesame seeds thickly over the top.
7. In the tandoor these bake against the wall until deep gold and crisp through. At home: bake on a preheated steel or heavy tray at 200°C for 18–25 minutes until evenly golden and rigid — a done bakerkhani feels light for its size and taps hollow-crisp.
8. Cool 10 minutes before eating; the layers set and crispen as steam escapes. Store airtight up to a week and re-crisp in a low oven.
Waza tips:
- Ghee then flour on every layer — fat alone welds the layers back together; the flour dusting is what keeps them distinct.
- The intermediate rests are not optional: laminated dough that is rolled without resting snaps its layers and bakes bready.
- Bake to a deeper gold than looks polite; a pale bakerkhani is raw and pasty at the centre of the coil.
- It should crackle audibly when broken — that sound is the quality test at the kandur.
Common mistakes:
- Rolling the final round thin like a paratha, which crushes the coil and erases the flaky layers.
- Using melted (liquid) ghee for laminating — it soaks in rather than sitting between the layers; it must be soft but plastic.
- Pulling it out golden but soft; bakerkhani finishes crisping only when baked fully dry.
- Overloading with sugar based on Dhaka-style recipes — the Kashmiri version is only faintly sweet, letting ghee and sesame lead.
At home: The tandoor gives bakerkhani fierce wall contact plus radiant heat from the coals; a home oven's gentler, even heat actually suits this bread better than the other kandur loaves, because the layers need time to dry and set. Use a baking steel or heavy tray preheated at 200°C, keep the bread in the lower-middle of the oven so the sesame top does not scorch before the core crisps, and resist opening the door in the first 15 minutes. The result is very close to the bakery original, if slightly less smoky; a 30-second pass under the broiler at the end recovers some of the tandoor's toasted-sesame char.
Serving: Serve with noon chai, broken and eaten slowly — it is the bread of unhurried company. Also sent, by tradition, on trays to in-laws for engagements and births, alongside other kandur specialties.

chunks.title: Basrakh
chunks.text:
Basrakh is on Wazwan Way under Street Food. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim.
Basrakh is a Kashmiri festive sweet: a stiff ghee dough shaped into small bowls, fried slowly until crisp and dipped in cardamom sugar syrup.
Basrakh is bound to the ceremonial economy of Kashmiri family life: sources consistently describe it as an engagement and wedding sweet, sent between families as a token of goodwill, and as a winter treat shared at large gatherings. The shaping is its craft signature — each piece is formed into a hollow dome over the end of a pestle (tschoute in Kashmiri), so it fries light and shatters rather than sitting dense. Unlike the syrup-soaked sweets of the plains, basrakh is finished with a crystallised sugar coat, closer in spirit to a frosted shortbread than to gulab jamun. Written documentation is sparse — it survives mainly in home kitchens and local halwais — which makes it one of the Valley's less exported traditions.

chunks.title: Recipe: Basrakh
chunks.text:
Recipe for Basrakh, as written on Wazwan Way.
Basrakh is a Kashmiri festive sweet: a stiff ghee dough shaped into small bowls, fried slowly until crisp and dipped in cardamom sugar syrup.
Prep 53 min. Cook 50 min. Level: Involved.
Ingredients:
- For the dough: 2 cups all-purpose flour (maida)
- ½ cup ghee
- 1 tsp cardamom powder
- 2 tbsp powdered sugar
- A pinch of salt
- ¼ cup water, or as needed
- Oil, for deep-frying
- For the syrup: 1 cup sugar
- 1 cup water
- ½ tsp cardamom powder
- A few saffron strands, optional
- Dry fruits of your choice, to finish
Method:
1. Mix the flour, powdered sugar, salt and cardamom, and rub in the ghee until the mixture looks like breadcrumbs.
2. Add the water a little at a time and knead to a stiff dough. Rest it for at least 30 minutes.
3. Divide the dough into small balls, or roll it out about ¼ inch thick, and shape the pieces into small bowls.
4. Fry on a low to medium heat until golden brown and crisp. Drain and leave to cool completely.
5. Boil the sugar, water, saffron and cardamom and simmer to a one-string syrup.
6. Dip the fried basrakh in the warm syrup to coat them, leave them in it for a minute, then set them on a plate and top with dry fruits.
7. Let them cool completely: the syrup hardens to a crunchy coating. They keep in an airtight container for up to a week.
Tips:
- Rub the ghee in until the flour looks like breadcrumbs before any water goes in.
- Fry slowly, and cool the basrakh completely before the syrup.
- The syrup is ready at one-string consistency.
Serving: Serve on the tea tray at celebrations with kahwa or noon chai, or boxed as a gift between families — its traditional role at engagements and weddings.

chunks.title: Cardamom Kahwa (Elaichi Kahwa)
chunks.text:
Cardamom Kahwa (Elaichi Kahwa) is on Wazwan Way under Beverages. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
Kashmiri green tea brewed light and gold with crushed green cardamom, a stick of cinnamon and slivered almonds — the kahwa of everyday hospitality, with cardamom leading where saffron usually reigns.
Kahwa is Kashmir's welcome ritual, traditionally drawn from the samovar into small cups all afternoon. The saffron-heavy version is the showpiece; this cardamom-forward brew is its daily working form, made when guests arrive unannounced or the household simply wants warmth. The rules are gentleness itself: green tea steeped, never boiled to bitterness, whole spices bruised rather than powdered, and almonds slivered into the cup so the last sip has texture. Sugar or honey to taste, always light.

chunks.title: Recipe: Cardamom Kahwa
chunks.text:
Recipe for Cardamom Kahwa, as written on Wazwan Way.
Kashmiri green tea brewed light and gold with crushed green cardamom, a stick of cinnamon and slivered almonds — the kahwa of everyday hospitality, with cardamom leading where saffron usually reigns.
Serves 4. Prep 5 min. Cook 12 min. Level: Easy.
Ingredients:
- 2 tsp Kashmiri green tea leaves (kahwa leaves or gunpowder green)
- 800 ml water
- 6 green cardamoms, bruised
- 1 small cinnamon stick
- 2 cloves (optional)
- 2 tsp sugar or honey, or to taste
- 10-12 almonds, blanched and slivered
- 2-3 dried rose petals, to finish (optional)
Method:
1. Bring the water to a boil with the cardamom, cinnamon and cloves and simmer 5 minutes so the spices open.
2. Take the pan off the boil, add the green tea leaves, and steep at a bare murmur for 2-3 minutes.
3. Sweeten with sugar or honey and stir once.
4. Divide the slivered almonds among small cups.
5. Strain the kahwa hot over the almonds and finish, if you like, with a rose petal.
Waza tips:
- Steep, don't boil, the leaves — boiled green tea turns harsh in a minute.
- Bruise the cardamom, never grind it; the tea should be clear gold, not cloudy.
Common mistakes:
- Long steeping for 'strength', which only adds bitterness.
- Drowning it in sugar — kahwa is meant to finish clean.
At home: Gunpowder or any unflavoured green tea stands in for kahwa leaves; a saucepan replaces the samovar without apology.
Serving: Serve hot in small cups after meals or alongside bakerkhani; the almonds at the bottom are eaten last.

chunks.title: Czochworu (Czochworu / Tsochworu)
chunks.text:
Czochworu (Czochworu / Tsochworu) is on Wazwan Way under Bakery. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
Bagel-like tandoor-baked bread topped with sesame.
Czochworu is a small, round, bagel-like bread with a soft interior and a hard crust topped with sesame seeds.
Where girda owns the Kashmiri morning, czochworu owns the evening: bread surveys of the Valley consistently describe it as the afternoon-to-evening bake at the kandur, the bread put out for drop-in guests because it is festive without being elaborate. Its bagel-like boil-then-bake method — rare in South Asian breadmaking — is its defining technical feature, gelatinising the surface so the crust turns glossy and crackling. The ring shape and sesame crust invite the bagel comparison that nearly every English-language account makes, though the czochworu predates any such framing and belongs entirely to the kandur repertoire. Naming varies by district — telvor/tilvor ('til' meaning sesame) and czochworu describe the same family of ring breads.
Another classic kandur bread, Czochworu has been the traditional tea-time companion for students and office workers in the afternoon.
Tip: Best sliced in half with butter spread inside.

chunks.title: Recipe: Czochworu
chunks.text:
Recipe for Czochworu, as written on Wazwan Way.
Czochworu is Kashmir's answer to the bagel — a palm-sized ring of yeasted dough, briefly boiled and then baked so it comes out of the tandoor with a crisp, deeply browned base and a soft, chewy sesame-crusted crown. It is the late-afternoon bread, bought warm on the way home and eaten with noon chai before dinner.
Serves 8 rings. Prep 48 min. Cook 30 min. Level: Involved.
Ingredients:
- 320 g all-purpose flour (maida), plus extra for dusting
- 30 g milk powder (or replace the kneading water with milk)
- 1 tsp active dry or instant yeast
- 1 tbsp sugar
- 1.5 tsp salt
- 2 tbsp neutral oil or soft ghee
- 180–200 ml lukewarm water, as needed
- 1 tsp flour whisked into 3 tbsp milk, for brushing
- 3 tbsp white sesame seeds (some kandurs use poppy seeds)
Method:
1. Dissolve the sugar in 120 ml lukewarm water, stir in the yeast and leave 10 minutes until frothy.
2. Mix the flour, milk powder and salt, add the yeast water, oil and enough extra water to form a soft dough. Knead 10–12 minutes until smooth and elastic — it starts sticky and comes together with kneading.
3. Oil the dough and bowl, cover, and rise about 2 hours in a warm place, until doubled.
4. Divide into 8 balls. Poke a floured finger through the centre of each, twirl to open the hole to 3–4 cm (it closes up as the dough proves and bakes), and flatten slightly into a ring.
5. Set the rings on greased, floured trays with space between, cover with a damp cloth, and prove 30 minutes until puffy.
6. Bring a wide pan of water to a rolling boil. Lower in 2–3 rings at a time and boil about 2 minutes total, 1 minute per side — this is the step that builds the crackling crust. Do not crowd the pan.
7. Lift onto a greased tray and let the surface dry 5–7 minutes.
8. Brush the tops with the flour-milk paste and sprinkle heavily with sesame seeds.
9. Bake on a lined tray in a preheated 220°C oven, middle rack, until the rings are deep golden with a hard, browned base — roughly 20–30 minutes depending on size. In the tandoor the base browns hard against the floor while the crown stays softer; judge by colour and a crisp knock on the bottom, not the clock.
10. Cool briefly on a rack. Best eaten warm the same day; they revive well in a hot oven for 3–4 minutes.
Waza tips:
- The boil is non-negotiable — skip it and you have baked a soft roll, not a czochworu.
- Make the centre hole bigger than looks right; a proud ring closes into a dimple by the time it is baked.
- The flour-milk wash is the kandur's glue and glaze in one: it holds a thick sesame crust and browns to a lacquer.
- Eat the contrast: crisp base, chewy crown. If the whole ring is uniformly soft or uniformly hard, something went wrong.
Common mistakes:
- Boiling too long, which thickens the crust into leather and wrinkles the surface.
- Baking straight from the boil while the surface is wet, so the sesame slides off and the crust steams instead of crisping.
- Under-proving before the boil — dense rings sink and stay dense.
- Crowding the boiling pan, dropping the water temperature and gumming the rings together.
At home: This is the kandur bread that translates best to a home kitchen, because the bagel method already assumes a boil plus an ordinary bake. The main gap is the tandoor floor, which hard-toasts the base: reproduce it by baking on a preheated baking steel or inverted cast-iron pan at 220°C, or by giving the boiled rings 2 minutes base-down in a dry cast-iron skillet before they go in the oven. One published home recipe bakes them a full 30–35 minutes at 220°C; smaller rings in a well-preheated oven can be done in 20 — go by deep colour and a hollow-crisp base.
Serving: Serve warm in the late afternoon with noon chai or kahwa — its traditional slot — split and buttered if you like. It also stands in well at breakfast beside girda.

chunks.title: Czochworu: Without an oven: in a pressure cooker
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Czochworu page: Without an oven: in a pressure cooker.
Czochworu is baked by the kandur in a tandoor. At home it can be baked on the hot wall of a pressure cooker.
The dough is 1½ cups flour, 1 tsp instant yeast and 1 tsp sugar frothed in ½ cup warm water, ½ tsp salt and 1 tbsp oil or melted butter, left to double for 1–1½ hours. Without being knocked back it is shaped into rings; each is boiled for 30–60 seconds a side in water with sugar and baking soda, brushed with milk and scattered with sesame or poppy seeds.
For the baking, the gasket and the whistle come off the cooker's lid, the empty cooker is heated for 10 minutes and salt water is sprinkled inside. Each ring is wetted underneath and stuck to the inside of the cooker, covered with the lid and cooked for 2–3 minutes; then the cooker is turned over the flame for 5–7 minutes, until the bread has golden spots on both sides.

chunks.title: Daeni Phoul (Dani Phol)
chunks.text:
Daeni Phoul (Dani Phol) is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: Medium. Tradition: Wazwan (Muslim). In the feast: the gravies.
A rich mutton drumstick preparation from the traditional Wazwan spread.
Dani Phol centers on a prized drumstick cut of mutton and is valued for its depth, marrow richness, and slow-cooked texture. It is one of the dishes that gives Wazwan its reputation for layered meat craftsmanship.
On the trami, presentation is rank: whole cuts served on the bone signal generosity, and the drumstick — phol — is among the handsomest. The waza's method is a patient braise in the Wazwan's red register of Kashmiri chilli, fennel and sonth, with praan (shallot paste) for body, until the meat can be pulled with the fingers but the piece still holds its shape for serving. It is a dish about the dignity of a good cut treated simply.
Dani Phol is a testament to the Kashmiri appreciation for specific, prized cuts of meat. Centered around the mutton drumstick or shin, this dish was historically favored for its depth of flavor and the richness of the marrow, which slowly renders into the surrounding gravy during the long cooking process. It is a prime example of the slow-cooking traditions that define Wazwan, where time and precise temperature control are just as important as the spices used, resulting in a dish that commands respect at any grand banquet.
Tip: Best for diners who enjoy richer cuts of meat and want to move beyond the most famous Wazwan dishes into the deeper feast repertoire.

chunks.title: Recipe: Daeni Phoul
chunks.text:
Recipe for Daeni Phoul, as written on Wazwan Way.
Whole mutton drumsticks — the shank end of the leg — braised slowly in a spiced red gravy until the meat loosens around the bone. Dani phol is one of the Wazwan spread's stately meat-on-the-bone courses.
Serves 4. Prep 15 min. Cook 1 h 30 min. Level: Involved.
Ingredients:
- 4 mutton or lamb shanks/drumsticks, about 250 g each, trimmed
- 5 tbsp mustard oil
- 2 tbsp shallot or small-onion paste (praan), browned
- 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
- 1 tbsp fennel powder
- 1 tsp dry ginger powder (sonth)
- 150 g yogurt, whisked
- 2 black cardamoms, 4 cloves, 1 cinnamon stick
- Salt to taste
- 700 ml hot water
Method:
1. Heat the mustard oil to smoking in a wide, heavy pot; settle it and add the whole spices.
2. Brown the shanks on all sides, unhurried, 8-10 minutes.
3. Add the browned shallot paste and turn the shanks in it.
4. Mix the chilli powder to a slurry with a little water and stir it in until the oil runs red.
5. Lower the heat and add the whisked yogurt gradually, turning the shanks until it is absorbed.
6. Add fennel, sonth, salt and the hot water; cover and braise at a bare simmer for 60-70 minutes, turning the shanks twice.
7. Uncover and reduce the gravy until it coats the meat richly; the shanks should be yielding but whole. Serve one per person.
Waza tips:
- Choose shanks of even size so they finish together.
- The braise must never gallop — a hard boil tightens shank meat before it surrenders.
Common mistakes:
- Rushing the browning, which is where half the gravy's colour lives.
- Boiling the yogurt in over high heat and splitting the gravy.
At home: Lamb shanks from any butcher are the natural substitute; a heavy casserole in a low oven (150°C) replicates the waza's steady fire.
Serving: Serve whole over rice with the gravy spooned around, and eat with the fingers as intended.

chunks.title: Dhaniwal Korma
chunks.text:
Dhaniwal Korma is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim. It is one of the seven dishes commonly listed as essential to a Wazwan. In the feast: the gravies.
A mutton curry enriched with yogurt and finished with coriander.
Daniwal Korma is a refined Wazwan meat course made with mutton, yogurt, spices, and coriander. It is gentler than the fiercer red gravies and brings freshness through its coriander finish.
Daniwal Korma appears in Wikipedia's list of the seven dishes generally regarded as mandatory in a Wazwan, valued precisely for the contrast it provides: a light, mellow, herb-lifted course between the chilli-heavy ones. It breaks from the pan-Indian korma template — there are no nut pastes and no cream, just churned yogurt, whole aromatics and quantities of fresh coriander added in stages so the herb registers both as background flavour and fresh finish. Beyond its Wazwan role the dish has no widely documented origin story, and we found no credible historical claims worth repeating.
Daniwal korma is lamb or mutton braised in a yogurt gravy flavoured with fresh coriander (Wikipedia); Outlook India describes it as "mutton cooked in a lot of coriander". In Kashmiri, daniwal means coriander and korme or korma a braise (Wikipedia). Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes notes that it can be made with parsley instead of coriander, and gives a chicken version, kokur danival kormeh, in a curd gravy with saffron and fresh coriander. It is one of the seven dishes Wikipedia lists as a must at a Wazwan. In Outlook India's account of the order, it comes after rista and rogan josh and before marchwangan korma, aab gosht, yakhni and gushtaba. The name is also written dhaniwal.
Tip: Try this if you want something fragrant and balanced rather than fiery. It pairs especially well with rice in the middle of a larger Wazwan meal.
Daniwal korma: mutton in a curd gravy with turmeric, dry ginger and saffron, finished with fresh coriander. A Wazwan essential: history and the wazas' recipe.

chunks.title: Recipe: Dhaniwal Korma
chunks.text:
Recipe for Dhaniwal Korma, as written on Wazwan Way.
Daniwal korma as a waza cooks it: small pieces of mutton boiled and washed, fried in plenty of desi ghee with garlic and whole spices, cooked tender on their own stock, then joined by boiled curd, raw onion paste, turmeric and dry ginger. Saffron goes in near the end, and the fresh coriander that names the dish goes on just before serving.
Serves 4–6. Prep 23 min. Cook 1 h 8 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 1 kg mutton, in small pieces
- The stock from boiling the mutton, as needed
- 250 g curd (yogurt)
- 2 tbsp garlic paste
- 2 medium onions, ground raw to a paste
- 150–200 g desi ghee
- 1½ tsp turmeric powder
- 1 tsp dry ginger powder (sonth)
- 2 small pieces of cinnamon
- 4–5 green cardamom pods
- 3–4 cloves
- A generous pinch of saffron
- Salt, to taste
- Fresh coriander, chopped, to finish
Method:
1. Boil the mutton, strain it and wash it well. Keep the stock.
2. Put the mutton in a large pot with the ghee, garlic paste, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves and salt. Set it on the heat and fry well.
3. Add the stock a little at a time and keep cooking until the mutton is tender.
4. In a separate pan, bring the curd to the boil.
5. Add the boiled curd to the mutton with the onion paste, turmeric and dry ginger. Cook until the flavours have come together, the mutton is completely tender and the gravy has thickened.
6. Add the saffron and cook a little longer.
7. Scatter with fresh coriander before serving.
Waza tips:
- Add the stock a little at a time while the mutton fries in the ghee.
- The curd is boiled in its own pan before it joins the mutton.
- The onion paste goes in raw, with the turmeric and dry ginger.
- Saffron goes in near the end, and the coriander just before serving.
Common mistakes:
- Adding the curd unboiled.
- Adding red chilli; the waza's version has none.
At home: A home version pressure-cooks the mutton with the whole spices and whisks the yogurt over a high flame, stirring all the time, until it boils; an egg or 2 tbsp of gram flour in the yogurt stops it splitting.
Serving: Served over rice; at a Wazwan it comes just before marchwangan korma. At home it pairs well with plain rice and a sharp mooli (radish) chutney.
About this recipe: Adjust the spices, ghee and stock to your taste and to the consistency you want.

chunks.title: Dhaniwal Korma: How it tastes and looks
chunks.text:
The sources agree on a yogurt gravy with plenty of fresh coriander (Wikipedia; Outlook India). None of them mentions chilli, and none describes the colour. Wikipedia's Wazwan article describes lamb roasted with yogurt, spices and onion purée, topped with coriander leaves (Wikipedia).
Our recipe below follows a waza's version, credited with the recipe: the curd is boiled before it goes in, the gravy takes turmeric, dry ginger and saffron, and the coriander is added fresh before serving.

chunks.title: Dum Aloo (Dama Oluv)
chunks.text:
Dum Aloo (Dama Oluv) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Kashmiri Pandit.
Potatoes cooked in yogurt gravy in the Kashmiri style.
Dum aloo, dum olav in Kashmiri, is a Kashmiri Pandit dish of small potatoes, deep-fried and then cooked slowly in a spiced yogurt gravy that is red from Kashmiri chilli rather than hot.
Dama Oluv is one of the defining dishes of Kashmiri Pandit cuisine and a fixture of vegetarian feast menus in the valley. Its identity rests on technique rather than ingredients: pricking the fried potatoes (families traditionally used a knitting needle or a sharpened twig) so the yogurt gravy penetrates them completely during the slow dum. Multiple sources stress the contrast with Punjabi dum aloo — the Kashmiri original uses no onion, garlic, tomato or cream, relying instead on yogurt, Kashmiri chilli, fennel, dry ginger and asafoetida.
Dum aloo, dum olav in Kashmiri, means slow-cooked potatoes. Small potatoes are skinned and deep-fried, then cooked slowly in a spiced yogurt sauce (Wikipedia). It is part of the traditional cooking of Kashmiri Pandits (Wikipedia; JKTDC), and Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes files it among the vegetable side dishes, cooked with ginger powder and fennel. It isn't a standard Wazwan course. Wikipedia's Wazwan article includes dum aelve, potatoes in yogurt gravy, but notes that "it is rare", and Asia Media Centre reports that vegetarian dishes have been added to the originally lamb-centred feast only over the last few years.
Tip: A great pick for vegetarians and for travelers who want a familiar ingredient prepared in a distinctly Kashmiri way.

chunks.title: Recipe: Dum Aloo
chunks.text:
Recipe for Dum Aloo, as written on Wazwan Way.
Kashmiri dum aloo: baby potatoes pricked and fried golden, then simmered in a spiced yogurt gravy until the oil separates. This is a home recipe, and its own touch is to thicken the gravy with a paste of a few of the boiled potatoes.
Serves 4. Prep 23 min. Cook 50 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 500 g baby potatoes
- Oil, for deep-frying
- 2 bay leaves
- 1 tsp cumin seeds
- 2 black cardamom pods
- 4 green cardamom pods
- 4 cloves
- 1-inch piece of cinnamon
- 1 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder
- ½ tsp turmeric
- 1 tsp fennel powder
- 1 tsp dry ginger powder
- 1 tsp coriander powder
- 1 cup yogurt, whisked
- Salt, to taste
- Water, as needed
- ½ tsp garam masala, to finish
Method:
1. Pressure-cook the potatoes, peel them and prick them all over.
2. Blend 4–5 of the potatoes to a smooth paste. Deep-fry the rest until golden.
3. Heat a little of the frying oil in a pot and sauté the bay leaves, cumin, cardamoms, cloves and cinnamon.
4. Add the chilli, turmeric, fennel, dry ginger and coriander powders and cook on a low heat.
5. Stir in the whisked yogurt and cook until smooth.
6. Add the potato paste, the fried potatoes, salt and a little water. Cover and simmer until the gravy is thick and the oil separates.
7. Finish with the garam masala and serve hot.
Tips:
- Prick the potatoes after peeling, so the gravy gets in.
- The paste of boiled potato is what makes the gravy silky.
- Cook the powdered spices on a low heat before the yogurt goes in.
Serving: Serve hot with plain steamed rice. It sits naturally beside haakh and chaman qaliya in a Pandit vegetarian meal.

chunks.title: Dum Aloo: The gravy
chunks.text: The red comes from Kashmiri chilli, which colours food strongly but adds little heat (Wikipedia). Wikipedia's account of the Kashmiri dish makes the sauce with yogurt or khoya, often with cashew paste, and lists garlic among the spices (Wikipedia); Pandit homes that avoid onion and garlic (JKTDC) leave them out, and our recipe below uses asafoetida. Other versions, such as the Banarasi dum aloo, are made with tomatoes and onions (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: Dum Aloo: The pricking
chunks.text: The potatoes are pierced all over so the gravy soaks into them and they turn spongy. Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes calls this "the most skilful part" and has it done after frying (Wikipedia). Our recipe pricks them before frying, which also stops them bursting in the hot oil.

chunks.title: Girda (Girda / Tsot)
chunks.text:
Girda (Girda / Tsot) is on Wazwan Way under Bakery. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
Tandoor-baked breakfast bread.
Girda is a round, flat bread with finger impressions pressed into the dough, baked in a traditional clay tandoor (kandur).
Girda sits at the centre of the kandur waan (baker's shop) culture of the Valley: nearly every mohalla has its own wood-fired tandoor bakery, and the morning queue for fresh girda doubles as the neighbourhood's social bulletin board. Kandurs traditionally leaven the dough with a reserved piece of the previous day's dough fermented overnight, rather than commercial yeast. The rows of fingertip dimples pressed into the wet surface are the bread's signature, helping it bake flat against the tandoor wall. Both Kashmiri Muslim and Pandit households buy from the same kandur; the bakers themselves are traditionally Muslim artisans. It is emphatically a fresh bread — meant to be eaten the day it is baked.
Kashmir has a unique bakery culture (Kandur-wan). Girda is purchased fresh every morning by locals to eat with Noon Chai.
Tip: Eat it warm with a spread of butter, dipped in Noon Chai.

chunks.title: Recipe: Girda
chunks.text:
Recipe for Girda, as written on Wazwan Way.
Girda is the round, dimpled everyday bread of Kashmir — golden and blistered on top, pale and floury underneath, with a thin crisp shell over a soft, chewy crumb. Baked before dawn by the neighbourhood kandur and carried home warm, it is the bread most Kashmiris grow up eating for breakfast with a bowl of noon chai.
Serves 6 breads. Prep 38 min. Cook 13 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 400 g all-purpose flour (maida), plus extra for dusting
- 1.5 tsp instant yeast (kandurs use a reserved old-dough starter fermented overnight)
- 1 tbsp sugar
- 1.5 tsp salt
- 1 tbsp ghee, plus extra for greasing
- 240–260 ml lukewarm water, as needed
- 2–3 tbsp water or thin plain curd, for brushing the tops
- 1 tbsp poppy seeds or white sesame seeds (optional, traditional on some kandur girdas)
Method:
1. Stir the yeast and sugar into 120 ml of the lukewarm water and leave 10 minutes until frothy. (Skip the wait if using instant yeast — mix it straight into the flour.)
2. Combine the flour and salt, rub in the ghee, then add the yeast water and enough of the remaining water to form a medium-soft dough. Knead 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
3. Grease the dough and bowl lightly, cover, and let it rise until doubled — about 2 hours in a warm kitchen, or overnight in the refrigerator for deeper, kandur-style flavour (the traditional dough ferments overnight).
4. Punch down and divide into 6 balls. Rest 10 minutes under a cloth.
5. With wet palms, press each ball out into a round roughly 15 cm across and about 1 cm thick — traditionally spread by pressing with the flat of the palm rather than a rolling pin.
6. Brush the top with water or thin curd. While the surface is wet, press 3–4 rows of deep fingertip dimples across the middle of the bread, leaving a plain border at the rim. Sprinkle poppy or sesame seeds if using.
7. Bake in a tandoor slapped against the hot wall for 2–3 minutes until the top blisters and browns while the base stays pale — or follow the home-oven method: hottest setting (250–275°C), tray on the top shelf close to the broiler element, 5–7 minutes until the top is deep golden and blistered, then 2–3 minutes more if the base needs setting.
8. Wrap in a clean cloth as they come out; the crust softens slightly and the crumb stays warm. Eat the same day.
Waza tips:
- The dimples must go in while the surface is wet — they hold their shape through baking and give girda its identity.
- Do not roll with a pin; palm-pressing keeps a slightly irregular, airy crumb that a rolling pin flattens out.
- Overnight fermentation is what separates a kandur girda from a quick naan — the faint sourness is the point.
- Underbake rather than overbake: girda should crackle at the crust and stay chewy inside, never biscuit-hard.
Common mistakes:
- Skipping the long ferment — a 45-minute dough tastes flat and tears instead of blistering.
- Making the dimples on a dry surface, so they puff out and vanish in the oven.
- Baking in the middle of the oven at moderate heat, which dries the bread through before the top colours.
- Rolling the dough thin like a chapati; girda is a plump 1 cm bread, not a flatbread.
At home: A domestic oven cannot match a tandoor's 400°C+ wall, so compensate with radiant top heat: preheat the oven at its maximum (250–275°C) with a baking steel or inverted heavy tray on the top shelf for at least 30 minutes, then bake the girda directly on it as close to the broiler/top coil as possible, switching to the broiler for the last 1–2 minutes to blister the top. Expect a slightly thicker, breadier result than the kandur's — the tandoor's one-sided wall contact is what keeps the base white while the face browns; at home the base will colour a little too. An overnight cold ferment recovers most of the flavour that commercial yeast shortcuts lose.
Serving: Serve warm, torn and buttered, with noon chai at breakfast — the classic Kashmiri morning. It also mops up harissa in winter and any curry at lunch.

chunks.title: Girda: Without an oven: girda in a pressure cooker
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Girda page: Without an oven: girda in a pressure cooker.
Girda can be made at home without yeast or an oven, on the hot wall of a pressure cooker.
1 cup flour is mixed with ¼ tsp baking soda, ½ tsp sugar and ½ tsp salt, then kneaded with 3 tbsp curd and warm water to a soft dough; 1 tbsp oil is worked in for 5–7 minutes and the dough rests for an hour under a damp cloth. It makes 4–5 thick discs, pressed in the middle with the fingertips to give the bread its dimples.
The cooker is used as for czochworu: gasket and whistle off, heated empty for 10 minutes, salt water sprinkled inside. Each girda is wetted underneath and stuck to the inside, covered and cooked for 2–3 minutes, then the cooker is turned over the flame for 5–7 minutes until the bread has golden spots. Brush them with butter or ghee.

chunks.title: Gushtaba
chunks.text:
Gushtaba is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim. It is one of the seven dishes commonly listed as essential to a Wazwan. In the feast: the last course; gushtaba always comes last.
Gushtaba is one of the most iconic and luxurious dishes of Kashmiri cuisine, especially served in the traditional Wazwan feast.
Gushtaba consists of finely pounded mutton meatballs cooked in a rich, creamy yogurt-based gravy. The texture is incredibly soft, almost melt-in-your-mouth, because the meat is traditionally hand-pounded rather than minced. Prepared with mutton, yogurt, ghee, cardamom, fennel powder and dry ginger, it is one of the grandest dishes in a Kashmiri Wazwan.
Widely called the 'dish of kings' in Kashmiri Muslim tradition, Gushtaba is served as the last meat course of the Wazwan, before dessert and kahwa — its arrival signals the end of the main meal. It shares its base with Rista: the same fresh mutton pounded with fat on stone with a goshpar mallet into a silken emulsion, but shaped into larger balls and cooked in yakhni-style yogurt gravy instead of the red chilli one — the white twin to Rista's red. The name is commonly explained through Persian roots as 'meat in broth', though as with most Wazwan etymologies the sources are traditional rather than documentary.
Gushtaba is a large ball of hand-pounded mutton and fat, cooked in yakhni, a white gravy of yogurt and mutton broth (Sahapedia; Wikipedia). Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes calls it "The Dish of Kings", and a Srinagar chef told Deccan Chronicle that it is "considered the king of all Kashmiri dishes". At weddings a waza brings the gushtaba to the guests (Reuters). Sahapedia describes a single gushtaba of 200 to 400 g shared by the four people at a trami, with the eldest dividing it. In August 2024 The Kashmir Wazwan Cooperative Limited applied for a geographical indication for "Goshtaba (Meat Products) of Kashmir" (application 1337). It was still at pre-examination when we checked in October 2026 (Intellectual Property India).
Tip: Gushtaba ends the main meal, so in a full Wazwan it comes last. In Srinagar, Outlook Traveller recommended Mughal Darbar for Wazwan in 2022, naming its rista and gushtaba.

chunks.title: Recipe: Gushtaba
chunks.text:
Recipe for Gushtaba, as written on Wazwan Way.
Gushtaba is the full stop of the Wazwan: large, cloud-soft meatballs of hand-pounded mutton and fat, simmered in a warm white gravy of churned yogurt perfumed with green cardamom and dried mint. When it arrives, everyone at the trami knows the savoury courses are over.
Serves 4–6 (makes 8–10 large meatballs). Prep 1 h 38 min. Cook 1 h 8 min. Level: Expert.
Ingredients:
- For the meatballs: 1 kg boneless mutton leg, very fresh, cubed
- 200 g mutton fat (suet), softened in warm water (a spoon of ghee may replace part of it)
- 1 tsp ground black cardamom seeds
- 1 tsp dry ginger powder (sonth)
- 1 tsp fennel (saunf) powder
- 1.5 tsp salt
- For the gravy: 750 g plain whole-milk yogurt, churned smooth
- 200 ml milk (optional, for extra body)
- 2 tbsp mustard oil
- 2 tbsp ghee
- 3 cloves
- 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped
- 3 tbsp praan (shallot) emulsion — fried shallots ground with hot water
- 1 tsp fennel powder and 1 tsp dry ginger powder (for the boiling stock)
- 8–10 green cardamom pods, lightly crushed
- 1/2 tsp ground black cardamom
- 1/4 tsp caraway seeds (shah zeera)
- 1 tsp garam masala
- 1 tbsp dried mint (or a small handful of fresh mint/coriander, chopped)
- Salt to taste
Method:
1. Pound the meat exactly as for Rista: beat the cubes with softened fat on a stone or heavy board, folding and re-pounding, until you have a completely smooth, sticky, pale paste with no visible grain (this takes noticeably longer than rista-fineness — the gushtaba paste should be even silkier). Knead in the black cardamom, sonth, fennel and salt.
2. With moistened palms, press and roll the paste into large compact balls, 5–7 cm across, pressing each twice so it is dense and crack-free.
3. Bring a pot of water to a simmer with a little salt, fennel powder and ginger powder. Poach the balls gently for about 30 minutes until set and cooked through. Lift them out; strain and reserve the poaching stock.
4. Churn the yogurt (with the milk, if using) until completely smooth — traditionally with a wooden churner, at home with a whisk or blender. Whisk in two ladles of the warm stock to temper it.
5. In the cleaned pot, heat the mustard oil, add the ghee, cloves and garlic, and fry until fragrant.
6. Pour in the tempered yogurt mixture and about 500 ml of the reserved stock, stirring constantly in one direction over medium heat until it comes to a gentle boil without splitting.
7. Add the poached meatballs and the praan emulsion. Simmer gently, uncovered, 20–25 minutes, shaking the pot occasionally, until the gravy thickens slightly and beads of ghee show on the surface.
8. Finish with the crushed green cardamoms, ground black cardamom, caraway, garam masala and dried mint. Simmer two minutes and serve each gushtaba with plenty of its white gravy.
Waza tips:
- Gushtaba paste is pounded finer than Rista's — wazas say you should be able to spread it like butter before shaping.
- Stir the yogurt gravy in one direction only and never leave it during the first boil; that is the moment it splits.
- Poach, don't fry: the balls must set in barely-simmering liquid or they toughen at the surface.
- Dried mint at the end is the signature aroma — add it late so it perfumes rather than stews.
Common mistakes:
- Under-pounding — the single most common failure; dense gushtaba misses the entire point of the dish.
- Adding cold yogurt straight to a hot pot, splitting the gravy; always churn smooth and temper with warm stock.
- Adding chilli or turmeric — the gravy is deliberately white, its heat coming only from black pepper-family aromatics.
- Hard-boiling the finished gravy, which curdles it and toughens the balls.
