At home: Use the same processor-plus-hand-beating method as Rista, keeping meat and fat cold, and beat a few minutes longer for the finer paste. Full-fat Greek-style yogurt let down with milk churns into a stable gravy; a teaspoon of rice flour or cornflour whisked into the yogurt is a pragmatic insurance against splitting, though no waza would use it. Shallots stand in for praan.
Serving: The final meat course of the Wazwan, served over rice as the closing statement before phirni and kahwa. At home it makes a stately centrepiece with plain rice.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: With chicken: a home-style gushtaba
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Gushtaba page: With chicken: a home-style gushtaba.
A lighter gushtaba can be made at home with chicken. It is a home cook's take on the dish, not the Wazwan's.
For the meatballs, 500 g boneless chicken is blended with 70 g rendered and cooled mutton fat (or ghee), 1 tsp salt, the seeds of 1 black cardamom pod, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 8–10 ice cubes to a smooth, sticky paste, shaped into balls and cooked in boiling water; 2 cups of the stock are kept.
For the gravy, 500 g yogurt is whisked with 1 egg or 2 tbsp gram flour and cooked, whisking all the time, until it boils. In go 1 black and 2 green cardamom pods, a small stick of cinnamon, 2 cloves, 1 tsp cumin seeds, ½ tsp each of fennel and dry ginger powder, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tbsp oil and salt. When it has thickened a little, the meatballs, the stock, 2 tbsp fried-shallot paste, ½ tsp mint powder and 1 tbsp ghee go in, and the pot is covered and simmered for a few minutes. Keep the chicken, fat and grinder cold, and use mutton fat for the Wazwan flavour.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: The gravy
chunks.text:
Sahapedia describes gushtaba's yakhni as yogurt and mutton broth with shallots, ginger, garlic and spices such as cinnamon and cardamom, topped with cumin and dried mint (Sahapedia). Onmanorama names curd, cardamom, dry ginger and fennel (Onmanorama). Neither lists tomato or chilli, though Wikipedia's Wazwan article calls the gravy "spicy" (Wikipedia).
The meatballs are boiled in water until soft and expanded, then cooked in the yakhni (Sahapedia).

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Its place in the feast
chunks.text:
Gushtaba ends the main meal: "As a rule, the meal must end with gushtaba" (Asia Media Centre). Its arrival tells guests the savoury courses are over (Wikipedia; Reuters). Desserts follow (Wikipedia), and kahwa closes the feast (Sahapedia). The sources we use record that it comes last, but not why.
Kashmiri hosts press food on their guests, and Onmanorama writes that Kashmiris consider it disrespectful to refuse a dish or an extra helping (Onmanorama). How Wazwan is served covers the order of the courses and the manners at the trami.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Gushtaba and rista
chunks.text: Both are made from the same pounded mutton and fat: gushtaba's balls are larger, rista's smaller (Sahapedia), and rista's gravy is red where gushtaba's is white (Wikipedia). Rista vs gushtaba compares them side by side, and rista has its own page.

chunks.title: Kabargah
chunks.text:
Kabargah is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: Medium. Tradition: Kashmiri Pandit.
Crispy fried mutton ribs cooked in milk and spices.
Kabargah consists of mutton ribs cooked in milk and spices, then dipped in a yogurt batter and shallow fried in pure ghee until crispy and golden.
Kabargah holds a place of honour at Kashmiri Pandit feasts and wedding meals, served early in the meal while the ghee is still audible. The two-stage method is the dish's identity: a slow milk simmer that tenderises the ribs and seasons them from within, followed by a hot ghee fry that sets the crust. True to Pandit kitchen rules it uses no onion or garlic, leaning instead on fennel, dry ginger and asafoetida. It is eaten with the fingers, and the test of a good kabargah is that the bone slides free.
Kabargah is the name Kashmiri Pandits commonly use for tabak maaz, the twice-cooked ribs of the Wazwan (Wikipedia). Its preparation involves simmering tender ribs in milk infused with cardamoms and sweet fennel before a final flash-fry.
Tip: Perfect as an appetizer. Squeeze fresh lemon juice on top before eating.
Kabargah: mutton ribs simmered in milk with fennel and cardamom, then batter-fried in ghee. The Kashmiri Pandit name for tabak maaz: history and recipe.

chunks.title: Recipe: Kabargah
chunks.text:
Recipe for Kabargah, as written on Wazwan Way.
Flat cuts of mutton rib simmered in milk perfumed with fennel and cardamom, then dipped in a light yogurt batter and shallow-fried in ghee until the edges crisp. Kabargah is the Pandit counterpart to the Wazwan's tabak maaz — richer for the milk, gentler for the absence of onion and garlic.
Serves 4. Prep 20 min. Cook 1 h 15 min. Level: Involved.
Ingredients:
- 800 g mutton ribs (breast/flank cuts), in flat 2-rib pieces
- 750 ml full-fat milk
- 250 ml water
- 1 tbsp fennel powder
- 1 tsp dry ginger powder (sonth)
- 4 green cardamoms and 2 black cardamoms, bruised
- 2 cloves and 1 small cinnamon stick
- 1 pinch asafoetida
- Salt to taste
- 150 g thick yogurt, whisked, for the batter
- 1 pinch turmeric (optional, for the batter's colour)
- Ghee for shallow-frying
Method:
1. Put the ribs in a wide pot with the milk, water, whole spices, fennel, sonth, asafoetida and salt.
2. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered, turning occasionally, until the ribs are fully tender and the liquid has nearly evaporated, 60-70 minutes.
3. Lift the ribs out carefully and let them cool enough to handle; they should hold their shape.
4. Whisk the yogurt with a little salt and the turmeric into a thin coating batter.
5. Heat ghee in a wide frying pan over medium heat.
6. Dip each rib piece in the yogurt batter, let the excess drip, and shallow-fry until golden brown and lightly crisp on both sides, 2-3 minutes a side.
7. Drain briefly and serve hot, sprinkled with a pinch of salt.
Waza tips:
- Let the milk reduce almost completely before frying — ribs lifted from wet milk will spit violently in the ghee.
- Fry in ghee, not oil; the flavour of kabargah is half milk, half ghee.
Common mistakes:
- Boiling the milk hard, which curdles it and toughens the meat.
- Skipping the batter — without it the crust burns before it crisps.
At home: Lamb breast or riblets from any butcher work well; the milk simmer can be done ahead and the ribs fried just before serving.
Serving: Serve as a starter or alongside rice and a yogurt dish; eat with the fingers while hot.

chunks.title: Kabargah: Kabargah and tabak maaz
chunks.text:
Wikipedia treats kabargah and tabak maaz as one dish under two names (Wikipedia), and its list of Kashmiri dishes says Kashmiri Pandits commonly call it kabargah. The list notes a small difference in method: kabargah is simmered on a low heat for longer and then fried very quickly, while tabak maaz is boiled with salt and garlic and has a slightly elastic texture (Wikipedia). JKTDC lists kabargah among the delicacies of Kashmiri Pandit cooking (JKTDC).
Tabak maaz has the Wazwan version, with how the wazas make it, and Kashmiri Pandit food covers the Pandit table more widely.

chunks.title: Harissa
chunks.text:
Harissa is on Wazwan Way under Street Food. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: Medium. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim.
A slow-cooked winter mutton and rice paste.
Harissa is a rich, smooth paste of mutton slow-cooked overnight with rice, spices, and oil, served hot with local baked flatbreads.
Harissa is a seasonal, artisan institution rather than a home dish: from roughly late autumn to early spring, specialist makers known as harisa guyr sell it by the morning bowl from shops concentrated in old Srinagar — Aali Kadal above all, with Saraf Kadal, Fateh Kadal and a few uptown addresses — several of them family businesses generations deep. The pot goes on the night before; the meat cooks down with rice and spices in a vessel set into a hearth, and is worked continuously until fibre and grain dissolve into one another. Its origin is traditionally traced to Central Asia and Persia, and popular accounts associate its arrival with the 14th-century Sufi saint Mir Syed Ali Hamadani — a widely repeated attribution rather than a documented fact, and best held loosely. What is certain is its status: for downtown Srinagar, harissa season is a calendar event, and the dish is a marker of winter identity. The name coincidence with Maghrebi harissa (a chilli condiment) is exactly that — a coincidence of Arabic-derived naming ('harasa', to pound/mash) applied to two unrelated foods.
Harissa is a winter breakfast made by specialist cooks and sold from shops in Srinagar's old city. Where it came from is a matter of tradition rather than record: one maker credits the Sufi saint Shah-i-Hamdan, others the Mughals, and it is often linked to Persian and Central Asian cooking. The pot goes on the night before over a wood fire, and the mutton and rice are worked until smooth.
Tip: Harissa is only made in winter, roughly from late autumn to March. It is a morning dish: shops in Srinagar's old city, especially around Aali Kadal, serve it early and often sell out by mid-morning, so go early and eat it hot with fresh bread from a kandur.
Harissa: Srinagar's winter breakfast of mutton and rice cooked overnight to a smooth paste, sold mornings in the old city from late autumn to March.

chunks.title: Recipe: Harissa
chunks.text:
Recipe for Harissa, as written on Wazwan Way.
Harissa at home: a stock from the mutton bones, the meat pressure-cooked with fennel and whole spices, cooked down for hours and thickened with rice flour until it mashes smooth.
Serves 6–8. Prep 38 min. Cook 4 h. Level: Expert.
Ingredients:
- 1.5 kg mutton on the bone
- 2–2.5 cups rice flour
- ½ cup fennel seeds
- Garlic paste, for the stock
- Salt, to taste
- ½ cup mustard oil, plus more to serve
- 2 tbsp fried shallot or onion paste
- For the spice bundle: 8–9 green cardamom pods, 3–4 black cardamom pods, 5–6 cloves and ½ tsp black peppercorns
- 1 large onion, finely sliced and fried, or fried shallots, to garnish
- Water, as needed
Method:
1. Take the meat off the bones. Boil the bones in a large pot of water with green cardamom and the garlic paste, then lower the heat and cook until you have a rich stock. Strain it, add any meat left on the bones to the rest, and discard the bones.
2. Pressure-cook the boneless mutton with the spice bundle, the fennel seeds, salt and water until it is falling apart. Take out the bundle and any membranes.
3. Pour the stock over the meat. Cover and cook on a low flame for 1–2 hours.
4. Mix the rice flour with water to a smooth slurry. Add it to the pot a little at a time, stirring continuously so that no lumps form.
5. Cook for 30–40 minutes more, stirring now and then, until the harissa is thick and velvety. Add the ½ cup of oil and the fried-onion paste.
6. Mash the meat into the gravy with a wooden spoon or a masher until smooth. Adjust the salt.
7. Serve hot, topped with mustard oil and fried onions.
Tips:
- Stir all the time while the rice-flour slurry goes in.
- The stock from the bones is what gives the harissa its depth.
- Mash until the meat disappears into the gravy.
Serving: Eaten at breakfast, scalding hot, with fresh tchot or girda bread torn and dipped straight into the bowl, ideally with noon chai alongside. In Srinagar it is a winter pleasure, from late autumn to March; out of season the shops simply stop making it.
About this recipe: This is a home version, thickened with rice flour and started in a pressure cooker; the harissa shops of Srinagar cook theirs overnight.

chunks.title: Kahwa
chunks.text:
Kahwa is on Wazwan Way under Beverages. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
Saffron-infused Kashmiri green tea with almonds.
Kahwa is an aromatic green tea brewed with saffron strands, cinnamon bark, cardamom pods, and served with a generous garnish of crushed almonds.
Kahwa is inseparable from the samovar — the coal-fired brass or copper urn with a central fire-chamber that keeps the tea perpetually hot, from which cups are refilled through long winter days and every Wazwan feast. Both the drink and the vessel speak to Kashmir's deep Persian and Central Asian inheritance: the samovar form travelled the same routes as the Persianate court culture, crafts, and Sufi networks that shaped the Valley from the fourteenth century onward, and Kashmiri kahwa culture is best understood inside that Persian-influenced world. The word is sometimes traced further back through trade etymologies, but the living tradition — saffron, cardamom, almonds, the samovar itself — is Kashmir's own, refined over centuries of local practice.
Kahwa has been drank in Kashmir for centuries. It was historically reserved for royalty and guests of honor as a warm welcome drink and digestive aid.
Tip: Always drink it hot. It is the perfect welcome drink when you arrive in the cool valleys of Kashmir.

chunks.title: Recipe: Kahwa
chunks.text:
Recipe for Kahwa, as written on Wazwan Way.
Kahwa is Kashmir's golden welcome: green tea simmered briefly with saffron, cardamom and cinnamon, poured over crushed almonds. Light, aromatic and barely sweet, it is drunk after heavy meals, offered to guests, and kept warm all day in the samovar.
Serves 4. Prep 5 min. Cook 13 min. Level: Easy.
Ingredients:
- 4 cups (about 950 ml) water
- 2 tsp Kashmiri green tea leaves (or a good whole-leaf green tea), lightly crushed
- 3-4 green cardamoms, crushed
- 1 small piece cinnamon (about 2.5 cm)
- 1-2 cloves (optional)
- A pinch of saffron threads, plus a few for the cups
- 8-10 almonds, blanched and crushed or slivered
- Sugar or honey to taste (traditionally light — about 2-3 tsp)
- Dried rose petals (optional, festive)
Method:
1. Bring the water to a boil with the crushed cardamom, cinnamon and cloves and simmer 4-5 minutes so the spices open fully — the spices go in before the tea, never after.
2. Add the saffron and simmer another minute until the water turns pale gold.
3. Add the green tea leaves, let the pot boil once, then take it off the heat and steep 2-3 minutes only. Long boiling turns the tea bitter and muddy.
4. Add sugar or honey to taste.
5. Put a spoonful of crushed almonds (and a thread or two of saffron) into each cup, strain the hot kahwa over, and serve immediately.
Waza tips:
- Spices first, tea last — the order is the whole technique. Green tea steeped more than a few minutes loses its lightness.
- Crush the almonds rather than slicing them thin; the coarse pieces at the bottom of the cup are meant to be eaten as the tea is finished.
- If saffron is scarce, bloom it in a spoon of warm water before adding — a few threads treated well outperform a pinch dumped in.
Common mistakes:
- Boiling the tea leaves hard, which makes the cup bitter and dark
- Adding milk (a different drink altogether)
- Overloading sugar until it tastes like syrup — kahwa is traditionally lightly sweetened
- Skipping the almonds, which are considered part of the drink, not a garnish
At home: A small saucepan replaces the samovar entirely; a thermos replicates its keep-warm role surprisingly well for a gathering. Gunpowder green tea is the closest widely available leaf to Kashmiri bombay tea. Skip milk — kahwa never takes it; that is noon chai's territory.
Serving: Served scalding hot in small cups after meals — obligatory after a Wazwan — or through the day in winter; it pairs naturally with Kashmiri breads and with sweets like Shufta.

chunks.title: Kahwa: Four kinds of kehwa
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Kahwa page: Four kinds of kehwa.
There is more than one kehwa. These are four, and each recipe makes two cups.
Kong kehwa, the saffron one, has no tea in it: 6–8 saffron strands are soaked in 2 tbsp hot water for 5 minutes; 2 cups of water are boiled with 2 pounded cardamom pods; the saffron and sugar or honey go in, and it simmers for 2–3 minutes and is served with almond slivers. Dodh kehwa is the same made with milk: 2 cups boiled with the saffron and cardamom, sweetened and simmered for 5 minutes.
Mulethi, or shangri, kehwa is 1 tsp liquorice root, 1 tsp sepistan and a small piece of cinnamon, lightly pounded, boiled in 2 cups of water with sugar for 8–10 minutes and strained. The green tea kehwa, dum tyoth, is 2 cups of water boiled with a small stick of cinnamon and sugar, then simmered for 3–4 minutes with 1 tsp green tea or noon chai leaves and strained.

chunks.title: Kahwa: A winter kehwa premix
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Kahwa page: A winter kehwa premix.
A ground mix of whole spices and herbs can be kept through the winter and brewed a cup at a time.
It is equal weights, 50 g each, of eight things: shanger, sonth (dried ginger), Bombay chai mix (a green tea), sapistaan (lisoda), black pepper, cinnamon, green cardamom and dried rose petals. They are cleaned and dried if they need it, ground coarse or fine, mixed and stored in an airtight jar.
To use it, ½ tsp of the mix is boiled in 1 cup of water for 5–7 minutes, strained, sweetened with honey and drunk warm.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Kulcha (Kulcha)
chunks.text:
Kashmiri Kulcha (Kulcha) is on Wazwan Way under Bakery. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
Small, round, crumbly afternoon bakery biscuits topped with poppy seeds.
Kashmiri Kulcha is a dry, hard, biscuit-like baked bread with a golden crumbly texture, traditionally topped with poppy seeds. Unlike the soft, leavened Punjabi Kulcha, the Kashmiri version is a small snack biscuit specifically baked by the Kandur to be enjoyed with afternoon tea.
Kulcha is the kandur bread with a shelf life. Where girda must be eaten the day it is baked, tins of kulcha sit in Kashmiri homes for weeks, brought out whenever tea is poured, and they travel — kulcha is the bread relatives carry out of the Valley. Kandurs bake both a salty (namkeen) and a mildly sweet version, and special runs are baked for Ramadan, Eid and family functions. The peanut pressed into the centre before baking is a small trademark flourish noted at traditional Srinagar bakeries. The ritual of dunking kulcha in noon chai and spooning up the softened crumbs is a fixture of Kashmiri tea culture.
Kashmiri Kulchas have been baked in neighborhood Kandur-wans for generations. There are sweet and savory versions, both of which are central to the valley's afternoon social gatherings. It is historically paired with Noon Chai or spiced saffron Kahwa.
Tip: Dip the hard Kulcha into your Noon Chai for a few seconds to soften it before taking a bite—the salty tea and crumbly biscuit flavor combination is a local favorite.
Kashmiri kulcha: a small, hard, crumbly biscuit topped with poppy seeds, baked by the kandur and dipped in noon chai. Sweet and savoury kinds, and the recipe.

chunks.title: Recipe: Kashmiri Kulcha
chunks.text:
Recipe for Kashmiri Kulcha, as written on Wazwan Way.
The Kashmiri kulcha has nothing to do with the soft stuffed kulchas of Punjab: it is a small, hard, crumbly biscuit-bread from the kandur's tandoor, usually salty, dusted with sesame and often pressed with a single peanut in the centre. It is built for dunking — its dry, short crumb drinks up noon chai without collapsing.
Serves 16–20 small kulchas. Prep 30 min. Cook 23 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 250 g all-purpose flour (maida)
- 100 g ghee, melted and cooled (the high moyan/shortening is what makes it crumbly)
- 1 tsp salt (for the classic namkeen kulcha; reduce to 1/2 tsp and add 3 tbsp powdered sugar for the sweet version)
- 1 tsp sugar
- 1/2 tsp baking powder
- 1/4 tsp instant yeast (optional — some bakers use a touch of yeast, others none)
- 1/4 tsp green cardamom powder (traditional in the sweet version; optional in the salty)
- 60–80 ml milk, as needed to bind
- 2 tbsp milk (or 1 beaten egg yolk) for brushing
- 2 tbsp white sesame seeds
- 16–20 raw peanuts, one per kulcha (optional, the kandur's trademark)
Method:
1. Whisk the flour, salt, sugar, baking powder, yeast (if using) and cardamom together.
2. Rub in the melted ghee until the mixture looks like damp sand and holds a print when squeezed — this shortening step, not kneading, decides the texture.
3. Add milk a spoonful at a time and press together into a firm, just-cohesive dough. Do not knead beyond bringing it together; working it develops gluten and toughens the kulcha.
4. Cover and rest 30–60 minutes (if you used yeast, let it sit the full hour in a warm spot).
5. Divide into 16–20 balls, flatten each slightly into a thick disc about 4–5 cm across, and set on a lined baking tray with space between.
6. Brush the tops with milk or egg yolk, sprinkle generously with sesame seeds, and press one peanut into the centre of each.
7. Bake at 180–190°C for 20–25 minutes until evenly pale gold and completely dry through — in the tandoor they bake at the cooler margin until they sound hollow and dry.
8. Cool fully on a rack; they crisp and set as they cool. Store airtight for up to 3 weeks.
Waza tips:
- The ghee-to-flour ratio is the recipe: skimp on the moyan and you get a hard rusk instead of a short, melting crumble.
- Bake low and slow relative to other tandoor breads — kulcha must dry out to the centre, not just brown.
- Handle the dough like pastry, not bread; the less you work it, the better it shatters.
- Salty kulcha with noon chai, sweet kulcha with lipton (sweet) chai — kandurs sell both for a reason.
Common mistakes:
- Kneading the dough smooth like a bread dough — the crumbliness comes from an unworked, shortcrust-style dough.
- Pulling them out as soon as they colour; an underdried kulcha turns leathery by the next day.
- Using soft or melted-hot ghee poured in at once, which makes the dough greasy instead of sandy.
- Making them large and thin — kulcha is a small, thick biscuit, not a cracker.
At home: This is the most home-oven-friendly of the kandur breads because it wants moderate, even heat rather than tandoor blast: a standard fan oven at 180°C reproduces it closely. The main translation is patience — bake until fully dry (a kulcha broken in half should show no moist centre) and let them cool completely before judging texture, as they harden off the tray. If your first batch is soft inside, return them to a 150°C oven for 10 minutes rather than raising the temperature.
Serving: Serve with noon chai, dunked whole and eaten by the spoonful as it softens — the definitive Kashmiri pairing. Also good alongside kahwa or afternoon tea from the tin.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Lassi (Gurus (churned buttermilk); salted mint lassi)
chunks.text:
Kashmiri Lassi (Gurus (churned buttermilk); salted mint lassi) is on Wazwan Way under Beverages. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
A creamy yogurt-based drink infused with saffron and dry fruits.
Kashmiri Lassi is a rich, creamy yogurt drink blended with saffron strands, crushed almonds, pistachios, and a touch of rose water. Unlike the thin lassis found in the plains, the Kashmiri version is thick, aromatic, and served chilled as a refreshing accompaniment to heavy meals or as a standalone summer cooler.
For centuries the churning of gurus was a household ritual across Kashmir: fermented milk worked in a clay or wooden vessel (tchod) with a long wooden churner (de'on) pulled by a rope (lam e raz), separating golden butter and leaving tart buttermilk behind. Kashmir Life records that gurus was served with spices, mint, salt and sugar, prized as a summer coolant and recommended by traditional hakims for digestion; a Kashmiri saying held that autumn gurus — made when grazing was richest — was fit for friends, while spring gurus was for enemies. Kashmiri food writers describe the tall glass of minted, cumin-spiced buttermilk as the standard close to a summer midday meal. The tradition is fading as machine skimming replaces hand churning, though it survives among herders in upland pastures. What is presented today as 'Kashmiri lassi' is essentially this salted-savory buttermilk idiom, made in modern kitchens from yogurt and cold water rather than churn-fresh buttermilk.
Yogurt-based drinks have been part of Kashmiri cuisine for centuries, especially during the warm summer months. The addition of saffron and dry fruits reflects Kashmir's access to premium ingredients from its own orchards and fields. Traditionally prepared at home using fresh curd, it has now become a popular offering at local cafes and street stalls across the valley.
Tip: Order it chilled after a heavy Wazwan meal — it helps with digestion and balances the rich, spicy flavors of the meats.

chunks.title: Recipe: Kashmiri Lassi
chunks.text:
Recipe for Kashmiri Lassi, as written on Wazwan Way.
Kashmir's everyday yogurt drink is not the thick, sweet, malai-capped lassi of Punjab. It is a thin, salted, mint-and-cumin-scented buttermilk — rooted in gurus, the hand-churned buttermilk that once accompanied nearly every summer afternoon meal in the Valley.
Serves 2. Prep 10 min. Level: Easy.
Ingredients:
- 400 g full-fat plain yogurt, well set and ideally a day old (a gentle sourness is traditional — gurus was made from fermented milk)
- 300–400 ml cold water, to taste (traditionally chilled spring water; more water gives the correct thin, drinkable body)
- 10–12 fresh mint leaves, plus a sprig to garnish
- 1/2 tsp roasted cumin powder
- 1/2 tsp salt, or to taste (a pinch of black salt is a common addition)
- Ice cubes, optional
- Pinch of sugar, optional (some households balance the salt with a whisper of sugar, as noted in accounts of gurus service)
Method:
1. Whisk the yogurt in a deep vessel until completely smooth — traditionally this was a rhythmic back-and-forth churning, not a quick stir; work it until no lumps remain and it turns glossy.
2. Add the cold water gradually, whisking or churning as you pour, until the drink is thin enough to gulp rather than sip. Kashmiri buttermilk is noticeably thinner than Punjabi lassi.
3. Bruise the mint leaves between your fingers (or pound briefly with a pinch of salt) and stir them in; for a smoother drink, blend the mint with a splash of the buttermilk first.
4. Season with salt and roasted cumin powder. Taste — it should be tart, saline and cooling, with mint as fragrance rather than a dominant flavour.
5. Whisk or blend vigorously once more until a light froth caps the surface (the froth is the traditional sign it has been churned enough).
6. Chill or pour over ice, garnish with mint, and serve in tall glasses alongside the midday meal.
Waza tips:
- Use yogurt that has sat a day past setting — the slight extra sourness mimics the fermented-milk tang of true gurus far better than fresh sweet curd.
- Do not thicken it. The single biggest tell of an inauthentic Kashmiri buttermilk is a thick, smoothie-like body; it should run off a spoon like milk.
- Salt after diluting, not before — the same quantity of salt tastes very different once the water goes in.
- If you can source real churned buttermilk (the by-product of butter-making), use it neat with just salt, mint and cumin — that is gurus proper.
Common mistakes:
- Making it thick and sweet like a Punjabi lassi — the Kashmiri idiom is thin, salted and savory.
- Skipping the roasted cumin, which supplies the drink's earthy backbone.
- Using ultra-fresh, barely-set yogurt with no tang, which produces a flat, milky drink.
- Over-blending the mint into green sludge; it should perfume the glass, not colour it.
At home: A blender does in twenty seconds what the de'on did in an hour: blitz yogurt, water, mint, salt and cumin together until frothy. Greek yogurt works if thinned with extra water. No specialty ingredients are needed — roasted cumin powder can be made by dry-toasting cumin seeds and crushing them.
Serving: Served chilled with the summer midday meal — it is the traditional companion to rice and haakh, and a cooling counterpoint to rich meat dishes. In winter, some households traditionally took it lukewarm with hot water whisked into the yogurt.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Pulao (Modur Pulao)
chunks.text:
Kashmiri Pulao (Modur Pulao) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
Sweet, fragrant saffron rice with nuts.
Modur pulao, Kashmir's sweet pulao, is basmati rice cooked with sugar, ghee and saffron, with fried almonds, raisins, dried dates and coconut.
This is celebration rice, cooked for festivals, weddings and large vegetarian feasts in Kashmir rather than for everyday meals. The 2006 Wazwan booklet used as reference presents it as a slow dum-cooked feast dish sealed with a rope of dough, a technique still described by home cooks. It appears in both Pandit and Muslim festive cooking; no credible source ties it to a single community or origin story, so none is claimed here. Its extravagance — saffron, ghee, almonds, dried fruit — reflects Kashmir's orchard-and-saffron economy more than any courtly legend.
Modur is Kashmiri for "sweet" (Grierson's dictionary gives "sweet, honied"), and modur pulao is Kashmir's sweet pulao: basmati rice cooked with sugar, ghee and saffron, with fried dry fruit, nuts and whole spices (De Leij: Culinary Art of Kashmir). A pulao is often part of a Wazwan. Wikipedia notes that a Kashmiri vegetarian pulao of spices, vegetables and dried fruit "is often included", and Onmanorama lists a Kashmiri pulao of basmati cooked in milk and ghee with saffron and dry fruit. Neither says it is sweetened, so it isn't clear that either is modur pulao. Pulaos have a long history at Kashmiri feasts: Kashmir Life, drawing on the 16th-century Tuhfat-ul-Ahbab, lists pulao, zard pulao and tursh pulao among the special foods of the time. The sources don't say whether any of these was modur pulao.
Tip: A great option if you prefer a sweet, rich, and completely non-spicy rice dish.

chunks.title: Recipe: Kashmiri Pulao
chunks.text:
Recipe for Kashmiri Pulao, as written on Wazwan Way.
Modur Pulao ('modur' means sweet in Kashmiri) is basmati rice cooked with sugar, ghee, saffron and whole warm spices, then strewn with fried nuts, raisins, dates and coconut shavings. It sits deliberately on the border between rice course and dessert — fragrant, golden and unapologetically rich.
Serves 6. Prep 30 min. Cook 53 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 500 g basmati rice, washed and soaked in water for 1-2 hours
- 200-250 g sugar (traditional feast versions run much sweeter)
- 125 g ghee
- A generous pinch of saffron threads, steeped in 3 tbsp warm milk or water
- 30 g almonds, blanched and halved
- 25 g raisins, stemmed and rinsed
- 50 g dried dates, soaked briefly, stoned and sliced
- 40 g dried coconut, shaved into thin slivers
- 1 tbsp melon seeds (optional, traditional)
- 6 green cardamoms, lightly crushed
- 2 black cardamoms, seeds crushed with 0.5 tsp black peppercorns
- 1 stick cinnamon (about 5 cm)
- 2 cloves
- 2 bay or cassia leaves
- 15 g fresh ginger, chopped fine (traditional; omit if you prefer a purely sweet profile)
- 1 tbsp crushed rock sugar / sugar candy (optional finish)
- 0.25 tsp salt
- 2-3 drops kewra water (optional)
Method:
1. Parboil the soaked rice in about 900 ml water (the soaking water is traditionally used) until it is roughly three-quarters cooked and the water is almost absorbed. Take it off the heat — the grains should still have a firm core.
2. Meanwhile make the syrup: dissolve the sugar in 300 ml water over low heat with the cinnamon, bay leaves, crushed black cardamom-pepper mix, chopped ginger and the saffron steeped in its liquid. Simmer gently for 5 minutes so the spices open up in the syrup.
3. In a small pan, heat the ghee with the cloves and fry the almonds, dates, coconut, melon seeds and finally the raisins (they colour fastest) until aromatic and lightly golden. Reserve a spoonful of the fried mixture for the top.
4. In a heavy, lidded pot, layer the parboiled rice, then pour over the spiced syrup, the ghee with its fried fruit and nuts, the green cardamoms and the salt. Fold together once, gently, with a flat spatula — do not stir vigorously.
5. Seal the pot: cover with the lid and, in the traditional manner, press a rope of kneaded wheat-flour dough around the rim (a tight lid weighted down works too).
6. Cook on the lowest possible heat (or over a tawa) for 20-30 minutes of slow dum, until the grains are cooked through, separate and slightly translucent — the aroma escaping the seal is the traditional signal that it is ready.
7. Open, sprinkle over the rock sugar and kewra water if using, fluff gently with a fork, and top with the reserved fried nuts and fruit. Serve hot.
Waza tips:
- Parboil the rice deliberately short of done — it finishes in the syrup, and fully cooked rice turns to pudding at the dum stage.
- Fold, never stir, once the sugar goes in; sugar makes hot rice fragile and vigorous mixing breaks every grain.
- Fry the raisins last and briefly — they balloon and colour in seconds.
- A dough-sealed lid is not theatre: trapping the steam is what makes the grains finish separate and glossy.
Common mistakes:
- Fully cooking the rice before adding the syrup, which guarantees a sticky, broken result
- Stirring the pot after sweetening instead of folding once and sealing
- Burning the ghee-fried fruit by adding everything to the pan at once
- Using so much sugar that the pulao can only be eaten as dessert (unless that is the intent)
At home: A heavy Dutch oven with foil under the lid replaces the dough seal convincingly. Cashews and pistachios are common modern additions if dried dates or melon seeds are hard to find. Start with the lower sugar quantity and adjust — served alongside savoury dishes, less sweetness reads better to most modern palates.
Serving: Serve hot as the festive rice of a vegetarian spread, alongside a sharp or spicy counterpoint such as dum aloo or chaman qaliya; it also stands alone as a sweet course.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Pulao: What goes in
chunks.text:
The colour and scent come from saffron. Kashmir's saffron is grown mainly around Pampore, which produces about 90% of India's crop (Wikipedia).
A published Kashmiri recipe for modur polav adds almonds, raisins, dried dates, dried coconut and melon seeds, with black and green cardamom, peppercorns, cinnamon, cassia leaves, cloves and fresh ginger, and finishes the rice with sugar candy and kewra. It allows a yellow food colour in place of saffron, and uses three parts sugar to two of rice (De Leij: Culinary Art of Kashmir). Our recipe below follows its method with much less sugar.

sources.label: De Leij: Culinary Art of Kashmir

chunks.title: Kashmiri Pulao: Who makes it
chunks.text: Modur pulav is cooked for special occasions in both Kashmiri Pandit and Kashmiri Muslim homes; our guide to Kashmiri sweets and desserts gives the sources. Kashmir's everyday rice, the base of most meals and of the Wazwan trami, is plain.

chunks.title: Lavasa (Lavas / Lavasa)
chunks.text:
Lavasa (Lavas / Lavasa) is on Wazwan Way under Bakery. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
Thin, soft baked unleavened flatbread.
Lavas is a thin, puffed unleavened flatbread baked in a tandoor, commonly wrapped around barbecue or harissa.
Lavas is Kashmir's utility bread and its wrap: the same sheet that accompanies morning noon chai is the jacket for masala tsot and the plate-and-napkin for charcoal-grilled tujji at Khayam Chowk. Kandur-culture accounts single out its baking position — laid on the tandoor floor so it cooks through gently without crisping — as the technique that separates it from every other bread in the oven. Its lineage connects to the wider lavash family of Persia and Central Asia, one of many Persian threads in Kashmiri food culture, though the Kashmiri loaf is smaller, softer and leavened. Both communities of the Valley eat it without variation.
Lavas has deep Central Asian roots. It acts as the primary wrap for street foods (Tujji) and winter Harissa in the valley.
Tip: Use it to scoop up hot Harissa or wrapped around skewered Tujji kababs.

chunks.title: Recipe: Lavasa
chunks.text:
Recipe for Lavasa, as written on Wazwan Way.
Lavas is the kandur's thin, soft, pale flatbread — pliable enough to fold around anything, mild enough to carry butter and jam at breakfast or a rack of street-side tujji at night. Unlike girda it is baked on the floor of the tandoor rather than slapped to its wall, which keeps it soft and white rather than blistered and brown.
Serves 8 flatbreads. Prep 25 min. Cook 18 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 300 g all-purpose flour (maida), plus extra for dusting
- 1 tsp instant yeast
- 1 tsp sugar
- 3/4 tsp salt
- 180–200 ml lukewarm water, as needed
- 1 tsp neutral oil, for the bowl
- Small bowl of water, for brushing before cooking
Method:
1. Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt. Add water gradually and knead 7–8 minutes to a smooth, medium-soft dough — softer than a chapati dough, firmer than a batter-slack naan dough.
2. Oil the dough lightly, cover, and prove in a warm place about 1 hour, until doubled.
3. Divide into 8 balls and rest 10 minutes under a cloth so they roll without springing back.
4. On a floured surface, roll each ball into a thin round or oval, 2–3 mm thick and about 20 cm across. Thinness matters more than shape.
5. In the tandoor, lavas is laid on the oven floor for under a minute per side until just cooked and still pale. At home: heat a heavy tawa or cast-iron pan over medium-high heat until water beads and skitters on it.
6. Brush one face of the rolled bread lightly with water and press that wet side down onto the hot tawa — the water glues it to the metal, tandoor-style, so it cooks flat without cushioning air.
7. Cook 40–60 seconds until the top surface dulls and bubbles rise, then release with a spatula and finish the second side 20–30 seconds — either flipped in the pan or kissed briefly over an open flame. Pull it while still soft and pale, with only faint freckles of colour.
8. Stack immediately inside a folded cloth so the breads steam each other soft. Repeat with the rest.
Waza tips:
- Pale is correct: a browned, crisped lavas has been overcooked and will crack when you try to roll it.
- The wet-side-down trick on the tawa is the honest home substitute for the tandoor floor — do not skip it.
- Keep the stack wrapped in cloth from the first bread; lavas dries out in minutes uncovered.
- Roll thinner than instinct suggests — it thickens as it puffs and relaxes.
Common mistakes:
- Chasing colour — golden-brown spots mean it is already on its way to becoming a cracker.
- Skipping the cloth wrap, which is what actually finishes the bread's softness.
- Rolling on a heavily floured board so the surface flour scorches on the tawa and tastes bitter.
- Under-proving the dough, which gives a dense, bready sheet instead of a supple wrap.
At home: The tandoor-floor bake translates better to a stovetop tawa than to a home oven: an oven's ambient dry heat browns and stiffens the bread before it finishes, while a hot cast-iron surface with the water-brushed face stuck to it mimics the gentle conductive bake that keeps lavas soft and white. If you must use an oven, bake on a preheated steel at 230°C for barely 60–90 seconds and pull it before it colours. Expect home lavas to be slightly thicker than the kandur's, whose long paddle and practiced stretch get it thinner than a rolling pin easily will.
Serving: At breakfast, spread with butter or jam beside noon chai. Its great second life is on the street: rolled around spiced white peas as masala tsot, or wrapped around charcoal tujji with radish chutney.

chunks.title: Marchhwangan Korma (Marchwangan Korma)
chunks.text:
Marchhwangan Korma (Marchwangan Korma) is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: High. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim. It is one of the seven dishes commonly listed as essential to a Wazwan. In the feast: the gravies.
An intensely spiced korma from the Wazwan tradition.
Marchwangan Korma is among the fiercer dishes in the Wazwan family, with a hot, dark-red gravy of Kashmiri chillies.
Marchwangan Korma is listed among the mandatory seven dishes of the Wazwan in Wikipedia's account of the feast, where it plays the role of the outright fiery course against the gentler yakhni and Aab Gosht. Unlike the Mughlai kormas its name evokes, it uses no nut pastes and in many renditions no yogurt either (Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes includes it) — the gravy is chilli paste, fat and reduced meat juices, with whole garam-masala aromatics underneath. Several published recipes note the absence of onion and garlic while others include shallot or garlic pastes, a genuine divergence between waza practice and home kitchens that we flag rather than settle. A sour note from tamarind water appears in a number of versions and is one of the dish's quieter signatures.
Marchwangan korma is mutton braised in a gravy made mostly with Kashmiri red chillies. Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes describes it as "meat cooked with spices and yogurt and mostly using Kashmiri red chillies and hot in taste", and Outlook India calls it "a fiery hot mutton cooked with Kashmiri red chilli". It is one of the seven dishes Wikipedia lists as a must at a Wazwan. The sources describe more than one version: Wikipedia's Wazwan article describes it there as chicken in a spicy browned-onion sauce, and its list of Kashmiri dishes has a chicken version, kokur martsawangan kormeh, alongside the mutton one. The name is also written marchhwangan.
Tip: Best for travelers who enjoy assertive spice. If you are sensitive to heat, try Daniwal Korma or Aab Gosht first.
Marchwangan korma: mutton braised in a hot, dark-red gravy of Kashmiri red chillies, the last hot dish of the Wazwan. Its history, where to eat it, recipe.

chunks.title: Recipe: Marchhwangan Korma
chunks.text:
Recipe for Marchhwangan Korma, as written on Wazwan Way.
Marchwangan korma as a waza cooks it: mutton boiled until tender, fried in mustard oil and ghee with garlic and whole spices, cooked down in its own stock with chilli water until the pot is nearly dry, and finished with a great deal of Kashmiri chilli powder. Kashmiri chilli is mild; the heat comes from how much of it goes in.
Serves 4–6. Prep 28 min. Cook 1 h 8 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 1 kg mutton
- 15–20 dried red chillies and water, for the chilli water
- 2 tbsp garlic paste
- 2–3 small pieces of cinnamon
- 4–5 green cardamom pods
- 5–6 cloves
- Salt, to taste
- 120 ml (½ cup) mustard oil
- 3 tbsp ghee
- The stock from boiling the mutton, as needed
- 1½ tsp turmeric powder
- 2 tbsp coriander powder
- 1 tsp dry ginger powder
- 1 tsp fennel powder
- 3–4 tbsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, to taste
Method:
1. Make the chilli water: soak the dried chillies, grind them with a little water, stir in more water and strain.
2. Wash the mutton and boil it until tender. Strain it and keep the stock.
3. Heat the mustard oil and ghee in a wide pot. Add the cooked mutton, garlic paste, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves and salt, and fry well until the mutton is coated.
4. Pour in the stock and the chilli water, then add the turmeric, coriander, dry ginger and fennel powders.
5. Cook, frying as the liquid goes, until the stock has reduced completely and the spices have gone into the meat.
6. Add the Kashmiri chilli powder and fry for a few minutes more, until the korma is deep red and the oil begins to separate.
Waza tips:
- The chilli goes in twice: as chilli water with the stock, and as chilli powder fried in at the end.
- Reduce the stock completely before the chilli powder goes in; the korma is fried at the end, not simmered.
- It is ready when it is deep red and the oil has begun to separate.
Common mistakes:
- Using a hot chilli powder in these quantities. The recipe is written for Kashmiri chilli, which is mild.
- Leaving stock in the pot. The korma is fried nearly dry before the chilli powder goes in.
At home: Adjust the chilli powder to the heat you want. Home versions differ from the waza's: one fries the mutton in smoked mustard oil and adds fried-shallot paste and dried mint.
Serving: At home, pair with plain rice and a cooling yogurt chutney.

chunks.title: Marchhwangan Korma: The name
chunks.text: In Kashmiri, marʦ is a red chilli, and Grierson's dictionary lists under it -wã̄gan-āra, "a chain or string of red chillis, dried and kept for winter use" (Grierson). Korma, from qormā, means braising: meat or vegetables braised with yogurt, water or stock (Wikipedia). Lamb and chicken kormas are common in the Wazwan (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: Marchhwangan Korma: How hot it is
chunks.text: Kashmiri chilli itself is mild, rated at 1,000–2,000 Scoville heat units and valued for the deep red colour it gives food (Wikipedia). Marchwangan korma uses a great deal of it and is described as hot (Wikipedia; Outlook India). How hot depends on the kitchen: India's Consumer Education and Research Centre put two branded "Kashmiri chilli" powders at 48,000 and 60,000 SHU (Wikipedia). If you're sensitive to heat, ask before you order. Is Kashmiri food spicy? covers the rest of the menu.

chunks.title: Marchhwangan Korma: Its place in the feast
chunks.text: In Outlook India's account of the Wazwan's order, marchwangan korma follows rista, rogan josh and daniwal korma, and comes before aab gosht, yakhni and gushtaba. The mutton dishes are eaten with rice or flat bread (Outlook India).

chunks.title: Masala Tsot (Masala Tsot / Masale Tsot)
chunks.text:
Masala Tsot (Masala Tsot / Masale Tsot) is on Wazwan Way under Street Food. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: High. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim.
Masala tsot is a Kashmiri street wrap: a soft lavasa spread with radish-and-onion chutney and a thick paste of boiled white peas, then rolled. This recipe uses no oil.
Masala tsot is consistently listed among the Valley's essential street foods, a working person's breakfast and a schoolyard favourite, prized for being cheap, filling and portable. It is a dish of assembly rather than cheffery — the kandur supplies the lavas, the vendor supplies the pea mash simmering in a deg and a bucket of radish chutney — which is why it never migrated into restaurant menus in its street form. Romy Gill documented a version in her Kashmir-to-Ladakh cookbook, bringing the wrap to an international audience. It has no meaningful sectarian split; it is simply what Srinagar eats on the move.

chunks.title: Recipe: Masala Tsot
chunks.text:
Recipe for Masala Tsot, as written on Wazwan Way.
Masala tsot is a Kashmiri street wrap: a soft lavasa spread with radish-and-onion chutney and a thick paste of boiled white peas, then rolled. This recipe uses no oil.
Serves 4. Prep 25 min. Cook 38 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- For the pea paste: 1 cup dried white peas (safed matar)
- Salt, to taste
- Water, for boiling
- For the chutney: 1 cup grated radish (mooli)
- ½ cup finely chopped onion
- 1–2 green chillies, finely chopped
- 1 tsp cumin seeds
- ½ tsp red chilli powder
- A handful of fresh coriander
- 2–3 tbsp yogurt
- Salt, to taste
- To assemble: Kashmiri lavasa or any soft roti
Method:
1. Rinse the peas and soak them overnight.
2. Drain them and pressure-cook with a pinch of salt and enough water until soft. Dry off any water that is left and mash the peas to a smooth, thick paste.
3. For the chutney, mix the grated radish, onion and green chillies with the salt, cumin, chilli powder, coriander and yogurt.
4. Lay a lavasa flat and spread it generously with chutney, then with a layer of the pea paste. Add another spoonful of chutney on top if you like it hot.
5. Roll it up tightly and serve at once.
Tips:
- Dry the cooked peas well before mashing, so the paste is thick.
- Serve as soon as it is rolled.
Serving: Serve as a standalone street-style breakfast or afternoon snack, with noon chai in winter. It pairs naturally with other Srinagar street food — nader monje on the side, halwa paratha after.

chunks.title: Methi Maaz
chunks.text:
Methi Maaz is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: High. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim. In the feast: on the trami.
A bold Wazwan preparation of tripe cooked with spices and dried fenugreek leaves.
Methi Maaz is one of the early ceremonial meat dishes served in Wazwan, known for its deep savory character and distinct fenugreek aroma. It brings a more rustic, traditional edge to the feast and is especially appreciated by diners who enjoy strong Kashmiri flavors.
Methi Maaz is traditionally among the first meat dishes served on the Wazwan trami — a sharp, bitter-edged opener before the procession of kebabs and gravies. The honest version of its story includes the offal: the classical preparation uses lamb tripe, stomach and intestine, boiled clean and then finely chopped by the waza with a heavy knife on a wooden block, a nose-to-tail thrift dish elevated into ceremony. It also appears as a garnish tradition on winter harissa in old Srinagar. Many contemporary home and restaurant versions substitute boneless mutton or keema for the offal — a legitimate evolution, but a substitution, and menus are not always candid about which one you're getting. The name is simply its two ingredients: methi (fenugreek) and maaz (meat).
Methi Maaz serves as one of the most vital introductory courses in a traditional Wazwan, establishing the complex flavor profile of the feast early on. Historically, this dish was developed to utilize every part of the sheep, transforming the tripe and intestines into a delicacy through the masterful use of dried fenugreek leaves (methi) and intense spices. The distinct, earthy bitterness of the fenugreek cuts through the richness of the meat, making it an essential palate-awakening dish that has been passed down through generations of Wazas.
Tip: This is a more traditional and intense dish than the best-known Wazwan staples, so try it if you want to taste something closer to the deeper ceremonial roots of the feast.
Methi maaz: tripe cooked with dried fenugreek leaves and spices, served early in the Wazwan with the tabak maaz. Its history, where to eat it and the recipe.

chunks.title: Recipe: Methi Maaz
chunks.text:
Recipe for Methi Maaz, as written on Wazwan Way.
Methi maaz as a waza cooks it: the sheep's stomach, tripe and intestines, cleaned, boiled tender and chopped small, then simmered in mutton stock with ghee, chilli water, garlic and a few spices until the gravy is thick. Dried fenugreek leaves, the methi of the name, go in at the end.
Serves 4–6 (small Wazwan-style portions). Prep 38 min. Cook 1 h 10 min. Level: Involved.
Ingredients:
- 500 g sheep's stomach, tripe and intestines, thoroughly cleaned
- 500 ml (2 cups) mutton stock
- 3 tbsp ghee, plus a little to finish
- 1 tsp dry ginger powder
- 1 tbsp garlic paste
- ½ tsp turmeric powder
- 120 ml (½ cup) chilli water: dried red chillies soaked, ground with a little water, thinned with more water and strained
- 1 small piece of cinnamon
- 3–4 green cardamom pods
- Salt, to taste
- Dried fenugreek leaves (methi), to finish
Method:
1. Clean the stomach, tripe and intestines thoroughly, then boil them until tender.
2. Drain and chop into small pieces.
3. Heat the ghee in a pot and add the cinnamon, cardamom, dry ginger, garlic paste, turmeric and chilli water.
4. Add the chopped offal and the stock.
5. Simmer on a low heat until the flavours are absorbed and the gravy has thickened.
6. Add the dried fenugreek leaves and finish with a little ghee.
Waza tips:
- Boil the offal until it is tender before chopping it, and chop it small.
- Cook it on a low heat until the gravy thickens.
- The dried fenugreek leaves go in last.
Common mistakes:
- Chopping the offal before it is tender.
- Rushing the simmer; the gravy should be thick.
At home: A butcher will usually clean the tripe and intestines for you; wash them again thoroughly before the first boil.
Serving: On the Wazwan trami it is served early and sparingly, alongside kebab and tabak maaz over rice. In winter Srinagar it famously rides on top of a plate of harissa. At home, treat it as a strong side to rice and a mild gravy dish.
About this recipe: We have no measured amount for the dried fenugreek leaves; add them to taste.

chunks.title: Muji Chetin (Muji Chetein)
chunks.text:
Muji Chetin (Muji Chetein) is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Medium. Tradition: Shared (variants noted). In the feast: on the trami.
A radish and walnut chutney that adds crunch and pungency to the feast.
Muji Chetin is a classic Kashmiri accompaniment made with radish and walnut, prized for the freshness and texture it brings next to richer Wazwan gravies.
Chutneys (chetein) are the sharp punctuation of a Kashmiri meal, and the radish version is among the most common, appearing at big dinners and everyday home meals alike. The 2006 booklet reference describes it as a side dish and appetiser served by the spoonful at large feasts. It belongs to both Pandit and Muslim tables; several sources describe radish chutney as a fixture at wedding feasts. Its pairing logic is seasonal and practical — winter radish is abundant exactly when the heaviest meat cooking happens.
Muji Chetin is a beloved, traditional Kashmiri accompaniment that pairs the sharp, peppery bite of raw radish with the earthy richness of local walnuts. Walnuts have grown abundantly in Kashmir for millennia and are deeply woven into the local diet. This chutney was historically crafted to provide a necessary textural crunch and a cleansing pungency alongside the soft, slow-cooked meats of the Wazwan. The interplay of the bitter radish, creamy walnut, and tangy yogurt reflects the sophisticated flavor-balancing techniques inherent in historic Kashmiri cooking.
Tip: Try a little with richer meat dishes to understand how condiments balance the structure of a Kashmiri feast.

chunks.title: Recipe: Muji Chetin
chunks.text:
Recipe for Muji Chetin, as written on Wazwan Way.
Muji Chetein is grated winter radish folded through thick curd with chilli and caraway — cold, sharp and cooling all at once. It takes minutes to make and does the quiet, essential work of cutting through Kashmir's rich meat and oil-heavy gravies.
Serves 6 (as a condiment). Prep 15 min. Level: Easy.
Ingredients:
- 250 g white winter radish (mooli/daikon), peeled
- 250 g thick fresh curd (yogurt), lightly whisked
- 0.5 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder
- 0.5 tsp salt
- 0.5 tsp sugar
- 1 pinch caraway seeds (shahi zeera)
- 2-3 green chillies, deseeded and finely chopped
- 2 tbsp walnuts, toasted and roughly crushed (optional)
Method:
1. Grate the radish on the coarse side of a grater, then squeeze it firmly in your hands or a clean cloth to press out the excess water — this single step decides whether the chutney is creamy or watery.
2. Whisk the curd smooth in a serving bowl with the salt, sugar, chilli powder and caraway seeds.
3. Fold in the grated radish (and crushed walnuts, if using) until evenly combined.
4. Scatter the chopped green chillies over the top, chill briefly, and serve cold the same day — the radish sharpens and weeps liquid as it sits.
Waza tips:
- Squeeze the radish harder than feels necessary; feast cooks wring it almost dry so the chetein holds its body on the trami.
- Use fresh, not sour, curd — the radish supplies the bite; the curd should supply calm.
- Make it last, closest to serving. This is a chutney with a shelf life measured in hours, not days.
Common mistakes:
- Skipping the squeeze, producing a thin, weepy raita rather than a chutney
- Making it hours ahead, by which time the radish has turned the curd watery and over-sharp
- Using sour curd that fights the radish instead of tempering it
At home: Daikon is a perfect substitute for Kashmiri muj, and Greek-style yogurt thinned slightly stands in well for hung curd. If raw radish reads too pungent, salt the gratings for ten minutes before squeezing — it mellows noticeably.
Serving: A spoonful per person alongside rice and rich gravies — it is a natural partner to Rogan Josh, Machh or Muj Gaad, echoing the same radish in a cold register.

chunks.title: Muji Chetin: Doon chetin, the walnut chutney
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Muji Chetin page: Doon chetin, the walnut chutney.
The walnut chutney served at Kashmiri weddings has radish in it too.
1 cup of soaked walnuts is chopped fine. Half a radish, half an onion and 3–4 green chillies are ground to a fine paste. ½ cup of thick curd is whisked with a little water until smooth, and the walnuts, the paste, salt and ½ tbsp cumin seeds are stirred in.

chunks.title: Muji Chetin: Gande chetin, the onion chutney
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Muji Chetin page: Gande chetin, the onion chutney.
The onion chutney of the feast is sharp, hot and sour. This quantity serves six to eight.
4 large onions are sliced thin and 8–10 green chillies chopped fine. Both are washed well in a large bowl, strained and squeezed dry. ¼ cup vinegar, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 tbsp red chilli powder and 1–1½ tsp salt are massaged in by hand, and the chutney rests for 15–20 minutes before it is served. A home version adds fresh coriander and mint.

chunks.title: Tujji (Tujji / Seekh Tujj)
chunks.text:
Tujji (Tujji / Seekh Tujj) is on Wazwan Way under Street Food. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: Medium. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim.
Tujji — the Kashmiri word for a skewer — is Srinagar's definitive street barbecue: small flattened pieces of mutton in a deep-red fennel-and-chilli marinade, threaded tight and grilled over glowing charcoal, then bundled into a soft lavas with radish chutney. On winter evenings, Khayam Chowk becomes a corridor of smoke and embers devoted to almost nothing else.
Tujji is street food with a geography: the lane of grill shops at Khayam Chowk in Srinagar — places like Gareeb Nawaz, run by the same families for decades — is where the dish's reputation was made, drawing crowds from across the city between sunset and late evening. Traditionally the meat is threaded on thin twigs of willow, a tree woven through Kashmiri material culture, though steel seekhs now dominate commercially. The serving ritual is fixed: hot skewers stripped into a fold of lavas with a battery of chutneys, eaten standing in the cold. One popular article traces tujji to Mughal royal kitchens, but that claim is uncorroborated elsewhere and is best treated as folklore; what is well documented is its standing as the Valley's favourite winter street food.

chunks.title: Recipe: Tujji
chunks.text:
Recipe for Tujji, as written on Wazwan Way.
Tujji — the Kashmiri word for a skewer — is Srinagar's definitive street barbecue: small flattened pieces of mutton in a deep-red fennel-and-chilli marinade, threaded tight and grilled over glowing charcoal, then bundled into a soft lavas with radish chutney. On winter evenings, Khayam Chowk becomes a corridor of smoke and embers devoted to almost nothing else.
Serves 4 (about 8 skewers). Prep 35 min. Cook 20 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 750 g boneless mutton (leg or shoulder), cut into small pieces about 3 cm across and lightly flattened
- 150 g thick plain curd, whisked (some Khayam stalls marinate without curd)
- 2 tbsp mustard oil
- 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste
- 1 tbsp Kashmiri red chilli powder (deep colour, moderate heat)
- 2 tsp fennel powder (saunf — the signature Kashmiri note)
- 1 tsp ground black pepper
- 1/2 tsp garam masala (or a pinch each of ground cinnamon, cardamom, clove and nutmeg)
- 1 tsp salt, or to taste
- 1 tsp lemon juice
- 1 tbsp raw papaya paste (optional tenderiser for tougher cuts)
- Ghee or mustard oil, for basting
- 8 thin skewers — traditionally stripped willow twigs, soaked 30 minutes; metal seekhs work
Method:
1. Whisk the curd with the mustard oil, ginger-garlic paste, chilli powder, fennel, pepper, garam masala, salt, lemon juice and papaya paste (if using) into a thick, brick-red marinade.
2. Massage the marinade into the flattened mutton pieces. Cover and refrigerate at least 4 hours, ideally overnight — street tujji gets its depth from a long marinade, and short-marinated meat tastes of surface spice only.
3. Light charcoal and let it burn down to glowing embers coated in grey ash — tujji is grilled over embers, never over flame.
4. Thread the meat snugly onto the skewers, pieces touching, so the meat stays juicy and the skewer looks like one ribbon of meat.
5. Grill close over the embers, turning every 2–3 minutes and fanning the coals, until the meat is browned at the edges with charred flecks and cooked through — roughly 15–20 minutes depending on the fire. Baste once or twice with ghee or mustard oil as it grills.
6. Rest the skewers 2–3 minutes off the heat.
7. Serve street-style: lay a warm lavas on the plate, strip the meat from the skewers onto it, add a spoonful of radish-curd chutney and a squeeze of lemon, and roll.
Waza tips:
- Embers, not flames — the grey-ashed coal stage is when the grilling starts; flames blacken the marinade before the meat cooks.
- Fennel powder is what makes it taste of Kashmir rather than of a generic seekh; do not substitute it away.
- Thread the pieces tight against each other; gaps let the edges dry out over the coals.
- Small, flattened pieces are the Khayam signature — big cubes stay raw inside at street-grill pace.
Common mistakes:
- Grilling over live flame, which chars the chilli to bitterness while the centre stays raw.
- A one-hour marinade — the colour will be there but the flavour will not.
- Using large cubes seekh-kebab style instead of small flattened pieces, changing the cook time and texture entirely.
- Skipping the resting bread-and-chutney service; dry tujji on a plate misses half the dish.
At home: Without a charcoal sigri, the best home translation is a heavy grill pan or cast-iron skillet ripping hot, with the skewered meat seared and turned exactly as over coals, finished with a 30-second smoke: place a piece of lit charcoal in a small steel bowl among the cooked skewers, spoon ghee over it, and cover for a minute (the dhungar method). An oven broiler at maximum with skewers on the top rack, turned twice, also works — expect less char and smoke than Khayam Chowk delivers. Chicken can substitute for mutton with the marinade unchanged and 10–12 minutes of cooking.
Serving: Serve rolled in warm lavas with radish-and-curd chutney (mujj chetin) and green chutney — the Khayam Chowk street format. As a starter, pile the skewers over sliced onion with lemon wedges and the same chutneys.

chunks.title: Nadru Gaad
chunks.text:
Nadru Gaad is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: Medium. Tradition: Kashmiri Pandit.
Kashmiri fish curry cooked with lotus stems.
Nadru Gaad pairs tender lake fish with fresh lotus stem slices, cooked together in a rich spice-infused red gravy.
Both halves of this dish come out of the same water: gaad from the lakes and rivers, nadru from the lake beds beneath them, which gives the pairing an easy logic Kashmiris have cooked by for generations, particularly in Pandit households through winter and on Gaada Batta. The nadru simmers until just tender while keeping its crunch, the fried fish holds its shape in the gravy, and the chilli-and-fennel base ties them together. It ranks among the most loved of all Pandit fish preparations.
Lotus stems (Nadru) harvested from Dal and Anchar lakes have been eaten in Kashmir since ancient times. Pairing them with local fish represents the traditional lakeside diet of the valley.
Tip: A great local specialty. The lotus stems absorb the delicious fish gravy and become extremely flavorful.

chunks.title: Recipe: Nadru Gaad
chunks.text:
Recipe for Nadru Gaad, as written on Wazwan Way.
Fried freshwater fish and crescent slices of lotus stem simmered together in a red, fennel-deep gravy — the lake's fish and the lake's vegetable in one winter pot. Nadru gaad is lake cooking, literally.
Serves 4. Prep 25 min. Cook 45 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 600 g firm freshwater fish steaks (carp or trout), patted dry
- 250 g lotus stem (nadru), scrubbed, in diagonal slices
- 6 tbsp mustard oil
- 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
- 1 tbsp fennel powder
- 1 tsp dry ginger powder (sonth)
- 1/2 tsp turmeric, plus a pinch for the fish
- 1 pinch asafoetida
- Salt to taste
- 550 ml hot water
Method:
1. Rub the fish with salt and a pinch of turmeric; rest 10 minutes.
2. Wash the nadru slices thoroughly, checking the channels for grit.
3. Heat the mustard oil to smoking in a wide pan and fry the fish golden on both sides; lift out gently.
4. In the same oil, fry the nadru 3-4 minutes until the edges colour, and set aside.
5. Add the asafoetida, then the chilli powder slurried in water, stirring until the oil runs red; add turmeric, fennel, sonth and salt.
6. Add the hot water and the nadru and simmer, covered, for 15 minutes until the stem is nearly tender.
7. Return the fish, spoon gravy over, and simmer gently, unstirred, for 8 minutes. Rest briefly and serve.
Waza tips:
- Grit hides in nadru's channels — wash like you mean it.
- Fish and nadru finish at different speeds; stagger them exactly as the steps say.
Common mistakes:
- Simmering the fish from the start — it goes in last and barely cooks.
- Letting the nadru soften fully; it should keep a clean bite against the fish.
At home: Frozen lotus stem and trout or tilapia steaks reproduce the dish faithfully outside Kashmir.
Serving: Serve over steamed rice with the gravy poured generously.

chunks.title: Nadru Yakhni
chunks.text:
Nadru Yakhni is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
Lotus stem cooked in a soothing yogurt and fennel curry.
Nadru Yakhni is a comforting vegetarian Kashmiri dish built on lotus stem slices, yogurt, fennel, and warming spices that create a balanced, aromatic gravy.
Nadru Yakhni is one of the signature dishes of the Kashmiri Pandit kitchen, cooked without onion, garlic or tomato, and it remains a fixture at Pandit feasts and fast-adjacent vegetarian meals; Kashmiri Muslim households cook and love it too, so it should not be read as exclusively Pandit property. Its cultural weight comes from the lotus stem itself: nadru is harvested from the valley's lakes and carries strong associations with home for the Kashmiri diaspora. The yakhni treatment — yogurt, fennel, sonth, no turmeric or chilli — marks it as part of the same white-gravy family as the mutton original, and it is one of the most widely documented Kashmiri vegetarian recipes, appearing everywhere from community cookbooks to Saveur.
The lotus stem, or Nadru, has been an integral part of the Kashmiri diet for centuries, deeply intertwined with the region's abundant lakes. Nadru Yakhni represents a harmonious blend of local agriculture and traditional cooking techniques. The yogurt-based Yakhni gravy itself has ancient origins in the valley, originally used to preserve and flavor meats and vegetables during harsh winters. Over generations, this comforting, fennel-scented vegetarian dish has become a beloved staple in both Kashmiri Pandit and Muslim households, celebrating the unique aquatic bounty of the valley.
Tip: A great pick for vegetarians seeking something authentically local rather than generic North Indian options.

chunks.title: Recipe: Nadru Yakhni
chunks.text:
Recipe for Nadru Yakhni, as written on Wazwan Way.
Crisp-tender rounds of lotus stem simmered in a churned yogurt gravy scented with fennel and dried ginger. Nadru Yakhni takes the vegetable Kashmir loves most — pulled from the Dal and Anchar lakes — and treats it with the same white-gravy reverence usually reserved for mutton.
Serves 4. Prep 20 min. Cook 45 min. Level: Easy.
Ingredients:
- 500 g lotus stem (nadru), about 2–3 stems
- 400 g full-fat yogurt, whisked smooth
- 3 tbsp mustard oil
- 1 tsp cumin seeds
- 3 cloves
- 3 green cardamom pods, lightly crushed
- 1 black cardamom pod
- 1 small piece cinnamon (about 2 cm)
- 2 tsp fennel powder
- 1 tsp dried ginger powder (sonth)
- 1 generous pinch asafoetida (hing)
- Salt to taste, about 1.5 tsp
- 1/2 tsp crushed dried mint leaves (optional, to finish)
Method:
1. Scrape the lotus stems well, trim the ends and slice diagonally into rounds about 1 cm thick. Wash thoroughly in several changes of water, working your fingers into the hollow channels — mud hides there, and one gritty piece ruins the pot.
2. Boil the sliced nadru in about 750 ml of lightly salted water for 15–20 minutes, until tender but still holding a slight bite at the centre. Do not cook it to mush. Reserve the cooking water.
3. Whisk the yogurt with the fennel powder and dried ginger powder until completely smooth, then thin it with a ladle or two of the warm nadru cooking water.
4. Heat the mustard oil in a heavy pan until its rawness cooks off, then take it briefly off the heat and add the cumin, cloves, cinnamon, both cardamoms and the asafoetida. Let them crackle gently for a few seconds.
5. Pour in the yogurt mixture and return the pan to medium heat, stirring continuously in one direction until it comes to a boil and no longer threatens to split.
6. Add the boiled nadru along with enough of the reserved cooking water to make a pourable gravy. Season with salt and simmer gently, uncovered, for 10–15 minutes, until the gravy thickens slightly and a thin sheen of oil shows at the edge.
7. Crush the dried mint between your palms over the pot, if using, stir once and serve hot.
Waza tips:
- Buy lotus stems that feel heavy and snap cleanly; limp, dark stems turn fibrous when cooked.
- The nadru should finish cooking in the yogurt gravy, not before it — pull the boil slightly early so the last 10 minutes of simmering marry the two.
- Full-fat, just-set yogurt gives the gravy body; sour or watery curd makes a thin, aggressive yakhni.
- Keep the flame low once the yogurt is in. This dish is coaxed, never boiled hard.
Common mistakes:
- Under-washing the stems and serving grit in the gravy — the most common and least forgivable error.
- Overboiling the nadru until it collapses; it should keep a gentle crunch.
- Adding the yogurt to a screaming-hot pan without stirring, causing it to curdle instantly.
- Reaching for turmeric out of habit — the gravy must stay white.
At home: Frozen or vacuum-packed lotus stem from Indian and East Asian grocers works well — rinse thoroughly and reduce the first boil to around 10 minutes. A pressure cooker (one whistle) can replace the initial boil. If fresh nadru is unavailable entirely, the same gravy takes well to raw banana or arbi, though the dish then loses its name.
Serving: Serve with plain steamed rice, ideally alongside a dry vegetable or a chutney for contrast. In Pandit festive meals it often sits beside Dum Aloo and Chaman.

chunks.title: Nadur Monji (Nadur Monje)
chunks.text:
Nadur Monji (Nadur Monje) is on Wazwan Way under Street Food. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Medium. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
Batons of lotus stem in a thin, chilli-flecked rice-flour crust, deep-fried until shatteringly crisp outside and juicy-crunchy within. Nadru Monje is Kashmir's best-loved street snack — the thing you eat hot from a paper cone on a cold afternoon.
Lotus stem (nadru) harvested from Dal and Anchar lakes is one of Kashmir's signature ingredients, and monje are its most democratic form: fried-to-order street food rather than feast cooking. Vendors' carts selling nadru monje are a familiar sight around Srinagar, notably near the Hazratbal shrine, and the snack is beloved across both communities — a rare Kashmiri deep-fried street food in a cuisine dominated by slow gravies. The classic coating is rice flour (not besan alone), seasoned with Kashmiri chilli and salt; the traditional partner is a sharp walnut (doon) chutney.

chunks.title: Recipe: Nadur Monji
chunks.text:
Recipe for Nadur Monji, as written on Wazwan Way.
Batons of lotus stem in a thin, chilli-flecked rice-flour crust, deep-fried until shatteringly crisp outside and juicy-crunchy within. Nadru Monje is Kashmir's best-loved street snack — the thing you eat hot from a paper cone on a cold afternoon.
Serves 4 as a snack. Prep 20 min. Cook 23 min. Level: Easy.
Ingredients:
- 400 g lotus stem (nadru), scrubbed, peeled and cut into finger-length batons or thick diagonal slices
- 100 g rice flour
- 2 tbsp gram flour (besan) — optional, helps the crust cling
- 2 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder
- 1/2 tsp carom seeds (ajwain) or cumin seeds
- 1/4 tsp asafoetida (hing) — optional
- 1 tsp salt, or to taste
- About 100-120 ml water, added little by little
- Oil for deep-frying (mustard oil is traditional)
Method:
1. Clean the lotus stems fastidiously: scrape the skin, slice open lengthwise if thick, and wash under running water, working a finger or brush through the channels — mud hides inside them. Drain well.
2. In a bowl, toss the drained nadru with the rice flour, besan (if using), chilli powder, carom seeds, asafoetida and salt so every piece is dusted.
3. Sprinkle in the water a little at a time, turning with your hands, until the flour just clings to the wet pieces as a thin, rough coating — a shaggy coat, not a pourable batter.
4. Heat the oil in a kadhai to medium-hot (a test piece should rise steadily with a lively sizzle). If using mustard oil, let it smoke once first, then settle back to frying temperature.
5. Fry the coated pieces in batches, without crowding, turning occasionally, until deep golden and audibly crisp — roughly 6-8 minutes per batch. The stem inside should stay slightly crunchy; that contrast is the point.
6. Drain on paper and serve immediately, scattered with a pinch of chilli powder or chaat masala if you like.
Waza tips:
- Rice flour, not besan, is what gives street-style monje their glassy crunch — besan is only a binder here, if used at all.
- Keep the coating thin; a thick batter turns the fritters into pakoras and hides the lotus stem's texture.
- Fry at a steady medium heat — too hot and the crust browns before the stem loses its rawness.
- Serve within minutes. Monje are street food precisely because they don't wait.
Common mistakes:
- Half-hearted washing, which leaves grit in the stem's channels — the one unforgivable failure.
- Making a thick, wet batter instead of a thin clinging coat.
- Slicing the stem paper-thin so it turns leathery, or so thick it stays raw at the core.
- Letting fried monje sit and steam themselves soft before serving.
At home: Vacuum-packed or frozen lotus stem from Asian groceries works — thaw, rinse and dry well before coating. If you find cleaning whole stems tedious, buy pre-sliced rings. Any neutral oil substitutes for mustard oil at a small cost in flavour. An air-fryer version (brushed with oil, 200°C) crisps acceptably but never quite matches the deep-fried original.
Serving: Eat hot as a snack with walnut (doon) chutney, onion chutney or a plain green-chilli chutney, ideally with noon chai or kahwa. They also work as a crisp opener before a Kashmiri dinner.

chunks.title: Nadur Monji: Another lotus-stem snack: nadre churme
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Nadur Monji page: Another lotus-stem snack: nadre churme.
Nadre churme are crushed, fried pieces of lotus stem tossed in a sour, hot spice mix. This is one home version.
2–3 cleaned lotus stems are cut into large pieces and crushed gently, without mashing them. They can be tossed with 1–2 tbsp rice flour or cornflour and salt for extra crispness, or fried as they are, and are deep-fried until golden and crisp.
The spice mix is ½ tsp salt, 1 tsp chaat masala and ½ tsp each of red chilli powder, coriander powder, roasted cumin powder and dried mint. It is sprinkled over the hot churme with a squeeze of lemon, and they are served at once.

chunks.title: Nadur Monji: A nadru chaat
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Nadur Monji page: A nadru chaat.
This chaat is a new idea, not a traditional dish: crisp slices of lotus stem take the place of papdi, over yogurt with saffron and caramelised onion, a pomegranate chutney and a walnut and mint chutney.
For the yogurt, a medium onion, thinly sliced, is caramelised until golden with a pinch of salt in 1 tsp ghee or oil and folded into 1 cup of thick whisked yogurt with 2 pinches of saffron; allow ½ tsp salt in all, and ½ tsp sugar if liked. For the pomegranate chutney, ½ cup of juice is simmered until slightly thick, then 1 tbsp jaggery or sugar, ½ tsp each of Kashmiri chilli powder, roasted cumin powder and fennel powder, and salt go in; it is cooked to a syrup and cooled. The walnut chutney is ¼ cup walnuts, ½ cup coriander leaves, ¼ cup mint leaves, 1–2 green chillies, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 2 tbsp yogurt, salt and 2–3 tbsp water, blended smooth.
One medium lotus stem is sliced paper-thin and coated with 2 tbsp cornflour, ½ tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, ½ tsp dried mint powder, salt and 1–2 tbsp of water, then fried until crisp and golden. To serve, the saffron yogurt is spread on a plate, both chutneys go over it, then the crisp nadru, and it is finished with pomegranate seeds, thin slices of apple or pear and mint leaves, and eaten at once.

chunks.title: Noon Chai
chunks.text:
Noon Chai is on Wazwan Way under Beverages. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
Traditional pink salted tea brewed with milk.
Noon Chai (also called Sheer Chai) is a pink salted tea brewed from special green tea leaves, baking soda, milk, and salt.
This is the tea of Kashmiri mornings and evenings, brewed in the samovar and drunk with breads from the local kandur (baker) — czot, kulcha, bakarkhani — into which it is unashamedly dunked. The pink is a genuine chemical signature: boiling extracts polyphenols from the green tea, the alkaline bicarbonate shifts them to a deep red, and milk turns that red to pink; vigorous aeration — pouring or ladling the concentrate from a height, repeatedly — deepens and stabilises the colour. Salt rather than sugar reflects both taste and mountain practicality, though sweetened versions exist (notably outside the Valley, where 'Kashmiri chai' is often served pink and sweet). It is drunk across all communities and is as close to a daily ritual as Kashmiri food offers. The authentic Kashmiri Noon Chai is salted — that is the Valley's canonical cup. A sweetened pink version served with nuts exists as a later adaptation in Pakistan and the diaspora, but it is a departure from, not a variation of, the traditional preparation.
This pink tea is the daily morning and afternoon beverage for almost every Kashmiri. Its unique color comes from the chemical reaction of tea leaves with baking soda under prolonged boiling.
Tip: It is salty, not sweet! Try it with local baked breads like Girda or Bakerkhani.

chunks.title: Recipe: Noon Chai
chunks.text:
Recipe for Noon Chai, as written on Wazwan Way.
Noon chai is Kashmir's salted pink tea: tea leaves boiled down with a pinch of baking soda, shocked with cold water, then simmered with milk and salt. This is the traditional method; a quicker pressure-cooker method is below.
Prep 5 min. Cook 50 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 1 heaped tsp Kashmiri tea leaves
- ¼ tsp baking soda
- 2 cups water
- 1 cup cold water
- 2 cups full-fat milk
- ½ tsp salt, or to taste
- 1 tbsp malai (cream), optional
Method:
1. Roast the tea leaves in a heavy pan on a low flame for 10–20 seconds.
