2. Add the baking soda and the 2 cups of water. Boil on a medium heat for 10–15 minutes, until it has reduced by half and turned a deep reddish brown. Repeat this twice.
3. Add the cup of cold water and whisk hard for 2–3 minutes.
4. Simmer for another 10 minutes; the tea turns a dark ruby pink.
5. Add the milk, stirring gently, and simmer slowly for 10 minutes, until it is a creamy rose pink.
6. Add the salt and, if you like, the malai. Serve hot with lavasa, girda or bakerkhani.
Tips:
- Long brewing is the key: reducing the tea is what develops the colour.
- Air matters: whisk the tea, or pour it, to bring out the pink.
- The cold water deepens the colour.
- Simmer slowly once the milk is in.
Serving: Drunk at breakfast and again in the late afternoon, always with bread — czot, kulcha, sheermal or bakarkhani — for dunking; at weddings and winter gatherings it is served from the samovar with a cap of malai.

chunks.title: Noon Chai: In a pressure cooker
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Noon Chai page: In a pressure cooker.
There is a quicker way. Put 2 cups of water, 1 heaped tsp of tea leaves and ¼ tsp of baking soda in a pressure cooker and stir. Cook on a high flame to the first whistle, then on a low flame for 5 minutes, and let the pressure fall by itself.
Open the cooker, add 1 cup of cold water and stir hard. Add 1 cup of milk, or more, bring to a gentle boil and simmer for 5–7 minutes, until the tea is a rich pink. Add ½ tsp of salt and a spoonful of malai if you like, and strain into cups.

chunks.title: Noon Chai: With tomle sott, roasted rice flour
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Noon Chai page: With tomle sott, roasted rice flour.
Tomle sott is rice that has been slowly roasted and stone-ground to a fine powder. It is traditionally mixed into hot salted noon chai at breakfast or with the evening tea.
A spoonful goes into the cup and makes the tea filling. We have no quantities for making the sott itself.

chunks.title: Phirni
chunks.text:
Phirni is on Wazwan Way under Desserts. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
Kashmiri phirni: semolina cooked slowly in full-fat milk with sugar, coconut, almonds and raisins, set in earthen bowls under roasted poppy seeds.
Phirni is honestly pan-Indian: a milk-and-ground-rice pudding made for Eid, weddings and celebrations across the subcontinent, and no source supports claiming it as a Kashmiri invention. What Kashmir contributes is its own idiom: the saffron-forward Kong Phirin, made with semolina rather than ground rice ('kong' means saffron), served chilled in clay shikoras, and associated by sources with Muslim festive cooking, Ramadan and Eid in the Valley — including a living tradition of phirni-makers in Srinagar. This entry gives the classic ground-rice method with the Kashmiri semolina-saffron variant documented alongside, and keeps all origin claims deliberately modest.

chunks.title: Recipe: Phirni
chunks.text:
Recipe for Phirni, as written on Wazwan Way.
Kashmiri phirni: semolina cooked slowly in full-fat milk with sugar, coconut, almonds and raisins, set in earthen bowls under roasted poppy seeds.
Prep 13 min. Cook 30 min. Level: Easy.
Ingredients:
- 1.5 litres full-fat milk
- ½ cup semolina (suji)
- ½ cup sugar, or to taste
- 2–3 tbsp dried coconut, thinly sliced
- 2 tbsp almonds, chopped
- 1 tbsp raisins
- 1 tbsp melon seeds
- 2 tbsp poppy seeds
- Earthen bowls, for setting
Method:
1. Soak the semolina in a little of the milk for 10–15 minutes.
2. Boil the rest of the milk and let it reduce a little, about 10 minutes.
3. Add the coconut, almonds, raisins and melon seeds, the sugar and the soaked semolina.
4. Cook on a low heat, stirring continuously, until slightly thick but still pourable.
5. Dry-roast the poppy seeds in a separate pan.
6. Pour the phirni into the earthen bowls and top with the poppy seeds.
7. Leave it to cool completely; it thickens and turns creamy as it cools.
Tips:
- Soak the semolina first: it prevents lumps.
- Cook it low and slow, and stop while it is still pourable. It thickens as it cools.
- The earthen bowls and the poppy seeds are part of the dish.
Serving: Served cold in individual bowls at the end of festive meals — in the Kashmiri context especially at Eid and Ramadan gatherings; it also closes a heavy Wazwan-style dinner gracefully.
About this recipe: This phirni is made with semolina, not ground rice.

chunks.title: Plain Steamed Rice (Batta)
chunks.text:
Plain Steamed Rice (Batta) is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted). In the feast: on the trami.
The base of the entire trami.
Traditional steamed basmati rice served as the foundational canvas for the Wazwan feast.
Kashmiris are rice eaters before anything else; 'batta khyov?' — have you eaten rice? — is simply how one asks if someone has eaten. The wazwan itself is served over rice heaped on the shared trami, and the daily table is unthinkable without it. The valley's preference is for soft, short-grain rice cooked with a little more water than pilaf traditions use, so the grains cling gently and carry gravy. No salt is strictly required; the dishes over it do the seasoning.
Historically, high-quality local Kashmiri rice like Mushk Budji or classic Basmati is used to form a large mound in the copper trami platter.
Tip: It is shared among four guests and forms the base for all subsequent meat courses.

chunks.title: Recipe: Plain Steamed Rice
chunks.text:
Recipe for Plain Steamed Rice, as written on Wazwan Way.
Plain short-grain rice steamed soft and slightly clinging — the foundation of the trami and of every Kashmiri meal. In Kashmir, batta is not a side; everything else on the plate exists to be eaten with it.
Serves 4. Prep 5 min. Cook 25 min. Level: Easy.
Ingredients:
- 400 g short-grain rice (Kashmiri budgi or any soft short-grain)
- 750 ml water
- Salt, a small pinch (optional)
Method:
1. Wash the rice in several changes of water until the water runs nearly clear.
2. Bring the measured water to a rolling boil in a heavy, lidded pot.
3. Add the rice and the pinch of salt if using, stir once, and boil uncovered until the water falls level with the rice, 8-10 minutes.
4. Drop the heat to its lowest, cover tightly, and steam for 10-12 minutes.
5. Rest off the heat, covered, for 5 minutes, then loosen gently and serve in a generous mound.
Waza tips:
- Kashmiri batta should be soft and lightly clinging — measure water for tenderness, not separateness.
- Never stir while it steams; the crust that forms at the base is the cook's private reward.
Common mistakes:
- Cooking it fluffy and separate like pulao rice — wrong dish, wrong texture.
- Serving it sparse; Kashmiri gravies assume a full plate of rice.
At home: Any soft short-grain rice reproduces batta faithfully; avoid aged long-grain basmati, which is the opposite texture.
Serving: Heap it and ladle any Kashmiri gravy over — rogan josh, yakhni, haakh or matschgand.

chunks.title: Rista
chunks.text:
Rista is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: High. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim. It is one of the seven dishes commonly listed as essential to a Wazwan. In the feast: the gravies.
Silky meatballs cooked in a bright red Kashmiri gravy.
Rista brings together carefully pounded meatballs and a saffron-tinted, chili-forward gravy that stands out for its elegant texture and bright appearance.
Rista is one of the mandatory dishes of the Wazwan and typically arrives in the earlier courses, one meatball per diner, four to a trami, with gravy. Its identity rests on the pounding: cubes of fresh, warm meat are beaten with a wooden mallet called a goshpar (the booklet's 'Goshpar'; some sources spell it goshpare) on a flat stone, with warmed fat worked in at intervals, until the muscle fibres and connective tissue break down into an emulsified paste. This is the same base mince used for Gushtaba — Rista is the red, chilli-saffron expression of it and Gushtaba the white, yogurt one, which is why the two are always discussed as a pair. The mawal (cockscomb flower) decoction that colours the gravy is a distinctly Kashmiri technique with no common substitute outside the valley.
Rista is mutton pounded by hand into a smooth paste, rolled into balls and cooked in a red gravy of Kashmiri chilli, fennel and saffron (Wikipedia; Asia Media Centre). It is one of the seven dishes Wikipedia lists as a must at a Wazwan. The pounding gives the meatballs a texture so hard to achieve that rista and gushtaba are rarely found outside the valley (Wikipedia). Each rista weighs about 80 to 100 g, and one is served to each person around the trami (Sahapedia), so four to a trami. Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes gives the same count for palak rista: four small pieces on a trami for four guests.
Tip: This is ideal for tourists who want a classic Wazwan dish with more visual drama and a punchier flavor profile than Gushtaba.
Rista: mutton pounded by hand into smooth meatballs in a red gravy of Kashmiri chilli, fennel and saffron. Its place in the Wazwan, history and recipe.

chunks.title: Recipe: Rista
chunks.text:
Recipe for Rista, as written on Wazwan Way.
Rista at home: chilled mutton mince and fat worked to a smooth paste in a grinder, rolled into balls and boiled in spiced mutton stock with fried-onion paste and ghee. At a Wazwan the meat is pounded by hand on stone; our story on rista describes that.
Prep 1 h 30 min. Cook 30 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- For the meatballs: 500 g mutton mince (keema)
- 150 g mutton fat, rendered and cooled until semi-solid
- 1 tsp salt
- 1 egg
- ¼ tsp green cardamom seeds
- ¼ tsp black cardamom seeds
- 1 litre mutton stock
- For the gravy: 3–4 green cardamom pods, 2 black cardamom pods, 2–3 cloves, 2–3 black peppercorns, 1 bay leaf and 1–2 sticks of cinnamon
- 1–2 tbsp chilli powder
- ½ tsp turmeric
- ½ tsp dry ginger powder
- 1 tbsp coriander powder
- ½ tbsp fennel powder
- 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste
- ½ cup fried-onion paste
- 2 tbsp ghee
- Mawal (cockscomb flower) extract for colour, optional
Method:
1. Chill the mince in the freezer for 1–2 hours, until half frozen. Grind it for 1–2 minutes in short pulses, so that it does not warm up.
2. Add the cooled fat, the salt and the cardamom seeds and grind to a smooth paste. Add the egg and mix well.
3. With wet hands, roll the paste into medium balls with no cracks.
4. Warm the stock, put the balls in and bring it to the boil once, so that they hold their shape.
5. Add the whole spices, the powdered spices, the ginger-garlic paste, the fried-onion paste, the ghee and the colour to the stock.
6. Boil for 20–25 minutes, until the ristas have swollen and the gravy is thick and glossy. Serve hot.
Tips:
- Keep the meat cold: a grinder heats it, and warm meat spoils the texture.
- The fat must be completely cool before it goes in.
- Leave no cracks in the balls, and set them in warm stock before the gravy is built.
Serving: In the Wazwan, one rista per diner, four to a trami, comes with a ladle of gravy early in the meat courses. At home, serve over plain rice with the gravy flooding the plate.
About this recipe: This is a home version, made in a grinder for cooks without the stone and mallet. At a Wazwan the meat and fat are pounded by hand, as our story on rista describes.

chunks.title: Rista: How it's made
chunks.text:
The meat is pounded straight after slaughter, before rigor mortis sets in, with a wooden mallet on a flat stone (Sahapedia; Wikipedia; Reuters). Fresh sheep fat is worked in until the paste turns light pink, then black cardamom seeds and salt; Sahapedia lists nothing else (Sahapedia). The meat is folded as it is beaten, which works air in and keeps the balls light (Wikipedia).
Sahapedia describes the balls being boiled in water until soft and expanded before they go into the gravy (Sahapedia). At weddings the meat is still pounded by hand (Reuters).

chunks.title: Rista: The gravy
chunks.text: Its red comes from Kashmiri chillies, which give food a deep colour without much heat (Wikipedia), and from mawal, dried cockscomb flowers boiled into a red colouring (Wikipedia; Asia Media Centre). Wikipedia's Wazwan article says it is coloured with alkanet, ratan jot. The gravy is scented with saffron and fennel (Wikipedia; Asia Media Centre).

chunks.title: Rista: Rista and gushtaba
chunks.text:
Both are made from the same pounded mutton: gushtaba's balls are larger and rista's smaller (Sahapedia). Rista comes early, straight after the trami's first dishes (Outlook India; Gulf News). Gushtaba, in a white yogurt gravy with mint, ends the main meal (Wikipedia; Asia Media Centre).
Rista vs gushtaba compares the two side by side, and gushtaba has its own page.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh
chunks.text:
Rogan Josh is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: Medium. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim. It is one of the seven dishes commonly listed as essential to a Wazwan. In the feast: the gravies.
A signature Kashmiri lamb curry layered with aromatic spices.
Rogan Josh is one of the most celebrated dishes from Kashmir, known for its vivid red color, tender meat, and deeply fragrant gravy built with fennel, dry ginger, and Kashmiri chilies.
Rogan Josh is one of the seven dishes generally counted as mandatory in a full Wazwan, served in the earlier meat courses of the feast. The Kashmiri Muslim version is built on praan (Kashmiri shallots) and garlic, which the Pandit tradition deliberately avoids — the two communities cook recognisably different dishes under the same name. What is served in most restaurants outside Kashmir is a third thing again: onion-tomato gravies and heavy yogurt marinades are shortcuts of the restaurant trade (ratan jot, by contrast, is the traditional colouring of the Pandit version), whereas the wedding version cooked by wazas over firewood takes its red from soaked Kashmiri chillies and a mawal decoction and its body from the meat's own stock and fat. The name is usually read through Persian as 'red' or 'clarified fat' (rogan) plus 'heat/intensity' (josh); sources disagree on the exact reading, so we don't press the etymology further. Its deeper origin is commonly linked to Persianate cooking arriving with Central Asian influence in Kashmir, but precise dates and courtly origin stories in circulation are not reliably documented.
Where the name comes from is uncertain. Read as Persian, roghan means ghee or oil and josh means to stew or braise, so the name would mean "stewed in ghee". Another reading takes roghan as the Kashmiri word for "red", giving "red meat" or "red juice" (Wikipedia). Onmanorama glosses josh as cooking on high heat. Wikipedia, drawing on the food historian Lizzie Collingham, describes rogan josh as a Persian dish of meat fried in hot butter that the Mughals brought to North India in the 16th century. Escaping the summer heat of the plains in Kashmir, they coloured and flavoured their food with Kashmiri herbs. The chillies that now make it red reached India with the Portuguese early in the 16th century (Wikipedia). We have found no more precise record of where the dish began.
Tip: Order it with plain steamed rice, the way it is eaten in Kashmir.
Rogan josh: Kashmiri mutton in a red gravy of chilli water, fried shallots and ghee, one of a Wazwan's seven essentials. Its history and the wazas' recipe.

chunks.title: Recipe: Rogan Josh
chunks.text:
Recipe for Rogan Josh, as written on Wazwan Way.
Rogan josh as a waza cooks it for a wedding: the mutton is boiled, skimmed and washed first, then cooked down in its own stock with ghee, fried-shallot paste and chilli water until the gravy is thick and red. There is no tomato and no yogurt in it.
Serves 4–6. Prep 30 min. Cook 1 h 15 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 1 kg mutton, cut into medium pieces
- Water, to boil the mutton
- About 1 litre of the stock from boiling the mutton
- 120 ml (½ cup) chilli water: dried red chillies soaked, ground with a little water, thinned with more water and strained
- 4 tbsp fried-shallot (praan) paste; fried onions, ground to a paste, if you have no shallots
- 3–4 green cardamom pods
- 2–3 cloves
- About 1 tbsp turmeric powder
- 120 ml (½ cup) ghee
- Salt, to taste
Method:
1. Put the mutton in a large pot, cover it with water and bring it to the boil. Skim off all the scum as it rises.
2. Strain the mutton and keep the stock. Wash the mutton well.
3. Return the mutton to the pot with about 1 litre of the stock. Add the cardamom, cloves and turmeric and boil until the raw smell of the turmeric has gone.
4. Add the shallot paste, the chilli water and the ghee, and bring back to the boil.
5. Cover and cook until the mutton is completely tender and the stock has reduced to a thick gravy.
6. Add salt before serving.
Waza tips:
- The mutton is boiled, skimmed and washed before anything else; the stock that is left is the cooking liquid.
- Chilli water and fried-shallot paste are the base of this dish. Make both before you start.
- Boil the turmeric in the stock until its raw smell has gone before the paste, chilli water and ghee go in.
- Salt goes in at the end.
Common mistakes:
- Adding tomatoes or a browned-onion base, which makes a different curry.
- Stopping before the stock has reduced to a thick gravy.
At home: If you have no shallots, fry onions, grind them and use that paste. A home rogan josh that pressure-cooks raw mutton with onions, garlic, oil and ground spices is not what a Wazwan serves: a home kitchen has neither the high heat nor the mutton stock.
Serving: Serve ladled directly over plain steamed rice. In a Wazwan it arrives in the earlier meat courses on the shared trami; at home it needs nothing more than rice and perhaps a raw onion-radish chutney.
About this recipe: The quantities are halved from a recipe for 2 kg of mutton.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: Hindi rogan josh, with yogurt and tamarind
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Rogan Josh page: Hindi rogan josh, with yogurt and tamarind.
The Wazwan has a second, lesser-known rogan josh, called Hindi rogan josh. It is tangy, from yogurt and tamarind. A waza makes it like this, for four or five.
750 g cooked mutton goes into a heavy pan with 2 tbsp garlic paste, 2 black and 4 green cardamom pods, 2 small pieces of cinnamon, 5–6 cloves, salt, ½ cup mustard oil and 2 tbsp desi ghee. On the heat, 1½ cups mutton stock, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ cup fried shallots and 1½ cups whisked yogurt are added and cooked until the yogurt is worked in.
Then 2 tbsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, ¼ cup tamarind water and ½ cup onion paste go in. The pan is covered and simmered until the gravy thickens and the mutton is tender. Add the tamarind a little at a time.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: Two versions
chunks.text:
Kashmiri Muslim and Kashmiri Pandit cooks both make rogan josh, in different ways (JKTDC; Wikipedia).
- Kashmiri Muslim, the Wazwan version. The base is praan, a shallot grown in Kashmir, with garlic (Sahapedia). The red comes from Kashmiri chillies and mawal, dried cockscomb flowers boiled to make a red colouring (Wikipedia; Onmanorama). Azmat Ali Mir, who owns a Kashmiri restaurant in Bangalore, says mustard oil is preferred for home cooking but an authentic Wazwan can only be cooked in ghee (Asia Media Centre).
- Kashmiri Pandit. Traditionally made without onion, garlic or shallots (JKTDC; Wikipedia); yogurt and asafoetida give the gravy its body (Wikipedia). The red comes from Kashmiri chillies and ratan jot, the root of alkanet (Wikipedia), which is fried in hot oil because its dye dissolves in oil but not in water (Wikipedia). A Pandit writer describes a good rogan josh as cooked with little water and plenty of mustard oil (Outlook India). Many Pandit families now use onion and garlic in some dishes (JKTDC).
The colourings aren't strictly divided between the two: Wikipedia's Wazwan article describes the red gravy of rista, a Wazwan dish, as coloured with alkanet (Wikipedia). For the Pandit table more widely, see Kashmiri Pandit food.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: Why there's no tomato
chunks.text: Rogan josh cooked in Kashmir has no tomato. Wikipedia calls tomato an incorrect substitute, used when mawal and ratan jot can't be found (Wikipedia), and British Indian restaurants make the dish red with tomatoes and red peppers (Wikipedia). Tomatoes only found their way into Indian curries after Europeans introduced them (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: How it's eaten
chunks.text:
With rice. In most Kashmiri cooking bread isn't part of the meal and is eaten with tea instead (Wikipedia), although Outlook India notes that the mutton dishes of a Wazwan are served with rice or flat bread (Outlook India). The rice prized for Wazwan is mushk budji, a short-grain variety (Asia Media Centre) grown in the higher reaches of the valley, which received a GI tag in February 2022 (Wikipedia).
At a Wazwan, rogan josh comes after the trami's first dishes, methi maaz and rista (Outlook India).

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The cuts
chunks.text: Sahapedia describes rogan josh made with pieces of about 70 to 80 g cut from the lower ribs, the lower back (bukhtor), the chest and the neck. They are simmered in a gravy of garlic, ginger, red chilli powder, clove, cardamom, cinnamon and praan paste, and served hot with rice (Sahapedia).

chunks.title: Ruwangan Chaman
chunks.text:
Ruwangan Chaman is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Medium. Tradition: Kashmiri Pandit. In the feast: alongside.
Paneer cooked in a tomato-based Kashmiri gravy.
Ruwangan Chaman is one of the recognizable vegetarian dishes that enters the broader Wazwan world, using fried paneer and a bright tomato gravy to add color and contrast.
Ruwangan Chaman belongs to the Kashmiri Pandit repertoire of paneer dishes that substitute for meat on ritual and festive vegetarian menus, cooked without onion or garlic and seasoned instead with asafoetida and the classic fennel-ginger pair. It is common enough to have a Wikipedia entry of its own, and it exists in two documented forms: the fresh-tomato version made in season, and Ruwangan Hachi Chaman, made through the winter with sun-dried tomatoes — a reminder of Kashmir's tradition of drying summer vegetables (hachi) against the snowed-in months. Alongside lyodur (yellow) and wuzij (red-chilli) chaman, it completes the trio of classic Pandit paneer gravies.
Ruwangan Chaman highlights the beautiful synergy between fresh paneer (chaman) and tangy tomatoes (ruwangan), a relatively recent but immensely popular addition to the Kashmiri culinary canon. Tomatoes were introduced to the valley much later than ancient staples like lotus stem and greens, but they were quickly embraced for the vibrant color and acidity they brought to gravies. This dish has become a festive vegetarian staple, showcasing how Kashmiri chefs successfully integrated new ingredients while maintaining the region's signature slow-cooked, spice-infused techniques.
Tip: A useful dish for mixed groups where some diners want a vegetarian Wazwan-style option without stepping too far from classic Kashmiri flavors.

chunks.title: Recipe: Ruwangan Chaman
chunks.text:
Recipe for Ruwangan Chaman, as written on Wazwan Way.
Fried paneer simmered in a brick-red gravy of fresh tomatoes sharpened with Kashmiri chilli, fennel and dry ginger. Ruwangan is Kashmiri for tomato, and this is the tangier, summery cousin of the yellow Chaman Qaliya.
Serves 4. Prep 15 min. Cook 33 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 400 g paneer, cut into 2.5 cm cubes or thick triangles
- 4-5 tbsp mustard oil
- 500 g ripe tomatoes, pureed (about 5-6 medium), or 400 ml good passata
- 1 generous pinch asafoetida (hing)
- 2.5 cm piece of cinnamon
- 2 cloves
- 1 black cardamom pod
- 2 green cardamom pods, lightly crushed
- 2 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, mixed into 3 tbsp water
- 1 1/2 tsp fennel powder
- 3/4 tsp dry ginger powder (sonth)
- 1/4 tsp turmeric powder
- 1/4 tsp caraway seeds (shahi zeera), lightly crushed
- 1 1/4 tsp salt, or to taste
- 300 ml hot water
- 1/2 tsp sugar (optional, if the tomatoes are very sharp)
Method:
1. Heat the mustard oil in a wide pan until it just smokes, then lower to medium. Fry the paneer in batches until light golden on all sides (about 5-6 minutes), and slip the fried pieces into a bowl of warm salted water to keep them tender.
2. Leave about 2 tablespoons of oil in the pan. On medium heat, add the asafoetida, cinnamon, cloves and black cardamom and let them crackle for 30 seconds.
3. Add the Kashmiri chilli paste (chilli powder mixed with water) and stir briskly for 20-30 seconds until the oil turns red — the water protects the chilli from burning and fixes the colour.
4. Pour in the tomato puree with the turmeric and salt. Cook on medium heat, stirring now and then, until the puree thickens, loses its raw smell and the oil starts to show at the edges (roughly 8-10 minutes).
5. Stir in the fennel powder and dry ginger powder, then add the hot water and bring to a simmer. Taste — if the tomatoes are aggressively sour, balance with the sugar.
6. Drain the paneer and add it to the gravy. Simmer gently, uncovered, for 10-12 minutes, until the gravy is glossy, coats the paneer and has thickened to a spoonable consistency with oil visible on the surface.
7. Finish with the crushed green cardamom and caraway seeds, cover, and rest off the heat for 5 minutes before serving.
Waza tips:
- Cook the tomato base until oil visibly separates before adding water — an undercooked tomato masala tastes raw no matter how long the paneer simmers afterwards.
- Kashmiri chilli powder is there for colour and gentle warmth; do not swap in hot chilli powder at the same quantity.
- Fennel and dry ginger go in after the tomatoes have cooked down — added too early they can turn bitter.
- In winter, Kashmiri households make this with soaked sun-dried tomatoes (ruwangan hachi), which give a deeper, almost smoky gravy — worth trying if you can find them.
Common mistakes:
- Burning the chilli powder by adding it dry to hot oil — always slake it in water first.
- Not cooking the tomatoes down fully, which leaves the gravy thin and raw-tasting.
- Using regular hot chilli powder in Kashmiri quantities, making the dish fiery instead of warm and red.
- Simmering the paneer too long or too hard, which toughens it.
At home: Canned tomato puree or passata works well and gives a more consistent colour than pale supermarket tomatoes. Pan-sear the paneer in less oil if you prefer, or skip frying altogether and add plain cubes for a lighter, softer result. Any heavy-bottomed pan replaces the traditional pot; just keep the simmer gentle.
Serving: Serve hot with plain steamed rice, as part of a Pandit vegetarian spread alongside haakh and dum aloo. It also pairs well with phulka or lavasa for a simpler meal.

chunks.title: Saffron Phirni (Kong Phirin)
chunks.text:
Saffron Phirni (Kong Phirin) is on Wazwan Way under Desserts. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
The classic ground-rice and milk pudding dyed a deep evening gold with Kashmiri saffron, set in shallow clay bowls. Saffron phirni is the dessert that lets Pampore's most famous crop speak almost alone.
Kashmir grows India's finest saffron on the karewa plateaus of Pampore, and this phirni is the sweet built to honour it: the trio of milk, ground rice and kong needs nothing else beyond cardamom and a scatter of nuts. The saffron is bloomed in warm milk first so its colour and perfume open fully. Served at weddings and Eid tables, it is judged on three things — the grain of the rice, the depth of the gold, and how cleanly it releases from the clay bowl's rim.

chunks.title: Recipe: Saffron Phirni
chunks.text:
Recipe for Saffron Phirni, as written on Wazwan Way.
The classic ground-rice and milk pudding dyed a deep evening gold with Kashmiri saffron, set in shallow clay bowls. Saffron phirni is the dessert that lets Pampore's most famous crop speak almost alone.
Serves 6. Prep 15 min. Cook 35 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 70 g short-grain rice, soaked 2 hours
- 1 litre full-fat milk
- 120 g sugar
- 1/2 tsp saffron threads (a generous pinch)
- 5 green cardamoms, seeds ground
- Slivered almonds and pistachios, to finish
Method:
1. Warm 3 tbsp of the milk and steep the saffron in it; set aside to bloom.
2. Drain the rice and grind it with a splash of milk to a coarse, semolina-like paste.
3. Bring the remaining milk to a boil in a heavy pan, then lower the heat.
4. Stir in the rice paste, loosened with warm milk, and cook on low, stirring constantly, until thick and no longer raw-tasting, 20-25 minutes.
5. Add the sugar, cardamom and the bloomed saffron with its milk and cook 5 minutes more until glossy and evenly gold.
6. Pour into shallow bowls — clay if you have them — cool, and chill at least 3 hours; finish with slivered nuts.
Waza tips:
- Bloom the saffron; threads thrown straight into the pot give colour in streaks and perfume not at all.
- Keep the grind coarse — phirni's texture is its identity.
Common mistakes:
- Skimping on saffron and compensating with food colour — the perfume is the point.
- Pouring it deep, which never sets to the proper sliceable surface.
At home: Packet ground rice and any good saffron work; use a few more threads if your saffron is not Kashmiri.
Serving: Serve cold in its setting bowl at the end of a rich meal.

chunks.title: Seekh Kebab (Seekh Kabab (Waza style))
chunks.text:
Seekh Kebab (Seekh Kabab (Waza style)) is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: Medium. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim. In the feast: on the trami.
Minced meat roasted on skewers over hot coals and served as a key Wazwan course.
In the Wazwan's opening arrangement, the trami arrives with its rice quartered and topped by seekh kababs alongside methi maaz and tabak maaz — Wikipedia's account describes the platter 'divided by two seekh kababs', making this one of the feast's structural dishes rather than a side. The Kashmiri version is distinguished by its seasoning: fennel and dry ginger where other regional seekhs lean on garam masala, cumin and raw onion, and a smoother, pounded texture in waza hands. It is grilled over charcoal at weddings, though a tawa (griddle) finish is common and accepted elsewhere. Beyond its role in the feast, the seekh's broader history belongs to the whole subcontinent and no uniquely Kashmiri origin claim is supportable.

chunks.title: Recipe: Seekh Kebab
chunks.text:
Recipe for Seekh Kebab, as written on Wazwan Way.
Two seekh kababs lie across the mound of rice on every trami before a Wazwan even begins — long fingers of fennel-scented pounded mutton, pressed onto flat skewers and cooked over charcoal. The waza's seekh is sparer than its Punjabi and Pakistani cousins: no onion crunch, no green chilli bite, just meat, fat and the Kashmiri spice signature.
Serves 4–6 (makes 10–12 kababs). Prep 35 min. Cook 23 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 750 g mutton mince from shoulder, fine-ground twice or briefly pounded, with its fat retained (aim for roughly 20% fat)
- 50 g mutton fat, minced, if the meat is lean
- 2 tsp fennel (saunf) powder
- 1.5 tsp dry ginger powder (sonth)
- 1/2 tsp ground black cardamom seeds
- 1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
- 1/2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder (optional — many waza seekhs are pale)
- A small pinch of saffron soaked in 1 tbsp warm milk (optional, for the wedding-style tint)
- 1 tbsp ghee, melted, plus more for basting
- 1.25 tsp salt
- Flat metal skewers (wide, sword-style if available)
Method:
1. Chill the mince thoroughly. Combine it with the minced fat, fennel, sonth, black cardamom, pepper, chilli and saffron milk if using, salt and the melted ghee.
2. Knead and slap the mixture against the bowl for 5–8 minutes until it turns sticky and cohesive — it should cling to an upturned hand. Rest it, covered and cold, for 20–30 minutes.
3. With wet palms, take a ball of mixture, mould it around a flat skewer and press-squeeze it along the length into an even cylinder about 2 cm thick, sealing the ends onto the metal.
4. Cook over medium-hot charcoal, turning every couple of minutes and basting with ghee, until evenly browned outside and just cooked through (8–12 minutes) — the kabab should stay juicy, not blister dry. On a stove, cook on a hot tawa or under a grill, turning and basting the same way.
5. Rest for two minutes, slide off the skewers whole, and serve hot.
Waza tips:
- Fat is non-negotiable — a lean seekh crumbles off the skewer and eats dry; wazas keep the mince visibly rich.
- Knead until sticky; it is the worked meat proteins, not egg or binder, that hold the kabab on the skewer.
- Keep the mixture cold right up to skewering, and wet your hands so the surface stays smooth.
- Moderate coals, frequent turning: the Kashmiri seekh is gently coloured, never charred black.
Common mistakes:
- Using lean supermarket mince, the main cause of kababs breaking on the skewer.
- Loading the mix with onion and green chilli, which makes a fine Punjabi seekh but not a waza one.
- Cooking over fierce heat until charred outside and raw within.
- Skipping the kneading and resting, so the kababs slump off the skewer.
At home: A cast-iron griddle or oven grill setting replicates the tawa method well; thread the kababs on soaked wooden skewers or shape free-form fingers if flat skewers are missing. Ask the butcher for shoulder mince with fat, or add ground lamb fat/butter. Resist adding raw onion or egg — chilling and kneading solve the binding problem the traditional way.
Serving: In the Wazwan, two kababs top the rice on each trami as part of the opening course. On their own, serve hot off the skewer with lavasa or rice and a walnut or mint-yogurt chutney.

chunks.title: Seekh Kebab: Without a grill or skewers: a home method
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Seekh Kebab page: Without a grill or skewers: a home method.
Kashmiri kababs need coals, a grill and skewers. This is a way of making them in a kitchen that has none of the three.
250 g boneless mutton, with 25–30 per cent fat, is chopped fine on a board with 1½ tbsp chilli powder, 2 tsp fennel, 1 tsp dry ginger powder, 1 tsp black cardamom powder, ½ tsp black pepper and salt. 1 tbsp cumin seeds, a handful of chopped coriander and 1 egg are mixed in, and the mince rests in the freezer for at least 30 minutes.
Skewers are folded out of thick aluminium foil, the mince is shaped on to them with wet hands, and they are laid across a smoking-hot pan so that the meat does not touch it. They cook on a high flame for 10–15 minutes, turned all the time. If the meat has no fat, add ghee and never oil.

chunks.title: Seekh Kebab: Lahabi kabab, the boat-shaped kebab of the feast
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Seekh Kebab page: Lahabi kabab, the boat-shaped kebab of the feast.
Lahabi, or lahabdar, kabab is a Wazwan kebab shaped like a boat and cooked in gravy. A waza makes it like this.
500 g boneless mutton is chopped fine with salt and 1 tbsp red chilli powder and passed through a mincer once or twice. 1 egg, ½ tbsp dried mint, ½ tbsp turmeric and ½ tbsp cumin seeds are added, and it is minced again until smooth, then shaped by hand into boats.
1 litre of mutton stock is boiled with ½ tbsp turmeric and 1 tbsp red chilli powder. The kebabs go in, followed by 2–3 cloves, 1 tbsp garlic paste, 3–4 green cardamom pods, ¼ tbsp dry ginger powder, 1–2 tbsp ghee, ½ cup whisked curd and a little onion or shallot paste to thicken. They simmer until the gravy is thick and the ghee separates.

chunks.title: Shami Kabab
chunks.text:
Shami Kabab is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: Medium. Tradition: Wazwan (Muslim). In the feast: on the trami.
Soft, spiced patties of finely minced mutton and chana dal, pan-seared in ghee until crusted outside and meltingly tender within.
Shami Kabab is a griddle kabab of twice-ground mutton cooked down with split chana dal and whole spices, then pounded to a smooth paste, bound with egg, and shallow-fried into flat discs. In the Kashmiri kitchen it belongs to the kabab family served alongside the Wazwan, prized for a soft, almost creamy interior against a browned crust. The dal is not a filler but the dish's signature, giving the kabab its characteristic bind and gentle nuttiness.
Shami kabab sits in the kabab register of the Kashmiri table, cooked for guests and festive meals and sold at the valley's better kabab counters. Its identity is the two-stage method: a slow simmer that marries mutton and chana dal into one tender mass, then a hot ghee fry that sets a thin crust. Unlike the skewered seekh, it is a griddle kabab — flat, soft, and eaten with chutney and onions.
The shami kabab travelled into the subcontinent with Central Asian and Mughal cooks and settled across the north, Kashmir included, where kabab-making is a respected craft. The name is popularly tied to the Levant (‘Shaam’), and the dish's defining trick — simmering minced meat with chana dal until both collapse into one paste — made it a way to stretch and soften meat into an elegant, spoon-tender kabab fit for a feast.
Tip: Eat it hot off the griddle with a squeeze of lemon, sliced onions and a sharp mint or onion chutney; the best versions are soft enough to break with the side of a fork.

chunks.title: Recipe: Shami Kabab
chunks.text:
Recipe for Shami Kabab, as written on Wazwan Way.
Minced mutton simmered with chana dal and whole spices until dry, ground to a smooth paste, bound with egg and shallow-fried into soft, crusted patties. A kabab defined by the meeting of meat and dal.
Serves 4. Prep 30 min. Cook 40 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 500 g mutton mince (leg), with a little fat
- 100 g chana dal (split Bengal gram), soaked 1 hour
- 1 onion, roughly chopped
- 4 cloves garlic and 1 inch ginger
- 3-4 dried Kashmiri chillies
- 4 cloves, 4 green cardamoms, 1 black cardamom, 1 small cinnamon stick
- 1 tsp cumin seeds
- 1 tsp fennel powder
- Salt to taste
- 1 egg, beaten, to bind
- A handful of chopped coriander and mint
- Ghee for shallow-frying
Method:
1. Put the mince, drained chana dal, onion, ginger, garlic, whole spices, cumin, fennel and salt in a heavy pot with just enough water to cover.
2. Simmer, covered, until the meat and dal are completely soft and the water has all but evaporated, 30-35 minutes.
3. Cool the mixture, pick out the whole spices, and grind it to a smooth, stiff paste with no free moisture.
4. Work in the chopped coriander and mint and the beaten egg until the paste holds together firmly.
5. With moist hands, shape the paste into flat discs about a centimetre thick.
6. Heat ghee in a wide pan over medium heat and shallow-fry the kababs until deep golden and crusted on both sides, 3-4 minutes a side.
7. Drain briefly and serve hot with lemon, onion rings and chutney.
Waza tips:
- Cook the mixture until truly dry before grinding — any moisture and the kababs fall apart in the pan.
- Chill the shaped kababs for 15 minutes before frying so they hold their form.
Common mistakes:
- A wet paste, which spreads and breaks on the griddle.
- Frying on high heat, which colours the crust before the centre warms through.
At home: Twice-minced lamb and ordinary chana dal reproduce this anywhere; a food processor grinds the cooked mixture in seconds.
Serving: Serve as a starter or alongside the Wazwan with mint chutney, sliced onion and lemon.

chunks.title: Sheera
chunks.text:
Sheera is on Wazwan Way under Desserts. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
Semolina roasted golden in ghee, then drawn out with hot sweet milk into a soft, spoonable pudding scented with cardamom and saffron. Sheera is the looser, milkier sibling of suji halwa — comfort measured in spoonfuls.
Where suji halwa firms up and holds its shape, sheera stays soft and flowing, enriched with milk rather than plain water — the version made for breakfast trays, convalescents and small household celebrations. In Kashmir it belongs to the budget sweet tier: pantry staples, one pan, twenty minutes. Its quality lives entirely in the roast — semolina taken slowly to gold in good ghee — and in serving it warm, before it tightens.

chunks.title: Recipe: Sheera
chunks.text:
Recipe for Sheera, as written on Wazwan Way.
Semolina roasted golden in ghee, then drawn out with hot sweet milk into a soft, spoonable pudding scented with cardamom and saffron. Sheera is the looser, milkier sibling of suji halwa — comfort measured in spoonfuls.
Serves 4. Prep 5 min. Cook 20 min. Level: Easy.
Ingredients:
- 150 g fine semolina (suji)
- 5 tbsp ghee
- 500 ml full-fat milk, hot
- 150 ml water, hot
- 120 g sugar
- 4 green cardamoms, seeds ground
- 1 pinch saffron threads, bloomed in warm milk (optional)
- 10-12 raisins and a handful of slivered almonds
Method:
1. Melt the ghee in a heavy pan, add the raisins and almonds, and lift them out once the raisins swell.
2. Add the semolina to the same ghee and roast on low-medium heat, stirring constantly, until golden and nutty, 8-10 minutes.
3. Dissolve the sugar in the hot milk and water.
4. Pour the sweet milk into the semolina in a stream, stirring — it will sputter and seize, then loosen.
5. Cook on low, stirring, until the semolina swells and the sheera turns soft and pourable, 5-6 minutes.
6. Fold in the cardamom, saffron and the fried raisins and nuts, and serve warm.
Waza tips:
- The roast is the flavour — pale semolina makes paste, not sheera.
- Keep it looser than feels right; it thickens noticeably as it stands.
Common mistakes:
- Adding cold milk, which lumps the semolina.
- Walking away during the roast; semolina colours unevenly the moment it is unattended.
At home: Nothing exotic here — fine semolina, ghee and milk from any grocery reproduce it exactly.
Serving: Serve warm in small bowls, on its own or beside morning noon chai.

chunks.title: Sheermal
chunks.text:
Sheermal is on Wazwan Way under Bakery. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Kashmiri Muslim.
Sheermal is the kandur's festive loaf: a round, faintly sweet flatbread kneaded with milk and ghee instead of water, painted with saffron milk so it bakes to a burnished apricot gold. Soft, rich and perfumed with cardamom, it is the bread of Eid mornings, wedding trays and special-occasion breakfasts.
The name is Persian — sheer, milk — and the bread arrived in the subcontinent along Persian and Mughal routes; Lucknow, Hyderabad and Iran all have their own versions, and Kashmir's kandurs absorbed it into their tandoor repertoire. In the Valley it is an occasion bread rather than a daily one: Srinagar's old bakeries run special batches for Ramadan and Eid, and Pampore — the saffron town — is noted for its sheermal, some versions studded with dried fruit. It shares the ceremonial-tray culture of bakerkhani, travelling to in-laws and gracing celebration spreads. The saffron wash is not garnish; with Pampore's saffron fields an hour from Srinagar, it is the local crop on the local bread.

chunks.title: Recipe: Sheermal
chunks.text:
Recipe for Sheermal, as written on Wazwan Way.
Sheermal is the kandur's festive loaf: a round, faintly sweet flatbread kneaded with milk and ghee instead of water, painted with saffron milk so it bakes to a burnished apricot gold. Soft, rich and perfumed with cardamom, it is the bread of Eid mornings, wedding trays and special-occasion breakfasts.
Serves 6 breads. Prep 35 min. Cook 15 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 300 g all-purpose flour (maida)
- 60 g ghee, melted, plus extra for brushing
- 40 g sugar
- 1/2 tsp salt
- 1 tsp instant yeast (some versions use baking powder instead)
- 150–170 ml warm milk, for the dough
- 20–25 saffron strands, steeped 30 minutes in 3 tbsp warm milk
- 1/2 tsp green cardamom powder
- 1 tsp kewra or rose water (optional)
- 1 tbsp melon seeds, chopped pistachios or almonds, to finish (optional, Pampore-style)
Method:
1. Steep the saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk for at least 30 minutes — the wash should be a deep marigold before you use it.
2. Whisk the flour, sugar, salt, yeast and cardamom. Add the melted ghee and rub through, then knead with warm milk (and the kewra water, if using) to a soft, supple dough, about 8 minutes. The dough is kneaded entirely with milk — no water — which is the bread's defining richness.
3. Cover and rise 1–1.5 hours in a warm spot until noticeably puffed (milk-and-ghee doughs rise slower than lean ones).
4. Divide into 6 balls, rest 10 minutes, then roll each into a round about 5 mm thick and 12–14 cm across.
5. Dock the surface all over with a fork so the bread stays flat and even rather than ballooning.
6. Brush generously with the saffron milk, edge to edge, and scatter with seeds or nuts if using.
7. Bake on a preheated tray or steel at 180–190°C for 10–15 minutes until the top is a deep saffron gold with toasted freckles — in the tandoor it takes a couple of minutes against the wall.
8. Brush immediately with ghee as they come out, and keep wrapped in a cloth. Serve warm.
Waza tips:
- Steep the saffron properly — a pale, hurried wash gives a yellow-stained bread instead of that deep bakery amber.
- Docking is what keeps sheermal an even, tender flat loaf; undocked, it puffs like naan and dries out.
- The ghee brush at the end is half the bread's character; do it while the surface is oven-hot so it drinks it in.
- Moderate oven, not tandoor-hot: the milk sugars scorch quickly, so sheermal bakes cooler than girda or lavas.
Common mistakes:
- Baking at tandoor temperatures, which burns the milk-and-sugar crust before the crumb cooks.
- Kneading with water 'to save milk' — the flavour and keeping quality both come from the all-milk dough.
- Skipping the dock, so the bread balloons, bakes unevenly and staling fast.
- Using saffron colour or turmeric instead of real saffron; the aroma, not just the hue, is the point.
At home: Sheermal is genuinely at home in a domestic oven — its enriched, sugar-and-milk dough prefers 180–190°C to a tandoor's ferocity, which is why even bakery recipes quote conventional temperatures. Bake on a preheated tray for a gently crisped base, keep the breads mid-oven so the saffron top colours without burning, and tent with foil for the last minutes if the edges darken early. A stovetop version also works: cook docked rounds on a heavy covered tawa over low heat, saffron side up, until set, then flash the top under a broiler.
Serving: Serve warm with noon chai or kahwa at a festive breakfast, or alongside rich mutton dishes — sheermal with a spoonful of gravy is a classic pairing across the sheermal belt. It also holds its own plain, with a smear of butter.

chunks.title: Shufta
chunks.text:
Shufta is on Wazwan Way under Desserts. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Kashmiri Pandit.
A rich sweet mixture of dry fruits, paneer, and honey.
Shufta is a decadent dessert packed with almonds, walnuts, pistachios, cashews, raisins, dry dates, and fried paneer, all coated in a saffron-infused honey syrup.
Shufta stands apart from the subcontinent's milk sweets: it is an assembly of textures — chewy dates and raisins, crisp nuts, soft syrup-glazed paneer — bound in a spiced syrup where black pepper and dry ginger answer the sugar. Rooted in the Pandit festive kitchen and cooked across communities for weddings, Herath (Shivratri) and celebration dinners, it is served warm in small portions. The pepper is not a flourish but the signature; without it the dish is merely sweet.
Shufta has historically been served at weddings and special celebrations, symbolizing wealth and luxury because of its use of premium dry fruits.
Tip: Extremely rich. Share a small bowl with friends at the end of your meal.

chunks.title: Recipe: Shufta
chunks.text:
Recipe for Shufta, as written on Wazwan Way.
Fried cubes of paneer tossed with ghee-plumped dry fruits in a thick saffron syrup that carries an astonishing crack of black pepper. Shufta is Kashmir's festival sweet — dessert built like a jewel box.
Serves 6. Prep 20 min. Cook 25 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 250 g paneer, in small cubes
- 3 tbsp ghee, plus more for frying the paneer
- 12 dates, pitted and halved
- 3 tbsp raisins
- 10 dried apricots, halved (optional)
- 50 g walnut kernels
- 50 g almonds and cashews, mixed
- 2 tbsp fresh or dry coconut slivers (optional)
- 150 g sugar
- 150 ml water
- 1 pinch saffron threads, bloomed in warm water
- 1/2 tsp freshly cracked black pepper
- 1/2 tsp dry ginger powder (sonth)
- 4 green cardamoms, seeds ground
- A few dried rose petals, to finish (optional)
Method:
1. Fry the paneer cubes in ghee to a light gold and set aside.
2. In the 3 tbsp ghee, fry the nuts until just coloured, then add the dates, raisins, apricots and coconut and toss until the raisins swell; set aside with the paneer.
3. In the same pan, boil the sugar and water to a light syrup, 5-6 minutes.
4. Add the saffron water, black pepper, sonth and cardamom to the syrup.
5. Return the paneer and fruits and simmer, folding gently, until the syrup thickens and coats everything in a glossy sheath, 6-8 minutes.
6. Rest 5 minutes, scatter with rose petals, and serve warm in small bowls.
Waza tips:
- Grind the pepper fresh and add it to the syrup, not the fruit — it must permeate, not sit in pockets.
- Stop while the syrup still flows; it firms considerably as it cools.
Common mistakes:
- Omitting or fearing the black pepper, which is the dish's identity.
- Overcooking the syrup to crystallisation, which turns the shufta grainy.
At home: All ingredients travel — any Indian grocery covers the list; firm tofu can stand in for paneer in a pinch.
Serving: Serve warm in small portions at the end of a festive meal, with kahwa alongside.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz
chunks.text:
Tabak Maaz is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted). It is one of the seven dishes commonly listed as essential to a Wazwan. In the feast: on the trami.
Crisp-fried lamb ribs with a rich, smoky finish.
Tabak Maaz is prepared by simmering ribs until tender, in their own stock in the wazas' kitchens and in milk in others, before frying them in ghee until the exterior turns deeply golden and crisp.
Tabak Maaz is counted among the mandatory Wazwan dishes and is typically already on the trami among the opening items. It is genuinely shared across both Kashmiri communities: the same twice-cooked ribs are known as Kabargah (or Kabarg) especially among Kashmiri Pandits, and Pandit recipe sources title the dish 'Tabak Maaz or Kabarg' as one preparation. Only a minority of sources — including the 2006 booklet — draw a technical distinction, reserving 'Kabargah' for ribs dipped in a spiced curd batter and deep-fried in ghee. Because most reputable sources treat the two names as one dish, we present a single entry with the batter-fried Kabargah finish documented as a variant rather than a separate recipe.
Tabak maaz is lamb ribs cooked twice: simmered with spices until tender, then fried in ghee until crisp outside and soft inside (Wikipedia; Sahapedia). It is served hot and dry and, like the rest of the Wazwan, eaten with the fingers (Wikipedia; Outlook India; JKTDC). It is one of the seven dishes Wikipedia lists as a must at a Wazwan, and it comes first: two pieces sit on each trami with the seekh kebabs and methi maaz before any gravy arrives (Wikipedia; Asia Media Centre; Outlook India). Gulf News describes diners having "less than ten minutes" to finish that first course before the next dish appears. In August 2024 The Kashmir Wazwan Cooperative Limited applied for a geographical indication for "Tabakmaaz (Meat Products) of Kashmir" (application 1336). It was still at pre-examination when we checked in October 2026 (Intellectual Property India).
Tip: Eat it hot, straight from the pan. At a Wazwan it is one of the first dishes on the trami.
Tabak maaz: lamb ribs simmered tender in their own stock, then fried in ghee until crisp. First on the trami at a Wazwan. Its history and the wazas' recipe.

chunks.title: Recipe: Tabak Maaz
chunks.text:
Recipe for Tabak Maaz, as written on Wazwan Way.
Tabak maaz as a waza cooks it: mutton ribs boiled and washed, simmered again in their own stock with cloves, garlic and turmeric until completely tender, then trimmed and fried in plenty of ghee until crisp. The wazas' pot holds water and stock, not milk; our story on the dish sets out who uses which.
Serves 4–6. Prep 18 min. Cook 1 h 28 min. Level: Involved.
Ingredients:
- 1 kg mutton ribs; ask the butcher to separate them
- Water, for the first boil
- The stock from the first boil
- 4–5 cloves
- 10–12 garlic cloves
- 1 tbsp turmeric powder
- Salt, to taste
- Ghee, plenty, for frying
Method:
1. Put the ribs in a large pot of water and bring to the boil. Skim off the scum that rises.
2. Keep boiling until the ribs are partly cooked. Lift them out and wash them well; keep the stock.
3. Cut the ribs into manageable pieces and return them to the stock. Add the cloves and garlic, then the turmeric and salt.
4. Simmer until the ribs have taken up the flavour of the stock and are completely tender.
5. Take the ribs out and let them cool a little. Chop off the excess bone to leave neat pieces that keep their rib shape.
6. Lay the ribs on a wide tawa or heavy frying pan, add plenty of ghee and fry, turning as needed, until golden-brown and crisp. Serve hot.
Waza tips:
- The ribs are cooked twice in liquid before they meet the ghee: a first boil in water, then a simmer in their own stock with cloves, garlic, turmeric and salt.
- Trim the excess bone after the second cooking, once the ribs have cooled a little.
- Use plenty of ghee, and fry until the ribs are crisp.
Common mistakes:
- Frying before the ribs are completely tender; the ghee only crisps them.
- Letting them wait after frying. They are served hot.
At home: A wide, heavy frying pan stands in for the waza's tawa. Fry the ribs in batches so that each piece sits flat in the ghee.
Serving: In the Wazwan it is among the first items on the trami, eaten with the fingers alongside rice and chutney. It also works as a stand-alone starter — two rib pieces per person with lemon and onion.
About this recipe: The Waza family's published recipe, quoted in our story on tabak maaz, has the same two cookings and adds dry ginger and black cardamom to the second pot.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: How the wazas make it
chunks.text:
A waza family's published recipe boils the whole rack of ribs in water, skimming it until the water runs clear, then adds garlic and salt and boils it until the membrane between the ribs can be pierced with a thumb. Only then is the rack cut into eight rectangles, boiled again with turmeric, dry ginger, cloves, black cardamom and salt, and fried in pure ghee until reddish brown (Scroll, from the Roli Books cookbook Wazwaan).
Sahapedia describes fatty ribs simmered in water with cardamom, cinnamon, ginger powder, garlic paste and cloves, then cut and fried in ghee until crisp and caramelised outside and succulent inside, a balance that earns a waza particular praise (Sahapedia).
Other accounts differ on the liquid. Wikipedia has the ribs simmered in milk (Wikipedia), and Onmanorama describes them cooked in ghee and then simmered in yogurt until dry (Onmanorama). Our recipe below follows the wazas' method: water for the first boil, then the ribs' own stock. A Srinagar chef told Deccan Chronicle that tabak maaz is deep-fried in ghee and that the chest gives "the required softness and taste" (Deccan Chronicle).

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Tabak maaz and kabargah
chunks.text:
Kashmiri Pandits commonly call the dish kabargah (Wikipedia), and JKTDC lists kabargah among the delicacies of Kashmiri Pandit cooking (JKTDC). Wikipedia treats the two names as one dish (Wikipedia), though its list of Kashmiri dishes notes a small difference in method: kabargah is simmered on a low heat for longer and then fried very quickly, while tabak maaz is boiled with salt and garlic and has a slightly elastic texture (Wikipedia). In Pandit homes that avoid onion and garlic (JKTDC), the garlic is left out.
Kabargah has its own page, with a Pandit recipe.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: The name
chunks.text: In Kashmiri, tabakh is a large dish, plate or tray (Grierson) and māz is meat (Grierson). Kashmir Life, describing feasts in the 16th-century Tuhfat-ul-Ahbab, notes that food was served in a copper tabak, "maybe a forerunner of traem of today" (Kashmir Life). How the dish came by its name isn't recorded.

chunks.title: Tosha
chunks.text:
Tosha is on Wazwan Way under Street Food. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
Small cylinders of soft flour-and-khoya dough fried gently in ghee, then rolled in warm sugar syrup until they wear a fine sweet glaze. Tosha is a festival sweet — modest to look at, rich to eat.
Tosha belongs to the family of syrup-finished fried sweets shared across North India that found a home in Kashmiri bakeries and festive trays, handed around at weddings, Eid and winter gatherings with noon chai or kahwa. Unlike gulab jamun it is not soaked but glazed: the fried pieces take a short turn in thick syrup so the outside crystallises lightly while the crumb stays tender. Good tosha is fried low and slow — colour rushed over high heat means a raw centre.

chunks.title: Recipe: Tosha
chunks.text:
Recipe for Tosha, as written on Wazwan Way.
Small cylinders of soft flour-and-khoya dough fried gently in ghee, then rolled in warm sugar syrup until they wear a fine sweet glaze. Tosha is a festival sweet — modest to look at, rich to eat.
Serves 6. Prep 25 min. Cook 30 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 150 g plain flour (maida)
- 100 g khoya (mawa), crumbled, or full-cream milk powder
- 2 tbsp ghee, for the dough, plus more for frying
- 1/4 tsp baking soda
- 4-5 tbsp milk, to bind
- 200 g sugar
- 120 ml water
- 4 green cardamoms, seeds ground
- Slivered pistachios or almonds, to finish
Method:
1. Rub the 2 tbsp ghee into the flour, then work in the khoya and baking soda until the mixture looks like damp crumbs.
2. Add milk a spoon at a time and gather a soft, smooth dough; rest it 15 minutes under a cloth.
3. Shape the dough into small cylinders or ovals about the size of a thumb, with no surface cracks.
4. Heat ghee over low-medium heat and fry the pieces slowly, turning, until they are an even deep gold, 8-10 minutes per batch.
5. Boil the sugar and water with the cardamom to a sticky one-string syrup.
6. Roll the warm fried pieces in the syrup off the heat until glazed all over, then lift them onto a plate before they clump.
7. Scatter with slivered nuts and let the glaze set before serving.
Waza tips:
- Fry at a lazy sizzle; tosha should colour in minutes, not seconds.
- Glaze in batches and keep the syrup just warm — cold syrup crystallises coarse and snowy.
Common mistakes:
- Kneading the dough hard, which makes the crumb tight and bready.
- Soaking instead of glazing — tosha is not meant to be syrup-logged.
At home: Full-cream milk powder moistened with a little cream substitutes for khoya where it is unavailable.
Serving: Serve at room temperature with kahwa or noon chai.

chunks.title: Walnut Halwa (Doon Halwa)
chunks.text:
Walnut Halwa (Doon Halwa) is on Wazwan Way under Desserts. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted).
Ground Kashmiri walnuts roasted slowly in ghee with milk and sugar until they gather into a dark, fudgy halwa that smells of toasted orchards. Doon halwa is the valley's walnut crop at its most indulgent.
Kashmir grows most of India's walnuts — doon — and the harvest works its way into chutneys, breads and this halwa, a winter and festival sweet sold in Srinagar's old-city sweet shops and made at home for guests. Unlike flour halwas it is nearly all nut: ground walnuts take the place of semolina, so the cooking is a patient low roast that must never scorch. A properly made doon halwa is moist, coarse-grained and bitter-edged under the sweetness, the way walnuts themselves are.

chunks.title: Recipe: Walnut Halwa
chunks.text:
Recipe for Walnut Halwa, as written on Wazwan Way.
Ground Kashmiri walnuts roasted slowly in ghee with milk and sugar until they gather into a dark, fudgy halwa that smells of toasted orchards. Doon halwa is the valley's walnut crop at its most indulgent.
Serves 6. Prep 15 min. Cook 40 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 250 g walnut kernels, plus a few halves to finish
- 4 tbsp ghee
- 2 tbsp fine semolina (optional, for binding)
- 350 ml full-fat milk
- 130 g sugar
- 4 green cardamoms, seeds ground
- 1 pinch saffron threads, bloomed in warm milk (optional)
Method:
1. Pulse the walnuts to a coarse meal — stop well before they turn to paste.
2. Melt the ghee in a heavy pan, add the walnut meal (and semolina if using) and roast on low heat, stirring constantly, until darker by a shade and richly fragrant, 12-15 minutes.
3. Warm the milk with the sugar until dissolved.
4. Pour the sweet milk into the walnuts carefully — it will sputter — and stir.
5. Cook on low, stirring, until the halwa absorbs the milk, thickens, and begins to leave the sides of the pan, 15-18 minutes.
6. Stir in the cardamom and saffron, cook 2 minutes more until the ghee glistens at the edges, and serve warm topped with walnut halves.
Waza tips:
- Walnuts scorch quietly and turn bitter — keep the flame low and the spoon moving.
- Stop grinding at coarse meal; over-ground walnuts release oil and make the halwa greasy.
Common mistakes:
- Roasting on high heat to save time, which bitters the entire batch.
- Adding all the milk at once cold, which seizes the roast.
At home: Any fresh walnut works, but taste them first — stale walnuts make a rancid halwa no sugar can rescue.
Serving: Serve warm in small portions with kahwa; it is rich enough that a little satisfies.

chunks.title: Waza Kokur (Dum Kokur)
chunks.text:
Waza Kokur (Dum Kokur) is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: Medium. Tradition: Shared (variants noted). In the feast: the gravies.
Whole chicken cooked in the traditional style of a Kashmiri Waza.
Waza Kokur is a ceremonial chicken course in Wazwan, often served as halves or as whole birds cooked in the elaborate style of the master Waza. It adds variety to the broader meat-heavy progression of the feast.
Dum Kokur belongs to the dum tradition of covered, slow, low-heat cooking that runs through Kashmiri and broader North Indian kitchens (the same principle behind Dum Aloo). It is a popular home and festive dish in both communities, On Wazwan Way, Dum Kokur and Waza Kokur name the same dish — this one. (Dhaniwal Korma, the coriander korma, is a separate preparation and is cross-referenced, not merged.) Unlike the yakhni family, Dum Kokur happily uses Kashmiri chilli for colour and, in most modern recipes, onion and ginger-garlic — with Pandit cooks historically omitting the garlic. It has no fixed slot in the formal Wazwan; its home is the family table.
While lamb and mutton heavily dominate the Wazwan feast, Waza Kokur was introduced to add variety and a lighter protein option to the elaborate sequence of courses. The traditional preparation of this chicken dish involves cooking whole halves of the bird in a delicately spiced, saffron-infused gravy, a technique perfected by the master Wazas over centuries. It highlights the adaptability of Kashmiri feast cooking, ensuring that even within a rigid, historic culinary structure, there is a balanced progression of flavors and textures for the guests.
Tip: A good choice if you want something more approachable than lamb-heavy dishes while still staying within the structure of a true Wazwan meal.

chunks.title: Recipe: Waza Kokur
chunks.text:
Recipe for Waza Kokur, as written on Wazwan Way.
Bone-in chicken marinated in yogurt, fennel and Kashmiri chilli, then cooked down slowly under a lid — on dum — until the moisture concentrates and the oil rises through a clinging red-gold masala. It is the chicken dish Kashmiris make when they want depth rather than delicacy.
Serves 4. Prep 23 min. Cook 53 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 1 kg bone-in chicken, cut into large pieces
- For the marinade: 150 g full-fat yogurt, whisked
- 2 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder (colour-forward, mild)
- 2 tsp fennel powder
- 1 tsp dried ginger powder (sonth)
- 1/2 tsp turmeric
- 2 tsp ginger-garlic paste (Pandit-style: use crushed fresh ginger only, no garlic)
- 1.5 tsp salt, or to taste
- For the pot: 4 tbsp mustard oil
- 1 medium onion, finely sliced
- 1 bay leaf
- 1 piece cinnamon (about 3 cm)
- 4 cloves
- 4 green cardamom pods, crushed
- 2 black cardamom pods, crushed
- 1 tsp roasted cumin powder
- 1/2 tsp garam masala (to finish)
Method:
1. Whisk together all the marinade ingredients, coat the chicken thoroughly and set aside for at least 2 hours (refrigerated), ideally 3.
2. Heat the mustard oil in a heavy, lidded pot until its rawness cooks off. Add the bay leaf, cinnamon and cloves and let them crackle.
3. Add the sliced onion and fry over medium heat, stirring, until evenly golden brown (roughly 8–10 minutes) — this is the body of the gravy, so take it to true colour without burning.
4. Add the marinated chicken along with every scrap of the marinade. Sear over medium-high heat for 5–6 minutes, turning, until the masala clings and the yogurt's raw smell cooks off.
5. Stir in the roasted cumin powder and both crushed cardamoms. Add about 250 ml of water, scrape the base, and bring to a simmer.
6. Cover with a tight lid, drop the heat to low, and cook on dum for 25–30 minutes, disturbing it only once or twice, until the chicken is completely tender.
7. Uncover and simmer gently until the gravy tightens around the chicken and the oil separates and pools at the edges — the visual signal that the dum has done its work (roughly 8–10 minutes).
8. Dust with garam masala, cover for a final 2 minutes off the heat, and serve.
Waza tips:
- The dish is ready when you see oil, not when the clock says so — 'tel upar aana' (oil rising) is the only doneness test that matters.
- Marinate in yogurt long enough for the fennel and sonth to penetrate; a rushed 20-minute marinade gives a coated chicken, not a seasoned one.
- Seal the lid with a rope of atta dough for a truer dum if your lid is loose.
- Use Kashmiri chilli generously and hot chilli sparingly — the target is a deep brick colour with gentle warmth.
Common mistakes:
- Lifting the lid repeatedly during the dum stage, venting the steam that is supposed to do the cooking.
- Pale, undercooked onions, which leave the gravy watery and sweet in the wrong way.
- Using hot red chilli in Kashmiri-chilli quantities and scorching the dish.
- Stopping before the oil separates, which leaves the masala tasting raw.
At home: Any heavy lidded pot or Dutch oven delivers a respectable dum; in a pinch, finish the covered stage in a 160°C oven for even, unattended heat. If mustard oil is unavailable, use ghee — the dish tolerates richness better than the yakhni family does. Bone-in thighs and drumsticks alone work better than breast, which dries out during the dum.
Serving: Serve with plain rice or Kashmiri girda bread. It sits well next to a white dish — Kokur Yakhni or a raita — that offsets its depth.

chunks.title: Waza Kokur: A home version, battered and fried
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Waza Kokur page: A home version, battered and fried.
A home version of the feast's chicken is boiled in its marinade, then battered and fried until crisp.
500 g of chicken pieces, cut deeply, are marinated for at least 2 hours, or overnight, in ½ cup white vinegar with 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 tbsp red chilli powder, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp fennel powder, 1 tsp cumin powder, 1 tbsp coriander powder, 1 tbsp meat masala, ½ tsp dry ginger powder and salt.
The chicken is boiled in the marinade for about 15 minutes, until four-fifths cooked, then coated in a thick batter of the same spice mixture with ½–1 cup of cornflour and deep-fried in batches until golden and crisp, 5–7 minutes a piece.

chunks.title: Waza Kokur: Dum kokur, a home dish
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Waza Kokur page: Dum kokur, a home dish.
Dum kokur is also the name of a home dish: chicken cooked on dum with yogurt, saffron and mint and finished with a little honey.
750 g of chicken is marinated for at least 2 hours, and preferably overnight, in 2 cups of thick whisked yogurt and ¼ cup of saffron milk with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 handfuls of chopped fresh mint, 4–5 chopped green chillies, 2 tbsp Kashmiri chilli powder, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp fennel powder, 1 tbsp coriander powder, salt and 2 tbsp mustard or cooking oil.
In a deep, heavy pan, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3–4 green cardamom pods, 1 black cardamom pod, 3–4 cloves and a small stick of cinnamon go into hot oil, then 2 thinly sliced onions, fried golden brown, and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste. The marinated chicken is added and brought to the boil, with 1 tsp dried fenugreek leaves and ½–1 tsp chilli flakes. It is covered and cooked on a low heat until the chicken is done, the gravy thick and the oil separating, and 1–2 tsp of honey is stirred in at the end.

chunks.title: Waza Palak
chunks.text:
Waza Palak is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Wazwan (Muslim). In the feast: alongside.
Spinach cooked in the traditional style of Kashmiri master chefs.
Waza Palak brings spinach into the Wazwan repertoire, offering a softer green note within an otherwise meat-forward feast. It serves as a balancing course with earthy character and gentle seasoning.
The waza's spinach is a different creature from the home pot of palak: praan (browned shallot paste) gives it sweetness and body, the oil is unapologetic, and the leaves are cooked until they collapse into a dense, spoonable green that holds its place on the trami. It is one of the few green vegetables granted a seat at the wazwan, often paired with paneer or served straight. The dish should taste of smoke, sweetness and iron in that order.
Waza Palak brings a crucial touch of vibrant green and earthy flavor to the predominantly meat-heavy Wazwan spread. Historically, leafy greens have always played a significant role in the Kashmiri diet due to the region's agricultural cycles, and integrating them into the grand feast was a way to provide balance and aid digestion. Prepared with a gentle hand and subtle spices, this dish demonstrates the Waza's ability to elevate humble, everyday vegetables into a course worthy of a celebratory banquet.
Tip: A smart choice if you want a lighter, greener dish between richer meat courses or if your table wants more balance in the feast.

chunks.title: Recipe: Waza Palak
chunks.text:
Recipe for Waza Palak, as written on Wazwan Way.
Spinach cooked down glossy and dark in mustard oil with browned shallots, whole spices and a measured hand of Kashmiri chilli — spinach as the wazas plate it, rich enough to sit beside the meat courses.
Serves 4. Prep 15 min. Cook 30 min. Level: Easy.
Ingredients:
- 600 g spinach, washed and roughly chopped
- 4 tbsp mustard oil
- 2 tbsp browned shallot paste (praan) or 2 small shallots, sliced and browned
- 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
- 1 tsp fennel powder
- 1/2 tsp dry ginger powder (sonth)
- 2 cloves and 1 green cardamom
- Salt to taste
Method:
1. Heat the mustard oil to smoking in a heavy pan, settle it, and add the cloves and cardamom.
2. Add the shallot paste and fry until it deepens a shade.
3. Add the chilli powder with a splash of water and stir until the oil colours.
4. Pile in the spinach with salt, cover, and let it collapse, 4-5 minutes.
5. Uncover and cook on a brisk flame, stirring, until the water is gone and the spinach turns dark, glossy and thick, 12-15 minutes.
6. Stir in fennel and sonth, cook 2 minutes more, and serve.
Waza tips:
- Cook past the bright-green stage — waza palak is meant to be deep, dark and concentrated.
- The oil should re-emerge at the edges when the dish is done.
Common mistakes:
- Serving it wet — the dish must hold its shape on the spoon.
- Skipping the shallots, which supply the sweetness that balances the mustard oil.
At home: Frozen leaf spinach, squeezed dry, collapses the timeline; brown ordinary shallots if praan paste is not on hand.
Serving: Serve alongside rogan josh or yakhni with rice; it also pairs naturally with fried paneer.

chunks.title: Waza Palak: With meatballs: palak riste
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Waza Palak page: With meatballs: palak riste.
The wazas also cook spinach with small meatballs, as palak riste. A waza makes it like this.
For the riste, 500 g of boneless mutton and about 150 g of mutton fat are pounded separately on stone until smooth, then pounded together, the fat at about 30 per cent, into a fine paste. Small balls of it are boiled gently in water with 3–4 green cardamom pods, a piece of cinnamon, 1 tsp garlic paste, 1 tsp dry ginger powder, ½ tsp turmeric and salt. Once they are cooked, 2 tbsp fried-shallot paste and ½ cup of chilli water go in and the pot simmers on a low heat.
For the spinach, 500 g is blanched, strained, squeezed dry and roughly chopped, then fried with 1 tbsp garlic paste and salt in 2 tbsp oil. 2 tbsp desi ghee is added, then the riste with their gravy, and the two simmer together for a few minutes.

chunks.title: Wazwan Mushroom (Kanaguchhi Yakhni)
chunks.text:
Wazwan Mushroom (Kanaguchhi Yakhni) is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted). In the feast: alongside.
A mushroom-based Wazwan preparation that adds a softer vegetarian note to the feast.
Wazwaan Mushroom is a rarer mushroom-centered dish within the broader Wazwan repertoire. It brings an earthy texture and a change of pace from the dominant meat courses.
Morels (Morchella species) cannot be commercially cultivated; every guchhi is found wild, mostly at 2,000–3,500 metres in Kashmir, Himachal and Uttarakhand forests after spring snowmelt, which is why sources including Village Square call them the world's priciest mushrooms — reported retail figures for dried guchhi range roughly from ₹20,000 to ₹40,000+ per kilogram depending on grade (Village Square, Himalayan Kart and Kashmiri retailer listings; figures vary widely by source and season). In Kashmir they are a festive ingredient rather than an everyday one. Kashmiri Pandit cuisine holds them especially dear as a luxurious vegetarian centrepiece — kanaguchhi yakhean (morels in rich yogurt gravy) and kan gucch pulao appear in Pandit household repertoires and on celebratory menus — while Kashmiri Muslim cooking also embraces morels, including with meat (kanaguchhi gosht, lamb-and-morel yakhni). Wikipedia's survey of Kashmiri dishes lists morel preparations across both traditions. The yogurt-fennel-ginger yakhni treatment given here, with asafoetida and no onion or garlic, follows the form documented on Kashmiri home-cooking sites. On Wazwan Way this dish carries the house name "Wazwan Mushroom" — a branding choice; its traditional name is Guchhi Yakhni (Kanaguchhi Yakhni).
Mushrooms, particularly wild varieties foraged from the surrounding forests, have a special, seasonal place in Kashmiri culinary history. Wazwaan Mushroom is a relatively rare but highly esteemed dish within the traditional feast, offering a meaty, umami-rich texture that appeals to both vegetarians and meat-eaters alike. The preparation mirrors the careful, slow-cooked techniques used for premium meats, highlighting how traditional Wazas have adapted their historic spice blends to complement the earthy, delicate nature of local fungi.
Tip: This is worth trying if you want a vegetarian Wazwan dish that feels more unusual and less commonly seen than standard paneer or potato options.

chunks.title: Recipe: Wazwan Mushroom
chunks.text:
Recipe for Wazwan Mushroom, as written on Wazwan Way.
Kashmir's wild morels — guchhi or kanaguchhi — are among the most expensive foods the Valley produces, foraged by hand from Himalayan forests for a few weeks each spring. Cooked waza-style in a yogurt, fennel and dried-ginger gravy, their honeycombed caps soak up the yakhni like nothing else in the Kashmiri repertoire.
Serves 3–4. Prep 35 min. Cook 30 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 25–30 g dried guchhi/morels (about 15–20 medium mushrooms; buy whole, not pieces, to judge quality)
- 500 ml warm water, for soaking
- 400 g full-fat plain yogurt, whisked completely smooth
- 3 tbsp mustard oil (or ghee)
- 1/8 tsp asafoetida (hing)
- 1/2 tsp cumin seeds
- 2 green cardamom pods, lightly cracked
- 1 black cardamom pod
- 2 cloves
- 2 tsp fennel powder (saunf)
- 1 tsp dried ginger powder (sonth)
- Salt, to taste
- 1/2 tsp black cumin (shahi jeera), for finishing
- 1 crushed black cardamom, for finishing (optional, waza-style)
Method:
1. Soak the dried morels in the warm water for 20–30 minutes until soft and pliable (some cooks use hot water for 15 minutes; either works, but do not shortcut — a stiff morel hides grit).
2. Lift the morels OUT of the soaking water with your fingers — never pour the bowl through a sieve, or the grit settled at the bottom goes straight back over the mushrooms.
3. Halve each morel lengthwise and rinse under running water, rubbing gently inside the honeycomb pits — sand and forest grit lodge deep in the ridges, and this step is non-negotiable. Squeeze gently and set aside.
4. Strain the soaking liquid through muslin or a coffee filter, leaving the last gritty spoonful behind, and reserve about 250 ml — it carries deep morel flavour into the gravy.
5. Heat the mustard oil in a heavy pan until it just smokes, then lower the heat. Fry the morels 2–3 minutes until lightly seared and aromatic; remove and set aside.
6. In the same oil over low heat, add the asafoetida, cumin seeds, cracked green cardamom, black cardamom and cloves; let them sizzle 15–20 seconds.
7. Whisk the fennel powder, dried ginger powder and salt into the yogurt along with a splash of water. With the pan on low heat, pour in the yogurt and stir continuously in one direction until it comes to a full boil — constant stirring is what keeps a yakhni from splitting (roughly 6–8 minutes; the gravy is ready to move on when it looks glossy and small beads of fat appear at the edges).
8. Add the fried morels and the strained soaking liquid. Simmer uncovered on low heat for 15–20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the morels are tender through and the gravy has body — it should coat the back of a spoon but still pour, looser than a cream sauce.
9. Finish with black cumin and crushed black cardamom, simmer one minute more, and take off the heat. Rest 5 minutes before serving; the gravy settles and the morels finish drinking it in.
Waza tips:
- Buy whole dried morels and inspect the stems — broken pieces and dust-heavy bags are how poor grades are moved at guchhi prices.
- The soaking liquid is half the dish. Strain it obsessively and use it; discarding it throws away the flavour you paid for.
- Stir the yogurt in one direction only and never leave it before the first boil — a split yakhni cannot be rescued.
- Morels must never be eaten raw or barely cooked; a proper simmer is traditional and also what renders them safe and tender.
Common mistakes:
- Pouring the soaking bowl through a strainer over the morels, re-depositing the grit you just soaked out.
