- Skipping the lengthwise halving — whole morels hide sand (and occasionally insects) inside the hollow cap.
- Adding cold yogurt to a hot pan and walking away, guaranteeing a curdled gravy.
- Drowning the morels in a thick, over-reduced gravy; a yakhni is delicate and pourable, and the morel must stay the star.
At home: If guchhi is beyond reach, imported dried morels behave identically, and in a pinch dried shiitake or fresh button mushrooms can carry the same yakhni gravy — honest, though no longer the same dish. Ghee substitutes cleanly for mustard oil. Use a heavy-bottomed pan and full-fat yogurt at room temperature to make the no-split boil far more forgiving; a teaspoon of the yogurt whisked with rice flour is a pragmatic (non-traditional) insurance policy against curdling.
Serving: Serve hot over plain steamed rice, which is how every source presents it. On a festive Pandit menu it stands as a luxurious vegetarian main; alongside a wazwan-style spread it plays the rich vegetarian counterpoint to the meat courses.

chunks.title: Wazwan Mushroom: With ordinary mushrooms: a quick curry
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Wazwan Mushroom page: With ordinary mushrooms: a quick curry.
A quick Wazwan-style mushroom curry uses canned or fresh button mushrooms and takes about 15 minutes.
1 cup of yogurt is whisked with 2–3 green cardamom pods, a small stick of cinnamon, 3–4 cloves and 1 tbsp gram flour over a high flame until it boils and thickens a little, and is set aside.
In another pan 2 medium onions, thinly sliced, are fried golden in 2–3 tbsp oil. In goes 1 cup of mushrooms (halved, if fresh), then salt, a pinch of turmeric and red chilli, coriander, cumin, fennel and dry ginger powders to taste. The yogurt is poured in and cooked until the oil starts to separate, and the curry is finished with 1 tsp dried mint and fresh coriander.

chunks.title: Yakhni (Neni Yakhni)
chunks.text:
Yakhni (Neni Yakhni) is on Wazwan Way under Wazwan. Diet: Non-veg. Spice level given on the site: Mild. Tradition: Shared (variants noted). In the feast: the gravies.
A curd-based Kashmiri gravy that also appears as a dish in the Wazwan repertoire.
Yakhni is a yogurt-based gravy associated with several Kashmiri preparations and also appears in Wazwan as a notable part of the feast structure. Its flavor is soothing, aromatic, and gently spiced.
The word yakhni comes from Persian, where it means 'store of food' (in the northern subcontinent it now means stock), and in Kashmir it names a whole family of curd-based dishes rather than a single recipe. Mutton yakhni appears both on the Wazwan trami and in everyday home cooking, and it is the dish Kashmiris reach for when they want comfort rather than fire. Both communities cook it, with a meaningful split: Kashmiri Muslim wazas often enrich the gravy with praan (a fried shallot emulsion) and sometimes garlic, while the Kashmiri Pandit version omits onion and garlic entirely and leans on asafoetida. The two-stage method — boiling the meat with whole fennel and ginger, straining, then rebuilding the gravy on curd — is the older, more formal technique recorded in mid-20th-century household cooking and in the 2006 booklet reference.
The word yakhni is Persian, where it means "store of food". A meat stew of that name began in medieval Iranian cooking and spread east and west; in the northern Indian subcontinent the word now means a meat stock or broth (Wikipedia). In Kashmir it has meant meat cooked in curd since at least the 16th century. Kashmir Life, drawing on the Tuhfat-ul-Ahbab, lists yakhni ("meat cooked in curd") among the special foods of 16th-century feasts, with kabab and pulao, and notes that these dishes point to the Persianate world. Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes says instead that it came to Kashmir with the Mughal emperor Akbar, who annexed it in 1586. We have found no earlier record. Both spellings, yakhni and yakhin, are in use (Wikipedia).
Tip: If you enjoy milder gravies, yakhni is one of the most approachable dishes in a Wazwan.

chunks.title: Recipe: Yakhni
chunks.text:
Recipe for Yakhni, as written on Wazwan Way.
Yakhni is mutton in a yogurt gravy with fennel, dry ginger and dried mint. This is a home version: the mutton is pressure-cooked, and an egg whisked into the yogurt keeps it from curdling.
Prep 20 min. Cook 50 min. Level: Moderate.
Ingredients:
- 500 g mutton, preferably fatty
- 2–3 green cardamom pods, 1 black cardamom pod, 1 stick of cinnamon and 4–5 cloves
- Salt, to taste
- 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste
- 2–3 cups water, for cooking the mutton
- 1 cup yogurt
- 1 egg
- 3 tbsp mustard oil
- 2 shallots or onions, thinly sliced
- 1 tsp fennel powder
- 1 tsp dry ginger powder
- ½ tsp garam masala
- 1 tbsp ghee
- 1 tbsp dried mint powder
Method:
1. Pressure-cook the mutton with the whole spices, salt, ginger-garlic paste and water until tender, 3–4 whistles. Keep the stock.
2. Whisk the yogurt with the egg until smooth. Cook it over a high flame, stirring all the time, until it boils.
3. Heat the mustard oil and fry the sliced shallots until golden brown. Blend them to a smooth paste.
4. To the boiled yogurt add the fennel, dry ginger and garam masala, then the cooked mutton, its stock, the ghee and the shallot paste.
5. Sprinkle in the dried mint and simmer for 10–15 minutes.
6. Serve hot with steamed rice.
Tips:
- The egg is there to stop the yogurt curdling; keep stirring until it boils.
- Fry the shallots to a golden brown before blending them.
- Be generous with the dried mint.
Serving: Ladle it directly over hot plain rice — the classic pairing. At a Wazwan it comes late, the last of the gravies before gushtaba.
About this recipe: This is a home version, with a pressure cooker and an egg in the yogurt.

chunks.title: Yakhni: What yakhni is
chunks.text:
In Kashmir, yakhni is a light, yogurt-based meat dish, usually mutton, flavoured with fennel, ginger and cardamom and eaten with rice (Wikipedia). Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes describes it as a mild mutton gravy without turmeric or chilli powder (Wikipedia), and Gulf News describes the Wazwan yakhni as mutton "stewed in curd and some delectable herbs", "sumptuous and thick" (Gulf News).
The two communities make it differently. Pandit cooks traditionally rely on asafoetida and curd rather than onion and garlic (JKTDC), while the yakhni Sahapedia describes for gushtaba, a Wazwan dish, includes shallots, ginger and garlic paste (Sahapedia).

chunks.title: Yakhni: Its place in the feast
chunks.text: At a Wazwan, yakhni comes late. Outlook India's account of the order runs from methi maaz, rista and rogan josh through daniwal korma, marchwangan korma and aab gosht to yakhni, "the finishing dish served in wazwan before gushtaba" (Outlook India). Gulf News also has it "towards the close" (Gulf News). How Wazwan Is Served covers the order of the courses.

chunks.title: Yakhni: Other yakhnis
chunks.text: The same curd gravy goes into other dishes. Wikipedia's Wazwan article describes it as the gravy typically made for gushtaba, "although it is also part of other dishes" (Wikipedia). Its list of Kashmiri dishes includes vegetable yakhnis of lotus stem (nadir yakhean), bottle gourd (al yakhean), mushrooms, bitter gourd and fried aubergine (Wikipedia). Sahapedia calls nadru, lotus stem, a staple of Kashmiri households and names nadru yakhni as a common way of cooking it (Sahapedia).

chunks.title: Shabdeg
chunks.text:
Shabdeg is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Non-veg.
Shabdeg is a Kashmiri winter dish that usually cooks overnight. This home version, with country chicken and pumpkin, is made in about an hour.
Shabdeg is a traditional Kashmiri winter dish that usually cooks slowly overnight. This is a quick home version: country chicken and fried pumpkin with dried plums, made in a pressure cooker in about an hour.

chunks.title: Recipe: Shabdeg
chunks.text:
Recipe for Shabdeg, as written on Wazwan Way.
This is a modern, fast version of shabdeg. The chicken is cooked under pressure with fried-onion paste and Kashmiri spices, and the fried pumpkin and dried plums go in for the last few minutes. Any chicken can be used in place of country chicken.
Serves 3–4.
Ingredients:
- 700–800 g country chicken, or any chicken
- 3 tbsp oil
- 1 tsp cumin seeds
- 1 bay leaf, 3–4 cloves, 3 green cardamom pods, 1 black cardamom pod and a small stick of cinnamon
- 2 medium onions, sliced
- Salt, to taste
- 1½ tbsp ginger-garlic paste
- ½ tsp turmeric
- 2 tbsp Kashmiri red chilli powder
- 1 tbsp coriander powder
- 1 tbsp fennel powder
- ½ tsp dry ginger powder
- 1 tsp garam masala
- ½ tsp black pepper
- ½–1 tsp ver masala (Kashmiri masala paste), optional
- 3 tbsp fried-onion paste
- 1 cup fried pumpkin cubes
- 10–12 dried plums (aloo bukhara)
- 1–1½ cups water
Method:
1. Heat the oil in a pressure cooker. Add the cumin seeds and whole spices and let them give up their aroma.
2. Add the sliced onions and salt and fry until golden brown. Stir in the ginger-garlic paste.
3. Add the turmeric, chilli powder, coriander powder, fennel powder, dry ginger powder, garam masala and black pepper. Cook for 30–40 seconds.
4. Add the chicken and fry until it changes colour and is coated in the spices.
5. Stir in the ver masala, if you are using it, and the fried-onion paste.
6. Pour in the water, close the lid and cook under pressure until the chicken is about four-fifths done: roughly 10–15 minutes, depending on the chicken.
7. Add the fried pumpkin and the dried plums. Cover and simmer on a low heat for 5–7 minutes, then serve.
Tips:
- The ver masala is optional, but it does a great deal for the aroma.
- How long the chicken needs under pressure depends on the bird.

chunks.title: Dagith Haakh (Pounded collard greens)
chunks.text:
Dagith Haakh (Pounded collard greens) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Veg.
Dagith haakh is Kashmiri pounded collard greens: boiled, squeezed and pounded, then cooked in mustard oil with garlic, green chillies and fried onion.
Dagith haakh is pounded haakh, Kashmiri collard greens. The leaves are boiled, squeezed dry and pounded to a coarse mash, then cooked in mustard oil with a paste of garlic and green chillies, a few ground spices and fried onion. It is eaten with steamed rice.

chunks.title: Recipe: Dagith Haakh
chunks.text:
Recipe for Dagith Haakh, as written on Wazwan Way.
Mustard greens or spinach can be used in place of haakh; the method is the same.
Ingredients:
- 500 g fresh haakh (collard greens), or mustard greens or spinach
- ¼ tsp baking soda
- Water, for boiling
- 4–5 green chillies, or to taste
- 6–7 cloves garlic
- 3–4 tbsp mustard oil
- 1 large onion, thinly sliced
- 1 tsp cumin seeds
- 2 dried red chillies
- 1 tsp coriander powder
- ½ tsp cumin powder
- 1 tsp fennel powder
- ½ tsp dry ginger powder
- Salt, to taste
Method:
1. Wash the greens well and tear them roughly. Add them to boiling water with the baking soda and cook until tender.
2. Drain the greens, squeeze out the water and pound them to a coarse mash.
3. Crush the green chillies and garlic to a coarse paste in a mortar.
4. Heat the mustard oil and fry the sliced onion until golden brown. Lift it out and keep it aside.
5. In the same oil, add the cumin seeds and dried red chillies, then the garlic and chilli paste, and fry for 1–2 minutes.
6. Stir in the pounded greens, the salt and the coriander, cumin, fennel and ginger powders. Cook for a few minutes.
7. Add a little water and the fried onion and cook until the oil separates. Serve hot with steamed rice.

chunks.title: Tchok Wangan (Sour aubergines)
chunks.text:
Tchok Wangan (Sour aubergines) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Veg.
Tchok wangan is Kashmiri sour aubergine: fried in mustard oil, then simmered in a hot, tangy gravy soured with lemon, tamarind or raw grape juice.
Tchok wangan, khatte baingan in Hindi, is aubergine fried in mustard oil and simmered in a sour, chilli-red gravy. The sourness comes from lemon juice, tamarind, vinegar or the juice of raw grapes.

chunks.title: Recipe: Tchok Wangan
chunks.text:
Recipe for Tchok Wangan, as written on Wazwan Way.
Small aubergines are slit into quarters and fried until soft before they meet the gravy. Adjust every spice to your own taste.
Ingredients:
- 6–8 small aubergines (brinjal), slit into quarters
- 4–5 tbsp mustard oil
- 1 tbsp cumin seeds
- 2 tbsp Kashmiri red chilli powder
- ½ tsp turmeric
- ½ tbsp fennel powder
- ½ tsp dry ginger powder
- 1 tbsp coriander powder
- 2–3 cloves
- About 1 cup water
- 6–7 green chillies
- 1½–2 tbsp lemon juice, tamarind pulp, vinegar or raw grape juice, to taste
- ¼ tsp garam masala
- Salt, to taste
Method:
1. Heat the mustard oil until it smokes, lower the flame and fry the aubergines until golden and soft. Lift them out.
2. In another pan, heat 1–2 tbsp of the same oil. Add the cumin seeds and let them splutter.
3. Lower the flame, add the red chilli powder and fry it for a few seconds, then pour in the water. Add the rest of the ground spices and the cloves.
4. Add the fried aubergines and the green chillies. Cover and simmer on a low heat for 5–6 minutes, until the aubergines have taken up the gravy.
5. Stir in the lemon juice, or whichever souring you are using, and the garam masala. Cook for 2–3 minutes.
6. Let it rest for a while before serving.
Tips:
- It tastes even better the next day.
- Use whichever souring you have: lemon juice, tamarind pulp, vinegar or raw grape juice.

chunks.title: Tchok Wangan: Another version, with onion, garlic and sour grape juice
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Tchok Wangan page: Another version, with onion, garlic and sour grape juice.
There is a second way of making the dish. ½ kg of long Chinese aubergines are each cut into 4 long pieces, washed, drained and salted, then fried golden brown in 2 cups of refined or mustard oil in a deep pan and lifted out.
2 cups of sliced onions are cooked in the same pan on a medium flame. A handful of garlic, 4–5 green chillies, 2 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp ginger powder, 1 tbsp cumin seeds, 3 tsp fennel powder, salt and some water go in and cook until the spices are done.
The gravy is brought to the boil and the fried aubergines are boiled in it for 5 minutes. 1 cup of sour grape juice (or tamarind pulp, lemon or vinegar) is added, and it boils for 2 minutes more, or until the oil separates.

chunks.title: Bezze Wangan (Roasted aubergine mash)
chunks.text:
Bezze Wangan (Roasted aubergine mash) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Veg.
Bezze wangan is Kashmiri-style baingan bharta: aubergines roasted over coals, mashed, and cooked in mustard oil with pounded garlic, chillies and coriander.
Bezze wangan is the Kashmiri way with baingan ka bharta. Aubergines are charred over live coals or a gas flame, peeled and mashed, then cooked in mustard oil with fried onion and a freshly pounded paste of garlic, green chillies and coriander.

chunks.title: Recipe: Bezze Wangan
chunks.text:
Recipe for Bezze Wangan, as written on Wazwan Way.
Two things matter here: roasting the aubergines over coals where you can, and pounding the paste fresh in a mortar.
Ingredients:
- 2 large aubergines (brinjal)
- 1 bowl cold water, for peeling
- 6–7 cloves garlic
- 2 green chillies, or to taste
- 1 small bunch fresh coriander
- 3 tbsp mustard oil, or any cooking oil
- 1 large onion, finely sliced
- ½ tsp cumin seeds
- ½ tsp coriander powder
- ¼ tsp dry ginger powder
- Salt, to taste
Method:
1. Roast the aubergines over live coals, or on a gas flame, turning them until the skin is charred and the flesh soft.
2. Drop them into the cold water, peel off the burnt skin and mash the flesh with a fork.
3. Pound the garlic, green chillies and coriander leaves coarsely in a mortar.
4. Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai and fry the onion until golden brown. Add the cumin seeds, coriander powder, dry ginger powder and salt.
5. Mix in the mashed aubergine and the pounded paste. Cook on a medium heat, stirring now and then, until the oil separates.
6. Serve hot with Kashmiri roti, paratha or plain rice.
Tips:
- Live coals are better than a gas flame for roasting.
- It tastes even better the next day.

chunks.title: Teher (Turmeric rice with fried onions)
chunks.text:
Teher (Turmeric rice with fried onions) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Veg.
Teher is Kashmiri turmeric rice dressed with mustard oil, cumin and fried onions, cooked and shared out on happy occasions.
Teher is rice boiled with turmeric, finished on dum, and dressed with hot mustard oil, cumin and crisp fried onions. In Kashmiri households it is cooked to mark a happy or auspicious occasion and shared out as tabarruk, blessed food.

chunks.title: Recipe: Teher
chunks.text:
Recipe for Teher, as written on Wazwan Way.
Teher is served plain, mixed gently just before serving, and needs nothing alongside it.
Ingredients:
- 2 cups rice, such as basmati
- Water, for boiling
- ½ tsp turmeric powder
- Salt, to taste
- 3–4 tbsp mustard oil
- 2 medium onions, thinly sliced
- 1½ tsp cumin seeds
Method:
1. Wash the rice and soak it for 20–30 minutes.
2. Bring plenty of water to the boil in a large pot with the turmeric and salt. Add the rice and cook until it is 70–75 per cent done, with a bite still in the grain.
3. Drain the rice completely and return it to the pot. Cover tightly and leave on a very low heat (dum) for 8–10 minutes, until it is cooked through and fluffy.
4. Heat the mustard oil in a pan until it smokes, then lower the heat. Fry the sliced onions until deep golden and crisp.
5. Spread the rice on a large plate. Sprinkle it with a little more salt and the cumin, pour the oil over it and top with the fried onions.
6. Mix gently just before serving, so that every grain is coated.

chunks.title: Nadru Kofta (Nadre Machh)
chunks.text:
Nadru Kofta (Nadre Machh) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Veg.
Nadru kofta, or nadre machh, is grated lotus stem bound with gram flour, fried in mustard oil and simmered in a spiced yogurt gravy. A Kashmiri recipe.
Nadru kofta, also called nadre machh, is koftas of grated lotus stem bound with gram flour and spices, fried in mustard oil and then simmered in a tangy yogurt gravy. It is served with steamed rice or plain roti.

chunks.title: Recipe: Nadru Kofta
chunks.text:
Recipe for Nadru Kofta, as written on Wazwan Way.
Soft koftas in a hot, tangy gravy: they are fried first and finish cooking in the yogurt.
Ingredients:
- For the koftas: 2 cups lotus stem (nadru), grated or finely minced
- 3–4 tbsp gram flour (besan), or more
- 2 green chillies, finely chopped
- ½ tsp ajwain (carom seeds)
- 1½ tbsp red chilli powder
- 1 tbsp coriander powder
- 1 tsp cumin seeds
- 1 tsp fennel powder
- Salt, to taste
- Mustard oil, for frying
- For the gravy: 1 cup yogurt, whisked
- ½ tsp turmeric powder
- 1 tsp red chilli powder, or to taste
- 1 tsp fennel powder
- ½ tsp dry ginger powder
- ½ tsp cumin seeds
- 2 tbsp mustard oil
- 2–3 cloves, 2–3 green cardamom pods and 1 bay leaf
- A pinch of asafoetida
- 1½ cups water
- Salt, to taste
- 1 tsp garam masala
- 2 tbsp dried fenugreek leaves (kasuri methi)
Method:
1. Wash and peel the lotus stem. Grate or mince it finely and squeeze out the water.
2. Mix it with the gram flour, green chillies, the kofta spices and salt until it comes together like a dough. Shape it into small oval koftas.
3. Heat mustard oil in a deep pan until it smokes, then lower the heat. Fry the koftas until golden brown and lift them out.
4. Whisk the yogurt with the turmeric, chilli powder, fennel powder, dry ginger powder and cumin seeds.
5. For the gravy, heat the 2 tbsp of mustard oil until it smokes and lower the heat. Add the cloves, cardamom, bay leaf and asafoetida and fry for a few seconds.
6. Pour in the yogurt mixture slowly, stirring all the time so that it does not curdle. Add the water and salt and simmer for 5–7 minutes.
7. Slide in the koftas and cook on a low heat for 5–7 minutes, so that they take up the gravy. Add the garam masala and dried fenugreek leaves, turn off the heat and let it rest for a few minutes before serving.
Tips:
- Squeeze the water out of the grated lotus stem before mixing; add more gram flour if the mixture needs it.
- Add the yogurt slowly and keep stirring, so that it does not curdle.

chunks.title: Gaade te Hoakh Syun (Fish with dried vegetables)
chunks.text:
Gaade te Hoakh Syun (Fish with dried vegetables) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Non-veg.
Gaade te hoakh syun is Kashmiri fish with dried vegetables: fried fish layered over lotus stem with sun-dried tomatoes and aubergines, simmered until thick.
Gaade te hoakh syun is fish with dried vegetables. Pieces of fish are fried crisp in mustard oil, layered over fried lotus stem with soaked sun-dried tomatoes and aubergines and a tomato purée, and simmered with whole and ground spices until the gravy is absorbed. The fish and the dried vegetables are served in two separate dishes.

chunks.title: Recipe: Gaade te Hoakh Syun
chunks.text:
Recipe for Gaade te Hoakh Syun, as written on Wazwan Way.
This recipe is for 1 kg of fish. The spice quantities are a guide; use them to your own taste.
Ingredients:
- 1 kg fish, cleaned and cut into small pieces
- 1 tsp turmeric powder and 1 spoon salt, to marinate the fish
- 50 g sun-dried tomatoes
- 50 g sun-dried aubergines (brinjal)
- 250 g lotus stem (nadru)
- 4–5 tomatoes, puréed
- Mustard oil, for frying, and 1 cup of the same oil for the pot
- 2–3 spoons salt
- 5 spoons red chilli powder
- 2 spoons turmeric powder
- 2 spoons coriander powder
- 1 tbsp cumin seeds
- 2 black cardamom pods, 3 green cardamom pods, 1 small stick of cinnamon and 3 cloves
- 2 spoons ginger-garlic paste
- 2 spoons ver masala, optional
- Water
Method:
1. Pat the fish dry and rub it with the 1 tsp turmeric and 1 spoon of salt. Leave it for 1–2 hours.
2. Soak the dried tomatoes and dried aubergines in warm water for 10–15 minutes.
3. Heat mustard oil until it smokes and fry the fish until golden brown and crisp.
4. Clean the lotus stem, cut it into small pieces and shallow-fry it until it turns light brown.
5. In a large pot, lay the lotus stem at the bottom, then the fish, with the soaked dried vegetables and the tomato purée.
6. Pour in water until the fish is half covered. Add the salt, ground spices, cumin, whole spices, ginger-garlic paste, the ver masala if you are using it, and 1 cup of the mustard oil the fish was fried in.
7. Mix the spices in, cover and simmer until the gravy is absorbed and thick.
8. Let it rest until it has cooled, then serve the fish and the dried vegetables in two separate dishes.
About this recipe: The spice amounts are in spoons, with no size given; treat them as a guide and season to your own taste.

chunks.title: Paneer Kaliya (Kashmiri Pandit style)
chunks.text:
Paneer Kaliya (Kashmiri Pandit style) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Veg. Tradition: Kashmiri Pandit.
Paneer kaliya is a Kashmiri Pandit dish: paneer soaked in turmeric water, fried in mustard oil and simmered in a milk gravy with fennel and dry ginger.
Paneer kaliya is fried paneer in a mild milk gravy, spiced with fennel, dry ginger and turmeric. It belongs to Kashmiri Pandit cooking, and this recipe has no onion, garlic or chilli in it.

chunks.title: Recipe: Paneer Kaliya
chunks.text:
Recipe for Paneer Kaliya, as written on Wazwan Way.
The paneer is soaked in boiling turmeric water, and that water then goes into the gravy with the milk. Serve it with steamed rice or Kashmiri naan.
Ingredients:
- 250 g paneer, cubed
- 2 cups water
- 1 tsp turmeric powder, for the soaking water and the gravy
- 2 tbsp mustard oil
- 1 tsp fennel seeds
- 2–3 green cardamom pods
- 1 stick cinnamon
- 2–3 cloves
- 1 tsp dry ginger powder
- 1 tsp cumin powder
- 1 cup milk
- ½ cup cream, optional
- Salt, to taste
- 2 tbsp dried fenugreek leaves (kasuri methi)
- ½ tsp garam masala
- Fresh coriander, to garnish (optional)
Method:
1. Bring the 2 cups of water to the boil with turmeric. Add the paneer cubes and let them soak for 10 minutes. Keep the water.
2. Heat the mustard oil in a pan until it just begins to smoke. Fry the paneer cubes until golden and set them aside.
3. In the same pan, fry the fennel seeds, cardamom, cinnamon and cloves for 1–2 minutes, until fragrant.
4. Lower the heat and add turmeric, the dry ginger powder and the cumin powder, stirring quickly so that they do not burn. Pour in the turmeric water, the milk and the cream, and add salt.
5. Add the fried paneer and simmer on a low heat for 10–12 minutes, so that it takes up the gravy. Add the dried fenugreek leaves.
6. Sprinkle the garam masala over, stir once more and garnish with fresh coriander if you like.

chunks.title: Alle Korme (Bottle gourd korma)
chunks.text:
Alle Korme (Bottle gourd korma) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Veg.
Alle korme is a mild bottle gourd korma: lauki softened in ghee, then cooked with a paste of fried onions and cashews, milk and cream. Serves 3–4.
Alle korme, lauki ka korma, is bottle gourd cooked slowly in ghee with a paste of fried onions and cashews, milk and a little cream. It is a mild, aromatic korma.

chunks.title: Recipe: Alle Korme
chunks.text:
Recipe for Alle Korme, as written on Wazwan Way.
The gourd is cooked in ghee until it is soft and its moisture has gone before the spices, the paste and the milk go in.
Serves 3–4.
Ingredients:
- 500 g bottle gourd (lauki), peeled and cut into thin slices or strips
- 2 tbsp ghee
- 1 tsp salt, or to taste
- ½ tsp turmeric powder
- 1 tsp fennel powder
- ½ tsp dry ginger powder
- 1 tsp cumin powder
- 1 tbsp coriander powder
- ½ cup fried onions
- 12–15 cashews
- 1 cup milk
- 3 tbsp fresh cream
- 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander
Method:
1. Heat the ghee in a pan. Add the sliced gourd and the salt and cook on a medium heat until it is soft and its moisture has dried off.
2. Add the ground spices and mix well.
3. Grind the fried onions and cashews to a smooth paste and add it to the pan.
4. Pour in the milk and a little of the cream, stir and cover. Cook on a low heat until it comes together into a rich gravy.
5. Finish with the rest of the cream, if you like, and the chopped coriander.

chunks.title: Tchok Mujje (Sour radish)
chunks.text:
Tchok Mujje (Sour radish) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Veg.
Tchok mujje is Kashmiri sour radish: slices of radish fried in mustard oil, then simmered with tamarind and spices until soft.
Tchok mujje, khatti mooli, is a sour radish curry: sliced radish fried golden in mustard oil and simmered in tamarind water with fennel, dry ginger and red chilli. Like tchok wangan, the sour aubergine dish, it is fried first and then simmered in a sour gravy.

chunks.title: Recipe: Tchok Mujje
chunks.text:
Recipe for Tchok Mujje, as written on Wazwan Way.
The radish is fried golden before it meets the sour gravy. Serve it hot with rice or roti.
Ingredients:
- 2–3 medium radishes (mooli), peeled and sliced
- 2–3 tbsp mustard oil
- 1 tsp cumin seeds
- Whole spices, such as cloves, cinnamon and cardamom
- 1 tsp fennel powder
- 1 tsp dry ginger powder
- 1 tbsp red chilli powder
- ½ tsp turmeric powder
- 1 tbsp coriander powder
- Tamarind, soaked in warm water, for its pulp
- Water, as needed
- Salt, to taste
- 2–3 green chillies
Method:
1. Soak the tamarind in warm water and press out the pulp.
2. Heat the mustard oil and fry the sliced radish until golden brown. Lift it out.
3. Pour off the extra oil, leaving 1–2 tbsp in the pan. Add the cumin seeds and whole spices.
4. Turn off the flame and add all the ground spices.
5. Turn the flame back on and add water, the tamarind pulp and salt. Mix well.
6. Add the fried radish and the green chillies and bring to the boil.
7. Cover and cook until the radish is soft and the oil begins to separate.
Tips:
- Add the ground spices with the flame off: it keeps them from burning.
About this recipe: There is no set quantity for the whole spices or the tamarind; add them to your taste.

chunks.title: Tchaer Chetin (Raw apricot chutney)
chunks.text:
Tchaer Chetin (Raw apricot chutney) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Veg.
Tchaer chetin is a Kashmiri chutney of raw apricots pounded with soaked dried red chillies and salt: sour, hot and coarse. Three ingredients.
Tchaer chetin is a chutney of three things: sour raw apricots, dried red chillies soaked until soft, and salt, ground together into a thick, coarse paste. It is sharp and hot.

chunks.title: Recipe: Tchaer Chetin
chunks.text:
Recipe for Tchaer Chetin, as written on Wazwan Way.
The chillies are ground first, and the apricots are crushed into them only briefly.
Ingredients:
- 1 cup raw apricots, washed, stoned and sliced
- 4–6 dried red chillies
- Salt, to taste
- A few drops of water, only if needed
Method:
1. Soak the dried red chillies in warm water for 15–20 minutes, until soft.
2. Grind them with salt to a coarse paste.
3. Add the sliced apricots and crush again, until the chutney is slightly chunky.
4. Add a few drops of water only if it needs them.
Tips:
- Keep it thick and coarse rather than smooth.

chunks.title: Garlic Scape Pickle
chunks.text:
Garlic Scape Pickle is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Veg.
A Kashmiri pickle of garlic scapes: the shoots are dried for a day or two, mixed with chilli, cumin, pickling spices and oil, and left for about two weeks.
This is a pickle of garlic scapes, the shoots of the garlic plant, mixed with salt, red chilli, cumin, a pickling masala and oil and left in a warm place for about two weeks.

chunks.title: Recipe: Garlic Scape Pickle
chunks.text:
Recipe for Garlic Scape Pickle, as written on Wazwan Way.
This recipe is for 1 kg of scapes. The pickle is eaten with rice or roti.
Ingredients:
- 1 kg garlic scapes
- 1 cup salt
- 1½ cups red chilli powder
- ½ cup cumin (zeera)
- For the achaar masala: 4 tbsp coriander seeds
- 3 tbsp mustard seeds
- 1 tbsp ajwain (carom seeds)
- 3 cups oil
Method:
1. Pick mature garlic scapes, wash them and leave them to dry for 1–2 days.
2. Add the salt, spices and oil to the scapes and mix very well.
3. Pack the pickle into an airtight container and close the lid tightly. Keep it in a warm place.
4. It takes about two weeks to be ready.
Tips:
- How much of each spice to use is a matter of taste.

chunks.title: Demin (Fried tripe)
chunks.text:
Demin (Fried tripe) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Non-veg.
Demin is Kashmiri fried tripe: sheep tripe cleaned, pressure-cooked with whole spices, fried in mustard oil and simmered in a light onion masala.
Demin is sheep tripe, cooked until tender, fried in mustard oil and simmered in a light onion masala made with its own stock. The tripe is cleaned and boiled twice before it is fried, and the dish is finished with dried fenugreek leaves and ghee.

chunks.title: Recipe: Demin
chunks.text:
Recipe for Demin, as written on Wazwan Way.
This recipe is for 1 kg of tripe. The quantities are a guide to adjust to taste.
Ingredients:
- 1 kg sheep tripe, cleaned
- 1 tsp turmeric, for the first boil
- 2 bay leaves, 1 black cardamom pod, 3 green cardamom pods, a 1-inch stick of cinnamon and 4 cloves
- 4–5 cups water, for pressure-cooking
- 4 tbsp mustard oil
- 2 medium onions, thinly sliced
- 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste
- 1 tsp red chilli powder
- ½ tsp turmeric powder
- 1 tsp coriander powder
- 1 tsp salt, or to taste
- 1 tbsp dried fenugreek leaves (kasuri methi)
- 1 tbsp ghee
Method:
1. Soak the tripe in hot water for 5–6 minutes. Pull off the outer layer and wash the tripe thoroughly.
2. Boil it in water with the 1 tsp of turmeric for 5–10 minutes. Throw the water away and rinse the tripe again.
3. Pressure-cook the tripe with the whole spices and the 4–5 cups of water until tender. Keep the stock.
4. Cut the tripe into bite-sized pieces. Heat the mustard oil, fry the pieces until lightly golden and lift them out.
5. In the same pan, fry the sliced onions until lightly golden. Add the ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
6. Add the chilli powder, turmeric, coriander powder and salt with a splash of the stock, and cook the masala well.
7. Return the tripe to the pan with the dried fenugreek leaves and enough stock to make a light gravy. Cover and simmer for 10–15 minutes.
8. Finish with the ghee and serve hot.
Tips:
- Take the outer membrane off completely, for the best texture.
- The first boil with turmeric helps with any strong smell.
- Cook the tripe until it is tender but not falling apart.
- Frying the cooked tripe before it simmers adds flavour and improves the texture.
- Always keep the cooking stock: it gives the dish its body.

chunks.title: Thoole Tchaman (Steamed eggs)
chunks.text:
Thoole Tchaman (Steamed eggs) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Egg.
Thoole tchaman is a Kashmiri dish of steamed eggs: beaten with milk, turmeric and crushed spring onion greens, set like paneer and cut into cubes.
Thoole tchaman looks like paneer but is made of eggs: beaten with milk, turmeric and hand-crushed spring onion greens, steamed until set, cooled and cut into soft, spongy cubes. The name roughly means "paneer made from eggs".

chunks.title: Recipe: Thoole Tchaman
chunks.text:
Recipe for Thoole Tchaman, as written on Wazwan Way.
The crushed greens of spring onion (puch gande) or shallot (puch praan) are what lift its flavour and texture.
Ingredients:
- 5 eggs
- ½ cup milk
- Salt, to taste
- ¼ tsp turmeric powder
- 2 tbsp spring onion greens or shallot greens, crushed by hand
Method:
1. Put the eggs, milk, salt and turmeric in a bowl and add the crushed greens.
2. Whisk or blend until smooth and well combined.
3. Pour the mixture into a greased mould or container.
4. Steam for about 15 minutes, or until set.
5. Let it cool completely, then cut it into cubes.
6. Use the cubes in curries, stir-fries or salads.

chunks.title: Baegli (Crispy fava beans)
chunks.text:
Baegli (Crispy fava beans) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Veg.
Baegli are fava beans. In this Kashmiri recipe they are blanched, skinned, split and roasted or fried until crisp, then tossed with salt and spices.
Baegli are fava beans. The fresh beans are blanched, slipped out of their skins, split and roasted in the oven until crisp and golden, then tossed with a seasoning of your choice while still warm. A deep-fried version follows the recipe.

chunks.title: Recipe: Baegli
chunks.text:
Recipe for Baegli, as written on Wazwan Way.
This recipe is for 2 cups of shelled beans. The seasoning is left open: there are six to choose from.
Ingredients:
- 2 cups fresh fava beans (baegli), shelled
- 1 tbsp oil
- Salt, to taste
- To season, any of: garlic powder, Kashmiri red chilli powder, cumin powder, black pepper, dried mint powder, chaat masala
Method:
1. Blanch the shelled beans in boiling water for 2–3 minutes.
2. Move them to cold water and slip off the outer skins.
3. Pat them dry and split each bean in half.
4. Toss with the oil and salt and spread on a baking tray in a single layer.
5. Roast at 180°C for 20–30 minutes, stirring every 8–10 minutes, until crisp and golden.
6. Toss with the seasoning while still warm. Leave them for 5–10 minutes: they turn crunchier as they cool.
Tips:
- The drier the beans, the crisper they come out.
- Splitting the beans helps them crisp faster.
- Do not crowd the tray.

chunks.title: Baegli: Deep-fried instead of roasted
chunks.text:
A variation given on Wazwan Way's Baegli page: Deep-fried instead of roasted.
The beans can be fried instead of roasted. They are blanched, skinned and dried thoroughly, as above, and split in half.
They are fried in medium-hot oil until golden and crisp, drained well and seasoned at once, while hot. Avoid very high heat, which burns the outside before the inside has crisped.

chunks.title: Handh te Kokur (Dandelion greens with chicken)
chunks.text:
Handh te Kokur (Dandelion greens with chicken) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Non-veg.
Handh te kokur is a Kashmiri dish of dandelion greens and chicken, traditionally cooked for mothers after childbirth.
Handh te kokur is dandelion greens cooked with chicken and its stock, a little fat and a few warming spices into an earthy broth. In Kashmir it is traditionally cooked for mothers recovering after childbirth.

chunks.title: Recipe: Handh te Kokur
chunks.text:
Recipe for Handh te Kokur, as written on Wazwan Way.
The greens are blanched and squeezed several times to take out their bitterness, then pounded, not blended.
Ingredients:
- 2 bunches dandelion greens (handh)
- 500 g chicken on the bone, and its stock
- 5–6 cloves garlic, minced
- Salt, to taste
- Water, as needed
- 1–2 tbsp rendered mutton fat or ghee
- 1 small onion, finely sliced
- 1 small cardamom pod
- A small piece of cinnamon
- 1 tsp fennel powder
- ½ tsp black pepper
- A pinch of dry ginger powder
Method:
1. Wash the dandelion greens thoroughly.
2. Blanch them in boiling water, strain and squeeze out the water. Fresh greens usually need this about three times; dried greens are more bitter and may need four or more.
3. Pound the greens rather than blending them, for the coarse traditional texture.
4. Cook the chicken slowly with garlic, salt and water to make a stock.
5. Soften the onion and minced garlic gently in the mutton fat or ghee.
6. Add the whole spices, the ground spices, the chicken with its stock and the pounded greens. Simmer gently until it comes together as a broth.
Tips:
- How many times the greens are boiled depends on how bitter they are.
- Cook it at a slow simmer.

chunks.title: Kutta Hua Ghosht (Shredded dry mutton)
chunks.text:
Kutta Hua Ghosht (Shredded dry mutton) is on Wazwan Way under Kashmiri Cuisine. Diet: Non-veg.
Kutta hua ghosht is Kashmiri-style dry mutton, pressure-cooked with onions, garlic, chillies and achari masala, then pounded until stringy.
Kutta hua ghosht is dry, shredded mutton: boneless meat cooked in mustard oil with onions, garlic, dried red chillies and achari masala until the water has gone, then lightly pounded so that the fibres come apart, and finished with fried onions, fresh mint and lemon. It is a hot, sharp dish.

chunks.title: Recipe: Kutta Hua Ghosht
chunks.text:
Recipe for Kutta Hua Ghosht, as written on Wazwan Way.
The mutton is cooked until dry and then pounded lightly, so that it shreds. Serve it hot with rice and extra lemon.
Ingredients:
- 600–700 g boneless mutton
- 4 tbsp mustard oil
- 2 medium onions, sliced
- 12–15 cloves garlic (about 3 tbsp chopped)
- 6–8 dried red chillies
- 2–3 green chillies
- 1 tsp cumin seeds
- About 1½ tsp salt, or to taste
- 1 tbsp red chilli powder
- 1 tbsp coriander powder
- 1 tsp cumin powder
- ½ tsp garam masala
- 1½ tbsp achari masala
- 1–1½ cups water, enough to cook the mutton
- ½ cup fried shallots or onions
- ½ cup chopped fresh mint, loosely packed
- 2 tbsp lemon juice
Method:
1. Heat the mustard oil until it smokes.
2. Add the mutton, onions, garlic, dried red chillies, green chillies, salt, cumin and ground spices.
3. Add the achari masala, pour in the water and pressure-cook until the mutton is tender.
4. Open the cooker and cook on until the water has dried off completely.
5. Pound the mutton lightly, so that the fibres separate.
6. Add the fried onions, mint and lemon juice and fry for a minute or two.

chunks.title: Chicken Kanti
chunks.text:
Chicken Kanti is on Wazwan Way under Street Food. Diet: Non-veg.
Chicken kanti is a Kashmiri snack of crisp fried chicken tossed on a high flame with marinated onions and tomatoes. A recipe with no MSG or food colour.
Chicken kanti is a Kashmiri snack: cubes of boneless chicken, marinated and fried crisp in mustard oil, then tossed on a high flame with onions and tomatoes that have sat in vinegar and spices. This version uses no MSG and no food colour.

chunks.title: Recipe: Chicken Kanti
chunks.text:
Recipe for Chicken Kanti, as written on Wazwan Way.
The chicken and the vegetables are marinated separately. Serve the kanti hot with naan or paratha.
Ingredients:
- For the chicken: 500 g boneless chicken, cut into cubes
- 1 tbsp vinegar
- 2 tbsp yogurt
- 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste
- 2 tbsp red chilli powder, or to taste
- ½ tsp black pepper powder
- 1 tsp cumin powder
- 1 tbsp coriander powder
- 1 tsp fennel powder
- ½ tsp turmeric powder
- 2 tsp dried fenugreek leaves (kasuri methi)
- ½ cup cornflour, enough to coat
- Salt, to taste
- For the onions and tomatoes: 2 medium onions, thinly sliced
- 2 medium tomatoes, thinly sliced
- 2–3 green chillies, slit
- 4–5 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- ½ tsp cumin seeds
- ½ tsp dried fenugreek leaves
- 1 tbsp vinegar
- 1–2 tbsp red chilli powder
- ½ tsp turmeric powder
- 1 tsp fennel powder
- 1 tbsp coriander powder
- Salt, to taste
- To cook: ½ cup mustard oil
- Fresh coriander, to garnish
Method:
1. Mix the chicken with the vinegar, yogurt, ginger-garlic paste, ground spices, dried fenugreek leaves, cornflour and salt. Leave it for 30 minutes.
2. In another bowl, mix the onions, tomatoes, green chillies and garlic with their spices, the cumin seeds, dried fenugreek leaves, vinegar and salt. Work it together with your hands and leave it for at least 1 hour.
3. Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it starts to smoke, then lower the flame to medium. Fry the chicken until crisp and golden brown and lift it out.
4. Pour off about four-fifths of the oil, keeping just enough to stir-fry. Add the onion and tomato mixture and cook on a high flame, stirring all the time, until the oil separates but the onions still have some crunch.
5. Add the fried chicken and toss everything together on a high flame.
6. Garnish with fresh coriander.

chunks.title: Mutton Kanti
chunks.text:
Mutton Kanti is on Wazwan Way under Street Food. Diet: Non-veg.
Mutton kanti is a Kashmiri snack of marinated boneless mutton, pressure-cooked and dried off, then tossed with onions, tomato and capsicum.
Mutton kanti is small cubes of boneless mutton, marinated in yogurt, vinegar and spices, cooked until tender and dry, and tossed with barely cooked onions, tomato and capsicum.

chunks.title: Recipe: Mutton Kanti
chunks.text:
Recipe for Mutton Kanti, as written on Wazwan Way.
The mutton needs at least 2 hours in its marinade. Adjust all the spices to your own taste.
Ingredients:
- For the mutton: 500 g boneless mutton, cut into small cubes
- 5 tbsp yogurt
- 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste
- 1 tsp red chilli powder
- ½ tsp turmeric powder
- 1 tsp coriander powder
- 1 tsp garam masala
- 1 tsp salt, or to taste
- 1 tbsp vinegar
- For the vegetables: 2 medium onions, sliced
- 1 large tomato, diced
- 1 medium capsicum, diced
- 2 green chillies, slit
- ½ tsp cumin seeds
- ½ tsp dried fenugreek leaves (kasuri methi)
- 1 tbsp vinegar
- Salt, to taste
- To cook: 2 tbsp mustard oil, or vegetable oil
- About ¼ cup water
- Fresh coriander, to garnish
Method:
1. Mix the mutton with the yogurt, ginger-garlic paste, chilli powder, turmeric, coriander powder, garam masala, salt and vinegar until it is evenly coated. Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, and overnight if you can.
2. Mix the onions, tomato, capsicum and green chillies with the cumin seeds, dried fenugreek leaves, vinegar and salt. Leave for about 30 minutes.
3. Heat mustard oil in a pressure cooker over a medium heat until it smokes. Add the mutton and fry until it has changed colour and browned on all sides.
4. Add about ¼ cup of water, close the lid and pressure-cook for 3–4 whistles, or until the mutton is tender.
5. Release the pressure, open the cooker and cook uncovered on a medium heat until the moisture has gone and the masala coats the meat.
6. In another pan or wok, heat a tablespoon of mustard oil on a high heat. Add the vegetables and fry for 2–3 minutes, so that they are just cooked and still crunchy.
7. Add the mutton, mix well and cook for 2 minutes more. Garnish with fresh coriander.

chunks.title: Kabab Kanti
chunks.text:
Kabab Kanti is on Wazwan Way under Street Food. Diet: Non-veg.
Kabab kanti is a Kashmiri snack: ready-made mutton kebabs cut up and fried crisp, then tossed on a high flame with spiced onion, tomato and capsicum.
Kabab kanti is kanti made with kebabs. Mutton kebabs are cut into bite-sized pieces and fried crisp, then tossed in a very hot pan with garlic and with onion, tomato and capsicum that have sat in vinegar and spices. It is served with naan and chutney.

chunks.title: Recipe: Kabab Kanti
chunks.text:
Recipe for Kabab Kanti, as written on Wazwan Way.
It starts from four mutton kebabs that are already made; the cooking is all frying and tossing on a high flame.
Ingredients:
- 4 ready-made mutton kebabs
- Oil, for frying
- 1 large onion, thinly sliced
- 1 large tomato, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 1 small capsicum, thinly sliced
- 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
- ½ tsp turmeric
- ½ tsp cumin powder
- ½ tsp coriander powder
- ½ tsp dried fenugreek leaves (kasuri methi)
- 1–2 tbsp vinegar
- Salt, to taste
- 2 tbsp oil, for tossing
- 1 tbsp garlic, finely chopped or sliced
- Fresh coriander, chopped
- Naan and chutney, to serve
Method:
1. Cut the kebabs into bite-sized pieces and fry them until crisp and golden. Lift them out.
2. Mix the onion, tomato and capsicum with the chilli powder, turmeric, cumin, coriander powder, dried fenugreek leaves, vinegar and salt. Let them sit for a few minutes.
3. Heat the 2 tbsp of oil in a pan until properly hot. Add the garlic and fry it briefly.
4. Add the vegetables and toss on a high flame, so that they cook quickly and keep their crunch.
5. Add the fried kebab pieces and toss until everything is combined.
6. Finish with fresh coriander and serve hot with naan and chutney.
Tips:
- Keep the pan really hot and do not overcook the vegetables: the slight crunch is what makes it.

chunks.title: Tcher Tchot (Rice-flour bread)
chunks.text:
Tcher Tchot (Rice-flour bread) is on Wazwan Way under Bakery. Diet: Veg.
Tcher tchot is a thin Kashmiri bread of rice-flour batter with ghee and cumin, cooked on a hot tawa like a dosa and eaten hot with noon chai.
Tcher tchot is Kashmiri rice bread: a thin, crêpe-like round made from a pourable batter of rice flour, ghee and cumin seeds, spread on a hot tawa and cooked until soft with lightly crisp edges. It is served hot with noon chai.

chunks.title: Recipe: Tcher Tchot
chunks.text:
Recipe for Tcher Tchot, as written on Wazwan Way.
This recipe is for 1 cup of rice flour. The batter is thin enough to pour, and each bread is steamed under a lid before it is crisped.
Ingredients:
- 1 cup short-grain rice flour
- 1 tsp salt, or to taste
- 1 tsp cumin seeds
- 1 tbsp ghee or oil for the batter, and more for the tawa
- Water, as needed
Method:
1. Whisk the rice flour, salt, cumin and melted ghee together in a bowl.
2. Add water a little at a time until you have a thin batter that pours, like a dosa batter.
3. Heat a tawa and grease it lightly.
4. Pour on a ladleful of batter and spread it thin at once, in circles, as for a dosa.
5. Cover with a lid and let it steam for 30–40 seconds.
6. Drizzle a little ghee round the edges and cook until lightly crisp but still soft. Serve hot with noon chai.

chunks.title: Nishasta Halwa (Wheat starch halwa)
chunks.text:
Nishasta Halwa (Wheat starch halwa) is on Wazwan Way under Desserts. Diet: Veg.
Nishasta halwa is a Kashmiri-style halwa of wheat starch cooked in ghee with saffron, sugar and nuts until thick and glossy. Makes 2–3 servings.
Nishasta halwa is made from nishasta, wheat starch, soaked to a slurry and cooked slowly in ghee with saffron and sugar until it thickens and turns glossy, then finished with chopped nuts.

chunks.title: Recipe: Nishasta Halwa
chunks.text:
Recipe for Nishasta Halwa, as written on Wazwan Way.
The starch has to soak for 2–3 hours before it is cooked, so start well ahead.
Serves 2–3.
Ingredients:
- 4 tbsp nishasta (wheat starch)
- 1 cup water for soaking, and 1 cup for cooking
- 2–3 tbsp ghee
- 6–8 saffron strands, soaked in 1 tbsp warm water or milk
- 4–5 tbsp sugar, or to taste
- ¼ tsp cardamom powder, optional
- 2–3 tbsp chopped almonds, walnuts and cashews
- Poppy seeds, to garnish
Method:
1. Mix the nishasta with 1 cup of water and leave it to soak for 2–3 hours. Stir it well into a smooth slurry with no lumps.
2. Melt the ghee in a heavy pan on a low flame and add the saffron with its soaking liquid.
3. Pour the slurry slowly into the ghee, stirring all the time. Add the second cup of water.
4. Add the sugar and stir until it dissolves, then the cardamom if you are using it.
5. Keep cooking on a low flame, stirring regularly, until the halwa thickens and turns glossy and the ghee begins to separate at the sides.
6. Stir in the chopped nuts and serve hot, sprinkled with poppy seeds.

chunks.title: Ahdoos, Residency Road, Regal Chowk
chunks.text:
Ahdoos (also listed as Ahdoo's Hotel): Named in guides and press, Residency Road, Regal Chowk, Srinagar.
Ahdoos is the restaurant of Ahdoo's Hotel on Residency Road, at Regal Chowk in central Srinagar. A bakery from 1918 that was a restaurant by the 1920s. Kashmir Life calls it the first restaurant in the Valley to serve Wazwan. It sells Wazwan dishes by the plate next to its own bakery.
Does it serve Wazwan? Yes. Ahdoos sells Wazwan dishes by the plate. Google's menu highlights list gushtaba, rista, mutton rogan josh, tabak maaz, nadru yakhni, lahabi kabab and Kashmiri pulao (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026), and Kashmir Life calls it the first restaurant in the Valley to serve Wazwan (Kashmir Life, 2 Apr 2025).
How Wazwan is sold there: Thali or plate: Single Wazwan (2018); Single dishes; Delivery: Listed on Google.
Dishes named in the research: Gushtaba, rista, rogan josh, tabak maaz, yakhni, nadru yakhni, lahabi kabab.
Price reported: About ₹1,500 for two (Outlook Traveller, Jan 2024).
Address: Ahdoo's Hotel, Residency Road, Regal Chowk, Srinagar 190001 (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026).
Phone: +91 70515 10634 (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026).
Hours: Daily 12–10 pm (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026).
Its Google Maps listing showed 4.1 from 4,324 reviews on 10 November 2026; that is Google's figure, not Wazwan Way's rating.
Wazwan Way has not phoned or visited; every fact is from the sources named, checked 10 November 2026.

chunks.title: Ahdoos: what the sources say
chunks.text:
Ahdoos, Residency Road, Regal Chowk, Srinagar.
Wazwan offered: Wazwan dishes by the plate. A food blogger in March 2018 was served one single-person Wazwan on a metal trami and told it could not be shared (Mohamushkil blog, 27 Mar 2018). Google's menu highlights list gushtaba, rista, mutton rogan josh, tabak maaz, nadru yakhni, lahabi kabab and Kashmiri pulao (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026).
Dishes in the press: Tabak maaz, rogan josh, gushtaba and rista (So City, 3 May 2018). Rogan josh and yakhni (Outlook Traveller, Feb 2022). Kashmiri kebabs, haak and Wazwan dishes (Outlook Traveller, 15 Jan 2024).
Other food: Its own bakery, with bakarkhani and katlam (So City, 3 May 2018), now branded Crème (Kashmir Life, 2 Apr 2025). Google's description adds Mughlai and Chinese staples (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026).
Prices: About ₹1,500 for two (Outlook Traveller, 15 Jan 2024), the same figure as (Curly Tales, 20 Sep 2022). TravelTriangle gives ₹350 for two (TravelTriangle, Dec 2024), far below every other estimate. No menu prices were found online.
Ordering: Google lists dine-in, takeaway and delivery and shows an Order online button (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026). A Swiggy listing exists but showed closed when checked (Swiggy listing). The hotel website, ahdooshotel.com, would not open on 10 Nov 2026.
Setting: A 3,000 sq ft restaurant in a hotel that added guest rooms in 1944 (Kashmir Life, 2 Apr 2025). Google lists outdoor seating, a private dining room and reservations, recommended for lunch and dinner (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026).

chunks.title: Ahdoos: what the sources say
chunks.text:
Ahdoos, Residency Road, Regal Chowk, Srinagar.
History: Haji Mohammad Sultan opened the bakery in 1918 as Ahdoo & Sons, named after his father Ahad (Kashmir Life, 2 Apr 2025). It was a restaurant by the 1920s (The Tribune, 2018), and Kashmir Life says it was the first in the Valley to serve Wazwan (Kashmir Life, 2 Apr 2025). His grandson Hayat Bhat runs it (Kashmir Life, 2 Apr 2025). It marked 100 years in 2018 (WION, 2018).
Google listing: 4.1 from 4,324 reviews. A second listing, Ahdoos Hotel, has 4.1 from 2,180. Cards and NFC payments; free car park and street parking (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026).
Google's review summary: Google's AI summary says diners praise the authentic Wazwan, the mutton dishes, vegetarian dishes such as dum aloo and nadru yakhni, the service and the bakery, and that some find it overpriced (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026).
Elsewhere: TripAdvisor 4.1 from 1,242, as shown on (Wanderlog).
Notes and caveats: A 2024 report of a trami served during Rahul Gandhi's visit is known only from a search snippet (LatestLY, search snippet only). Kashmir Life and The Hans India both say the 1918 bakery had Maharaja Hari Singh's patronage (Kashmir Life, 2 Apr 2025) (The Hans India, 25 Jan 2020), but he became Maharaja in 1925. A Hindustan Times feature from June 2018 was not read (Hindustan Times, 24 Jun 2018 (not read)).

chunks.title: Mughal Darbar (upstairs), Residency Road, first floor
chunks.text:
Mughal Darbar (upstairs): Named in guides and press, Residency Road, first floor, Srinagar.
This Mughal Darbar is the upstairs restaurant on Residency Road in central Srinagar, the one behind mughal-darbar.com. The only restaurant here that publishes a full Wazwan price list, from a trami for four to a 10 kg majma. Its website says Haji Mohammad Ibrahim Mugloo founded it in 1984 and his sons run it.
Does it serve Wazwan? Yes. Its website sells a Full Wazwan Trami for four at ₹6,200, a Wazwan Full Plate for one at ₹1,300, a 10 kg Wazwan Majma at ₹10,000 and single Wazwan dishes from ₹310 to ₹720, prices seen on 10 Nov 2026 (mughal-darbar.com, seen 10 Nov 2026).
How Wazwan is sold there: Trami: For 4 · ₹6,200; Thali or plate: For 1 · ₹1,300; Single dishes: ₹310–720; Delivery: Tins to your door; Majma or events: 10 kg · ₹10,000.
Dishes named in the research: Tabak maaz, rista, gushtaba, rogan josh, mutton yakhni, methi korma, mirchi korma, dhani phol, lahabi kebab, seekh kebab, waza kokur, Kashmiri pulao.
Price reported: Trami for 4 ₹6,200; plate ₹1,300 (own site, 10 Nov 2026).
Address: Upstairs, Residency Road, Srinagar (mughal-darbar.com, seen 10 Nov 2026).
Phone: 0194-2476998 · +91 94190 07528, and five more numbers on its website (mughal-darbar.com, seen 10 Nov 2026).
Hours: 9:30 am–9 pm (TravelTriangle, Dec 2024).
Wazwan Way has not phoned or visited; every fact is from the sources named, checked 10 November 2026.

chunks.text:

chunks.title: Mughal Darbar (upstairs): what the sources say
chunks.text:
Mughal Darbar (upstairs), Residency Road, first floor, Srinagar.
Press: A food blogger ate a mini Wazwan for three here in March 2018, ₹770 in all, with tabak maaz, rista, gushtaba, rogan josh and mirchi korma (Mohamushkil blog, 27 Mar 2018). TravelTriangle lists it on the first floor (TravelTriangle, Dec 2024).

chunks.title: Mughal Darbar (ground floor), Residency Road near the GPO, Munshi Bagh
chunks.text:
Mughal Darbar (ground floor): Named in guides and press, Residency Road near the GPO, Munshi Bagh, Srinagar.

The Mughal Darbar most visitors find on Google, with 8,103 reviews. Its website lists Wazwan dishes with prices, Google's menu shows a Wazwan trami, and it runs a bakery and a Bemina branch.
Does it serve Wazwan? Yes. Its website lists Wazwan dishes by the plate, such as gushtaba and aab gosh (mughaldarbar.in, seen 10 Nov 2026), and Google's menu highlights include a Wazwan trami, without a price (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026).
How Wazwan is sold there: Trami: On Google's menu, no price; Single dishes: ₹300–650; Delivery: Website cart.
Dishes named in the research: Gushtaba, aab gosh, waza chicken, nadru yakhni, methi korma, rogan josh, seekh kebab.
Price reported: Gushtaba (4) ₹650; aab gosh ₹600 (own site, undated).
Address: Ground floor, Residency Road, near the GPO, Munshi Bagh, Srinagar 190001 (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026).
Phone: +91 70065 90221 (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026).
Hours: Daily 10 am–11 pm, from 9 am on Thursday (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026).
Its Google Maps listing showed 3.7 from 8,103 reviews on 10 November 2026; that is Google's figure, not Wazwan Way's rating.

Mughal Darbar (ground floor), Residency Road near the GPO, Munshi Bagh, Srinagar.

chunks.title: Mughal Darbar (ground floor): what the sources say
chunks.text:
Mughal Darbar (ground floor), Residency Road near the GPO, Munshi Bagh, Srinagar.

Shamyana, Boulevard Road, Ghat No. 2 (Dalgate), Srinagar.

chunks.title: Stream Restaurant, Boulevard Road, opposite Ghat No. 2
chunks.text:

Website: upstairs: mughal-darbar.com, built by Kashmir Online (mughal-darbar.com, seen 10 Nov 2026); ground floor: mughaldarbar.in, built by Marina Technologies (mughaldarbar.in, seen 10 Nov 2026).
Where: upstairs: Upstairs, Residency Road (mughal-darbar.com, seen 10 Nov 2026); TravelTriangle says first floor (TravelTriangle, Dec 2024); ground floor: Ground floor, Residency Road near the GPO, Munshi Bagh (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026).

Founder named: upstairs: Haji Mohammad Ibrahim Mugloo, 1984, by its own account (mughal-darbar.com, seen 10 Nov 2026). His 2018 obituary calls him the owner of Mughal Darbar on Residency Road (Kashmir Life, 20 Aug 2018).; ground floor: Not named on its website (mughaldarbar.in, seen 10 Nov 2026). Kashmir Life profiles a Mughal Darbar founded in 1984 by Ghulam Qadir Grustoo that added a bakery in 1992, without naming a floor (Kashmir Life, 2 Apr 2025)..
On Google: upstairs: No Srinagar listing found; ground floor: 3.7 from 8,103 reviews; Bemina branch 3.7 from 303 (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026).

chunks.title: Srinagar restaurants that serve Wazwan: what the research found
chunks.text:
Wazwan Way's directory lists 29 places in Srinagar, researched on 10 November 2026 from Google Maps listings, the places' own pages, press and guides. No restaurant was phoned or visited.
Only one restaurant publishes a full Wazwan price list. Mughal Darbar (upstairs) sells a trami for four at ₹6,200, a one-person plate at ₹1,300 and a 10 kg majma at ₹10,000 on its own website, seen 10 Nov 2026 (mughal-darbar.com, seen 10 Nov 2026). Elsewhere the prices are journalists' estimates for two, delivery-app figures or Google users' per-person ranges.
Most places sell Wazwan as a thali or by the plate. Kareema, JJ Foods, Salam e Wazwan, Dawat E Wazwan, Wazwan Stories, Authentic Wazwan and Wazwan Box all list a Wazwan thali. A trami for four with a stated size appears only at Mughal Darbar (upstairs) and on a Zomato listing in Rainawari.
Two different businesses trade as Mughal Darbar on Residency Road. The upstairs one has no Google listing; the ground-floor one holds the listing with 8,103 reviews. See the two compared.
The old city has strong review evidence and little web presence. Shahi Pakwaan in Nowhatta has 86 Google reviews that mention Wazwan and no website. In Wazpora, JJ Foods and Lazeez Wazwan are run by waza families and were profiled by Greater Kashmir in 2026 (Greater Kashmir, 18 Jan 2026).
Stream is not confirmed as a Wazwan restaurant. Stream has the most Google reviews here, 13,327, but only two June 2026 reviews mention a Wazwan thali.
Bismillah on Jawahar Nagar is now marked permanently closed on Google. So City recommended its trami and its sweet pulao with walnut chutney in 2018 (So City, 3 May 2018).

Kareema's Wazwan thali was recommended by Outlook Traveller in 2022 (Outlook Traveller, Feb 2022); JJ Foods, Salam e Wazwan, Dawat E Wazwan, Wazwan Stories and Authentic Wazwan list a Wazwan thali on Google; and Mughal Darbar (upstairs) sells a Wazwan Full Plate for one at ₹1,300 (mughal-darbar.com, seen 10 Nov 2026).

chunks.title: Srinagar restaurants that serve Wazwan: How much does Wazwan cost at a restaurant in Srinagar?
chunks.text:
How much does Wazwan cost at a restaurant in Srinagar?
The figures found run from a ₹200 mini Wazwan thali on Swiggy (Swiggy listing) to ₹6,200 for a trami for four (mughal-darbar.com, seen 10 Nov 2026). In January 2024 Outlook Traveller put a meal for two at about ₹800 to ₹1,500 at the restaurants its city guide names (Outlook Traveller, 15 Jan 2024), and Google users report paying ₹400 to ₹1,400 per person at most of the Wazwan places listed here. Every price on these pages carries its date.

chunks.title: Srinagar restaurants that serve Wazwan: Which Srinagar restaurants deliver Wazwan?
chunks.text:
Which Srinagar restaurants deliver Wazwan?
Mughal Darbar (upstairs) delivers Wazwan packed in tins (mughal-darbar.com, seen 10 Nov 2026). Google lists delivery for Ahdoos (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026), JJ Foods (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026), Salam e Wazwan (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026) and Wazwan Stories (Google Maps, 10 Nov 2026), among others, and Wazwan Box sells Wazwan thalis through Zomato (Zomato, search snippet), though Google warns it may be closed. Nobody here tested a delivery.

chunks.title: Srinagar restaurants that serve Wazwan: Is Mughal Darbar upstairs or on the ground floor?
chunks.text:
Is Mughal Darbar upstairs or on the ground floor?
Both. Two separate businesses trade as Mughal Darbar a few steps apart on Residency Road, with different websites and phone numbers, and no source explains how they are related. Mughal Darbar: two restaurants, one name compares them.

chunks.title: Srinagar restaurants that serve Wazwan: Which was the first restaurant in Kashmir to serve Wazwan?
chunks.text:
Which was the first restaurant in Kashmir to serve Wazwan?
Kashmir Life calls Ahdoos the first restaurant in the Valley to serve Wazwan (Kashmir Life, 2 Apr 2025). It began as a bakery in 1918 (Kashmir Life, 2 Apr 2025) and had become a restaurant by the 1920s (The Tribune, 2018).

chunks.title: Wazpora, the wazas' quarter of Srinagar
chunks.text:
Several of the newer Wazwan restaurants sit in Wazpora, near Rajouri Kadal in the old city, where the hereditary cooks live.
Greater Kashmir describes Wazpora, in Downtown Srinagar, as the home of the traditional cooks, and reports that fewer young people are joining the trade. It names JJ Foods, Lazeez Wazwan and Wazwan Hut as Wazpora's Wazwan eateries (Greater Kashmir, 18 Jan 2026).
In 2022 The Hindu called it the oldest colony of the waza cooks and counted nine Wazwan eateries there as tourists found their way in (The Hindu, Sep 2022 (republished copy)).
Reuters quotes Ghulam Nabi Baba, 74, who has cooked at weddings for nearly six decades. He says Wazwan began as seven mutton dishes and now runs to about 20, that an average wedding uses about 200 kg of meat, and that his son now runs a restaurant (Reuters, 30 Sep 2026). Greater Kashmir put his age in the early 60s in 2023 (Greater Kashmir, 21 Mar 2023). Al Jazeera's photographs from the same reporting show meat pounded for rista and gushtaba and copper pots over wood fires (Al Jazeera photos, 30 Sep 2026).
Kashmir Observer places Wazpora close to the Bohri Kadal and Saraf Kadal stretch of the old city (Kashmir Observer, 4 Jul 2021).

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Tabak maaz, the ribs that open a Wazwan: what its name means, the two cookings, the milk-or-water question, kabargah, and the GI application.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text:
The trami comes to the four of you under a copper cover, the sarposh (Outlook India). When it is lifted, the rice is already dressed: two seekh kebabs crossing it into quarters, four pieces of methi maaz, two chickens, and two pieces of tabak maaz (Wikipedia; District Budgam). At the wedding a Gulf News writer attended, the guests had "less than ten minutes to finish it off" before the cooked courses began arriving (Gulf News). So the first thing most people ever taste of a Wazwan is a piece of rib: simmered until the bones slip, then fried in ghee until it is "reddish brown all over" (Scroll, from the Waza family's cookbook).
Tabak maaz is the plainest of the seven essential dishes and the one with the most disagreement about how it is made. It is cooked twice; on that everyone agrees. What it is simmered in before the frying, whether it is the same dish as the Kashmiri Pandits' kabargah, what its name has to do with a plate, where the sheep whose ribs these are come from, and why a people who once avoided ghee fry their first wedding dish in it are the questions this story works through. For what the dish is, with a recipe and where to eat it, see tabak maaz; for the application to register it as a geographical indication, see the GI guide.

sources.label: Scroll, from the Waza family's cookbook

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: What tabak maaz is
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Tabak maaz is lamb ribs cooked twice: "initially braised with ground spices, then browned in ghee", in Wikipedia's summary (Wikipedia). It is one of the seven dishes Wikipedia lists as "a must" at a Wazwan and one of the seven the Waza family's cookbook calls indispensable (Wikipedia; Roli Books), and a 2016 review of the feast's meat products names it with kabab, aab gosh, rogan josh, yakhni, rista and goshtaba (Rather, Masoodi and Akhter). Unlike the gravies that follow it, it comes dry: "a glossy meat made of lamb ribs, fried thoroughly and served in dry form" (Outlook India). Doctors who recorded a Srinagar wedding feast in 2012 described it the same way, "made up of rib cage of sheep, cooked in ghee and served as dry pieces", two to four pieces to a trami (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, SKIMS, 2012). In August 2024 The Kashmir Wazwan Cooperative Limited applied to register "Tabakmaaz (Meat Products) of Kashmir" as a geographical indication; on 17 October 2026 the application was still at pre-examination (GI Registry, application 1336).

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The plate in the name
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Kashmiri has words for ribs. Grierson's Dictionary of the Kashmiri Language gives pōwaca, "the ribs (of man or beast)", pāha-lara, "the ribs (spoken of as a whole)", and lar, "a bone of the side, a rib" (Grierson, pp. 810, 684, 529). The dish uses none of them. Māz is meat (Grierson, p. 615), and tabakh is a large dish, plate or tray (Grierson, p. 962). Tabak maaz is, literally, plate-meat. Which plate is not recorded, but two threads lead somewhere. The first is old. Kashmir Life, summarising the Tuhfat-ul-Ahbab, a Persian work completed in the early 17th century, describes 16th-century feasts at which food was served on a dastarkhwan in a copper tabak, "maybe a forerunner of traem of today", and at grand ceremonies the tabak came "covered with sarposh" (Kashmir Life). The covered copper plate the modern trami arrives under had a name four centuries ago, and it was tabak. The second thread is a recipe. A Kashmiri cookbook first published in 1988 gives one method under the double name "Kabargah Ta Tabaq Maz", and its tabaq maz is cooked in plates.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The plate in the name
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: The simmered, battered ribs are laid in a ghee-smeared baked clay plate, a tabaq, covered with a second plate, the rims sealed with wheat-flour dough, and the sealed plates set over a slow charcoal fire with coals on top for about an hour, until the meat is deep brown; the earthenware, the book says, gives the dish a special flavour and aroma, and it "should always be served steaming hot" (Kaul Kilam, Culinary Art of Kashmir). It is the only method we have found that puts a plate into the cooking rather than the serving. Whether the dish was named for the clay plates it was once cooked between, or for the copper plate it was served on, nobody has written down; both fit the word. The only other origin claim we found is a single remark by the former tourism director M. Saleem Beg that the dish "seems to have travelled from Kazakhstan", offered without evidence (Daily Excelsior). The two materials, clay and copper, divide along a line the dictionary draws.

sources.label: Kaul Kilam, Culinary Art of Kashmir

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The plate in the name
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Grierson's entry for trömi is "a copper dish (used only by Musalmāns) out of which food is eaten", and trāmi-bata is the food served in those copper vessels to the Muslim guests at a wedding feast; a separate word, ṭôku, covers food served to each guest on a platter of their own (Grierson, pp. 1026 and 991). Walter Lawrence, writing in 1895, saw the other material on the table. When "the professional cook is called in some taste is displayed in the preparation and arrangement of viands", he wrote, and "the earthenware platters filled with brightly-coloured foods make a pretty show"; elsewhere in the book he notes that rough earthenware supplied all the wants of the Kashmiri peasant, metal being seldom used for household purposes (Lawrence, p. 253). So the Valley of the 1890s ate off clay and feasted, when Muslim and able, off copper; a dish named for a plate had both to choose from. Our history of Wazwan follows the copper. The spelling varies with the writer: tabakh maaz on Wikipedia, tabaq maz in the cookbook, tabakmaz in Beg's essay, "Tabakmaaz" in the doctors' paper and on the GI register. The Kashmiri Pandit name for the dish is kabargah, also written qabargah (Wikipedia; Wikipedia).

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The sheep
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Every account of tabak maaz starts with a rib cage, and in Kashmir the rib cage starts a long way from the kitchen. The Valley has kept sheep for as long as anyone has written about it, and it has never kept enough. Lawrence was clear about the quality. "The choicest mutton in Kashmir is raised in the village of Nandpur on the Dal lake", where the sheep grazed the tender grass of the made land called demb; "the mutton of Kashmir is throughout excellent"; the Kashmiri "considers two-year-old wether mutton as the best"; and the sheep of the valley "have been pronounced by a competent authority to be as good as the Southdowns" (Lawrence, p. 363). He was equally clear about the quantity. "In spite of the number of sheep in Kashmir it is often difficult to obtain mutton in the villages", because villagers kept their flocks for wool and for warmth, penned on the ground floor of the house through the winter, and sold them to the city butchers rather than eating them; and a sheep that sickened in the close winter pens was killed and eaten by its owner as braxy mutton (Lawrence, pp. 360 to 363).

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The sheep
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: The cultivator, he reckoned, ate mutton "perhaps five times in the month" (Lawrence, p. 254). The sheep he described still exist, and are now counted as breeds. A 2022 review by animal scientists at the Sher-e-Kashmir agricultural university lists the Valley's own, with their standing: the Gurez, "registered (with NBAGR)", found "only in Gurez and Tulail Tehsils of the Bandipora district", reared by the Dard people, known for "good-quality mutton" and "the biggest sheep breed of Kashmir"; the Karnah, of the Kupwara hills, "under the threat" of disappearing through random cross-breeding; the Poonchi, "primarily reared for both mutton and wool"; and the Bhakarwal, the migratory sheep "reared mainly by the nomadic tribe called the Bhakarwals", hardy, good climbers, some of them fat-tailed (Hamadani and others, Indian Journal of Animal Sciences, 2022). Together Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh had 8.32 million and 7.37 million livestock and poultry at the 20th Livestock Census, of which sheep were 36.84 per cent, and the two territories "stand 6th with regard to the population of sheep" in India (Hamadani and others, 2022). The Kashmir region's sheep alone numbered 3.4 million at the previous census (Rural21). Most of those sheep are no longer the sheep Lawrence saw.

sources.label: Hamadani and others, Indian Journal of Animal Sciences, 2022

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The sheep
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: From the 1960s the state's sheep husbandry department crossed Valley ewes with imported rams to make a new animal: "Kashmir valley ewes were crossed with Australian Merino rams", the first-generation ewes "were bred to Delaine rams of the USA", and the second generation was bred among itself "after proper selection" until "a breed with steady and uniform characters evolved which was named as Kashmir Merino" (Rural21). The department's director, Abdul Salam Mir, told a reporter in 2019 that "the quality of sheep which we had before 1990s, used to be low on both meat and wool", and that the Merino was "far more productive both in terms of mutton and wool"; his department ran eight breeding farms and had distributed about 29,000 rams into private flocks (Village Square; Rural21). The 2022 review puts the result in a sentence: "Nearly 43% sheep have already been converted into crossbred", and about 80 per cent of the native breeds were being crossed with exotic fine-wool sheep, which is why the Karnah and the Gurez are now listed as endangered (Hamadani and others, 2022).

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The sheep
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: The rib on the trami, in other words, is as likely to come from a sheep that is half Australian and a quarter American as from one Lawrence would have recognised. It is more likely still to come from Rajasthan. The government's own figures, tabled in the state's legislative council and reported in 2012, put the Valley's mutton consumption at 2,53,88,000 kg a year, worth Rs 761 crore, of which 1,44,08,000 kg was imported, "most of the mutton imports" from Rajasthan: 56 per cent of the meat from outside (Kashmir Life). Two years later a Kashmir Life editor wrote that "the state's overall requirement for mutton has crossed 560 lakh kilograms", that "the government said that 55% of this volume is net import", and that "the voracious mutton eating habits have given the Wazwaan country a new identity"; the sheep, he added, were "stuffed in trucks beyond capacity" and "for most of the distance between Rajasthan to Srinagar, they are kept hungry and thirsty" (R. S. Gull, Kashmir Life). In 2019 the sheep husbandry director gave demand as 31 million kg and imports as 17.7 million kg, "well over 50% of mutton from outside the state" (Village Square).

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The sheep
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: In 2021 the department's data showed about 22 lakh sheep slaughtered a year in the Valley and "a meager 6.5 lakh sheep are raised locally", so that local production was "just 30% of the total consumption"; the director blamed "harsh winter for six months", which made it "very difficult for the farmers to raise sheep on a big scale" (Greater Kashmir). And in February 2026 a three-part series in Kashmir Times put local production at 30,000 tonnes against consumption of "around 60,000 tonnes annually", filled by "approximately 14 lakh sheep and goats annually" from Rajasthan, Haryana, Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh, draining "between Rs 1,000 and Rs 1,400 crore" a year; the carcasses of the imported breeds weigh "around 12 kilograms", and the whole trade travels one road, the Jammu-Srinagar highway, which landslides, weather and security closures can cut (Rao Farman Ali, Kashmir Times). A mutton dealers' office-bearer named the supply chain: Ujlan-Jaisalmer, Jaipal Basti, Jaisalmer and Sikar, in Rajasthan (Rao Farman Ali, Kashmir Times). The figures do not agree with one another, and they should not be expected to: they come from different years, different departments and different definitions of "Kashmir". What they agree on is the shape.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The sheep
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: The Valley eats roughly twice the mutton it raises, has done so for at least fifteen years, and buys the difference from the plains. The reasons given are the same in 1895 and 2026: a six-month winter, flocks kept for wool rather than meat, and pastures that are shrinking (Lawrence, p. 363; Kashmir Times). The herders who move sheep between those pastures, the Bakarwals and Gujjars, sell to the dealers on their autumn migration down from the high meadows, which is also the wedding season (Greater Kashmir); the 2012 figures were accompanied by the complaint that most of the meadows along the Line of Control had been closed to herdsmen "mostly from Pir Panchal region" of Rajouri and Poonch (Kashmir Life). What that means for a wedding became plain in the summer of 2026.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The sheep
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: "Around 500 kilogrammes of mutton and 150 kilogrammes of chicken are consumed at an average Kashmiri wedding", the Press Trust of India reported, and more than a tonne at a lavish one; when Punjab levied a four per cent charge on livestock trucks crossing the state, which the president of the Valley's mutton dealers' association called a "Goonda Tax", the dealers suspended imports, a Budgam dealer who had paid his supplier in Rajasthan said he had "not received any sheep in the past month", and a father in Hyderpora with a son's wedding fixed for 25 July said, "We might have to postpone it" (PTI via Outlook Business). The chief minister wrote to his counterpart in Punjab; the levy was withdrawn within days (Daily Pioneer). A veteran waza put the quantities in his own terms to Reuters that autumn: "Normally, at an average marriage we cook 200 kgs of mutton"; forty years earlier, at a village wedding in Delina, he had cooked 4,500 kg (Reuters). Two pieces of tabak maaz to a trami, and a hundred tramis to a wedding, is a great many rib cages; and almost none of them, now, from Nandpur on the Dal.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The first cooking: water, milk or yogurt?
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Every source has the ribs simmered before they are fried. They do not agree on what in. Water, say the wazas. The one published recipe from a waza family, in the Roli Books cookbook Wazwaan, uses water and nothing richer. The whole rib cage goes into boiling water and is skimmed "until the water runs clear"; garlic goes in, then salt, and the ribs boil, covered, until the membrane between them can be pierced with a thumb. They are drained, cooled and washed, and the water is kept.
