Only then is the rack cut, with a heavy knife, into eight rectangular pieces, which go back into the reserved water with salt, dry ginger, cloves, black cardamom and turmeric "until the bones can be extracted from the membrane easily" (Scroll, from Wazwaan). A Srinagar waza describes the same first step, whole ribs boiled with salt and garlic (The Kashmir Walla), and Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes has the Wazwan version "boiled with salt and garlic" (Wikipedia). Sahapedia's account has fatty ribs simmered with cardamom, cinnamon, ginger powder, garlic paste and cloves (Sahapedia).

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The first cooking: water, milk or yogurt?
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: A chef's notes from a cooking session with a Gulmarg waza have the rib cage boiled for about two hours in stock with turmeric, fennel seeds, cardamom, cinnamon and salt (Chef Jolly). Milk, say others. Wikipedia's own article on the dish has the ribs "simmered in milk and spices and then fried" (Wikipedia); a news-agency feature has them "cooked in milk and then fried in clarified butter" (Anadolu Agency); the Budgam district administration has them "braised with ground spices and milk" (District Budgam). Yogurt, say others still. The Hindu's 2012 account, as Wikipedia's Wazwan article quotes it, has "ribs of lamb simmered in yogurt till tender, then fried" (Wikipedia), and an IANS feature reverses the order altogether: "glossy ribs cooked in ghee then simmered in yogurt till dry" (Onmanorama). The 1988 cookbook splits the difference, simmering the ribs in water with half a teacup of milk (Kaul Kilam). And the chef's notes offer the one explanation on record for the split: "pundits boil the ribs in milk, whereas stock is preferred by Muslims" (Chef Jolly). That is one cook's observation rather than a documented rule, but it fits the pattern: the wazas' published method uses water; the milk versions come from general descriptions of "Kashmiri" cooking.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The first cooking: water, milk or yogurt?
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Our own recipe follows the wazas: water for the first boil and the ribs' own stock for the second. What goes into the pot is less disputed. The ribs are the point: "It is important to use the chest for the required softness and taste," Bashir Ahmad Choncha of Choncha Foods told Deccan Chronicle (Deccan Chronicle), and in the wazas' division of a carcass the ribs go to tabak maaz while the back leg goes to gushtaba and the bony pieces to rogan josh (Kashmir Life). The cookbook wants pieces of roughly two inches by four with the fat and skin left on, two or three bones to a piece, 25 to 30 pieces from a kilo (Kaul Kilam); at a working-class wedding in Srinagar a reporter watched the ribs being "hacked into shape" (Outlook Traveller).

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The second cooking: ghee
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: The frying is what makes the dish. The Waza family's recipe calls for 475 g of pure ghee to a kilo of ribs. The boiled pieces are laid in a large pan without overlapping, the ghee is poured over them, and they are fried, turning occasionally, "until they are reddish brown all over"; the ghee is drained off before serving (Scroll, from Wazwaan). Choncha calls it "deep fried in ghee" and "a very rich dish" (Deccan Chronicle); the Gulmarg waza's version was shallow-fried "bone side down, using a weight on top to press it" (Chef Jolly). Sahapedia describes the result as crisp and caramelised on the outside (Sahapedia); Outlook Traveller's glossary has "unspiced rib cuts fried to a crisp" (Outlook Traveller). That crispness is the dish's whole argument. The fat between the rib bones renders in the first cooking and sets in the second, so the piece comes to the trami glossy and dry, to be eaten with the fingers off the rice before the gravies arrive. It was the favourite dish of a Polish bride who held her wedding reception in Srinagar: "Tabakhmaaz is my favorite," she told The Wire, which describes it simply as "pieces of lamb ribs fried in butter" (The Wire).

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The second cooking: ghee
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: The ghee is a puzzle of its own, because the Valley did not use it. Lawrence found in the 1890s that "clarified butter (ghi) is not much eaten", since Kashmiris believed it irritated the throat; in another passage he records that they avoided ghi, calling it the butter of India, and cooked instead with large quantities of vegetable oil (Lawrence, p. 254). Yet the Valley made a great deal of it. Lawrence lists ghi as by far the most important of Kashmir's exports to the Punjab, made mostly from buffalo milk by the Gujar herders and sold through Punjabi middlemen, who adulterated it with walnut oil; cow's-milk ghi, he noted, was reckoned the most delicate, buffalo ghi next, goat's rank (Lawrence, chapter on exports and the pages on cattle). Grierson's dictionary has the word, gĕv, clarified butter, made from butter boiled gently, strained and allowed to cool, and it records at least one meat dish cooked in it, a kabab, under shömi (Grierson, pp. 316 and 882). So the ghee of tabak maaz was, a century ago, a product the Valley exported rather than ate, and a wedding that fried its ribs in it was spending something.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The second cooking: ghee
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: The pattern holds today in a smaller way: a Kashmiri restaurateur told Asia Media Centre that ghee is used for an authentic Wazwan and mustard oil at home (Asia Media Centre). The researchers who counted the calories in a wedding feast in 2012 found the cost. Their tabakmaaz, cooked in ghee, carried 1,470 calories per trami, or 367 for each of the four diners, more than the rogan josh (331) and the aab gosh (234), and less than the rista (454), the gushtaba (447) and the kebabs (740) among the mutton dishes; the whole chicken, also fried in ghee, carried the most of all (899) (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi). A 2026 public-health advisory in Srinagar named "Tabak Maaz" with the meatballs and kebabs among the dishes that account for most of a trami's 6,000 to 9,000 calories, and advised moderation rather than abstinence: "Wazwan is a celebration, not an everyday meal" (Kashmir Reader). Two pieces of rib, eaten in the first ten minutes, are a quarter of a day's energy.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: Tabak maaz and kabargah
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Kashmiri Pandits commonly call the dish kabargah (Wikipedia), and J&K Tourism lists kabargah among the delicacies of Kashmiri Pandit cooking (JKTDC). Are they one dish or two? The sources answer both ways. One dish, says Beg: tabakmaz in the Wazwan and kabargah on the Pandit table are "soft ribs from mutton", and "the method of preparation remains exactly the same for this dish" (Daily Excelsior). Two methods, says Wikipedia's list: kabargah is "simmered on a low heat for longer and then fried very quickly", while tabak maaz is boiled with salt and garlic and has a slightly elastic texture (Wikipedia). In Pandit homes that avoid onion and garlic, the garlic of the wazas' first boil is left out (JKTDC). The 1988 cookbook, written from the Pandit kitchen, treats the names as two finishes of one simmered rib. Its ribs are simmered once, in water and a little milk with chilli, ginger, aniseed, turmeric, asafoetida, garam masala, cloves and salt, until tender and the liquid absorbed. Then they part ways. For kabargah, each piece is dipped in a batter of curd beaten with chilli powder, garam masala and salt, and deep-fried slowly in ghee until brown.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: Tabak maaz and kabargah
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: For tabaq maz, the battered pieces are sealed between the clay plates and cooked over charcoal. The book adds a detail that turns the Wazwan order upside down: in Pandit homes the dish is "generally served as a last Meat Course" (Kaul Kilam). The same ribs open a Wazwan and close a Pandit feast. Kabargah has its own page, with a Pandit recipe, and Kashmiri Pandit food covers that table more widely. Lawrence recorded one thing about Pandit meat-eating that bears on the ribs. The Hindus of Kashmir, he wrote, were flesh-eaters who nevertheless avoided certain vegetables for their colour: "Tomatoes, the red-fleshed kabuli vegetable marrow, carrots, and red beans are an abomination to the Hindu" (Lawrence, p. 300). A rib fried brown in ghee offended no such rule, which may be one reason the dish could cross between the two kitchens with its method, as Beg says, "exactly the same". That is our inference, not Lawrence's. The headnote to the Waza family's cookbook draws the two traditions together rather than apart: it contrasts the Muslim wazwaan with the Pandits' butta, and says both favour lamb and cooking over wood fire (Scroll, from Wazwaan).

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: First on the trami
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text:
Tabak maaz does not come in a course; it is on the platter when the platter arrives. Wikipedia and the Budgam district administration list the trami's contents as rice quartered by two seekh kebabs, four pieces of methi maaz, two of tabak maaz, and two chickens, one white and one coloured with saffron (Wikipedia; District Budgam). The doctors' 2012 list, "in the order in which they are served", runs methi, chicken, kabab, tabakmaaz, then dani, the single piece of meat on the bone, before rista opens the gravies (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi). Every reported feast agrees on the company it keeps: seekh kebabs, methi maaz and chicken (Outlook India; Asia Media Centre; Onmanorama; JK Arts Foundation), with a large piece of mutton, the daeni phoul, in some accounts (The Kashmir Walla). Then the wazas start bringing the gravies, four pieces to a trami, and the long middle of the meal begins (Gulf News). For the order from there to gushtaba, see how Wazwan is served.
Its position explains its form. The first dishes are eaten fast, by hand, straight off the rice, before anything with a gravy has been served; a piece of fried rib with its fat set hard is built for exactly that.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The feast it opens, then and now
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: The feast tabak maaz opens is older than any description of the dish. Lawrence's account of a Muslim wedding in the 1890s is short: "the gorgeous groom sits on cushions and the feast commences, winding up with tea"; "a big feast is given on the marriage night", the tehl, and the guests leave next day; the groom's father paid the bride's a lagan chir of twenty to fifty rupees (Lawrence, pp. 268 to 269). Of the cultivators he wrote that they were "frugal in their expenditure and do not lavish money on marriage feasts or extravagances of a similar nature, as is the case in India", though he thought that might change (Lawrence, p. 397). Grierson's dictionary, compiled in the same decades, has the feast's vocabulary ready: yēra, "a marriage feast"; dah, "materials (flesh, spices, etc.) for a great feast"; wura-bal, "the place for the cooking-fires of a bridegroom's party"; dēg, "a large pile of rice cooked in a cauldron, for a wedding feast or the like"; and wāza, "a cook-person, one who is a cook by profession, and comes of a line, or caste, of cooks" (Grierson, pp. 1202, 199, 1138, 194 and 1178). It has changed, and the governments of the day have tried to change it faster.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: The feast it opens, then and now
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: A 1974 order limiting hosts to five dishes was set aside by a sessions judge who thought it would only waste meat; a February 2017 order capped weddings at seven meat dishes, seven vegetarian dishes and two sweets (Anadolu Agency; Gulf News/IANS). Ghulam Nabi Baba, who has cooked weddings for nearly sixty years, told Reuters that "there were only seven mutton dishes at that time. Over the centuries we added more, and now there are around 20 dishes" (Reuters). Through every count, the ribs have stayed on the rice at the start. Our gushtaba story tells what happens at the other end.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: Eating it for the first time
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Most visitors meet tabak maaz in a Srinagar restaurant, where it is served as a starter or as one plate among several; our guide to eating in Srinagar lists places that serve Wazwan — Ahdoos, Mughal Darbar and Shamyana were the only restaurants on all five published Srinagar lists we compared in September 2026 — and the cost guide covers prices. Expect pieces of rib that are crisp and brown at the edges and soft between the bones, with the fat left on, no gravy, and little spice; it is eaten with the fingers, with rice, and it comes first. If a menu lists kabargah instead, you now know what the difference is, and isn't.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: Frequently asked questions: What is tabak maaz?
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Lamb ribs cooked twice: simmered with spices until the bones loosen, then fried in ghee until reddish brown. It is served dry, on the rice, as one of the first dishes of a Wazwan, and is one of the seven dishes counted as essential to the feast.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: Frequently asked questions: What does tabak maaz mean?
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Plate-meat. In Kashmiri, tabakh is a large dish, plate or tray and māz is meat, according to Grierson's dictionary. Which plate it refers to isn't recorded: a copper tabak served food under a cover at 16th-century Kashmiri feasts, and a 1988 cookbook cooks its tabaq maz sealed between clay plates called tabaqs.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: Frequently asked questions: How is tabak maaz cooked?
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: The Waza family's published recipe boils the whole rib cage in water with garlic and salt until the membrane can be pierced with a thumb, cuts it into eight pieces, boils them again with turmeric, dry ginger, cloves and black cardamom, and fries them in pure ghee until reddish brown all over.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: Frequently asked questions: Is tabak maaz cooked in milk or water?
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Sources disagree. The wazas' own recipe and a Srinagar waza use water; Wikipedia's article on the dish, a news agency and the Budgam district page say milk; The Hindu and an IANS feature say yogurt. One chef who cooked with a Gulmarg waza reports that Pandits boil the ribs in milk while Muslims prefer stock.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: Frequently asked questions: Why is tabak maaz fried in ghee?
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: The frying sets the fat between the bones and gives the dish its crisp, glossy, dry finish, which suits a piece eaten by hand off the rice before any gravy arrives. The ghee is a feast ingredient: in the 1890s Walter Lawrence found that Kashmiris cooked with oil and exported their ghi, and a restaurateur today says ghee is for an authentic Wazwan and mustard oil for home.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: Frequently asked questions: How many calories are in tabak maaz?
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: At the Srinagar wedding studied by SKIMS researchers in 2012, the tabak maaz carried about 1,470 calories per trami, or 367 per diner. A 2026 health advisory named it among the dishes that make up most of a trami's estimated 6,000 to 9,000 calories.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: Frequently asked questions: Where does the mutton for tabak maaz come from?
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Mostly from outside Kashmir. Official figures reported between 2012 and 2026 put imports at 55 to 70 per cent of the Valley's mutton, trucked up the Jammu-Srinagar highway from Rajasthan, Haryana, Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh; Kashmir's own flocks, now largely Kashmir Merino crossbreds, supply the rest.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: Frequently asked questions: What is the difference between tabak maaz and kabargah?
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Kabargah is the Kashmiri Pandit name for the same ribs. One writer says the method is exactly the same; Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes says kabargah is simmered longer and fried faster; a Pandit cookbook dips the ribs in a curd batter before frying and leaves out garlic. In Pandit homes it is often the last meat course, where in a Wazwan it is among the first.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: Frequently asked questions: When is tabak maaz served at a Wazwan?
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: At the very start. It is on the trami when it arrives, with the rice, seekh kebabs, methi maaz and chicken, before any of the gravies are served.

chunks.title: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name: Frequently asked questions: Does tabak maaz have a GI tag?
chunks.page: Tabak Maaz: Ribs Cooked Twice, and the Plate in the Name
chunks.text: Not yet. An application for "Tabakmaaz (Meat Products) of Kashmir" was filed on 8 August 2024 and was still at pre-examination when we checked the register on 17 October 2026.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: Rista, the Wazwan's red meatball: how wazas pound it from fresh mutton, what colours its gravy, how it differs from gushtaba and where it comes in the meal.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text:
The first course is gone in minutes, eaten off the rice with the fingers: the kebabs, the ribs, the chicken (Gulf News). Then the wazas come out of the kitchen with the first pot, and what they ladle onto each trami is four meatballs the size of golf balls in a red gravy, one for each of the four diners (Gulf News; The Kashmir Walla). That is rista, and it has been in the making since the small hours, when the meat for it came off a stone slab under a wooden mallet (Reuters via Al Jazeera).
Rista is the Wazwan's opening gravy and its first test of the cook: the dish that shows whether the pounding was done right. This story covers how it is made, who makes it and with what, what the meat scientists of Srinagar found when they tried to make it in a laboratory, what makes it red, what it weighs and what it costs the body, where it comes in the meal, and how it relates to the dish it is always paired with. For what rista is, with a recipe and where to eat it, see rista; for a side-by-side with its white twin, see rista vs gushtaba.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: What rista is
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: Rista is a ball of mutton pounded with fat, boiled, and cooked in a red gravy. Wikipedia describes it as "meatballs in a red, paprika-saffron-fennel spice gravy" coloured with alkanet, and lists it among the seven dishes that are "a must" at a Wazwan (Wikipedia); the Waza family's cookbook counts it among the same seven (Roli Books), and a 2016 review of the feast's meat products names it with kabab, tabak maaz, aab gosh, rogan josh, yakhni and goshtaba (Rather, Masoodi and Akhter). Sahapedia gives the size, about 80 to 100 g, and the rule that goes with it: each guest at the trami gets one (Sahapedia). Doctors who recorded a Srinagar wedding feast in 2012 wrote it down the same way: "4 pieces of minced meat of spherical shape", four to a trami (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, SKIMS, 2012).

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: The name, and the family it belongs to
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text:
Its name, like those of rogan josh, yakhni, aab gosht and gushtaba, comes from Persian (Wikipedia, citing the 2016 review). A search of Grierson's Dictionary of the Kashmiri Language finds no entry for the word, though the dictionary does record a Kashmiri dish of "balls (or cakes) of this pounded meat fried in oil" (Grierson, p. 609), and it knows the tool: nal, a small stone mortar used for pounding pepper and other spices (Grierson, p. 632). The stone and the pounding were in the language before anyone wrote the dish down.
The wider family is older and larger. Kofta, the pounded meatball of Persian, Turkish and South Asian cooking, takes its name from the Persian koofta, "pounded meat". "The earliest known recipes are found in early Arab cookbooks", and they are "for large ground lamb meatballs triple-glazed in a mixture of saffron and egg yolk"; kofta "were also found in the Byzantine Empire"; a stuffed version, nargisi kofta, "was served at the Mughal court"; and across the family "sizes vary from that of a golf ball to that of an orange" (Wikipedia). When a former head of Kashmir University's Persian department listed the dishes that Persian cooks taught Kashmiris, kofta and rista were both on it (The Kashmir Walla, summarising Shams-ud-din Ahmad's Shah-i-Hamdan aur Kashmir). What the list does not say is how rista came to differ from the kofta it sits beside. Our history of Wazwan sets out what is documented about the feast's origins and what is only told; the short answer is that no document records when the Valley started pounding its meatballs on stone, or why.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: The pounding line
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: The clearest picture of rista being made is from a working-class wedding near Amira Kadal in Srinagar, where a reporter walking along the Jhelum in 2017 found 25 men cooking for 600 guests and a 12-course feast, "all meat". The host, Junaid Ali, was marrying off his daughter; asked how he could afford it, he said, "I'm a driver." Inside, "the waza or head chef sat harvesting choice boneless chunks from lamb legs for korma", "two men sat mincing lamb for waza sheekh", and then came what the reporter called "the gushtaba pounding pipeline: eight men, each with a stone mortar and a heavy wooden mallet. Starting with boneless chunks, each man pounded a spice into the meat before passing it on." The last man, "breathing a metronomic 'shhk shhk shhk', pounded in lamb fat, turning the mash pink", and "the end result were glistening oval discs" (Outlook Traveller). Those discs are the common stock of rista and gushtaba; the division into small red balls and large white ones comes later. Every other account describes the same work with fewer men.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: The pounding line
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text:
Kashmir Life has rista and gushtaba pounded by "a line of chefs using wooden mallets on stone slabs" (Kashmir Life); Gulf News has "Kashmiri walnut wood hammers on stone" (Gulf News); Reuters' photographs from 2026 show wazas pounding "with wooden mallets on stone slabs to prepare gushtaba and rista", and the agency reports that "the cooking method has changed little, with lightly spiced meat pounded by hand" (Reuters via Al Jazeera; Reuters). The mallet has three names in our sources. A 1988 cookbook calls it a goshpar; the Srinagar doctors who watched a wedding kitchen wrote that the meat "is minced on stony surfaces with a tukni (a wooden instrument)"; the reporters say mallet or hammer (Kaul Kilam; Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi; Reuters via Al Jazeera). The scale of the work depends on the wedding. "Normally, at an average marriage we cook 200 kgs of mutton," Ghulam Nabi Baba, 74, who learned the trade from his father in the cooks' quarter of Wazpora, told Reuters; forty years ago, at a village wedding at Delina in north Kashmir, he cooked 4,500 kg (Reuters). The Srinagar doctors found three to five kilograms of meat in a single trami for four (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi).
The back leg is the pounding cut; the ribs go to tabak maaz and the bony pieces to rogan josh and the kormas (Kashmir Life). Grierson's dictionary, a century ago, already had a word for a cook of this kind: wāza, "a cook-person, one who is a cook by profession, and comes of a line, or caste, of cooks" (Grierson, p. 1178). What does waza mean? follows the word.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: How it is made
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: Rista starts where gushtaba starts: with a sheep slaughtered that morning and a mallet. The meat is minced "directly after slaughter" with a wooden hammer on a flat stone, with fresh sheep fat and black cardamom pounded in; the paste is shaped into balls, smaller for rista and larger for gushtaba, and both are boiled (Sahapedia). It is folded as it is beaten, which works air into the paste and keeps the finished ball light (Wikipedia). Why the hurry? The waza Mohammad Shafi Khan says that if the mutton "is left idle and minced later" the ball cannot be made (The Kashmir Walla); Wikipedia's account, from The Hindu, is that the meat must be pounded before rigor mortis sets in, and that rista and gushtaba are rarely found outside the Valley because the texture is so hard to achieve (Wikipedia). Meat science agrees with the wazas, for reasons our gushtaba story sets out: before rigor, pounded and salted muscle holds water and binds in a way that rested meat cannot. A 2021 review describes pre-rigor muscle as having "excellent processing characteristics with high pH and relaxed microstructure" (Kim and others, Foods, 2021). Then the shaping and the first cooking.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: How it is made
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text:
A Kashmiri cookbook first published in 1988 rolls the same pounded mass "between the palms into 2–3 inch balls for goashtaba, or smaller, slightly flattened balls for rista or palak-rista" (Kaul Kilam, Culinary Art of Kashmir). The balls are boiled in water until they are soft and have expanded (Sahapedia); a chef who cooked with a Gulmarg waza describes both meatballs poached "in lamb stock flavoured with cinnamon and black cardamom" (Wikipedia, citing Chef Jolly). Only then do they meet the gravy. How big is a rista? The sources say golf ball, 80 to 100 g, and "smaller, slightly flattened" than a gushtaba, and the kofta family runs "from that of a golf ball to that of an orange"; rista sits at the small end and gushtaba, at 500 to 750 g in the 2012 paper's account, well past the large one (Gulf News; Sahapedia; Kaul Kilam; Wikipedia; Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi). The laboratory balls described below are 50 to 60 g, which is to say a small rista. Home versions do what home cooks must.
Wikipedia's article on the dish, following an NDTV recipe, has ground meat mixed with spices and eggs, rolled by hand, cooked in hot water for half an hour and then in the gravy (Wikipedia)); the 1988 cookbook kneads in arrowroot and allows a food processor for small batches (Kaul Kilam). Neither egg nor arrowroot appears in any account of a waza's kitchen.

sources.label: Kaul Kilam, Culinary Art of Kashmir

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: What the laboratory found
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: Rista has been studied in Srinagar's laboratories for nearly forty years, and the work is worth reading because it tests, one by one, the things the wazas insist on. The earliest study we have found is a 1988 veterinary thesis at the Indian Veterinary Research Institute, "Processing and preservation of Goshtaba and Rista (Kashmiri meat products)", by A. H. Samoon, which later papers still cite as the standard method (Jalal and others, Indian Journal of Animal Sciences, 2015). Samoon's published rista paper, in Meat Science in 1994, described the dish as "a popular emulsion type ground meat product of Kashmir (India)" and tested fat, freshness and the mallet. "Incorporation of lamb fat at 20% level was found optimum for processing Rista"; "both pre-rigor and chilled (post-rigor) meat were utilised"; adding 0.5 per cent sodium tripolyphosphate "improved product binding, texture and yield", and that improvement "was more pronounced in machine minced Rista samples processed from cold-boned lamb meat, as compared with hot-processed and hand minced product". Cooked rista kept "in satisfactory condition for 4 days" in a refrigerator (Samoon and Sharma, Meat Science, 199490052-3)).

sources.label: Jalal and others, Indian Journal of Animal Sciences, 2015

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: What the laboratory found
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: Read the other way round, that is the wazas' method stated as a result: fresh meat pounded by hand needs no phosphate to bind; chilled meat through a machine does. The Kashmir University group that took up the work in the 2010s uses the same vocabulary. Gushtaba, rista's twin, is "an emulsion type ground meat product", in which "considerable amount of animal fat (20 %) is used in its formulation to achieve a stable emulsion", and the laboratory makes it from "fresh mutton from hind leg portion", the wazas' cut, shaped into "compact balls of 60 mm diameter and 50–60 g weight" (Rather and others, Journal of Food Science and Technology, 2015). A veterinary group at the Sher-e-Kashmir agricultural university records the deadline in laboratory terms: their mutton and fat were "used for the preparation of the products within 2 h of post-mortem". Their standard formulation is bare: 90 parts boneless mutton to 10 of mutton fat, with 2.5 per cent salt, 10 per cent chilled water and 0.2 per cent large cardamom seeds, and they note that the traditional product "with an average fat content of 15–25% is having a high sensory appeal" (Jalal and others, 2015).

sources.label: Rather and others, Journal of Food Science and Technology, 2015

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: What the laboratory found
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: Salt, fat, black cardamom and fresh meat: the same four things Sahapedia's wazas pound in. The most recent paper we have found answers a question the wedding guest never asks. In 2016 six scientists at the same agricultural university, calling rista one of the "indigenous meat products of Kashmiri cuisine (Wazwan)", cooked batches of it from pure mutton, pure beef, pure buffalo and mixtures down to one part in a hundred, and showed that a DNA test could still find beef or buffalo in a cooked rista at the 1 per cent level, "processing, cooking, and non-meat ingredients" having no effect on the result. "Meat adulteration is a serious problem in the meat industry and needs to be tackled," they wrote (Bhat and others, Veterinary World, 2016). The paper does not say that any wedding rista has ever been adulterated; it says that if one were, the test would show it. That such a test was developed for rista, rather than for sausage, says something about where the dish stands in the Valley.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Why it is red
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: Rista's gravy is red the way rogan josh is red, and the sources name the same three colourings in different proportions. The first is Kashmiri chilli. Shafi Khan's rista goes into mutton stock with cardamom, cloves, garlic and Kashmiri chillies, "which add colour more than heat" (The Kashmir Walla); the chilli itself rates about 1,000 to 2,000 Scoville units (Wikipedia). The Gulmarg waza's version builds the gravy on "a cooked paste of praan, garlic, red onion and the extract of red dried chili", and the chef's verdict is that "rista is primarily red due to the red chilli, whilst gustaba is whiter" (Chef Jolly). What makes the chilli a dye rather than a heat is measurable. Kashmiri red chillies "are characterized by their ability to give a dark red colour to food and add flavour, while not allowing the food to become too pungent or spicy"; the Spices Board says they are grown mainly in Jammu and Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh and harvested in winter; the dried pod "appears wrinkled and rough, often brownish", but "contains densely concentrated red pigment material"; its ASTA colour value, the spice trade's measure of extractable colour, is 54.10, and its capsaicin, the heat, only 0.325 per cent (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Why it is red
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: Demand outruns supply, so Byadgi chillies from the south are "often used" as substitutes, and India's Consumer Education and Research Centre has tested two branded "Kashmiri" powders at 48,000 and 60,000 Scoville units, with brick powder recorded as "one of the forms of adulteration" (Wikipedia). Wikipedia's article on Kashmiri cooking adds that the chilli "is also added in excess sometimes to produce a red colour" (Wikipedia). Our Kashmiri red chilli guide and the marchwangan korma story go further into the pod. The second is mawal, the dried cockscomb flower that is boiled to make the red colouring used mostly in Wazwan (Wikipedia); Grierson's dictionary has it as mawal, "the cockscomb", a plant whose seed-cakes it records as a peasant food without a word about dye (Grierson, p. 611). Azmat Ali Mir, a Kashmiri restaurateur, credits it with the deep red of the feast's dishes, and the article that quotes her calls rista's gravy "saffron-based" (Asia Media Centre).

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Why it is red
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: Saffron is the third: Wikipedia's Wazwan article names it with fennel in the gravy and says the colour is helped along with alkanet, the root called ratan jot (Wikipedia); the chef's notes have rista "further enhanced in colour by saffron extract", with hot ghee or mustard oil poured over the finished dish and a garnish of fried praan paste (Chef Jolly). The result is what a Gulf News writer, at his cousin's wedding, called "a rich rouge gravy" (Gulf News). Is it hot? Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes calls the gravy "fiery red" (Wikipedia), which describes the colour; the waza's own description, colour more than heat, describes the taste, and the same Wikipedia article records that Kashmiri Muslim cooking "uses chilies in moderate quantity, and avoid hot dishes at large meals" (Wikipedia). Kitchens vary, and a Srinagar master chef has admitted to Kashmir Life that he is "not averse to using food grade colors" when the rest of the pot is honest (Kashmir Life). For how the colourings work, see our rogan josh story.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: What a rista costs
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: In the autumn of 2012 three researchers from the Sher-i-Kashmir Institute of Medical Sciences chose a wedding at random, had the vasta waza "keep a record of every ingredient used and the number of servings prepared", repeated the exercise three times, and worked out the calories from the National Institute of Nutrition's tables. Their rista, four balls to a trami, carried 1,814 calories, or 454 for each diner: the heaviest of the dishes served in a gravy, ahead of the gushtaba (447), the rogan josh (331), the marchwangan korma (265) and the aab gosh (234); only the kebabs (740) and the whole chicken fried in ghee (899) carried more. The trami as a whole held 18,484 calories before rice and 21,933 with it, "dishing up some 5483 calories to the invited person" (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, JMS SKIMS, 2012). The paper is a two-page brief report with a slip in it, its text giving the chicken's 3,597 calories to the rista, which its own table corrects; its fieldwork, a waza's weighed ingredient list at a real wedding, is the only such record we know of.

sources.label: Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, JMS SKIMS, 2012

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: What a rista costs
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: The authors' conclusion was not to give up the feast but to "reduce the amount served per person", and they noted in passing that a PubMed search for "Wazwan" found no earlier paper at all. A 2026 public-health advisory in Srinagar reached the same place by estimate: a trami for four "may contain between 6,000 and 9,000 calories", "approximately 1,500 to 2,250 calories per person", with "meatballs such as Rista and Gushtaba" among the main contributors, and it ended, "Wazwan is a celebration, not an everyday meal" (Kashmir Reader). The 2012 measurement and the 2026 estimate differ by a factor of two or more; what they share is the place of rista near the top of the list. The fat the eighth man pounds in is where the calories are. For every dish on that trami, see how many calories are in a Wazwan.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Where it comes in the meal
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: Rista comes early. In Shafi Khan's kitchen it is the first dish served after the trami, four balls to a platter (The Kashmir Walla). Gulf News calls it the second course, after the kebabs, ribs and chicken on the rice (Gulf News). Outlook India lists it after methi maaz and before rogan josh (Outlook India); Asia Media Centre has the same order (Asia Media Centre); the Srinagar doctors' list, "in the order in which they are served", has it sixth, after methi, chicken, kabab, tabakmaaz and dani, and first of the gravies (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi). Whatever the kitchen, it opens the gravies, and its white twin closes them: a feast that begins with a red meatball and ends with a white one. How Wazwan is served gives the whole order.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: The sheep behind the ball
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: Rista is made from a sheep that was alive that morning, and in Kashmir that sheep has usually come a long way. Walter Lawrence found in the 1890s that "the mutton of Kashmir is throughout excellent", the best of it from Nandpur on the Dal lake, but also that "in spite of the number of sheep in Kashmir it is often difficult to obtain mutton in the villages", where flocks were kept for wool and warmth; the cultivator ate mutton "perhaps five times in the month" (Lawrence, pp. 254 and 363). The Valley now eats roughly twice the mutton it raises. Figures reported between 2012 and 2026 put imports at 55 to 70 per cent of consumption, trucked up the Jammu-Srinagar highway from Rajasthan and beyond (Kashmir Life; Greater Kashmir; Kashmir Times), and when Punjab taxed those trucks in the summer of 2026 the dealers stopped importing and families began talking of postponing weddings; an average wedding, the Press Trust of India reported, consumes "around 500 kilogrammes of mutton and 150 kilogrammes of chicken" (PTI via Outlook Business). Our tabak maaz story follows the sheep from Lawrence's Nandpur to the Rajasthan mandis. For rista the point is a practical one: a dish that must be pounded within the hour of slaughter is made, now, from animals that arrived in the Valley by truck a day or two before.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Rista, gushtaba and the rest of the family
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text:
Rista and gushtaba are one meat in two dishes: the same pounded mutton and fat, shaped small for rista and large for gushtaba, cooked red for rista and white for gushtaba, served first and last (Sahapedia; Wikipedia). Our guide to rista vs gushtaba sets them side by side, and the gushtaba story explains why the larger ball comes last.
The family has grown around them. Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes records beef riste, palak riste cooked with spinach, and safed riste, a white version (Wikipedia); the 1988 cookbook knows palak-rista too (Kaul Kilam). A Srinagar chef told Kashmir Life in 2011 that rista and gushtaba, traditionally mutton, were by then also made with chicken and fish (Kashmir Life). And the dish has a restaurant life of its own: at a Srinagar hotel's Wazwan a reporter was served "rista haaq", tiny meatballs with the Valley's collard greens, "bright and toothsome" (Outlook Traveller). The Srinagar doctors noted in 2012 that "ready-made Wazwan is now available on a fly", and the laboratory papers above are, at bottom, attempts to make a rista that keeps: four days in 1994, twenty in 2015 (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi; Samoon and Sharma90052-3); Jalal and others).

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Eating it for the first time
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: Rista is the easiest Wazwan dish to order on its own, and most Srinagar restaurants serve it as a plate of two or three balls in gravy with rice; our guide to eating in Srinagar lists places, and the cost guide covers prices. Expect a ball that is springy rather than dense, a gravy that is red rather than hot, and a sheen of fat on top. At a trami, it is the first gravy to arrive, one ball per diner, and it is eaten with the rice and the fingers.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Frequently asked questions: What is rista?
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: A ball of mutton pounded with fat, about 80 to 100 g, boiled and then cooked in a red gravy of Kashmiri chilli, mawal, saffron and fennel. It is one of the seven essential dishes of a Wazwan and the first gravy served.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Frequently asked questions: How is rista made?
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: From a sheep slaughtered the same morning. The meat is pounded with a wooden mallet on a flat stone, with fresh fat and black cardamom worked in, until it is smooth and light; it is shaped into small balls, boiled in water or stock, and finished in the red gravy. Home recipes add egg or arrowroot; wazas use neither.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Frequently asked questions: What is the mallet called?
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: A 1988 Kashmiri cookbook calls it a goshpar; doctors who watched a Srinagar wedding kitchen call it a tukni, "a wooden instrument"; reporters describe walnut-wood mallets or hammers used on stone slabs. Grierson's dictionary records a small stone mortar for pounding spices, nal, but no entry for rista itself.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Frequently asked questions: Why is rista red?
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: From Kashmiri chilli, which colours strongly but is mild, and from mawal, the dried cockscomb flower, with saffron. Wikipedia's Wazwan article also names alkanet. There is no tomato.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Frequently asked questions: Is rista spicy?
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: Usually not very. The Kashmiri chilli that colours it rates about 1,000 to 2,000 Scoville units and has a capsaicin content of about 0.3 per cent, and a waza describes the chillies as adding colour more than heat. Kitchens vary, and some powders sold as Kashmiri have tested far hotter.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Frequently asked questions: How many calories are in rista?
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: At the Srinagar wedding studied by SKIMS researchers in 2012, the four rista on a trami carried about 1,814 calories, or 454 per diner, the most of any dish served in a gravy; only the kebabs and the whole chicken carried more. A 2026 health advisory estimated 1,500 to 2,250 calories per person for a whole trami and named rista among the main contributors.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Frequently asked questions: What is the difference between rista and gushtaba?
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: The same pounded mutton in two dishes. Rista is small, one per diner, in a red gravy, served early; gushtaba is large, one per trami, in a white yogurt gravy, served last.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Frequently asked questions: When is rista served at a Wazwan?
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: Early: the first gravy after the dishes that arrive on the trami, before rogan josh and the kormas.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Frequently asked questions: Is rista the same as kofta?
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: It belongs to the same family. Kofta takes its name from the Persian for "pounded meat", its earliest recipes are in early Arab cookbooks, and a Kashmir University Persian scholar lists both kofta and rista among the dishes Persian cooks taught Kashmiris. Rista is the Kashmiri Wazwan's own version: fresh-pounded mutton and fat, in a red gravy, one to a diner.

chunks.title: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone: Frequently asked questions: Can rista be made with beef?
chunks.page: Rista: The Meatball Pounded on a Stone
chunks.text: A beef version, beef riste, appears on Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes, and a Srinagar chef says chicken and fish versions exist. The Wazwan rista is mutton, and a 2016 study at Kashmir's agricultural university developed a DNA test that can detect beef or buffalo in a cooked mutton rista at the 1 per cent level.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: Aab gosht, the Wazwan's milk curry: what its name means, the ten litres reduced to one, which cut is used, and how it differs from Persian abgoosht.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text:
By the time aab gosht reaches the trami, the red dishes are behind you. Rista, rogan josh and the two kormas have come and gone, and the wazas now bring the pale ones: a piece of mutton in a gravy the colour of cream, then yakhni, then gushtaba (Outlook India). The cream is milk, and a great deal of it. "Ten litres of pure cow milk are reduced to one and then mixed with the mutton," Mohammad Shafi Khan, a second-generation waza from downtown Srinagar, told The Kashmir Walla (The Kashmir Walla).
Aab gosht is the gentlest of the seven essential Wazwan dishes and the one with the most misleading name. The name is Persian and means meat broth; the dish is Kashmiri and is made with milk. In Iran a dish of the same name is something else entirely. This story covers the two names, the two dishes, what milk meant in the Valley before anyone wrote the recipe down, the words Kashmiri has for it, the reduction and what it does, the cut, the spices, what the dish costs the body, and where it comes in the meal. For what the dish is, with a recipe and where to eat it, see aab gosht.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: What aab gosht is
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: Aab gosht is mutton cooked in reduced milk. Wikipedia describes "lamb chunks cooked with a fennel-based spice mixture, cardamom and partially evaporated milk" and lists it among the seven dishes that are "a must" at a Wazwan (Wikipedia); its list of Kashmiri dishes calls it "a famous milk-based curry cooked in spices and ghee over a low flame" (Wikipedia). The Waza family's cookbook counts it among the seven indispensable dishes (Roli Books), and a 2016 review of the feast's meat products names it with kabab, tabak maaz, rogan josh, yakhni, rista and goshtaba (Rather, Masoodi and Akhter). Reporters describe it as "sheep ribs cooked in a milk-based gravy and flavoured with green cardamoms and saffron" (Outlook India) and, more simply, "mutton in milk sauce" (Outlook Traveller). The Hindu's 2012 account, as Wikipedia quotes it, calls it "lamb cooked in sweet milk curry" (Wikipedia). Doctors who recorded a Srinagar wedding feast in 2012 were more anatomical: "1 piece of sacral area of vertebral column prepared in milk", one large piece to a trami (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, SKIMS, 2012).

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Two names, two dishes
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: The dish has a Persian name and a Kashmiri one, and they say different things. Aab gosht is Persian. The names of rogan josh, yakhni, aab gosht, rista and gushtaba all "stem from Persian sources", as Wikipedia puts it, citing the 2016 review (Wikipedia). In Persian, abgoosht means "literally 'meat broth'" (Wikipedia): āb, water, and gūsht, meat. When a former head of Kashmir University's Persian department listed the dishes that Persian cooks taught Kashmiris, aab gosht was on it, with kabab, rogan josh, korma, yakhni, pulao, kofta and rista (The Kashmir Walla, summarising Shams-ud-din Ahmad's Shah-i-Hamdan aur Kashmir). Kashmiri kept the Persian element and used it the Persian way. Grierson's Dictionary of the Kashmiri Language has no entry for aab gosht, but under gōshĕth, meat, it enters gusht-āba, "a rich soup of pounded or minced meat" (Grierson, p. 309): the same two elements in the other order, naming the dish for its liquid. In the Valley's kitchen vocabulary, āb meant the broth a thing was cooked in, whatever the broth was made of. Dodhe maaz is Kashmiri, and it describes what is in the pot. Dŏd is milk and māz is meat in Grierson's dictionary (Grierson, pp. 190 and 615): milk-meat.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Two names, two dishes
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes gives dodhe maaz as the dish's other name, and a Srinagar food writer's recipe is titled "Kashmiri Aab Gosh (Dodhe Maaz)" (Wikipedia; Rising Kashmir). So the Persian name records the idea of a meat broth, and the Kashmiri name records what Kashmir did with it. What Iran calls abgoosht is a different dish. It is "usually made with lamb, chickpeas, white beans, onion, potatoes, tomatoes, turmeric, and dried lime", a "hearty mutton Persian soup thickened with chickpeas", cooked and then strained, with the broth eaten first with bread and the solids mashed into a paste; it is served in stoneware crocks called dizi, which has become its other name (Wikipedia). No milk, and beans and potatoes that the Kashmiri dish has never had. Kashmir Life notes the contrast in standing too: aab gosht is "rich" in Kashmir, but the Iranian dish it is named for began as "poor man's food" (Kashmir Life). What travelled from Persia, on this evidence, was the name and the idea of meat in its liquid. The milk is Kashmir's.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Shir and āb: two Persian words, two Kashmiri liquids
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text:
There is a second Persian word for a liquid in the Kashmiri kitchen, and it went to a different dish. The salted tea that Kashmiris drink through the day is noon chai, from noon, salt, and it is also called sheer chai, from shir, which "means 'milk' in Persian"; Kashmiri Pandits call it sheer chai still (Wikipedia). It is "traditionally made from green tea leaves, milk, salt and baking soda, and is usually cooked in a samavar", the soda turning the brew red and the milk turning the red to pink, and it is "popularly consumed numerous times per day in Kashmir" (Wikipedia). Lawrence met it in the 1890s: tea, he wrote, was served either very sweet, as kahwa, or very salty, as shir, with milk, from a samovar, and eaten with wheaten bread (Lawrence, p. 254).
So Kashmiri took two Persian words for two of its milk preparations and crossed them. The milk tea got shir, milk; the milk curry got āb, water. That is not a muddle so much as a record of what each name was describing: the tea is named for what is added to it, the dish for the Persian category it was understood to belong to, meat in a broth. The Kashmiri names, dodhe maaz and noon chai, name the ingredient and the salt. Nobody has recorded when either Persian word attached itself, and we do not propose a date; the dictionary, the tea and the dish simply arrive together in the nineteenth-century record, with the words already in place.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Milk in the Valley, 1895
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: Why milk? The sources give no origin for the dish, so the honest answer is that nobody knows. But the Valley that made it was, by the one detailed account we have of its food before the twentieth century, a place awash in milk and short of almost every other richness. Walter Lawrence, the state's settlement commissioner, wrote in 1895 that the cultivator's diet was rice and other grains, vegetables, oil, salt and pepper, and milk without limit; that fowl was eaten about six times a month and mutton "perhaps five times in the month"; and that "clarified butter (ghi) is not much eaten", because Kashmiris believed it irritated the throat (Lawrence, pp. 253 to 254). Elsewhere he records that Kashmiris depended heavily on milk and wool, kept their cattle in byres on the ground floor of the house, and thought maize unpalatable without milk; that in the famine of 1878 people had lived on wild herbs "while skim milk lasted", and that herbs without milk proved fatal; that goat's milk was reckoned strengthening and milch goats were led from door to door to feed infants; and that tea was always taken with milk, salted or sweet (Lawrence, The Valley of Kashmir, found through the archive's full-text search).

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Milk in the Valley, 1895
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: The cows themselves were small. A cow giving four seers of milk a day, about four kilograms, was treasured; improved cows gave eight; rice straw and rice water were said to raise the yield; and a proverb warned that loud lowing and a large udder rarely meant much milk (Lawrence, chapter on cattle). The ghi the Valley did make was mostly from buffalo milk, made by the Gujar herders and sold to Punjabi middlemen, and was by far its most important export; cow's-milk ghi, Lawrence noted, was reckoned the most delicate (Lawrence, chapters on cattle and exports). Much of that milk came down from the hills with the herders. Lawrence records the Gujars giving away all of Friday's milk in charity; the Gujars and Pathans of the Lolab making a cheese he calls milk-bread, which he thought could supply the garrisons of upper India with cheese and butter; the village shepherd, the chaupan, taking as a perquisite the butter he made from sheep's milk; and the state taxing milch buffaloes for their summer grazing in the forests (Lawrence, chapter on cattle and the pages on the Gujars).

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Milk in the Valley, 1895
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: The same transhumant communities that bring the Valley its sheep in autumn, as our tabak maaz story describes, were its dairy in Lawrence's day. A wedding in October, when the flocks come down, is a wedding in the season of both. Milk was ritual as well as food. Lawrence records a feast of rice and milk at a child's first month, rice boiled in milk as the first solid food at six months, rice boiled in milk distributed when smallpox abated, and, at the spring of Khir Bhawani, the "milk goddess" of the Kashmiri Pandits, offerings of sugar, milk, rice and flowers; Hindus visiting her abstained from meat that day (Lawrence, pp. 260, 286 and 300). Grierson's dictionary, compiled in the same decades, has a matching omen: zang, a sign of good luck, its example "a dish of curds" placed on the right hand before starting an undertaking (Grierson, p. 1227). A dish that cooks the feast's mutton in ten litres of milk belongs to that Valley: one where milk was the ordinary abundance, ghee was something you sold, and a bowl of white was a good sign. That is context, not a cause; no source says the wazas chose milk for any of these reasons.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: The words for milk
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: Kashmiri distinguishes the milk in aab gosht from the curd in yakhni and gushtaba, and the dictionary shows how fine the distinctions run. Dŏd is milk (Grierson, p. 190). Zyonu is to curdle, and zyonu dŏd is curdled milk; caka is curds, curdled milk with the whey strained out; mana is "whey, the liquid of curds"; har is the scum that rises like cream on curds; aḍ is milk only half boiled; chôpu is the small churning-stick (Grierson, pp. 1239, 168, 572, 343, 12 and 163). The dishes follow the words. Yĕkhañĕ is "a kind of dish (consisting of meat cooked with spices in curdled milk)" (Grierson, p. 1192); kürü is "curdled milk cooked and spiced, used as a relish with other food"; trakānüja is "a drink made up of milk, curds, and water mixed in equal parts"; buröni is a salad of pounded radish in curds with cumin and salt, which is the radish chutney a Wazwan still serves between its heavy dishes (Grierson, pp. 468, 1024 and 124). What the dictionary does not record is any dish of meat cooked in fresh milk. Aab gosht, or dodhe maaz, is not there. Whether that means the dish is younger than the dictionary's informants, or only that no informant mentioned it, the dictionary cannot say; it records a kitchen in which milk was everywhere and curd was the usual medium for meat.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: A dish with a short paper trail
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: For a dish counted among the seven, aab gosht has left few marks on paper, and the gaps are themselves informative. Grierson's dictionary, compiled from the 1890s, has words for milk, curds, whey and a meat dish cooked in curd, and none for a meat dish cooked in milk. The 1988 Culinary Art of Kashmir, written from the Kashmiri Pandit kitchen with a separate section for the cuisine of the Valley's Muslims, has yakhni twice in its index and no dish of meat in milk at all (Kaul Kilam, index). The first written places we find the dish are the wazas' own canon, the Roli cookbook's list of seven indispensable dishes (Roli Books), the 2016 food-science review that names it among the feast's ethnic meat products (Rather, Masoodi and Akhter), and the 2012 medical paper that counted its calories (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi); Wikipedia's own article on it is a stub, and the one full recipe in a Kashmiri newspaper dates from 2023 (Rising Kashmir). None of that proves the dish is young; it proves that it belongs to the wazas' kitchen, which was not written down, rather than to the Pandit one, which was. Our history of Wazwan sets out how little of the feast's past is on paper at all.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: The milk: ten to one
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: The defining act of the dish is a reduction. Shafi Khan's ten litres to one is matched by Wikipedia's list, which records the same figure (The Kashmir Walla; Wikipedia). A chef who cooked with a Gulmarg waza describes fresh milk reduced "with cinnamon, green cardamom, paste of praan, garlic, ginger powder and fennel powder", the boiled meat then simmered in the milk sauce "until the flavour becomes well-rounded" (Chef Jolly). Ten to one is a long way to take milk. The nearest comparison in South Asian cooking is khoa, the milk solid that is the base of most of the subcontinent's sweets, made "by simmering full-fat milk in a large, shallow iron pan for several hours over a medium fire", at about 80 °C to avoid scorching, and for which "a concentration of milk to one-fifth volume is normal" (Wikipedia). The waza's reduction goes twice as far as the sweet-maker's, and does it in a copper deg over wood, with the aromatics in the milk from the start. Nobody has recorded how long it takes a wedding kitchen; the sources say only that the cooking begins around three in the morning and runs for about six hours (Onmanorama; The Kashmir Walla).

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: The milk: ten to one
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: Reducing ten litres of milk takes a wood fire and a morning, so most published recipes take a shortcut: milk powder. Sahapedia's account of the wazas' dish has full-cream dry milk added to the mutton stock, with ghee to finish, giving "a creamy soup" (Sahapedia); the Srinagar recipe uses 500 g of full-cream dry milk to a kilo of mutton, mixed with two or three cups of water or stock and brought to the boil before the boiled meat goes in, with two more cups of stock, fried shallot paste and ghee, and a scatter of almonds at the end (Rising Kashmir). Wikipedia's "partially evaporated milk" describes the same thing from the other direction (Wikipedia). Khoa and milk powder are, in the end, the same shortcut: milk with the water already taken out.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Milk in a copper pot
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: The reduction happens in the same pots as everything else. At the wedding Outlook Traveller watched in 2017, "in the kitchen tent, a dozen men worked over a raging fire fed by whole logs arranged along a trench", and "on it simmered enormous brass vats bearing aab gosht, rogan josh, rista, pulao" (Outlook Traveller). Other accounts call the vats copper: "nickel-plated copper daegs" in Outlook India, nickel-plated copper on fruit-tree logs in IANS's account (Outlook India; Onmanorama). The word is in Grierson's dictionary as dēg, "a large pile of rice cooked in a cauldron, for a wedding feast or the like", the cauldron having given its name to what was cooked in it (Grierson, p. 194). The plating matters more for this dish than for any other on the trami, and the dictionary says why. Its entry for zangāra, verdigris, notes that milk or curds in a metal vessel spoil under a verdigris scum (Grierson, p. 1227). A hundred years before anyone wrote "nickel-plated", Kashmiri already had a word for what bare copper does to milk. Ten litres reduced to one in a pot that is not lined would not be aab gosht; it would be the dictionary's zangāra.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Milk in a copper pot
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: The lining, the tinning that Kashmiri coppersmiths renew and the nickel that has replaced it in modern degs, is the unglamorous technology the dish depends on. Our history of Wazwan follows the copper. The sweetness that The Hindu noticed comes without sugar. Reduced milk is sweet in itself, and Khan adds cloves sautéed in pure ghee "for sweetness" (The Kashmir Walla). None of the accounts we have read adds chilli, tomato or turmeric; the dish is pale because nothing in it is red. Lawrence noted that Kashmiris liked their food very salty and were "very fond of tea and sugar", and that tea came either very sweet or salted (Lawrence, p. 254); a sweetish, salted milk gravy would not have surprised him.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Milk today
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: The Valley Lawrence described still milks small cows, and many more of them. Jammu and Kashmir has "1.76 million non-descript indigenous cattle" and "1.05 million buffaloes", according to a 2022 review by the Sher-e-Kashmir agricultural university, which quotes Lawrence's own description of the local cattle as "small, hardy and conservative in habits" (Hamadani and others, Indian Journal of Animal Sciences, 2022). The union government told the Lok Sabha in 2026 that the territory's milk production had risen from 2.82 million tonnes in 2022-23 to 2.97 million tonnes in 2024-25, and that the milk available per person had risen from 572 to 595 grams a day, against a national figure of 485 (Kashmir Life). Where the Valley imports more than half its mutton, as our tabak maaz story sets out, its milk is its own. Of the two main ingredients of aab gosht, the ten litres are the local one.

sources.label: Hamadani and others, Indian Journal of Animal Sciences, 2022

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: The cut and the spices
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text:
The sources name different cuts, and all of them are big. Sahapedia has meat from the lamb's tail, shoulder or shank, boiled until tender (Sahapedia); the Srinagar recipe has the same three (Rising Kashmir). Khan uses "one large piece from the lower back", slow-cooked in the milk (The Kashmir Walla); the Srinagar doctors' "sacral area of vertebral column" is the same place in a surgeon's words (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi). Two reporters say sheep ribs (Outlook India; Onmanorama). What they share is large pieces rather than small chunks, boiled first and finished in the milk; at the wedding the Srinagar doctors recorded, the dish came as one large piece to a trami of four (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi).
The spices are the Wazwan's gentle register. Sahapedia's list is shallot, garlic paste, ginger powder, fennel powder, cloves, green and black cardamom, cinnamon and salt (Sahapedia); the Srinagar recipe's is the same with fried shallot paste and ghee (Rising Kashmir). Wikipedia calls the mixture "fennel-based" (Wikipedia), and two accounts add saffron with the green cardamom (Outlook India; Onmanorama). Grierson's dictionary has the two foundation spices as bödiyāna, sweet fennel, whose kernels are pounded in a mortar, and shō̃ṭh, dry ginger (Grierson, pp. 89 and 899); see fennel and dry ginger.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: What it costs
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: For a dish built on ten litres of milk, aab gosht is the lightest meat on the trami. The three researchers from the Sher-i-Kashmir Institute of Medical Sciences who had a wedding's vasta waza "keep a record of every ingredient used" in 2012, and worked the calories out from the National Institute of Nutrition's tables, found the aab gosh carrying 934 calories per trami, or 234 for each of the four diners: less than the marchwangan korma (265), the rogan josh (331), the tabak maaz (367), the gushtaba (447) and the rista (454), and less than everything else they counted except the single piece of dani (177). The whole trami came to 21,933 calories with rice, "some 5483 calories to the invited person" (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, JMS SKIMS, 2012). The figures are from one wedding, repeated three times, and the paper is a two-page brief report; but they are the only weighed record of the feast we know of, and they put the milk dish where a diner would expect it, at the mild end. A 2026 public-health advisory in Srinagar, estimating 6,000 to 9,000 calories for a typical trami, named the rice, the meatballs, the kebabs, the tabak maaz and "gravies rich in fats and oils" as the main contributors, and did not name aab gosht at all (Kashmir Reader).

sources.label: Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, JMS SKIMS, 2012

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Where it comes in the meal
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: Aab gosht comes late. In Outlook India's account of the order it follows marchwangan korma and comes before yakhni and gushtaba (Outlook India); in Asia Media Centre's it follows rista, rogan josh and daniphol (Asia Media Centre). At the wedding the Srinagar doctors recorded it came ninth of eleven dishes, after the tomato paneer and before the spinach, the marchwangan korma and the goshtaba (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi), which is a reminder that kitchens differ in the middle of the meal even as they agree on its ends. It is served on the trami with rice (Sahapedia). Read across the accounts, the feast moves from red to white: the chilli-coloured dishes in the middle, then aab gosht, yakhni and gushtaba, each paler and milder than the last. That shape is our observation; the order is the sources'. How Wazwan is served gives the whole sequence.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Eating it for the first time
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: Most visitors meet aab gosht in a Srinagar restaurant, on its own or late in a set trami; our guide to eating in Srinagar lists places, and the cost guide covers prices. Expect a large piece of mutton in a pale, creamy gravy with the scent of fennel and cardamom and a faint sweetness, eaten with rice. It is mild; there is no chilli in it. And if you have eaten abgoosht in an Iranian restaurant, expect nothing like it.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: What is aab gosht?
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: Mutton, usually a large piece from the shoulder, shank, tail, lower back or ribs, boiled and then cooked in milk reduced with fennel, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, ginger, shallot and garlic. It is one of the seven essential dishes of a Wazwan and comes late in the meal.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: What does aab gosht mean?
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: The name is Persian and means meat broth: āb, water, and gūsht, meat. Its Kashmiri name, dodhe maaz, means milk-meat, which is what the dish is.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: Is aab gosht the same as Persian abgoosht?
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: No. The Iranian abgoosht is lamb with chickpeas, beans, onion, potatoes, tomatoes, turmeric and dried lime, strained and mashed, and served in a stone pot. The Kashmiri dish shares the name and nothing else: it is mutton in reduced milk with fennel and cardamom.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: How much milk goes into aab gosht?
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: A waza describes ten litres of cow's milk reduced to one for the wedding dish, twice the reduction used to make khoa for sweets. Published home recipes use full-cream milk powder instead, about 500 g to a kilo of mutton.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: Is aab gosht made with milk or yogurt?
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: Fresh milk. Kashmiri keeps the two apart: dŏd is milk and caka or zyonu dŏd is curd. Yakhni and gushtaba are cooked in curd; aab gosht, or dodhe maaz, is the Wazwan's one dish cooked in reduced fresh milk.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: Why is aab gosht sweet?
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: Because reduced milk is sweet in itself; no sugar is added. A Srinagar waza also sautés cloves in ghee "for sweetness". The Hindu described the dish as "lamb cooked in sweet milk curry".

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: Is aab gosht cooked in copper?
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: In nickel-plated or tinned copper degs over wood, like the rest of the feast; one reporter saw brass vats. Grierson's dictionary records that milk or curds spoil in a bare metal vessel under a scum of verdigris, which is why the lining matters more for this dish than for any other.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: Is there a Kashmiri Pandit aab gosht?
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: We have found none. The 1988 Pandit cookbook's index lists no dish of meat cooked in milk, and Grierson's dictionary records no such dish either; aab gosht appears in writing in the wazas' own list of seven and in later reporting, which places it with the Muslim feast rather than the Pandit table.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: Which cut of meat is used?
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: Large pieces: tail, shoulder or shank in Sahapedia's account, one large piece from the lower back in a waza's, "the sacral area of the vertebral column" in a medical paper's, sheep ribs in two reporters'. At the wedding a medical team recorded in 2012, it came as one large piece to a trami of four.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: How many calories are in aab gosht?
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: At the Srinagar wedding studied by SKIMS researchers in 2012, the aab gosh carried about 934 calories per trami, or 234 per diner, the lightest of the main mutton dishes they counted.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: Is aab gosht spicy?
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: No. Its flavour is fennel, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and ginger in reduced milk, with saffron in some accounts. None of the accounts we have read adds chilli, tomato or turmeric.

chunks.title: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: When is aab gosht served at a Wazwan?
chunks.page: Aab Gosht: The Milk Curry of the Wazwan
chunks.text: Late, among the pale dishes: after marchwangan korma and before yakhni and gushtaba in one account; after rista, rogan josh and daniphol in another; before the korma and the gushtaba at the wedding a medical team recorded.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course
chunks.text: Daniwal korma, the Wazwan's coriander course: what its name means, what korma means in Kashmir, how it is made, and where it comes in the meal.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course
chunks.text:
Between the two red dishes of a Wazwan comes a green one. After rogan josh and before marchwangan korma, in Outlook India's account of the order, the wazas serve daniwal korma, "mutton cooked in a lot of coriander" (Outlook India). A magazine glossary describes what arrives: "superbly tender meat on the bone, in a white gravy flavoured with coriander" (Outlook Traveller). It is the least written-about of the seven essential dishes, and the one whose name tells you most about it.
This is the story of a dish with a long name: what daniwal and korma each mean, where the herb and the word came from, why the herb is a spring plant at an autumn feast, what the dish is built on, what the sources agree and disagree on, how it is made, why it is not the korma the rest of the world knows, and where it sits in the meal. For what the dish is, with a recipe and where to eat it, see daniwal korma.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: What daniwal korma is
chunks.text: Daniwal korma is mutton braised in a yogurt gravy and finished with fresh coriander. Wikipedia's article on the dish calls it lamb or mutton "cooked in a yogurt-based gravy flavored with fresh coriander leaves" and "a staple of the Kashmiri Wazwan" (Wikipedia), and its Wazwan article lists it among the seven dishes that are "a must" at the feast (Wikipedia). The Waza family's cookbook names "dhaniwal korma" among the same seven (Roli Books), and the former tourism director M. Saleem Beg has "dhania kurma" in his list of seven standard dishes (Daily Excelsior). Reporters at weddings describe "mutton cooked in coriander" (Gulf News) and "mutton korma cooked in coriander and ghee with yogurt-based gravy" (Onmanorama).

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: The name: coriander, and a braise
chunks.text:
Both halves of the name are in the dictionaries.
Daniwal is coriander, and specifically the leaf. Grierson's Dictionary of the Kashmiri Language enters dāñĕwal as the greens of the coriander plant, and distinguishes it from dāñĕwal-gūjü, the powdered and sifted seed, and dāñĕwal-kulu, the shrub itself (Grierson, p. 232). The dish is named for the fresh herb, not the spice. A news feature cited by Wikipedia makes the same point in Hindi-Urdu terms: daniwal means coriander (Wikipedia, citing Times Now). Hindi and Urdu use one word, dhania, for both leaf and seed; Kashmiri, on the dictionary's evidence, used a suffix to tell them apart, and the dish takes the bare word, the leaf.
Korma is a braise. Wikipedia's article on the dish glosses "korme" or "korma" as braise, citing Merriam-Webster (Wikipedia), and its article on korma says that "the English name is an anglicisation of the Hindi-Urdu qormā", which in turn derives from "the Turkic qawirma, '[a] fried thing'", though "korma and modern Turkish kavurma are quite different dishes" (Wikipedia). The 2016 review of Wazwan's meat products says korma "has Turkish roots" (Wikipedia), and when a former head of Kashmir University's Persian department listed the dishes that Persian cooks taught Kashmiris, korma was among them (The Kashmir Walla, summarising Shams-ud-din Ahmad's Shah-i-Hamdan aur Kashmir). A search of Grierson's dictionary finds no entry for the word; it came into Kashmiri from outside, like the dish.
Daniwal korma, then, is coriander-braise: the name is a recipe.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: The herb
chunks.text: Coriander is one of the oldest cultivated flavourings in the world, and almost none of its history passes through Kashmir. The plant is native to the Mediterranean basin; seeds found at two sites in Israel may be "the oldest find of coriander in the world"; about half a litre of its fruits were recovered from the tomb of Tutankhamun, which suggests it was cultivated in Egypt, "as coriander does not grow wild in Egypt"; the Ebers Papyrus of about 1550 BCE lists its uses; a Linear B tablet from Pylos records it "cultivated for the manufacture of perfumes" in Mycenaean Greece; and the Torah uses it as a point of reference for the taste of manna (Wikipedia).
