The English name comes through Old French from the Latin coriandrum, and the Greek koríandron behind that may be related to kóris, the bed bug, the name given "on account of its fetid, bug-like smell" (Wikipedia). The Greeks were describing the green plant.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: The herb
chunks.text: Most people, Wikipedia says, "perceive the leaves as having a fresh, slightly citrus taste", from the aldehydes 2-decenal and 2-dodecenal; the dried seed tastes of linalool and pinene instead, lemony and warm; and a minority of people, because of a variation in an olfactory receptor gene, OR6A2, taste the leaf as soap (Wikipedia). That is the only dish on the trami whose main flavour a share of the guests are born unable to enjoy. In Indian cooking the two halves of the plant lead different lives. The seeds go into garam masala and the spice mixtures; the leaves are a garnish and a chutney herb, and, Wikipedia notes, "in Indian and Central Asian recipes, coriander leaves are used in large amounts and cooked until the flavor diminishes" (Wikipedia). Daniwal korma does both at once. It cooks the leaf into the gravy in quantity, as the Central Asian method does, and most recipes, our own included, add a second handful fresh at the end, as a garnish would. The Outlook glossary's "white gravy flavoured with coriander" is the cooked herb; the green flecks on top are the raw one.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: A cool-season plant at an autumn feast
chunks.text: Coriander is a plant of cool weather and short days. "Both temperature and day length influence flowering and seed set," says Jim Myers, who holds the vegetable breeding chair at Oregon State University; in midsummer the plant "bolts into small white flowers and produces seed within four to six weeks", while in cooler, shorter days it grows leaves "for several weeks or months before flowering", which is why the university's extension service tells gardeners to sow in early spring and again in late summer, and to "sow seeds in succession" for a steady supply of leaf (Oregon State University Extension). Wikipedia's account of the Kashmiri year, drawn from Kashmir Life, places the herb accordingly: "Coriander (danival) is a cool herb whose season predominates between spring and summer in cooler areas" (Wikipedia). The feast, though, is an autumn one. The Srinagar doctors who studied a wedding in 2012 chose the season because it is "when most of marriages in Kashmir take place" (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, SKIMS, 2012); Reuters' 2026 report on the wazas opens as "the wedding season opens in autumn" (Reuters via Al Jazeera).

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: A cool-season plant at an autumn feast
chunks.text: Where the coriander for an October wedding comes from, whether a late-summer sowing in the Valley, a cooler side-valley, or the markets of the plains, none of our sources records. What they do record is that the Valley thought about its foods in terms of season and temperament. Walter Lawrence noted in 1895 that grains, fruits and vegetables were "classed as hot or cold and combined with care", and that dried vegetables and fruits were important in the winter (Lawrence, p. 254); Kashmir Life's word for the herb, as Wikipedia relays it, is "cool". A green, cooling dish between the two chilli-red ones is a placement a Kashmiri cook would have had the vocabulary to explain; whether any waza explains it that way, we have not found written down. One more thing the Valley's larder says about the herb is what it does not contain. Kashmiris dry their summer vegetables for winter: "during summer, vegetables are peeled, chopped, salted and sun-dried to preserve them for winter", and the stock of hokh syun includes dried tomatoes, dried fenugreek leaves, dried lotus stem, "dried shallot leaves (praan)", dried mint, dried bottle gourd, dried turnip, dried quince, dried collard greens and dried spinach (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: A cool-season plant at an autumn feast
chunks.text: Fenugreek and mint are dried; coriander is not on the list, in that account or any other we have read. The herb that names this dish is, on the evidence, eaten green or not at all, which is one more reason the dish reads as a seasonal one even when it is served in October. Lawrence himself never mentions the herb. A full-text search of The Valley of Kashmir finds no "coriander" and no "dhania", and for that matter no "chillies"; his chapter on food names rice, vegetables, oil, salt and pepper, fowl, mutton and milk, and his chapter on crops is about grain, fruit and saffron (Lawrence, p. 253). The settlement commissioner counted what paid revenue. The herbs of the kitchen garden were below his notice, which is one reason the dictionary, compiled by a philologist from the speech of ordinary people, is the better witness to what Kashmiris cooked with.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: The base: praan and the stock
chunks.text: Every account of the dish names coriander and yogurt. What the wazas build those on is the same base that underlies most of the feast: a stock, and the Valley's shallot. "Much of Kashmiri cooking relies on a fragrant meat stock", and, in a sentence Wikipedia takes from a Kashmiri cookbook, "the main skill of a wazwan lies in the preparation of this stock made of onions and shallots" (Wikipedia). The shallot is praan. "Shallots, known as praan, stand out, lending its unique flavour to a multitude of Kashmiri dishes, from soups and stews, to curries and kebabs"; "many of Mughal Emperor Akbar's feasts in the 16th century featured shallots"; and one village in Bandipora, Buthoo, "has earned renown for producing prized organic shallots" (Wikipedia, citing Kashmir News Observer). A Kashmiri restaurateur in Bangalore calls praan "the life of Wazwan" (Asia Media Centre). Grierson's dictionary has no headword for shallot, but it has prān, "fried onions (as a seasoning)", with compounds for cooking a dish with them, and ganḍ, the ordinary onion bulb (Grierson, pp. 761 and 289). The dictionary's definition is a method as much as a word: praan is the onion in its fried, seasoning form, and that is how it goes into the korma.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: The base: praan and the stock
chunks.text:
How the praan is fried decides the dish, and the rule is stated in the same Wikipedia account, drawn from a Guardian recipe: "whole spices must be tempered, fried in oil – clove, cardamom, cinnamon, bay leaves. Fried too little, and the dish will be lifeless, without fragrance. A second too much, and one will be left with nothing but bitterness"; and at the end, "hot ghee or mustard oil is poured on top and garnished with fried praan (shallots) paste & saffron extract" (Wikipedia). Chef Jolly's "lightly roasted" until golden is that rule in a waza's hands. The dictionary's word for the result, bagāra, is oily or buttery cooked food, and the Hindustani cook's word for the technique, bagar, the tempering of spices in hot fat, is the one Wikipedia's korma article uses for the korma's finish (Grierson, p. 92; Wikipedia). The shallot leaves, too, are dried for winter as praan among the Valley's hokh syun (Wikipedia); the bulb goes into the korma, the leaf into the winter.
The 1988 Pandit cookbook from which Wikipedia takes its stock sentence belongs to the kitchen that does not use onions at all; the Pandit table replaces praan and garlic with asafoetida and dry ginger, a difference every source on the two cuisines records (Daily Excelsior; Wikipedia). Daniwal korma, with its praan and garlic roasted golden, is a Wazwan dish in the Muslim manner; we have found no Pandit version by that name. The online index of that 1988 cookbook, which has sections for the mutton dishes of Kashmiri Pandits and a separate one for the cuisine of the Valley's Muslims, lists no korma of any kind and no coriander dish (Kaul Kilam, Culinary Art of Kashmir, index). Kashmiri Pandit food covers the other table.

sources.label: Kaul Kilam, Culinary Art of Kashmir, index

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: The seed that stays out of the pot
chunks.text:
The dish is named for the leaf, and the spice box of the Wazwan explains why it had to be. Coriander seed, which the plains grind into every garam masala, is almost absent from the feast's recipes. Sahapedia's rogan josh is seasoned with garlic, ginger, red chilli, clove, cardamom, cinnamon and praan; its aab gosht with shallot, garlic, ginger powder, fennel powder, cloves, cardamoms and cinnamon; its gushtaba gravy with shallots, ginger, garlic, cinnamon, cardamom, cumin and dry mint (Sahapedia). The Waza family's tabak maaz uses turmeric, dry ginger, cloves and black cardamom (Scroll, from Wazwaan); the 1988 cookbook's rogan josh uses chilli, turmeric, dry ginger, aniseed, cumin, garam masala and asafoetida (Kaul Kilam). The Valley's foundation spices are fennel and dry ginger, bödiyāna and shō̃ṭh in the dictionary (Grierson, pp. 89 and 899), and our guide to fennel and dry ginger sets out how they do the work that coriander seed and cumin do elsewhere.
So when the Wazwan wanted coriander, it did not reach for the ground seed it hardly used; it reached for the fresh plant, in quantity, and gave it a dish of its own. Grierson's distinction between dāñĕwal, the greens, and dāñĕwal-gūjü, the sifted powder, is the distinction the feast draws in practice. That is our reading of the recipes; no waza is on record explaining the choice.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: What the sources agree on, and don't
chunks.text:
Every account has the coriander and the yogurt. They part on the rest.
Wikipedia disagrees with itself. The body of its Wazwan article describes "lamb roasted with yoghurt, spices and onion puree, topped with coriander leaves"; the same article's list of dishes calls it "a mutton curry with coriander", and its list of Kashmiri dishes has "lamb cooked with coriander or parsley" (Wikipedia; Wikipedia). None of those three lines carries a citation, and "roasted" and "parsley" appear nowhere else. Every reported feast and every recipe has a braise, and coriander.
Colour is barely described. Outlook Traveller's "white gravy" is the only account that gives it one (Outlook Traveller); none of the sources mentions chilli. That places daniwal korma with the pale dishes of the feast, yakhni and aab gosht, rather than with rista and rogan josh, which take their red from Kashmiri chilli and mawal.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: How it is made
chunks.text: One step-by-step account comes from a chef's notes on cooking with a Gulmarg waza. The lamb is blanched and the scum removed; praan, the Kashmiri shallot, and garlic are "lightly roasted" until golden, and a little stock is added; the cooked lamb goes back in with fresh coriander and spices, and blanched almonds are optional (Chef Jolly). The yogurt that every other account names (Wikipedia; Onmanorama) gives the gravy its body and its paleness. The meat is on the bone: in the wazas' division of a carcass, the bony pieces go to rogan josh and the kormas (Kashmir Life). At the wedding Outlook Traveller watched, the head waza sat "harvesting choice boneless chunks from lamb legs for korma" (Outlook Traveller), so kitchens differ on the bone as on much else. The method is a korma's in the general sense Wikipedia gives the word: meat "braised with yogurt, water or stock, and spices", after being "first cooked briskly, or seared, using high heat, traditionally with ghee" (Wikipedia). The fat is the feast's. A Kashmiri restaurateur says ghee is used for an authentic Wazwan and mustard oil at home (Asia Media Centre); IANS has the korma "cooked in coriander and ghee" (Onmanorama).

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: How it is made
chunks.text: That ghee was, a century ago, a thing the Valley sold rather than ate: Lawrence found that "clarified butter (ghi) is not much eaten" and that Kashmiris cooked with vegetable oil, while ghi was the state's most important export to the Punjab (Lawrence, p. 254 and the chapter on exports). Our tabak maaz story follows the ghee. The coriander goes in at the end, which is why the dish tastes of the herb rather than of a spice. Our own recipe adds it once, fresh, just before serving. A chicken version exists. The waza Mohammad Shafi Khan names "daniwal korma kokar", chicken prepared with coriander, among the dishes hosts have asked for and wazas have added to the feast (The Kashmir Walla); Wikipedia notes, without a citation, that lamb and chicken kormas are both common in the Wazwan (Wikipedia).

sources.label: Lawrence, p. 254 and the chapter on exports

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: Not that korma
chunks.text: Outside Kashmir, korma means something else, and the something else has a documented history that the Kashmiri dish does not share. "Korma stems from Mughlai cuisine"; "kormas were prepared in the Mughal court kitchens", where, according to the food historian Neha Vermani, the dish is first mentioned in cookery books from the reign of Shah Alam; and "during the 18th century, cooks in the Mughal court enriched the Persian-style stew with almonds, garlic, spices, and yoghurt" (Wikipedia). In Hyderabad in 1832 a "korma" was a variety of pilau with thinly sliced meat. In the nineteenth century the dish split in two. A quarama from Lucknow "contained (among other ingredients) ghee, yoghurt, cream, crushed almonds, cloves, cardamom, and saffron; whereas an 1869 Anglo-Indian quorema or korma, 'different in substance as well as name', had no cream, almonds, or saffron, but added the then-standard British curry spices, namely coriander, ginger, and black peppercorns" (Wikipedia). From there it went, by way of the restaurant trade, to Britain, where "a typical korma as served in curry houses is a mildly spiced dish with a thick sauce" that "often features almonds, cashews or other nuts, and coconut", and where chicken korma is regularly named among the country's most popular curries (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: Not that korma
chunks.text:
The pot "may be sealed with dough during the last stages of cooking", the dum, and the spices finished in hot ghee, the bagar (Wikipedia). The only korma in that whole history to contain coriander is the Anglo-Indian one of 1869, and its coriander was the ground seed of the British curry powder. Kashmir's coriander korma is the opposite case: the fresh leaf, with no cream, no nuts and no curry powder. The two dishes share a word and a verb and nothing in the pot. That is our comparison; the sources describe each korma without mentioning the other. The Kashmiri korma shares the word and the braising and little more. Its base is yogurt and stock, its aromatics praan and garlic, and its flavour a fresh herb; nothing in the accounts above is sweet, creamy or thick with nuts, the optional almonds aside, and nothing is sealed under dough. The one sentence in Wikipedia's korma article that mentions the Valley, "in the traditional wazwan, a banquet produced by Hindu and Muslim cooks for a range of celebrations, lamb and chicken kormas are common elements", carries no citation and gets the feast's cooks wrong; the wazas are a Muslim guild (Wikipedia; Sahapedia).
The two kormas of the seven, daniwal and marchwangan, are named for what flavours them, coriander and chilli, not for a court. For the wider difference between the two kitchens, see Wazwan vs Mughlai; for the other korma, see our marchwangan korma story.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: The course that can go missing
chunks.text: Daniwal korma is one of the seven, and it is the one most easily left out. When the Srinagar doctors listed the dishes served at the wedding they studied in 2012, "in the order in which they are served", there were eleven, and daniwal korma was not among them: methi, chicken, kabab, tabakmaaz, dani, rista, roganjosh, tomato paneer, aab gosh, spinach, marchwangan korma and goshtaba (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi). That is one wedding, and the authors note that the number of dishes depends on "the nature of occasion and financial strength of host". But it fits what the wazas say about the seven: they are a norm, not a law. A veteran waza told Reuters that "there were only seven mutton dishes at that time", and that his trade has added a dozen more since (Reuters); Outlook India reports "no set rules" on which dishes a host serves (Outlook India). It also means that the one weighed record of a Wazwan's calories has no figure for this dish, and that the 2026 health advisory, which names rista, gushtaba, kebabs and tabak maaz, does not name it either (Kashmir Reader). On the evidence of its ingredients, a yogurt braise of meat on the bone without the meatballs' pounded fat, it is unlikely to be the heaviest thing on the trami; but that is a guess, and we would rather say so than invent a number.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: Where it comes in the meal
chunks.text: Daniwal korma comes in the middle. Outlook India's order has it after rogan josh and before marchwangan korma (Outlook India); at the wedding Gulf News describes it arrived in the run of dishes between the rista and the yakhni, with rogan josh, marchwangan korma and the greens (Gulf News). A pale, herbal dish between two red ones: that is where the wazas put it. How Wazwan is served gives the whole order.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: Eating it for the first time
chunks.text: Daniwal korma is the mild, fresh-tasting dish of the feast, and the easiest to like if red gravies are not for you. In a Srinagar restaurant it is served as a plate of mutton on the bone in a pale gravy flecked with green, eaten with rice; our guide to eating in Srinagar lists places, and the cost guide covers prices. If you dislike coriander, this is the one dish to pass on; if coriander tastes of soap to you, you now know why, and the wazas will not be offended.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: Frequently asked questions: What is daniwal korma?
chunks.text: Mutton on the bone braised in a yogurt gravy with praan and garlic and finished with a great deal of fresh coriander. It is one of the seven essential dishes of a Wazwan and is served in the middle of the meal.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: Frequently asked questions: What does daniwal mean?
chunks.text: Coriander leaf. Grierson's dictionary of Kashmiri enters dāñĕwal as the greens of the coriander plant, distinct from dāñĕwal-gūjü, the powdered seed.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: Frequently asked questions: What does korma mean in Kashmir?
chunks.text: A braise: meat cooked with yogurt, water or stock. The word is an anglicisation of the Hindi-Urdu qormā, from the Turkic qawirma, "a fried thing", and the 2016 review of Wazwan's meat products says it has Turkish roots.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: Frequently asked questions: What is praan?
chunks.text: The Kashmiri shallot, fried as a seasoning and pounded into a paste; a Kashmiri restaurateur calls it "the life of Wazwan". Grierson's dictionary defines prān as "fried onions (as a seasoning)". The village of Buthoo in Bandipora is known for it.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: Frequently asked questions: Does daniwal korma use coriander seed?
chunks.text: No. It is named for and made with the fresh leaf. Coriander seed is almost absent from the Wazwan's recipes, whose foundation spices are fennel and dry ginger; the one korma in the wider history of the word that contained coriander seed was an Anglo-Indian curry-powder version of 1869.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: Frequently asked questions: Is daniwal korma spicy?
chunks.text: No. None of the accounts we have read mentions chilli, and the one that describes the colour calls the gravy white. Its flavour is coriander, yogurt, shallot and garlic.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: Frequently asked questions: Why does coriander taste of soap to some people?
chunks.text: Because of a variation in an olfactory receptor gene, OR6A2, which makes some people sensitive to the aldehydes in the leaf. For everyone else the leaf tastes fresh and faintly citrus.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: Frequently asked questions: Is it the same as a Mughlai korma?
chunks.text: No. The Mughlai korma was enriched in the 18th-century court kitchens with almonds, garlic, spices and yoghurt, and the British curry-house korma is mild, thick and often made with nuts and coconut. The Kashmiri daniwal korma is yogurt and stock with praan, garlic and fresh coriander.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: Frequently asked questions: How many calories are in daniwal korma?
chunks.text: No published figure exists. The one study that counted a Wazwan's calories, at a Srinagar wedding in 2012, recorded eleven dishes, and daniwal korma was not among them; the 2026 health advisory does not name it.

chunks.title: Daniwal Korma: The Coriander Course: Frequently asked questions: When is daniwal korma served at a Wazwan?
chunks.text: In the middle of the meal: after rogan josh and before marchwangan korma in one account, in the run of dishes between rista and yakhni in another.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: Marchwangan korma, the Wazwan's hottest dish: what its name means, how much Kashmiri chilli goes in, and how it differs from rogan josh.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text:
Every Kashmiri house dries its chillies in autumn. Grierson's Dictionary of the Kashmiri Language has a word for the result: marʦ-wã̄gan-āra, "a chain or string of red chillis, dried and kept for winter use", with the note that "they are strung on a thread, like a necklace" (Grierson, p. 594). Those strings are the dish this story is about. Of all the chilli that goes into a wedding Wazwan, one estimate has three-quarters going into a single pot (Onmanorama). The pot is marchwangan korma, "a fiery hot mutton cooked with Kashmiri red chilli" (Outlook India), and it is the one dish on the trami that a Kashmiri will warn you about.
The warning needs qualifying, because the chilli in question is famous for being mild. This story covers the name, where the chilli came from and what the Valley called pepper before it arrived, what the chilli is and how hot the dish really gets, how heat is measured and why the measurements disagree, the application to protect the Valley's long chilli, how the dish differs from the rogan josh it sits beside, what it costs the body and what is served to cool it, and where it comes in the meal. For what the dish is, with a recipe and where to eat it, see marchwangan korma.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: What marchwangan korma is
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text:
Marchwangan korma is mutton braised in a thick gravy built on Kashmiri red chilli. Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes describes "meat cooked with spices and yogurt and mostly using Kashmiri red chillies and hot in taste", and its Wazwan article lists the dish among the seven that are "a must" at the feast (Wikipedia; Wikipedia). The Waza family's cookbook names "marchwagan korma" among the seven indispensable dishes (Roli Books), and the former tourism director M. Saleem Beg has "mirchi korma" in his seven (Daily Excelsior). At weddings, reporters have called it "fiery hot Kashmiri chilly korma" (Gulf News) and "mutton in a gravy red with Kashmiri chillies, flavoured with cardamom and coriander" (Outlook Traveller). Doctors who recorded a Srinagar wedding feast in 2012 wrote it down as "pieces of meat prepared in chilly soup", four to six pieces to a trami (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, SKIMS, 2012).
Its spelling is the least settled of the seven. Marchwangan, marchhwangan, martsewagan, martswangan, marchwagun, marchwagan, marchawangan and mirchi korma all appear in the sources above; they are one dish.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: The name: a string of chillies, and a braise
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text:
The first word is the chilli. Marʦ is Grierson's word for it, and the dictionary's gloss shows how the word was used: "long pepper, red pepper, a pod of red pepper, a red chilli, Capsicum sp." His compound for the dried string, marʦ-wã̄gan-āra, carries the element -wã̄gan-, and the dictionary's separate entry wã̄gun is the brinjal, or egg-plant, dried and kept for winter in the same way (Grierson, pp. 594 and 1102). Marchwangan, in other words, is the Kashmiri word for the chilli pod itself, formed from the chilli and the plant word it shares with the brinjal. That is our reading of the two entries; the dictionary does not spell it out.
The second word is the braise. Korma is an anglicisation of the Hindi-Urdu qormā, from "the Turkic qawirma, '[a] fried thing'", for meat "braised with yogurt, water or stock, and spices" after being seared "using high heat, traditionally with ghee" (Wikipedia), a word the 2016 review of Wazwan's meat products says "has Turkish roots" (Wikipedia). Marchwangan korma is chilli-braise, as daniwal korma is coriander-braise: the two kormas of the seven are named for what flavours them. Our daniwal korma story covers the other one, and the word's own journey from the Mughal court to the British curry house.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Pepper before chilli
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: The gloss on marʦ records something the dish's name has forgotten: the word is older than the pod. The first sense Grierson gives is "long pepper", Piper longum, the Indian spice that Europe bought before it bought chilli, and the dictionary has two more words for the same plant, maga and pipijü, and one, loṭu, for the cubeb, the "tail pepper" of the old trade (Grierson, pp. 594, 551, 749 and 535). Pepper was in the Kashmiri kitchen's vocabulary and in its mortar: the dictionary's nal is a small stone mortar used for pounding pepper and other spices. It was in the sickroom, where ʦhaṭh was "a meat gravy seasoned only with a little salt and pepper, given to sick people", and in the shepherds' camp, where ʦarŏn was a relish of sheep's or goat's liver spiced with very hot pepper and salt, also offered to demons (Grierson, pp. 632, 1063 and 1082). When the capsicum arrived, Kashmiri did what most languages did: it gave the new pod the old pepper's name. The Portuguese had done the same with Columbus, who "and his crew called the Capsicum fruits 'peppers'" (Wikipedia). A dish named for the red strings on the house front is, at one remove, named for a spice that came from the opposite direction.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Where the chilli came from
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text:
The chilli is the newest thing on the trami. "Capsicum plants originated in modern-day Peru and Bolivia, and have been a part of human diets since about 7,500 BC", and "chili peppers were cultivated in east-central Mexico some 6,000 years ago" (Wikipedia). A physician on Columbus's second voyage, Diego Álvarez Chanca, published the first European account of them in 1494; the Portuguese then carried them "first to Africa and Arabia" and on to their Asian ports, "including Goa, Sri Lanka, and Malacca"; and "the earliest known mention of the chili pepper in Chinese writing dates to 1591", the plant having probably entered China in the 1570s (Wikipedia; the Portuguese sentences are uncited on the page). A Malayalam news feature's summary of the Indian story is the usual one: the chilli came with the Portuguese in the sixteenth century, and before it India's heat was black pepper (Onmanorama).
When it reached Kashmir, nobody has recorded. The Valley's own chilli is the one the trade calls Kashmiri, grown, according to the Spices Board, "mainly in Jammu and Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh, but also in places such as Goa", and "harvested during winter" (Wikipedia). The Goa connection is worth noticing: the port where the Portuguese landed the plant still grows a chilli by the Valley's name. Whether the long, mild, deep-red Kashmiri pod was selected in Kashmir from the Portuguese stock, or came up from the coast already mild, is not something any source we have read can say. What can be said is that the feast's "fiery" dish depends on an American plant that has been in Asia for five hundred years at most, and that the Valley's oldest dictionary records it already strung on the house fronts.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Lawrence, 1895
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: The one detailed outsider's account of Kashmiri food before the twentieth century barely knows the chilli exists. A full-text search of Walter Lawrence's The Valley of Kashmir finds no "chillies", no "capsicum" and no "coriander"; his chapter on food lists rice and grains, vegetables, oil, "salt and pepper", fowl, mutton and milk, and records that Kashmiris liked their food very salty, that clarified butter was "not much eaten", and that the cultivator ate mutton "perhaps five times in the month" (Lawrence, pp. 253 to 254). "Red pepper" appears once, in the chapter on the Hindus, and it is telling. The Pandits, Lawrence wrote, had once eaten only water-chestnut on fast days, but "vegetable marrows, and red pepper are now freely eaten", a laxity his informants regretted; and they avoided a whole class of foods for their colour: "Tomatoes, the red-fleshed kabuli vegetable marrow, carrots, and red beans are an abomination to the Hindu" (Lawrence, p. 300). Red pepper, newly admitted on fast days, had passed the colour bar that tomatoes had not. That is all the 1895 record says about the pod. It says nothing about any dish made from it, which is one more reason to be wary of anyone who dates marchwangan korma.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Lawrence, 1895
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: Lawrence does record the larder the strings belonged to. Dried vegetables and fruits, he wrote, were important in the winter (Lawrence, p. 254); the dictionary's marʦ-wã̄gan-āra and its wã̄gun, the brinjal dried the same way, are two items from that larder. The larder is still kept. "During summer, vegetables are peeled, chopped, salted and sun-dried to preserve them for winter", and the stock of hokh syun runs to dried tomatoes, fenugreek leaves, lotus stem, shallot leaves, mint, bottle gourd, turnip, quince, collard greens and spinach (Wikipedia). The chilli strings on the house front are the red end of that store. A dish that uses three-quarters of a feast's chilli at an October wedding is a dish that draws on the summer's drying, and on the winter's.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: How hot is it?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: Here the dish and its reputation part company, because the Kashmiri chilli is mild. Kashmiri red chillies "are characterized by their ability to give a dark red colour to food and add flavour, while not allowing the food to become too pungent or spicy"; the dried pod "appears wrinkled and rough, often brownish when traditionally dried (long dry), but contains densely concentrated red pigment material"; its ASTA colour value, the spice trade's measure of extractable colour, is 54.10; its capsaicin, the compound that makes a chilli hot, is 0.325 per cent, and a 1999 study found 0.126 per cent; and on the Scoville scale it reads 1,000 to 2,000 units (Wikipedia). Wikipedia's article on Kashmiri cuisine calls powdered red chillies "moderately hot colouring agents" used in most meat dishes, and records that Kashmiri Muslim cooking "uses chilies in moderate quantity, and avoid hot dishes at large meals" (Wikipedia). A feast that avoids hot dishes, and one dish that is fiery: the contradiction resolves in the quantity. The chilli is mild; marchwangan korma uses a great deal of it. By the IANS estimate, three-quarters of all the chilli in a Wazwan goes into this dish alone (Onmanorama).

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: How hot is it?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: The scale on which the chilli is rated is older than most of the sources above and less exact than its numbers look. It is named for Wilbur Scoville, an American pharmacist whose 1912 "Scoville organoleptic test" dissolved an exact weight of dried pepper in alcohol, diluted it in sugar water, and gave the dilutions to a panel of five tasters until "at least three" could no longer detect any heat; the rating was that dilution, in multiples of 100 (Wikipedia). "A weakness of the Scoville organoleptic test is its imprecision due to human subjectivity", and tasters' palates tire quickly; modern laboratories measure capsaicinoids by chromatography instead and convert the result to Scoville units, but results can "vary widely (up to ± 50%) between laboratories" (Wikipedia). On that scale a bell pepper is 0, a jalapeño 2,500 to 10,000, a cayenne 25,000 to 50,000, pure capsaicin 16 million (Wikipedia). A Kashmiri chilli at 1,000 to 2,000 sits below the mildest jalapeño; what capsaicin it has works the way all capsaicin does, by binding "with pain receptors in the mouth and throat" (Wikipedia). Kashmiri has words for what capsaicin does.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: How hot is it?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: Grierson's khōla is the burning or stinging sensation caused by pepper and other pungent things, and bĕgarun describes food that has acquired an acrid, burning taste (Grierson, pp. 398 and 92). The Valley's chilli, on the trade's measurements, delivers less of the first than almost any chilli in India, which is why it is wanted everywhere. Vir Sanghvi "writes that a majority of the restaurant industry in India uses Kashmiri chillies or their powdered form", and chefs use it as a stand-in for the Goan peri-peri; "India is the largest consumer and producer", and the big spice brands all sell a powder by its name (Wikipedia). A chilli grown in two hill states and wanted by every tandoor in the country is a chilli that will be imitated. How hot the korma gets depends on the kitchen, and on the chilli. "Due to the high demand for Kashmiri chillis, substitutes such as Byadagi chillies are often used", and India's Consumer Education and Research Centre has tested two branded "Kashmiri chilli" powders at 48,000 and 60,000 Scoville units, with brick powder recorded as "one of the forms of adulteration" (Wikipedia). A powder labelled Kashmiri is not always the mild one, and a korma made from it is a different dish.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: How hot is it?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: The Valley's own chilli is also sometimes "added in excess" purely for colour (Wikipedia). A chef who cooked the dish with a Gulmarg waza noted its "sharpness due to the chili extract" (Chef Jolly). A Srinagar master chef has said he is "not averse to using food grade colors" when the rest of the pot is honest (Kashmir Life), which is a reminder that red and hot are not the same thing: the ASTA value measures the first and the Scoville number the second, and the Kashmiri chilli is high on one and low on the other. Our guide to Kashmiri red chilli covers the spice, and Is Kashmiri food spicy? the rest of the menu.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: A GI for the long chilli
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: The imitators got their protection first. The Spices Board's register of geographical indications for spices, as of 15 September 2026, runs to 47 entries, and the chillies on it include Guntur Sannam (registered 2010) and Byadagi (2011), both with the Spices Board itself as custodian, Goa's Khola chilli (2019) and Harmal chilli (2021), Nagaland's Naga Mircha, Mizoram's Mizo chilli, Manipur's Hathei, Tamil Nadu's Ramnathapuram Mundu and Virudhunagar Samba Vattal, Uttarakhand's Almora Lakhori, and Madhya Pradesh's Khargone Lal Mirch, registered in March 2026. Jammu and Kashmir appears twice on the list, for Kashmir saffron, registered on 1 May 2020 with the Directorate of Agriculture at Lalmandi, Srinagar, as its proprietor, and for Ramban's dried pomegranate seed, registered in January 2024. No Kashmiri chilli appears on it (Spices Board of India, list of spice GIs). The Byadagi that is sold in its place, and two chillies from the Goan coast where the Portuguese landed the plant, have the legal name that the Valley's own pod does not. The Valley is trying to change that.

sources.label: Spices Board of India, list of spice GIs

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: A GI for the long chilli
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text:
There are "government initiatives and incentives in Jammu and Kashmir to support and increase the production of the local variety of the Kashmiri chilli" (Wikipedia); on 4 June 2021 an adviser to the lieutenant governor, Farooq Ahmad Khan, visited Baramulla and, at a vegetable cluster at Sadderbal Palhalan in Pattan, launched "a special programme for revival of local Chilli known as 'Lal Mirchi'" (Kashmir Reader). Three years later the application came from the same tehsil. On 26 June 2024 a farmers' company in Pattan, Baramulla, the Shejaar Vegetable Producer Company Limited, applied to India's Geographical Indications Registry to register "Kashmiri Long Chilli" as a geographical indication in the agricultural class. The file lists a product specification, a historical background, a method of production, a statement of uniqueness and a map of the area; a formality check was recorded on 28 June 2024 and another on 25 September 2025; and when we checked on 17 October 2026 the status was "Pre Examination" (GI Registry, application 1295). It sits in the queue a few numbers before the two Wazwan applications, for tabak maaz and gushtaba, filed by The Kashmir Wazwan Cooperative in August 2024 (GI Registry, application 1336). None of the three has been examined.
If the long chilli's registration is granted, "Kashmiri" on a packet of chilli powder would, for the first time, have to mean something; our GI guide explains how the process works and how to check the register yourself.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Marchwangan korma and rogan josh
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: The two red mutton dishes of the Wazwan are easy to confuse and are not the same. The waza Mohammad Shafi Khan draws the line by the cut: marchwangan korma is "a dish made of smaller chunks of meat than used in roganjosh and cooked in a thick chilli gravy" (The Kashmir Walla). Rogan josh takes larger pieces on the bone and a gravy whose red comes as much from mawal, the cockscomb flower, as from chilli; marchwangan korma takes smaller pieces and gets its red and its heat from the chilli itself. Outlook Traveller's glossary adds cardamom and coriander to the korma's flavouring (Outlook Traveller); the Gulmarg waza's version was "pot roasted" (Chef Jolly). Both come from the bony portions of the carcass (Kashmir Life). The Srinagar doctors' portions tell the same story from the plate: four pieces of rogan josh to a trami, "4 - 6 pieces" of marchwangan korma (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi). For rogan josh's own story, see Rogan josh: the history, the name and the red.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Mutton, or chicken?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: Every reported feast has marchwangan korma as mutton (Outlook India; Gulf News; Onmanorama; The Kashmir Walla; Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi). Wikipedia's Wazwan article nevertheless describes it in its body as "chicken legs/thighs cooked in a spicy browned-onion sauce", without a citation, while the same article's list calls it "an extremely spicy lamb dish" (Wikipedia); the Budgam district administration's page repeats the chicken line (District Budgam). A chicken version does exist: Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes records "kokur martsawangan kormeh", citing a Delhi restaurant's menu (Wikipedia). On the evidence, the Wazwan dish is mutton, and the chicken is a restaurant variant. The mutton itself, as our tabak maaz story sets out, now comes mostly from Rajasthan and the plains: the Valley eats roughly twice the mutton it raises (Kashmir Times).

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: What it costs, and what cools it
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text:
For the hottest dish on the trami, marchwangan korma is a light one. The three researchers from the Sher-i-Kashmir Institute of Medical Sciences who had a wedding's vasta waza "keep a record of every ingredient used" in 2012, and worked the calories out from the National Institute of Nutrition's tables, found the korma carrying 1,059 calories per trami, or 265 for each of the four diners: more than the aab gosh (234) and the single piece of dani (177), less than the rogan josh (331), the tabak maaz (367), the gushtaba (447) and the rista (454). The whole trami came to 21,933 calories with rice, "some 5483 calories to the invited person" (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, JMS SKIMS, 2012). The figures are from one wedding, repeated three times, and the paper is a two-page brief report; it is the only weighed record of the feast we know of. A 2026 public-health advisory in Srinagar, estimating 6,000 to 9,000 calories for a typical trami, named the rice, the meatballs, the kebabs, the tabak maaz and "gravies rich in fats and oils" as the main contributors (Kashmir Reader); the korma is a gravy, and it is not named.
What the feast serves against the heat is a bowl of curd. The radish chutney, muji chetin, comes between the heavy dishes to help digestion (JK Arts Foundation); at the wedding Gulf News describes it arrived in the same run of courses as the korma (Gulf News). Grierson's dictionary had it a century ago as buröni, a salad of pounded radishes mixed with curd, seasoned with cumin and salt, and eaten uncooked (Grierson, p. 124). The pairing of the Valley's hottest braise with its oldest cold relish is not something any source explains; it is simply what the trami carries.

sources.label: Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, JMS SKIMS, 2012

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Where it comes in the meal
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: Marchwangan korma comes in the middle, among the heavy red dishes. Outlook India's order has it after rista, rogan josh and daniwal korma, and before aab gosht, yakhni and gushtaba (Outlook India); at the wedding Gulf News describes it arrived in the same run, with the greens and the radish chutney (Gulf News). At the wedding the Srinagar doctors recorded it came later still, eleventh of twelve, after the aab gosh and the spinach and immediately before the goshtaba (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi). Kitchens differ on exactly where; they agree that after the korma the feast turns pale, and that yakhni and gushtaba carry no chilli at all. It is the last hot thing you eat. How Wazwan is served gives the whole order.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Eating it for the first time
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: In a Srinagar restaurant, marchwangan korma is the dish to ask about before ordering; our guide to eating in Srinagar lists places, and the cost guide covers prices. Expect small pieces of mutton in a thick, dark red gravy, eaten with plenty of rice, and heat that varies from kitchen to kitchen. If you are sensitive to chilli, order rogan josh or daniwal korma instead and taste the korma from a companion's plate. At a wedding, it comes to the trami whether you asked for it or not, the radish chutney is there for a reason, and the yakhni that follows will put the fire out.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Frequently asked questions: What is marchwangan korma?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: Mutton, in smaller pieces than rogan josh, braised in a thick gravy built on Kashmiri red chilli, with yogurt and spices. It is one of the seven essential dishes of a Wazwan and the hottest.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Frequently asked questions: What does marchwangan mean?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: Chilli. Grierson's dictionary of Kashmiri gives marʦ for the red chilli and records the strings of dried chillies kept for winter; the -wã̄gan- in the word is the plant element shared with wã̄gun, the brinjal. Korma means braise, so the name is chilli-braise.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Frequently asked questions: How hot is marchwangan korma?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: Hotter than anything else on the trami, but by quantity rather than by the chilli's own strength. Kashmiri chilli rates about 1,000 to 2,000 Scoville units, below a mild jalapeño; the dish uses a great deal of it, by one estimate three-quarters of all the chilli in the feast. Kitchens vary, and some "Kashmiri chilli" powders have tested at 48,000 to 60,000 units.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Frequently asked questions: Where did Kashmir's chilli come from?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: From the Americas, by way of the Portuguese, who carried capsicums to Goa and their other Asian ports in the sixteenth century. When the plant reached Kashmir is not recorded; Grierson's dictionary, compiled from the 1890s, already has the word for a string of dried chillies, and Walter Lawrence's 1895 account of the Valley mentions "red pepper" once.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Frequently asked questions: Why do some "Kashmiri chilli" powders test so hot?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: Because the demand outruns the supply and substitutes are used: Byadagi chillies from Karnataka are common stand-ins, and India's Consumer Education and Research Centre found two branded "Kashmiri" powders at 48,000 and 60,000 Scoville units against the true chilli's 1,000 to 2,000. Brick powder has also been recorded as an adulterant. Byadagi has held a geographical indication since 2011; the Kashmiri long chilli's application was filed in 2024 and has not been examined.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Frequently asked questions: Is marchwangan korma mutton or chicken?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: Mutton, in every reported feast and in the wazas' own accounts. Wikipedia's uncited description of chicken legs in a browned-onion sauce is contradicted by its own list; a chicken version, kokur martsawangan kormeh, appears on restaurant menus.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Frequently asked questions: What is the difference between marchwangan korma and rogan josh?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: A waza puts it by the cut: the korma uses smaller chunks than rogan josh, in a thick chilli gravy. Rogan josh takes larger pieces on the bone and gets its red from mawal as well as chilli; the korma gets its red and its heat from the chilli alone.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Frequently asked questions: How many calories are in marchwangan korma?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: At the Srinagar wedding studied by SKIMS researchers in 2012, the korma carried about 1,059 calories per trami, or 265 per diner, less than rogan josh, tabak maaz, gushtaba or rista.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Frequently asked questions: Does Kashmiri chilli have a GI tag?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: Not yet. An application to register "Kashmiri Long Chilli" was filed on 26 June 2024 by a producer company in Baramulla and was at pre-examination when we checked the register on 17 October 2026.

chunks.title: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami: Frequently asked questions: When is marchwangan korma served at a Wazwan?
chunks.page: Marchwangan Korma: The Hottest Dish on the Trami
chunks.text: In the middle or towards the end of the meat courses, after rista, rogan josh and daniwal korma; before aab gosht in one account and after it in another; always before the pale dishes, yakhni and gushtaba. It is the last hot dish.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Gushtaba, the meatball that ends every Wazwan: what its name means, how wazas pound it from fresh-killed mutton, its yakhni gravy, and why it comes last.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text:
The sound comes before the dish. As the wedding season opens in autumn, Reuters reported in 2026, "the rhythmic thud of wooden mallets pounding lamb" carries through the courtyards and lanes of Kashmir (Reuters via Al Jazeera). At one Srinagar wedding a reporter counted eight men at it, each with a stone mortar and a heavy wooden mallet, each pounding one spice into the meat before passing it on; the last man pounded in the lamb fat, "turning the mash pink", and what came off the stones were "glistening oval discs" (Outlook Traveller). Hours later, in a white gravy of yogurt and broth, those discs will have swollen into the dish that tells four hundred guests the meal is over.
Gushtaba is the last dish of a Wazwan, and the one by which the cook is judged. "As a rule, the meal must end with gushtaba," a Kashmiri restaurateur told Asia Media Centre (Asia Media Centre). Every account of the feast agrees on that. This is the story of the dish behind the rule: what its name means, what the oldest Kashmiri dictionary knew about the cooks who make it, where it may have come from, why the meat has to be pounded within an hour of slaughter, what the food scientists of Srinagar found when they put it on the bench, what goes into its gravy, what it weighs and what it costs the body, how it is shared, and what it has come to stand for. For what the dish is, with a recipe and where to eat it, see gushtaba; for how it compares with its red twin, see rista vs gushtaba.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: What gushtaba is
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text:
Gushtaba is a large ball of mutton pounded with fat, boiled, and then cooked in yakhni, a white gravy of yogurt and mutton broth (Sahapedia). Wikipedia calls it "a velvety textured meatball in white yogurt gravy" and counts it among the seven dishes that are "a must" at a Wazwan (Wikipedia); the Waza family's cookbook lists it among the same seven (Roli Books), and a 2016 review of the feast's meat products names it with kabab, tabak maaz, aab gosh, rogan josh, yakhni and rista (Rather, Masoodi and Akhter). A second paper by the same Kashmir University group, published a year earlier, puts it even more plainly: "Goshtaba forms the essential item of Kashmiri wazwan" (Rather and others, Journal of Food Science and Technology, 2015).
It is big. Sahapedia records a single gushtaba of 200 to 400 g that serves the four diners at a trami, and a waza in downtown Srinagar describes one large meatball cut into four (Sahapedia; The Kashmir Walla). Researchers who recorded the dishes at a Srinagar wedding in 2012 described a "500 - 750 gms mutton ball" (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, SKIMS, 2012). Where each diner gets a rista of their own, the gushtaba is shared.

sources.label: Rather and others, Journal of Food Science and Technology, 2015

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: The name, and the titles
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text:
The dictionary of the Kashmiri language has the word. Under gōshĕth, "meat, flesh", Grierson's Dictionary of the Kashmiri Language enters gusht-āba: "a rich soup of pounded or minced meat" (Grierson, p. 309). The first half is gosht, meat. If the second is the Persian āb, water, which is the same element as in the Persian dish abgoosht, "water" plus "meat" (Wikipedia), then gushtaba is simply meat-broth: the dictionary's "rich soup", named for its gravy rather than its ball. The name is Persian in origin, like those of rogan josh, yakhni, aab gosht and rista (Wikipedia, citing the 2016 review). It is spelled many ways: Wikipedia's article is titled "Goshtaab", a 1988 Kashmiri cookbook writes "Goashtaba", the Srinagar doctors wrote "Goshtaba", and the application now before India's Geographical Indications Registry is for "Goshtaba (Meat Products) of Kashmir" (Wikipedia; Kaul Kilam; GI Registry, application 1337).
The titles are grander than the name. The 1988 cookbook says Muslims call it "The King of Dishes" or the "Dish of Kings" (Kaul Kilam). Wikipedia calls it the "king of Kashmiri wazwan" (Wikipedia). "It's considered the king of all Kashmiri dishes," Bashir Ahmad Choncha, who runs Choncha Foods in Srinagar, told Deccan Chronicle (Deccan Chronicle). Kashmir Life calls it "the finest delicacy of Wazwaan" and "the most eagerly awaited dish served at the end" (Kashmir Life; Kashmir Life). To the waza Mohammad Shafi Khan it is "the showstopper" (The Kashmir Walla); to a Gulf News writer at his cousin's wedding, "a yardstick to measure the chef's culinary skills" that "serves as a full stop" (Gulf News).

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: The cook, the kitchen and the feast, in the dictionary
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Grierson's dictionary was compiled from the 1890s and published between 1916 and 1932, and it knew the trade that makes gushtaba better than it knew the dish. Its entry for wāza is "a cook-person, one who is a cook by profession, and comes of a line, or caste, of cooks", and wāzagī is the profession itself (Grierson, pp. 1178 to 1179). Two other words, nözir and sŏlhöri, are glossed as a head cook, the figure a wedding kitchen now calls the vasta waza (Grierson, pp. 676 and 909). Under kömü the dictionary records a proverb that asks "what have cooks to do with kings" (Grierson, p. 444); the dish the cooks are judged by would, in time, be called the Dish of Kings. The feast is there too, word by word. Wura is a kitchen, and the dictionary notes that it is usually set up temporarily on the occasion of feasts; wura-bal is "the place for the cooking-fires of a bridegroom's party" (Grierson, p. 1138). Dēg is "a large pile of rice cooked in a cauldron, for a wedding feast or the like" (Grierson, p. 194), which is the word the wazas still use for their copper pots.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: The cook, the kitchen and the feast, in the dictionary
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Dah is "materials (flesh, spices, etc.) for a great feast" (Grierson, p. 199). Yēra is "a marriage feast" (Grierson, p. 1202). Trömi is "a copper dish (used only by Musalmāns) out of which food is eaten", and trāmi-bata is the food served in those copper vessels to the Muslim guests at a wedding feast (Grierson, p. 1026). Pötar is "eating from the same dish or at the same feast" (Grierson, p. 804), which is what four people at a trami do. And māzarath is "hospitable pressing to eat (at a feast)" (Grierson, p. 616): the custom, described below, by which the gushtaba is never refused. One more entry belongs here. Zang is an omen of good luck, and the dictionary's example is "a dish of curds" placed on the right hand before starting an undertaking (Grierson, p. 1227). Curds were auspicious in the Valley long before anyone wrote down that the feast should end in a dish of them. Whether that is why the last dish is white, nobody has recorded; the dictionary gives the custom and the dish, not the link between them.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Where it may have come from
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Less is documented about gushtaba's past than about its present. Wikipedia says the dish "is believed to have been introduced" during the reign of the Mughal emperors, as part of the Central Asian, Persian and Mughal influence on Kashmiri cooking, citing the food historian Colleen Taylor Sen (Wikipedia). The 2016 review's authors are blunter about the state of the record: the feast's "traditional knowledge is poorly documented" (Rather, Masoodi and Akhter), and no document records when or how Wazwan began at all (JK Arts Foundation). The wazas themselves keep a count rather than a date: "There were only seven mutton dishes at that time. Over the centuries we added more, and now there are around 20 dishes," Ghulam Nabi Baba, 74, whose forefathers settled in Srinagar's old city in the cooks' quarter of Wazpora, told Reuters in 2026 (Reuters). Two older threads are worth following. The first is the technique. Pounded meat shaped into balls has a Persian name of its own, kofta, a loanword from the Persian koofta, "pounded meat"; the earliest known recipes for it are in early Arab cookbooks, for "large ground lamb meatballs triple-glazed in a mixture of saffron and egg yolk", and a stuffed version, nargisi kofta, was served at the Mughal court (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Where it may have come from
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: When a former head of Kashmir University's Persian department, Shams-ud-din Ahmad, listed the mutton dishes that Persian cooks taught Kashmiris, he named kofta and rista among them, with kabab, rogan josh, korma, yakhni, pulao and aab gosht (The Kashmir Walla, which summarises his book Shah-i-Hamdan aur Kashmir). Gushtaba is not on that list by name, but its two halves are: the pounded ball and the curd gravy. The second is the gravy. The earliest description of Kashmiri feasting that Kashmir Life could find, in the Tuhfat-ul-Ahbab, a Persian work completed in the early 17th century, has 16th-century nobles and Sufi lodges serving kabab, pulao and yakhni, "meat cooked in curd" (Kashmir Life). Grierson's dictionary defines yĕkhañĕ the same way: "a kind of dish (consisting of meat cooked with spices in curdled milk)" (Grierson, p. 1192). Whether a pounded ball was cooked in that curd four hundred years ago, nobody has recorded. Our history of Wazwan sets out the rest of what is known, and what is only told.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: The feast in 1895
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text:
The fullest outside description of Kashmiri eating before the twentieth century is Walter Lawrence's, in The Valley of Kashmir (1895), written after years as the state's settlement commissioner. He does not name gushtaba, or any Wazwan dish. What he describes is the gap between everyday food and the food of a feast. The ordinary meal, he wrote, showed little taste; but when "the professional cook is called in some taste is displayed in the preparation and arrangement of viands", and "the earthenware platters filled with brightly-coloured foods make a pretty show" (Lawrence, p. 253). The ordinary cultivator ate fowl about six times a month and mutton "perhaps five times in the month"; clarified butter was "not much eaten", because Kashmiris believed it irritated the throat; and, in a judgement the feast has done nothing to soften, "the Kashmiri Musalman is extravagant and greedy" (Lawrence, p. 254).
His account of a Muslim wedding is brief. "The gorgeous groom sits on cushions and the feast commences, winding up with tea"; "a big feast is given on the marriage night", the tehl, and the next day the guests depart (Lawrence, p. 269). Of the agricultural classes he wrote that they were "frugal in their expenditure and do not lavish money on marriage feasts or extravagances of a similar nature, as is the case in India" (Lawrence, p. 397). Two things in those pages matter for this story. The professional cook was already a figure in the Valley's kitchens in the 1890s, called in for occasions. And the platters he filled were earthenware: the copper trami that Grierson's dictionary reserves for Muslim feasts does not appear in Lawrence's description of the groom's dinner. Whether that reflects what Lawrence saw or what he chose to write down, we cannot tell.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: The meat: why it is pounded within the hour
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Gushtaba is made from a sheep that was alive that morning. The meat is minced "directly after slaughter", Sahapedia says, with a wooden hammer on a flat stone, and fresh sheep fat and black cardamom are pounded in (Sahapedia). At a wedding the meat is prepared for cooking within one hour of butchering (Onmanorama). Shafi Khan, a second-generation waza, puts the rule plainly: "If the mutton is left idle and minced later, one can't make goshtab" (The Kashmir Walla). Wikipedia's account, drawn from The Hindu, is that the sheep must be slaughtered fresh and the meat pounded before rigor mortis sets in, and that the two meatball dishes are rarely found outside the Valley because the texture is so hard to achieve (Wikipedia). The cut is the back leg, which goes into gushtaba and kebabs while the ribs go to tabak maaz and the bony pieces to rogan josh and korma (Kashmir Life). The 1988 cookbook agrees: boneless leg, "preferably freshly slaughtered", with about 250 g of suet to the kilo, softened in hot water (Kaul Kilam). Then the pounding. The tool has three names in our sources.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: The meat: why it is pounded within the hour
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: The cookbook calls the wooden mallet a goshpar; the Srinagar doctors who watched a wedding kitchen in 2012 wrote that the meat "is minced on stony surfaces with a tukni (a wooden instrument)"; Reuters simply says wooden mallets on stone slabs (Kaul Kilam; Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi; Reuters via Al Jazeera). The meat is cubed on a block, pounded a few pieces at a time, and the warm suet is pounded in as it goes (Kaul Kilam). At weddings the mallets are walnut wood and the work is done by "a line of chefs" on stone slabs (Gulf News; Kashmir Life). The meat is beaten until it "loses its stringiness" (Onmanorama), until, as one account has it, "the nerves dissolve" (JK Arts Foundation). It is folded as it is beaten, which works air in and keeps the finished ball light (Wikipedia). "We pound the meat by hand for a very long time," says Choncha (Deccan Chronicle). The fat is not a garnish but the structure: the finished ball arrives, in the Gulf News writer's words, "marinated with blobs of golden fat" (Gulf News), and when the discs went into the gravy at the wedding Outlook Traveller watched, "the melting fat stretched the discs into enormous orbs" (Outlook Traveller).

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: The meat: why it is pounded within the hour
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: The wazas do not explain the hour's deadline in the language of science, but meat science explains it for them. As rigor mortis sets in after slaughter, the muscle's pH falls, the acid cancels the charges on the muscle proteins, and the proteins actin and myosin lock into actomyosin, which "physically reduces the space between protein chains": the meat holds less water. Before rigor, muscle is "the easiest form from which to extract the highly functional protein, myosin", and mixing salt into it at that stage preserves that state; products made this way have "a firmer texture ... with less cooking loss". Those are the findings of an Ohio State University meat scientist writing about sausage, where the window for salting pork is 90 minutes from bleeding (Lynn Knipe, Ohio State University). A 2021 review in Foods describes pre-rigor muscle as having "excellent processing characteristics with high pH and relaxed microstructure", and salt as the agent that improves its protein solubility, emulsifying capacity and water-holding capacity (Kim and others, Foods, 2021). None of this research is about gushtaba. But fresh-killed meat, pounded with fat and salt within the hour, is exactly the process it describes, and the spring and lightness that Kashmiris prize in the ball is what it predicts.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: The meat: why it is pounded within the hour
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Home cooks who cannot buy a sheep that morning reach for binders. The 1988 cookbook kneads in arrowroot and allows a food processor for small batches (Kaul Kilam); a Kashmiri home cook in Dubai who published a goshtaba recipe in Gulf News mixes egg whites and mustard oil into the mince (Abdul Rashid Waza, Gulf News). Wazas use none of these; they have the stone, the mallet and the hour.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: What the laboratory made of it
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Gushtaba has a small scientific literature of its own, almost all of it from Srinagar, and it confirms the wazas on every point they care about. The earliest work we have found is a 1988 veterinary thesis at the Indian Veterinary Research Institute, A. H. Samoon's "Processing and preservation of Goshtaba and Rista (Kashmiri meat products)", which later papers still cite as the standard method (Jalal and others, Indian Journal of Animal Sciences, 2015). Samoon's published study of rista, in Meat Science in 1994, tested the two things the wazas insist on, fresh meat and fat: "Incorporation of lamb fat at 20% level was found optimum", and both pre-rigor and chilled meat were used, with the hand-minced, hot-processed product binding better than machine-minced meat from chilled carcasses (Samoon and Sharma, Meat Science, 199490052-3)). The Kashmir University food technologists who took up the work in the 2010s describe gushtaba in the vocabulary of their trade: "an emulsion type ground meat product", in which "considerable amount of animal fat (20 %) is used in its formulation to achieve a stable emulsion" (Rather and others, 2015). Their laboratory version is instructive for what it keeps and what it shrinks.

sources.label: Jalal and others, Indian Journal of Animal Sciences, 2015

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: What the laboratory made of it
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text:
The meat is "fresh mutton from hind leg portion", the wazas' cut; the fat is adjusted to 20 per cent with mutton fat; the seasoning is 2.5 per cent salt, large cardamom and cumin; and the yakhni is "two parts of fresh curd" to one of water, with cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, ginger, aniseed, garlic, fried onion and salt, brought to the boil before the balls go in for 30 minutes. But the balls are "compact balls of 60 mm diameter and 50–60 g weight", a tenth of the wedding ball. The finished control product was 64 per cent water, 15 per cent protein and 17 per cent fat, with a pH of 5.3, and the tasting panel gave it 7.3 out of 9 (Rather and others, 2015). A veterinary group at the Sher-e-Kashmir agricultural university worked the same way, and their paper records the wazas' deadline in laboratory terms: the mutton and fat were "used for the preparation of the products within 2 h of post-mortem".
Their formulation was 90 per cent boneless mutton to 10 per cent fat, with 2.5 per cent salt, 10 per cent chilled water and 0.2 per cent large cardamom; they note that traditional goshtaba "with an average fat content of 15–25% is having a high sensory appeal", and they found that even their low-fat version kept for 20 days in a refrigerator (Jalal and others, 2015). The whole research programme, from xanthan gum and apple pomace to retort pouches, is an attempt to make a gushtaba that travels; none of the papers claims to have matched the wedding kitchen's ball. For the dish's texture the science has one consistent explanation, fresh meat and fat, and the wazas have had it for generations.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: The yakhni
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text:
The balls are boiled first, in water until they are soft and have expanded (Sahapedia), or, in the cookbook's method, for about half an hour with salt, aniseed and ginger powder, after which the broth is strained and kept (Kaul Kilam). Then they go into the yakhni.
Sahapedia describes the wazas' yakhni as yogurt and mutton broth with shallots, ginger, garlic, cinnamon and cardamom, topped with cumin and dry mint, "a creamy white soup" (Sahapedia). Shafi Khan's has yogurt, ghee and mutton stock with mild spices and dry mint (The Kashmir Walla); a news-agency account names curd, cardamom, dry ginger and fennel (Onmanorama). What it never has is chilli or turmeric: yakhni is the gravy made "without turmeric or chilli powder" (Wikipedia), which is why gushtaba is white where rista is red. The cookbook's method shows the one technical danger: the curd and broth are cooked with cloves and garlic, "stirred constantly so the curd doesn't split", with fried shallot and onion, over a low heat until the oil and ghee rise, and finished with garam masala, cinnamon, cardamoms and mint (Kaul Kilam). The former tourism director M. Saleem Beg compresses the whole dish into a phrase: "pounded mutton balls cooked in preheated curd" (Daily Excelsior).
The dried mint on top is the dish's signature scent, and the cumin its warmth; the gravy's heat, such as it is, comes from the spices, not from chilli. Wikipedia's Wazwan article calls the gravy "spicy" (Wikipedia); every detailed account lists cardamom, cinnamon, ginger, fennel, cloves and mint, and none lists chilli. For the spices themselves, see fennel and dry ginger.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: The last dish
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Every source has gushtaba at the end. Wikipedia: the main course "usually ends with gushtaba" (Wikipedia). Reuters: "the final dish of a Wazwan feast, signalling the end of the meal" (Reuters via Al Jazeera). Beg: "the final dish announcing the completion of servings" (Daily Excelsior). The 1988 cookbook: "the last Meat Dish in a 'Vazavan' Feast, before the Dessert" (Kaul Kilam). In Outlook India's account of the order, yakhni is "the finishing dish served in wazwan before gushtaba is served" (Outlook India). The Srinagar doctors' list of the eleven dishes served at the wedding they studied, "in the order in which they are served", ends with goshtaba (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi). A dessert such as phirni follows, and kahwa, poured from a samovar, closes the feast (Wikipedia; Gulf News; Sahapedia). None of these sources says why. What they do describe is how the last dish is eaten, and that may be the answer. Each diner at the trami has had a rista of their own; the gushtaba comes one to a trami, and the eldest of the four divides it (Sahapedia). Guests often take fresh rice just before it arrives (JK Arts Foundation).

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: The last dish
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: It is the richest thing on the table, the dish the cook is judged by, and the only one the four must share out among themselves. A feast that opens with the washing of hands and seats its guests in fours ends, in other words, with an act of division performed by the senior person at each platter. That reading is ours, not a source's; the sources give the rule and the ritual and leave the reason unsaid. They are clear about one more thing. Kashmiri hosts press food on their guests, and it is thought disrespectful to refuse a dish or an extra helping (Onmanorama). Grierson's dictionary had a word for the pressing, māzarath, a century ago. The gushtaba is not turned down. How Wazwan is served covers the rest of the manners at the trami.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: What a gushtaba weighs, and what it costs
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: In the autumn of 2012 three researchers from the Sher-i-Kashmir Institute of Medical Sciences, Mushtaq Ahmad of the medicine department and Sakina Akhter and Shariq Masoodi of endocrinology, chose a wedding at random, asked the host and the vasta waza for consent, and had the waza "keep a record of every ingredient used and the number of servings prepared". They repeated the exercise three times, because the meat in a trami for four "varies greatly (usually from 3 kg to 5 kg)", and worked out the calories from the National Institute of Nutrition's tables (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, JMS SKIMS, 2012). Their goshtaba was a "500 - 750 gms mutton ball", "prepared in spheres then cooked in curd", one to a trami. It carried 1,787 calories, or 447 for each of the four diners; across the eleven dishes they counted, the trami held 18,484 calories before rice, and 21,933 with the one or two kilograms of rice that each trami consumed. "Presuming that one Tramie will serve four persons, the total calories consumed on an average by each person would be 5483." Their title was "Wazwan the Kashmiri Cuisine - A Caloric Bomb". Two cautions.

sources.label: Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, JMS SKIMS, 2012

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: What a gushtaba weighs, and what it costs
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text:
The paper is a two-page brief report, and it contains a slip: its text says the dishes ranged "from 709±60 Calories in 'Dani' to 3597±1348 Calories in 'Rista'", but its own table gives the 3,597 figure to the whole chicken, fried in ghee, and rista 1,814. And its introduction repeats the Timur legend as fact, citing Wikipedia. What stands is the fieldwork: a waza's own ingredient list, weighed, at a real wedding. Gushtaba was the third heaviest mutton dish on the trami after rista and the kebabs, and the authors' advice was not to abandon the feast but "to reduce the amount served per person like decreasing the portion size". They also noted that a search of PubMed for "Wazwan" in a title found nothing; theirs was the first paper (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi). Fourteen years later a public-health advisory issued in Srinagar put the same point in gentler numbers: "a typical Wazwan trami serving four people may contain between 6,000 and 9,000 calories", or "approximately 1,500 to 2,250 calories per person", which can be "as much as 80 to 125 per cent of an average adult's daily calorie requirement in a single meal".
The advisory named "meatballs such as Rista and Gushtaba" among the main contributors, and ended: "Wazwan is a celebration, not an everyday meal. Enjoy our heritage, protect your health, and choose moderation" (Kashmir Reader). The 2012 and 2026 figures differ by a factor of two or more; the first was measured at one wedding, the second is an estimate for a typical one, and neither pretends to be the last word.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: The dish of state
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Gushtaba's titles have followed it out of the wedding tent. Kashmir Life prints, as folklore, the story of Bakhshi Ghulam Mohammad, who became the state's prime minister in August 1953, feeding gushtaba to the visiting Soviet leader (Kashmir Life; Wikipedia). The visit itself is a matter of record. Nikita Khrushchev and Nikolai Bulganin toured India in the autumn of 1955, and in India Khrushchev announced Soviet support for Indian sovereignty over Kashmir (Wikipedia; Wikipedia). Jawaharlal Nehru's letters from those weeks, published in his Selected Works, show the Srinagar leg being planned for 9 December: Bakhshi was to receive the two men at the airport and proposed a garden party at Shalimar and a banquet, and Nehru, accepting the garden party, wrote that he was "rather nervous of Kashmiri banquets. I fear that the food they will get there might upset them"; a week after the visit he wrote that it "had passed off so successfully" and that the Soviet leaders "spoke highly of" Bakhshi (Nehru Archive, letters of 23 November, 2 December and 17 December 1955). Whether gushtaba was on the table that December is not in the letters.

sources.label: Nehru Archive, letters of 23 November, 2 December and 17 December 1955

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: The dish of state
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: A news-agency feature goes further, saying that the famous photograph of Bakshi "thrusting goshtaba" at Khrushchev "is understood to have turned high tables of global diplomacy in India's favor"; the claim is attributed to no one, and we repeat it only as the story Kashmir tells (Anadolu Agency). That the story is told at all says what the dish means there. Wazwan has stayed on the diplomatic menu since, from the Pakistani delegation told in 2004 that they were in Kashmir "to taste Wazwan" to the governments that have tried to shrink the feast: a 1960s attempt to phase it out, a 1974 order limiting hosts to five dishes that a sessions judge set aside on the ground that it would only waste meat, and a February 2017 order capping weddings at seven meat dishes, seven vegetarian dishes and two sweets (Outlook India; Anadolu Agency; Gulf News/IANS). Through all of them, gushtaba has kept its place at the end.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Gushtaba today
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: The dish is changing at the edges and not at the centre. Rista and gushtaba are now also made with chicken and fish, a Srinagar chef told Kashmir Life in 2011, and the same chef, Bashir Ahmad Choncha, had moved into processed Wazwan (Kashmir Life). The Srinagar doctors noted in 2012 that "ready-made Wazwan is now available on a fly", so that Kashmiris were eating the feast "every now and then" rather than at weddings alone (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi). The wazas' children are leaving.
