"Our kids didn't continue the tradition of cooking in weddings because they said it's too hectic," Ghulam Nabi Baba told Reuters; his son has opened a restaurant instead, and other young cooks have followed him (Reuters; Reuters via Al Jazeera); younger men are leaving the trade (Sahapedia). At the centre, the meat is still pounded by hand on stone and cooked over wood (Reuters via Al Jazeera). The sheep that make it are, increasingly, not Kashmiri. "Normally, at an average marriage we cook 200 kgs of mutton," Baba says; forty years ago, at a village wedding in north Kashmir, he cooked 4,500 kg (Reuters).

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Gushtaba today
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: A news agency's estimate in 2026 was "around 500 kilogrammes of mutton and 150 kilogrammes of chicken" at an average wedding and more than a tonne at a lavish one (PTI via Outlook Business). Kashmir produces about half of what it eats; the rest comes up the highway in trucks from Rajasthan and beyond, and when Punjab levied a tax on those trucks in the summer of 2026 the dealers stopped importing and families began talking of postponing weddings (PTI via Outlook Business). Our tabak maaz story follows the sheep; it is the same animal, whichever dish it ends in. In August 2024 The Kashmir Wazwan Cooperative Limited applied to register "Goshtaba (Meat Products) of Kashmir" as a geographical indication. When we checked the register on 17 October 2026 the application was still at pre-examination (GI Registry, application 1337). Our GI guide explains what registration would mean and how to check the status yourself.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Eating it for the first time
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Weddings are private, so most visitors meet gushtaba in a Srinagar restaurant; our guide to eating in Srinagar lists places that serve it, and the cost guide covers prices. In a set Wazwan it comes last, so don't ask for it first. Expect one large ball in a white gravy, rich with fat and scented with dried mint, to be eaten with rice; on a shared trami, let the eldest divide it. It is mild. If you are offered more, the custom is to accept.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Frequently asked questions: What is gushtaba?
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: A large ball of mutton pounded with fat, boiled, and cooked in yakhni, a white gravy of yogurt and mutton broth scented with cardamom, fennel, dry ginger and dried mint. It is one of the seven essential dishes of a Wazwan and is served last.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Frequently asked questions: Why is gushtaba served last?
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Every account of the feast records that it ends with gushtaba, but none explains the rule. What the sources describe is that one gushtaba serves the four diners at a trami and the eldest divides it, where each diner has a rista of their own; the shared, richest dish closes the meal, and dessert and kahwa follow.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Frequently asked questions: What does gushtaba mean?
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Grierson's dictionary of Kashmiri enters gusht-āba under gōshĕth, meat, and defines it as "a rich soup of pounded or minced meat". If the second half is the Persian āb, water, the name means meat-broth. It is also called the Dish of Kings.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Frequently asked questions: How is gushtaba made?
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: From a sheep slaughtered the same morning. The leg meat is pounded with a wooden mallet on a flat stone within the hour, with fresh fat, black cardamom and salt worked in, until it is smooth and light; shaped into large balls; boiled; and then cooked in yakhni.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Frequently asked questions: How big is a gushtaba?
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Sahapedia gives 200 to 400 g for the ball that serves a trami of four; researchers who recorded the dishes at a Srinagar wedding in 2012 gave 500 to 750 g. Laboratory versions made for research are a tenth of that, about 50 to 60 g.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Frequently asked questions: How many calories are in gushtaba?
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: At the wedding studied by SKIMS researchers in 2012, the gushtaba carried about 1,787 calories per trami, or 447 per diner, and the whole feast about 5,483 per person including rice. How many calories are in a Wazwan? gives every dish. A 2026 public-health advisory in Srinagar estimated 1,500 to 2,250 calories per person for a typical trami.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Frequently asked questions: What is the difference between gushtaba and rista?
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Both start from the same pounded mutton. Rista is smaller, one per diner, in a red gravy coloured with Kashmiri chilli and served early; gushtaba is larger, one per trami, in a white yogurt gravy and served last. See our guide to rista vs gushtaba.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Frequently asked questions: Is gushtaba spicy?
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: No. Its gravy has no chilli or turmeric; its flavour comes from cardamom, cinnamon, fennel, dry ginger, cloves, cumin and dried mint.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Frequently asked questions: Does gushtaba have a GI tag?
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Not yet. An application for "Goshtaba (Meat Products) of Kashmir" was filed on 8 August 2024 and was still at pre-examination when we checked the register on 17 October 2026.

chunks.title: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball: Frequently asked questions: Can you refuse gushtaba at a Wazwan?
chunks.page: Gushtaba: Why the Wazwan Ends With a Meatball
chunks.text: Kashmiri hosts press food on their guests, and refusing a dish or an extra helping is considered disrespectful. The gushtaba is accepted, and shared.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: Where rogan josh comes from, what its name means, why it is red without tomatoes, how Kashmiri Muslim and Pandit cooks make it, and its place in the Wazwan.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text:
The cooking for a Kashmiri wedding starts in the dark. Accounts of the wazas' night agree on the hour: around 3 am, with the sheep slaughtered only hours before (JK Arts Foundation; Onmanorama). In the open kitchen Kashmiris call the vur, the fire is fed with logs and birch branches, the meat for the meatballs is pounded with walnut-wood hammers on stone, and the copper degs sit "under an autumn moon" (Gulf News). One of those pots holds rogan josh. Mohammad Shafi Khan, a second-generation waza from the Ahad family in downtown Srinagar, puts about twenty pieces of mutton into each utensil of it (The Kashmir Walla). Hours later it will reach the trami as a deep red gravy with its fat risen to the top, four pieces to a platter (Gulf News).
Rogan josh is the Kashmiri dish most of the world has heard of, and the one most of the world gets wrong. Outside the Valley its name sits on tomato-red curries that no Kashmiri kitchen would recognise. Inside it, two communities cook two different dishes under the same name. And the name itself has at least three explanations. This is the story of all of that: where the dish came from, what it is called and why, what makes it red, who cooks it and how, and where it sits in the feast. For the dish itself, the recipe and where to eat it, see rogan josh; this page is the long version of its history.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: What rogan josh is
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text:
Rogan josh is mutton or goat, usually on the bone, braised in a red gravy. In a Wazwan it is one of the seven dishes Wikipedia lists as "a must for these occasions", alongside tabak maaz, rista, daniwal korma, aab gosht, marchwangan korma and gushtaba (Wikipedia); the Waza family's own cookbook names the same seven as "an indispensable part of the feast" (Roli Books), and a 2014 essay in Dawn counts it "among the seven permanent dishes in wazwan" (Dawn). A 2016 review in the Journal of Ethnic Foods lists it among the key meat products of the feast, with kabab, tabak maaz, aab gosh, yakhni, rista and goshtaba (Rather, Masoodi and Akhter).
Its red comes from Kashmiri chilli and from a flower or a root, never from tomato (Wikipedia). It is eaten with rice: "with rice, not with a roti or a naan", as one Kashmiri hotelier put it (Vir Sanghvi).

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: The name: ghee, heat, or red?
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: Nobody agrees on what "rogan josh" means. The dish is also written roghan josh and roghan ghosht, and the Diner's Dictionary says it is unclear which name is the original (Wikipedia). The Persian reading is the most common. Roghan is ghee or oil, and jōš is to stew or braise, so the name would mean "stewed in ghee" (Wikipedia, citing Lizzie Collingham and the Oxford Dictionary of Foreign Words and Phrases). The food historian Lizzie Collingham writes that the Persian name "implies a stew of meat cooked in butter" (Dawn). A news-agency feature glosses it more vividly: "Rogan means fat and Josh means to cook on high heat" (Onmanorama). The Kashmiri reading points at the colour instead. Pat Chapman's India: Food and Cooking takes roghan as "red", which with gosht, meat, gives "red meat", or with a word for juice gives "red juice" (Wikipedia). Dawn reports that "some food historians" link the name to the colour for the same reason (Dawn). The dictionary of the Kashmiri language itself has the word, and it sides with the fat. Grierson's Dictionary of the Kashmiri Language glosses rōgan as "grease, varnish, polish; clarified butter, ghī" (Grierson, p. 828).

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: The name: ghee, heat, or red?
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: The Diner's Dictionary concludes that the exact etymology "remains uncertain" (Wikipedia), and that is where the evidence leaves it. What can be said is that the name, like those of yakhni, aab gosht, rista and gushtaba, comes from Persian (Wikipedia, citing the 2016 review). Whichever reading is right, both describe the finished dish. Kashmiri cooks judge rogan josh by its fat: a Kashmiri cookbook first published in 1988 has it simmered "until the meat is tender and the gravy is red, thick, and oily" (Kaul Kilam, Culinary Art of Kashmir), and a magazine glossary describes it as "mutton slow cooked in ghee and its own juices" (Outlook Traveller). Red, and glossed with oil: the name fits either way.

sources.label: Kaul Kilam, Culinary Art of Kashmir

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Where it came from: what's documented and what's told: The Mughal story
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text:
The account most often repeated comes from Collingham's Curry: A Tale of Cooks and Conquerors. In it, rogan josh began in Persia as a dish of meat cooked in butter, came to North India with the Mughals, and was changed in Kashmir, where the Mughal court went to escape the summer heat of the plains and where cooks adapted Kashmiri herbs for colour and flavour. From there it became a staple of Kashmiri cooking and a main dish of the Wazwan (Wikipedia). Quoted directly, Collingham says "Rogan Josh originated in Persia", that the Mughals' presence "encouraged a blossoming of Kashmiri cuisine", and that the dish "was perfected" in Kashmir; the Mughals, she adds, cultivated Persian flavourings such as saffron and asafoetida so their cooks had a steady supply (Dawn). Kashmir came under Mughal rule in 1586 (Wikipedia).
The food writer Vir Sanghvi tells the same story with the hedges left in. Rogan josh "came to India with the Mughals (we think) perhaps from Persia or some other part of the Middle East"; it was "cooked at Mughal courts everywhere" but "really found favour only in Kashmir"; and "it is the Kashmiris who created the version we know today" (Vir Sanghvi).

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Where it came from: what's documented and what's told: An earlier Persian route
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: A second account places the Persian lesson two centuries before the Mughals. Shams-ud-din Ahmad, a former head of the Persian department at Kashmir University, wrote in his book Shah-i-Hamdan aur Kashmir that Persian chefs taught Kashmiris a set of mutton dishes: kabab, roganjosh, korma, yakhni, pulao, aabgosh, kofta and rista. The context is the arrival of saints from Iran and Central Asia from the 14th century, among them the saint the article names as Sayeed Ameer Kabir Hamdani, the Shah-i-Hamadan of the book's title (The Kashmir Walla, which summarises the book). Mohammad Ashraf Wani, a former history professor at the same university, puts it this way: "Islam was not introduced in Kashmir just as a religion but more like a culture", the saints brought food, clothing and traditions with them, "that is when many dishes of wazwan were introduced", and the dishes were then changed until, in his words, "we won't find dishes with equal taste even in Iran and Central Asia" (The Kashmir Walla).

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Where it came from: what's documented and what's told: What the record holds
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text:
Neither account rests on a dated Kashmiri document that names the dish. No document records when or how Wazwan began; the accounts that circulate rest on word of mouth (JK Arts Foundation). The nearest thing to early evidence is a Persian work completed in the early 17th century, the Tuhfat-ul-Ahbab, which describes 16th-century feasts with kabab, pulao and yakhni; rogan josh is not among the dishes Kashmir Life names in its summary (Kashmir Life). Going further back, a Kashmir University historian, Professor Fayaz, told the same magazine that nothing like Wazwan appears in the Nilmat Puran or the Rajatarangini, and that experts who went looking for these dishes in Central Asia "could not find these there" (Kashmir Life). The wazas' own tradition, that their craft came with cooks from Samarkand in Timur's time, runs into the fact that Timur never entered Kashmir; our history of Wazwan sets out what is known.
So the firm ground is narrow: a Persian name, a dish that Kashmir made its own, and a feast whose documentation, in the words of the 2016 review, is "poorly documented" (Rather, Masoodi and Akhter). The Mughal summer and the Hamadani-era cooks are both plausible, both told by serious people, and neither is proven.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Why it is red
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: Rogan josh is red for three reasons, and the mix depends on who is cooking. Kashmiri chilli. The Kashmiri red chilli is grown for colour rather than heat. Wikipedia puts it at 1,000 to 2,000 Scoville heat units, low enough to use by the handful (Wikipedia). In Kashmir the whole dried chillies are de-seeded, soaked and ground to a paste (Wikipedia). Grierson's dictionary records the Kashmiri word for the chilli, marʦ, and a compound for "a chain or string of red chillis, dried and kept for winter use" (Grierson, p. 594): the strings of chillies drying on Srinagar's houses in autumn are the rogan josh of the coming winter. Mawal. The second colouring is a flower. Mawal is the dried cockscomb flower, boiled to make a red colouring that is used mostly in Wazwan (Wikipedia). Azmat Ali Mir, who runs a Kashmiri restaurant in Bangalore, credits it with the deep red of Wazwan dishes (Asia Media Centre). Collingham names "the dried flower of the cockscomb plant (maval)" as the colouring of the Kashmiri Muslim version (Dawn); the cookbook writer Camellia Panjabi adds that some cooks use praan, the local shallot, and mawal petals for colour and for a supposed "cooling" effect (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Why it is red
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text:
The waza Shafi Khan's rogan josh gets its dark red from red chillies and saffron ground in water together with cockscomb extract (The Kashmir Walla). Ratan jot. The third is a root. Ratan jot is alkanet, Alkanna tinctoria, whose dried flowers or root give a deep red (Wikipedia). Its dye dissolves in oil but not in water, which is why it is fried in hot oil first (Wikipedia). Wikipedia's article on Kashmiri cuisine associates it with Kashmiri Pandit cooking (Wikipedia), though not every Pandit account uses it: the hoteliers Vir Sanghvi consulted said Pandit cooks "will depend on Kashmiri red chillies and the browning of the yoghurt" for colour (Vir Sanghvi), and the 1988 cookbook's rogan josh gets its red from chilli powder and turmeric alone (Kaul Kilam). Saffron plays a part too. A chef's notes from Kashmir have rogan josh and rista "further enhanced in colour by saffron extract" (Wikipedia, citing Chef Jolly). And one Srinagar master chef was candid about what happens when the flowers run short: Bashir Ahmad Khan of Fateh Kadal told Kashmir Life he is "not averse to using food grade colors" so long as the other ingredients are unadulterated (Kashmir Life). What rogan josh is never red with is tomato.
Wikipedia calls tomato an incorrect substitute, used when mawal and ratan jot can't be found, and states flatly that "no authentic Kashmir-cooked version uses tomatoes" (Wikipedia). Tomatoes only entered Indian cooking after Europeans introduced them (Wikipedia); the dish is older than its British imitation, which is where the tomatoes come from, as the last section explains.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: The two rogan joshes
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: Kashmir has two kitchens, Kashmiri Muslim and Kashmiri Pandit, and both make rogan josh. The difference is the aromatics. The Wazwan version. The base of the Kashmiri Muslim dish is praan, a shallot grown in Kashmir, with garlic. Sahapedia's account of the wazas' rogan josh has the meat simmered in a gravy of garlic, ginger, red chilli powder, clove, cardamom, cinnamon and praan paste (Sahapedia). "They are the life of Wazwan," Azmat Ali Mir says of praan; she adds that mustard oil is preferred for home cooking but that an authentic Wazwan can only be cooked in ghee (Asia Media Centre). Reporters describe the wedding dish as shoulder meat cooked in praan paste, mawal flower essence, curd and Kashmiri chilli (Onmanorama), or "shoulder cuts cooked in flower essence, curd, and Kashmiri chilly" (Gulf News). Collingham sums it up as "lots of garlic and onion" with the cockscomb flower (Dawn). The Pandit version. Kashmiri Pandit kitchens traditionally used no onion or garlic. J&K Tourism describes the Pandit school by "the abundant use of heeng (asafoetida) and curd", notes that "originally, Kashmiri Pandits avoided onions and garlics but now many of them have acquired a taste for them", and adds that almost no Pandit dish is cooked without curd (JKTDC). M.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: The two rogan joshes
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text:
Saleem Beg, the former director general of tourism, puts the contrast in one sentence: "Pandit cuisine uses dried ginger and asafoetida ... generously, while Muslim cookery uses onions and garlic" (Daily Excelsior). Collingham agrees: Kashmiri Brahmans "avoid onions and garlic", so their rogan josh uses fennel seeds and asafoetida, and frying the asafoetida "released a garlicky flavour" that stands in for what is missing (Dawn). Vir Sanghvi's Kashmiri informants list the Pandit flavourings as saunth (dry ginger), aniseed, hing and dry spices, with garam masala sometimes going in at the end (Vir Sanghvi). A Pandit writer in Outlook describes a good rogan josh as cooked with little water and plenty of mustard oil (Outlook India). The published Pandit method bears this out. The 1988 Culinary Art of Kashmir makes its "Neni Rogan Josh" with mustard oil, curd, cloves, salt, a little sugar, red chilli powder, turmeric, dry ginger, aniseed, cumin, garam masala, a teaspoon of ghee and a pinch of asafoetida, and nothing from the onion family.
The curd-coated meat is fried in mustard oil until golden brown; the chilli, turmeric and sugar go in with half a cup of water and are stirred until the meat is brownish-red; then water, dry ginger and aniseed, and a slow simmer until the gravy is "red, thick, and oily" (Kaul Kilam). The same dish, or two? Sandeep Bamzai, a Kashmiri Pandit, has said the Muslim version is "completely different, not at all alike". Vir Sanghvi's verdict, having eaten both, is that they are "still recognisably the same dish" (Vir Sanghvi). Sources even disagree on the meat: J&K Tourism says Pandits prefer young goat (JKTDC), while Wikipedia's article says lamb or sheep (Wikipedia). For the Pandit table more widely, see Kashmiri Pandit food.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: The cut
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text:
Ask a waza what goes into rogan josh and the answer is a list of bones. Sahapedia describes pieces of about 70 to 80 g cut from the lower ribs, the lower back (bukhtor), the chest and the neck (Sahapedia). Shafi Khan's version uses medium chunks from the lower back (The Kashmir Walla). Bashir Ahmad Choncha, who runs Choncha Foods in Srinagar, told Deccan Chronicle that "for Rogan josh neck and shoulders of the meat are preferable" (Deccan Chronicle). Two wedding reports say shoulder (Onmanorama; Gulf News), and a 2011 account of the trade has rogan josh and korma made from the bony portions of the lamb, with the back leg kept for gushtaba and kebabs and the ribs for tabak maaz (Kashmir Life).
The common thread is meat on the bone from the back, ribs, shoulder and neck, not boneless cubes. Beyond that, the cut has always been a matter of means. Deepak Haksar of ITC Hotels, from a Kashmiri family, told Vir Sanghvi that "more prosperous families used better cuts of meat", naming "the whole machhli, the most tender part of the shoulder"; another Srinagar-born hotelier, Virender Razdan, said he never saw the lamb-shank version now sold in expensive restaurants as "Kareli Rogan Josh" while growing up in the Valley. Sanghvi's conclusion: "perhaps the cut you use is only a function of what you can afford", and what makes the dish is the spicing (Vir Sanghvi).
Freshness matters as much as the cut. At a wedding the meat is prepared for cooking within an hour of butchering (Onmanorama); the sheep are slaughtered only hours before the fires are lit (JK Arts Foundation).

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: How the wazas cook it
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: Rogan josh at a wedding is cooked by professionals. A Wazwan is made by a team of wazas under a head cook, the vasta waza, who may oversee 15 to 20 degs at once while apprentices chop, portion and pound (Asia Media Centre). They work in a temporary kitchen set up at the host's home (Sahapedia), and they talk to each other, one account says, in a code of their own (JK Arts Foundation). Our guide to the wazas covers the trade; what follows is the part that bears on this dish. The pots. The degs are copper, nickel-plated on the inside (Outlook India; Onmanorama). One chef, Nazir Ahmed Aram, says the pots have to have the right copper content (Wikipedia). At one working-class wedding in Srinagar a reporter counted the vessels as "enormous brass vats" on a trench of burning logs, their heat regulated by two men lifting a vat on or off the fire (Outlook Traveller). The fire. The wood is from fruit trees: apple, walnut or plum, with acacia and willow used occasionally (Sahapedia).

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: How the wazas cook it
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text:
The reasoning given for slow wood or charcoal heat is that the food "receives heat on two sides, top and bottom" and that "the best results are obtained by slow heat using charcoal" (Daily Excelsior). Reuters' photographs from 2026 show the dishes cooked in degchis over a wood fire, and the agency credits the fire with the feast's smoky flavour (Reuters via Al Jazeera). The hours. After a night of chopping and pounding, the cooking proper begins at dawn and takes about six hours (The Kashmir Walla); in the wedding season a waza's day can run to 18 or 20 hours (Sahapedia). Bashir Ahmad Khan's rule for all of it: "In wazwan hurry does not achieve the best curry" (Kashmir Life). The gravy. The wazas' rogan josh, as Sahapedia records it, is the meat simmered in garlic, ginger, red chilli powder, clove, cardamom, cinnamon and praan paste (Sahapedia). Panjabi's account of the dish adds bay leaves and notes that it is often finished with dampokhtak, the slow, sealed cooking of the Mughal kitchen (Wikipedia). The wedding version is "slow cooked in ghee and its own juices" (Outlook Traveller). It is done when the fat has risen: the rogan of the name, whichever way you read it. The serving.
The wazas themselves carry the pots to the tramis and serve "exactly four pieces of a course" onto the four quarters of each platter, one for each diner (Gulf News). The rice underneath, in the best feasts, is mushk budji, a short-grained aromatic variety grown in the higher reaches of the Valley (Asia Media Centre) that received a geographical indication in February 2022 (Wikipedia). For a home version with quantities, see the recipe on the rogan josh page.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Its place at the trami
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text:
Rogan josh comes early in the gravies. Outlook India's account of the order runs: seekh kababs, tabak maaz, a large piece of mutton and chicken on the trami first; then methi maaz, rista, rogan josh, daniwal korma and marchwangan korma; then aab gosht, yakhni and, last, gushtaba (Outlook India). Asia Media Centre's has rista, then rogan josh, then daniphol and aab gosht (Asia Media Centre). At the wedding Gulf News describes, rista came as the second course and rogan josh in the run of dishes that followed, between daniwal korma and marchwangan korma (Gulf News).
How fixed is the order? Within a kitchen, very: "when it comes to serving the various dishes, the order is set in stone", says Azmat Ali Mir (Asia Media Centre). Between kitchens, less so: Outlook notes there are no set rules about which dishes are served (Outlook India). What every account shares is that the heavy red dishes come in the middle, with a radish chutney served between them to help digestion (JK Arts Foundation; Onmanorama), and that gushtaba closes the meal. How Wazwan is served covers the trami, the hand-washing and the manners; Traditional Wazwan lists every dish in serving order.
The scale is worth knowing before you sit down. A news-agency feature estimates "easily 2 kg of mutton and chicken" served per person across a full wedding Wazwan (Onmanorama). Rogan josh is one course of many.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Rogan josh and its neighbours
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text:
Three other red or near-red dishes share the trami, and visitors confuse them.
- Marchwangan korma is the hot one. It is made, a waza says, with "smaller chunks of meat than used in roganjosh and cooked in a thick chilli gravy" (The Kashmir Walla); by one estimate "three-quarters of the chilly used in the entire wazwan is singularly used in this dish" (Onmanorama). Rogan josh is the milder, more aromatic of the two. Marchwangan korma has its own page.
- Rista shares rogan josh's colourings, chilli and mawal or alkanet, but is pounded meat shaped into balls rather than pieces on the bone (Wikipedia). See rista.
- Yakhni is the white opposite: a yogurt gravy without turmeric or chilli powder (Wikipedia). Daniwal korma is paler still, "a white gravy flavoured with coriander" (Outlook Traveller). See yakhni and daniwal korma.
For the wider confusion between Kashmiri and Mughlai cooking, see Wazwan vs Mughlai.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: The dish abroad: how rogan josh turned tomato-red
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text:
The rogan josh most of the world knows was made in Britain. Collingham traces the dish's path from a mildly spiced Persian stew to the herb-red Kashmiri dish and then to a British Indian restaurant dish made red with tomatoes and red peppers (Wikipedia, citing Collingham and the BBC's Sheila Dillon). Those restaurants mattered beyond Britain: Collingham notes that many foreign visitors, Americans among them, had their first taste of Indian food in them (Wikipedia). For such diners, rogan josh and the tomato version are the same thing.
The substitutions are well documented. Madhur Jaffrey's 1982 BBC book suggests "4 to 16 times as much paprika as cayenne" to copy the colour without Kashmiri chillies; Sanjeev Kapoor's restaurant version uses white and black cardamom, anise and bay leaves; Shivaji Rao Holkar's 1975 Cooking of the Maharajas describes a dish of meat and tomatoes; ready-made pour-over sauces are tomato-based; and Dharamjit Singh's Indian Cookery of 1973 already objected that tomatoes are not traditional (Wikipedia). Vir Sanghvi is blunter: a "dubious variation" of the dish "has long been a staple of the Kwality-Volga kind of restaurant" in India, the English curry-house version "tastes nothing like the real thing", and "the Punjabi restaurant variation is based on the Hindu recipe" (Vir Sanghvi).
None of this is a reason to avoid the dish outside Kashmir. It is a reason to know which rogan josh you are eating.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Eating it for the first time
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text:
Weddings are private, so most visitors meet rogan josh in a Srinagar restaurant, as a single dish or as part of a set trami. Our guide to eating in Srinagar lists places that serve it — Ahdoos, Mughal Darbar and Shamyana were the only restaurants on all five published Srinagar lists we compared in September 2026 — and the cost guide explains prices.
What to expect: a deep red gravy with a layer of oil on top, pieces of mutton on the bone, and no sweetness from tomato. Eat it with rice. Its heat varies from kitchen to kitchen: the chilli itself is mild, but India's Consumer Education and Research Centre found two branded "Kashmiri chilli" powders at 48,000 and 60,000 Scoville units (Wikipedia), so ask if you are sensitive. Is Kashmiri food spicy? covers the rest of the menu. If a menu offers a Pandit-style rogan josh, you now know what the difference is.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Frequently asked questions: What does rogan josh mean?
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: It is uncertain. Read as Persian, roghan means ghee or oil and josh means to stew or braise, so "stewed in ghee". Another reading takes roghan as the Kashmiri word for "red", giving "red meat" or "red juice". The Diner's Dictionary says the exact etymology remains uncertain, and Grierson's dictionary of Kashmiri glosses rōgan as grease or clarified butter.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Frequently asked questions: Where did rogan josh come from?
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: Its name is Persian. The food historian Lizzie Collingham writes that it originated in Persia, came to North India with the Mughals and was perfected in Kashmir, where the Mughal court spent its summers. A Kashmir University Persian scholar's account has Persian cooks teaching it to Kashmiris two centuries earlier, with the saints who came from Iran from the 14th century. No dated Kashmiri document names the dish, so neither account is proven.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Frequently asked questions: Why is rogan josh red?
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: From Kashmiri chilli, which colours strongly but is mild, and from mawal, the dried cockscomb flower, in the Kashmiri Muslim version, or ratan jot, the root of alkanet, in some Kashmiri Pandit versions. Saffron is sometimes added for colour. Authentic rogan josh cooked in Kashmir contains no tomato.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Frequently asked questions: Does rogan josh have tomatoes in it?
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: Not in Kashmir. Tomatoes came into the dish in British Indian restaurants, which used tomatoes and red peppers for the colour; tomato-based pour-over sauces followed. Wikipedia calls tomato an incorrect substitute used when mawal and ratan jot can't be found.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Frequently asked questions: Is rogan josh spicy?
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: Usually medium. Kashmiri chilli rates about 1,000 to 2,000 Scoville units, so the dish is red rather than hot, but some branded "Kashmiri chilli" powders have tested far hotter, and kitchens vary. The hot dish on the trami is marchwangan korma, not rogan josh.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Frequently asked questions: Which cut of meat is used for rogan josh?
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: Meat on the bone from the lower ribs, lower back, chest, neck and shoulder, in pieces of about 70 to 80 g, according to wazas and Srinagar chefs. Boneless cubes and lamb shanks are restaurant inventions.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Frequently asked questions: What is the difference between Kashmiri Muslim and Kashmiri Pandit rogan josh?
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: The Muslim, or Wazwan, version is built on praan (Kashmiri shallots) and garlic, coloured with mawal, and cooked in ghee at a feast. The Pandit version traditionally has no onion or garlic and relies on asafoetida, curd, dry ginger and fennel, with mustard oil. They are different dishes under one name, though many consider them recognisably the same.

chunks.title: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish: Frequently asked questions: When is rogan josh served at a Wazwan?
chunks.page: Rogan Josh: The History, the Name and the Red of Kashmir's Most Famous Dish
chunks.text: Early among the gravies: after the first dishes on the trami and after rista, before the korma dishes, aab gosht, yakhni and the closing gushtaba. The order is fixed within a kitchen but varies between them.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text: What to eat in Kashmir, from everyday rice and haakh to Wazwan, bakery breads, noon chai, street food and winter harissa, plus when and where to find each.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text:
Here's what to eat in Kashmir if you only have a few days:
- a plate of rice with haakh (collard greens), the Valley's everyday meal
- a Wazwan meal with rista, rogan josh and gushtaba
- noon chai with fresh bread from a neighbourhood kandur (baker)
- masala tsot and kebabs from the street
- in winter, a morning bowl of harissa
Between them, those five cover the Valley's everyday food, its famous feast, its bakery and tea culture, and its seasons.
This guide explains each one, where and when you'll find it, and what often gets mislabelled as "Kashmiri" on menus and travel lists. It covers the Kashmir Valley: Srinagar and the towns around it. Jammu and Ladakh each have their own, quite different food.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: Kashmiri food at a glance
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text:
Many visitors arrive thinking Kashmiri food is Wazwan, the famous multi-course feast. Wazwan is the ceremonial peak, but daily eating in Kashmir works on four layers:
- Everyday home cooking. Rice is the staple at almost every meal. It comes with vegetables, greens, yogurt-based gravies and, often, mutton.
- Wazwan. A formal feast cooked by professional chefs called wazas, for weddings and big occasions.
- Bakery and tea. Bread comes from the neighbourhood baker and is mostly eaten with tea rather than with main meals.
- Street food and seasonal specialities. Wraps, fritters, barbecue and winter harissa, tied closely to the time of day and the time of year.
Kashmir also has two main kitchen traditions, Kashmiri Muslim and Kashmiri Pandit (Hindu). They share most ingredients and techniques. The main difference is the aromatics: Muslim kitchens typically use onion, garlic and shallots, while Pandit kitchens use asafoetida and yogurt instead. Our guide to Kashmiri cuisine explained covers both traditions in depth.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: 1. Start with the everyday: rice, haakh and yogurt gravies
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text:
Rice has been Kashmir's staple for centuries. The Kashmiri phrase haakh-batte, "greens and rice", is the local equivalent of "bread and butter". If you eat one simple home-style meal on your trip, make it this one.
Haakh is collard greens cooked with mustard oil, water, a green chilli and often a pinch of asafoetida until tender. It's plain and deeply savoury.
Nadru yakhni is lotus stem simmered in a yogurt gravy scented with fennel and dry ginger. Nadru (lotus stem) grows in the Valley's lakes, and the harvest begins in September.
Dum olav (dum aloo) is potatoes, fried and then simmered in yogurt with fennel, ginger powder and cardamom. Kashmir's version is yogurt-based, although some food sites describe it as tomato-based.
Rajma gogji is kidney beans cooked with turnip, a staple of the colder months.
Look for these on the "Kashmiri" section of restaurant menus, or ask your host or guesthouse. They're everyday dishes, so they appear far less often on tourist menus than the Wazwan favourites. Dum olav has its own page if you want to know what to expect.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: 2. Try a Wazwan meal, and know what you're eating
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text:
Wazwan comes from waz (cook) and wan (shop). It's a multi-course feast built mostly on mutton and cooked by teams of wazas for weddings and major celebrations.
How many dishes it has depends on the occasion. A 2016 review in the Journal of Ethnic Foods puts it at anywhere between 7 and 36. The often-quoted 36 is the grand ideal, not the norm. Traditionally, four people share one large copper platter called a trami.
As a visitor, you'll most likely eat Wazwan at a restaurant in Srinagar. Restaurants usually serve it as a shared trami for a group or a single-person platter. Wedding Wazwan is by invitation only.
Dishes to look for:
- Tabak maaz: lamb ribs simmered until tender, then fried.
- Rista: meatballs in a red gravy of Kashmiri chilli, saffron and fennel.
- Rogan josh: mutton in a deep red, aromatic gravy. Its colour comes largely from Kashmiri chilli and traditional colourings, and its heat varies from cook to cook.
- Gushtaba: pounded meatballs in a yogurt gravy, traditionally the last main dish of the meal.
Start with What is Wazwan? for the full picture, and read How to Experience Wazwan before you book a table. For the seven dishes every Wazwan has, each with its own long story, see the core seven.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: 3. Drink noon chai and eat from the neighbourhood bakery
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text:
Kashmir's everyday tea is noon chai: salted, pink and made with milk. The tea is boiled for a long time with a pinch of baking soda and aerated by ladling. Milk then turns it pink, and salt is added. Kashmiri Pandits call it sheer chai. It's savoury rather than sweet, which surprises many first-timers.
Noon chai comes with bread from the neighbourhood kandur. Kandurs start baking before dawn, and what you'll find depends on the time of day:
- Girda (tsot): the round morning bread, marked with the baker's fingertips.
- Lavasa: a thin flatbread, soft or crisp.
- Tsochwor (tilvor): a sesame-topped, bagel-shaped bread for afternoon tea.
- Kulcha: a crumbly, biscuit-like bake, sweet or savoury.
- Sheermal: a mildly sweet milk bread especially associated with Pampore.
Kahwa is the other tea: green tea brewed with saffron, cinnamon and cardamom, served with almonds or walnuts. It's commonly served after Wazwan and at family dinners. For the difference between the two teas, see Kahwa vs. Noon Chai.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: 4. Eat on the street
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text:
Kashmiri street food is closely tied to place and time:
- Masala tsot is a lavasa bread spread with a radish-and-yogurt chutney and topped with boiled chickpeas. It's sold from mornings until early afternoon near shrines, colleges and courts. It's vegetarian. What masala tsot is.
- Kebabs and tujji (small pieces of mutton grilled on skewers) fill the evening air at Khayam Chowk, a well-known Srinagar barbecue street. It's busiest during Ramadan evenings.
- Around the Hazratbal shrine you'll find nadur monji (crisp lotus-stem fritters), fried fish and halwa with an enormous paratha. The bazaar is busiest on Fridays.
Our guide to Kashmiri street food covers where to go and when.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: 5. Eat with the seasons
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text:
What you can eat depends a lot on when you visit.
- Winter. Harissa is mutton and rice cooked overnight until smooth. It's a breakfast dish sold from early morning in Srinagar's old city, roughly from late autumn to March, and it usually sells out by mid-morning. Winter is also when households cook hokh syun, vegetables sun-dried months earlier. The coldest spell, Chillai Kalan, runs from 21 December to the end of January. See Kashmiri winter food.
- Autumn. The nadru harvest starts in September, and walnuts are harvested in autumn.
- Ramadan. Evenings bring crowds to Khayam Chowk, and some old-city makers sell phirni (a set pudding) only during this month.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: 6. Save room for something sweet
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text:
Phirni is one of Kashmir's best-known desserts. Locally called firin, it's a set pudding served in small clay bowls, and the saffron version is kong phirin. Some Srinagar makers use semolina rather than ground rice.
Other genuinely Kashmiri sweets include shufta, paneer and dry fruit in saffron syrup, which is associated with Kashmiri Pandit homes, and the fried celebration sweets basrakh and tosha.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: What to eat in Kashmir at a glance
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text:

| Nadru yakhni | Lotus stem in yogurt gravy | Homes and Kashmiri menus | Year-round (fresh nadru from September) |
| Rista and gushtaba | Mutton meatballs in red (rista) and yogurt (gushtaba) gravies | Wazwan restaurants, weddings | Year-round |
| Tabak maaz | Ribs simmered, then fried | Wazwan restaurants | Year-round |
| Noon chai with girda | Salted pink tea with bakery bread | Homes, bakeries, tea stalls | Mornings and afternoons |
| Masala tsot | Lavasa wrap with chickpeas and radish chutney | Stalls near shrines, colleges and courts | Mornings to early afternoon |
| Tujji and seekh kebab | Mutton grilled over charcoal | Khayam Chowk | Evenings |
| Harissa | Mutton and rice slow-cooked overnight | Old-city shops in Srinagar | Winter, early morning |
| Phirni | Set pudding in clay bowls | Old-city makers, especially in Ramadan | Some makers sell it only in Ramadan |

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: What isn't Kashmiri food, even if the menu says so
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text:
- Momos, thukpa and butter tea come from Tibetan and wider Himalayan food traditions (thukpa, for example, is eaten in Ladakh), not from the Kashmir Valley's cuisine. Several popular travel lists still include them in their "Kashmiri food" line-ups.
- "Kashmiri pulao" on Indian restaurant menus, a sweet rice with fruit and nuts, isn't the Valley's everyday rice. Plain steamed rice anchors Kashmiri meals, including the Wazwan trami. Kashmir's own sweet saffron rice, modur pulav, is made for special occasions.
- "Red means hot" isn't a reliable rule. Much of the red in Kashmiri food comes from Kashmiri chilli, which is prized for colour more than heat, and from traditional colourings such as dried cockscomb flower (mawal). Read more in Is Kashmiri food spicy?

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: Practical tips for eating in Kashmir
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text:
- Rice for meals, bread with tea. Don't expect rotis with lunch. Bread belongs to breakfast and tea time.
- Vegetarians eat well. Look for Pandit-style vegetable dishes and street snacks. Our guide to vegetarian food in Kashmir lists what to order.
- Pick busy stalls. For street food, choose places where food is cooked in front of you and turns over quickly.
- Plan around Fridays and Ramadan. Areas around major shrines such as Hazratbal are crowded on Fridays. During Ramadan, eating patterns shift towards the evening.
- Go early for harissa. In winter, most shops are sold out by mid-morning.
Planning a trip around food? Our 4-day Kashmir Food Trail itinerary puts Wazwan, bakeries, street food and kahwa into a day-by-day route.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: Frequently asked questions: What is the most famous food of Kashmir?
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text: Outside Kashmir, the best-known dishes come from the Wazwan feast: rogan josh, rista and gushtaba. Inside the Valley, everyday favourites matter just as much, especially haakh with rice, noon chai with fresh bread, and harissa in winter. Kashmir has no official "national dish", despite what some travel sites claim.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: Frequently asked questions: Is all Kashmiri food Wazwan?
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text: No. Wazwan is a formal feast cooked by professional wazas for weddings and big occasions. Everyday Kashmiri food is simpler: rice with vegetables, greens, yogurt-based gravies and mutton. It also includes a bakery and tea culture and a lively street-food scene.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: Frequently asked questions: What do Kashmiris eat every day?
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text: Rice is the staple of lunch and dinner. It comes with dishes such as haakh (greens), lotus stem, potatoes or paneer in yogurt gravies, beans, and often mutton or fish. Mornings and afternoons are for noon chai with breads from the local baker.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: Frequently asked questions: Is Kashmiri food very spicy?
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text: Mostly not. Kashmiri food is usually more aromatic than hot, built on fennel, dry ginger and cardamom. Its red colour comes largely from Kashmiri chilli, prized more for colour than heat, and traditional colourings. Some dishes, such as marchwangan korma, are deliberately hot, and heat varies from cook to cook.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: Frequently asked questions: Can vegetarians eat well in Kashmir?
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text: Yes, although Wazwan itself is built around meat. Kashmiri vegetarian dishes include haakh, nadru yakhni, dum olav, paneer dishes (tschaman) and rajma gogji. On the street, look for masala tsot and nadur monji.

chunks.title: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food: Frequently asked questions: When can I eat harissa in Kashmir?
chunks.page: What to Eat in Kashmir: A First-Timer's Guide to the Valley's Food
chunks.text: Harissa is a winter breakfast. Old-city shops in Srinagar sell it from early morning, roughly from late autumn to March, and it usually sells out by mid-morning. Opening months and times vary from shop to shop.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text: Kashmiri street food by time and place: masala tsot in the morning, Khayam Chowk kebabs at night, Hazratbal on Fridays and winter harissa, plus safety tips.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text:
Kashmiri street food runs on a timetable. In Srinagar:
- Mornings are for masala tsot, a thin lavasa bread topped with chickpeas and radish chutney.
- Evenings are for kebabs and tujji off the grills at Khayam Chowk.
- Fridays bring crowds to the food stalls outside the Hazratbal shrine.
- Winter mornings belong to harissa in the old city.
Most of it is cooked in front of you, and much of it is gone by a certain hour. This guide covers what to order, where locals go for it and when to turn up.
The places and timings come from reporting by Kashmiri and national media. Treat them as a starting point: stalls move, and seasons shift from year to year.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Kashmiri street food in Srinagar at a glance
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text:
| Food | What it is | Where to look | When | Vegetarian? |
| Masala tsot | Lavasa bread with boiled chickpeas and a radish-yogurt chutney | Outside shrines, colleges and courts | Morning to about 1–2pm | Yes |
| Tujji and seekh kebab | Mutton grilled on skewers over hot coals | Khayam Chowk | Evening; busiest at iftar in Ramadan | No |
| Nadur monji | Lotus stem fried crisp in a spiced rice-flour batter | Stalls outside Hazratbal shrine | Busiest on Fridays | Yes |
| Halwa-paratha | Sweet halwa with a giant fried bread | Outside Sufi shrines, including Hazratbal | Busiest on Fridays and religious anniversaries | Yes |
| Fried fish | Fish fried to order | Stalls outside Hazratbal shrine | Busiest on Fridays | No |
| Harissa | Mutton and rice cooked overnight into a smooth paste | Old-city shops around Aali Kadal, Nawakadal and Fateh Kadal | Winter, early morning | No |
| Rice plates | Rice with a single dish, meat or vegetable | Batte Gali, near Lal Chowk | Ask locally | Both |

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Morning: masala tsot outside shrines, colleges and courts
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text:
Masala tsot (also spelt masal tchot) is Srinagar's roadside breakfast, and the easiest vegetarian thing to eat on the move. The vendor:
1. takes a round of lavasa, the thin flatbread from the neighbourhood bakery;
2. spreads it with a chutney of radish and yogurt;
3. piles on boiled chickpeas.
It's eaten as a wrap. Much of the work happens before the stall opens: Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes notes that preparation starts the night before.
The chutney carries the flavour. Our masala tsot page describes it as fiery, but heat varies from vendor to vendor. Watch one being made before you ask for extra.
Where and when. In 2026, Kashmir Life reported on the Valley's roadside breakfast:
- Masala tsot sellers set up outside shrines, colleges and courts.
- Two examples it names are the shrine of Makhdoom Sahib and the Eidgah area.
- They sell until about 1 or 2pm.
If you want masala tsot, make it a morning plan. By mid-afternoon, most sellers have finished for the day.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Evening: kebabs and tujji at Khayam Chowk
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text:
When the light goes, the grills come alive at Khayam Chowk, Srinagar's well-known kebab street. Outlook Traveller pointed readers to its kebab stalls as far back as 2017. WazwanWay's own guide to eating in Srinagar sends visitors there in the evening too.
The street has a history that mirrors the city's. According to The Kashmir Monitor:
- The area once had a cinema, which shut amid militant violence in the early 1990s.
- Food took its place: what began as one kebab shop grew into more than a dozen eateries.
- The street is at its busiest at iftar, the evening meal that breaks the fast during Ramadan.
What to order:
- Tujji. Small pieces of mutton marinated with Kashmiri red chilli and ground spices, threaded on skewers and grilled. See tujji.
- Seekh kebab. Minced meat shaped around skewers and roasted over hot coals. The same kebab appears as a course in Wazwan; here it's fast food. See seekh kebab.
- Lavasa. Sahapedia's study of Srinagar's bakers describes lavasa as the bread that wraps barbecued meat, so expect your kebabs to come with it. See lavasa.
Timing tips:
- Khayam Chowk is an evening place. Go after sunset.
- Hours vary from stall to stall, so ask locally.
- In Ramadan the crowds peak at iftar. If you'd rather avoid the rush, plan around it.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Fridays: the stalls outside Hazratbal shrine
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text:
The food stalls outside Srinagar's Hazratbal shrine are the city's other well-known street-food stop. Writers who have walked the Hazratbal food trail describe stalls selling:
- Halwa-paratha. A sweet halwa served with a fried bread so large that a whole one weighs about a kilo. Slurrp's writer described it as about three feet across. The Kashmir Monitor notes that halwa-paratha is sold outside Sufi shrines more widely.
- Nadur monji. Lotus stem fried until crisp. See nadur monji. Lotus stem is one of the Valley's signature vegetables; read the story of nadru.
- Fried fish, cooked to order.
- Masala tsot, for anyone who arrives early.
When to go. Slurrp's account says the stalls are busiest:
- on Fridays, the main day of congregational prayer;
- on religious anniversaries at the shrine.
On an ordinary weekday you'll find it calmer.
Before you go. Hazratbal is a working shrine first and a food stop second. The stalls are outside, but dress and behave as you would at any place of worship.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Winter mornings: harissa in the old city
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Rice plates on a budget: Batte Gali, near Lal Chowk
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text:
Not all of Srinagar's street food is a snack. Near Lal Chowk, Batte Gali is a lane of low-cost eateries serving rice with a single dish. Batte is Kashmiri for rice, as in haakh-batte, "greens and rice".
Greater Kashmir's October 2023 report on the lane found:
- Its vendors said it had been feeding people for more than 50 years.
- One family said three of its generations had served there.
- In 2023, a non-vegetarian plate with one Wazwan dish cost Rs 100–150, and a vegetarian plate Rs 50.
Prices will have changed since then, and a one-dish plate isn't a full Wazwan.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Vegetarian street food
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text:
Khayam Chowk is all about meat, but vegetarians can still eat well on Srinagar's streets:
- Masala tsot, the morning wrap.
- Nadur monji, lotus stem fried crisp.
- Aloo monji, potato slices fried in a spiced rice-flour batter. See aloo monji.
- Halwa-paratha, outside the shrines.
- Vegetarian rice plates at Batte Gali.
Two cautions:
- Shared oil. Stalls that fry both fish and vegetables may use the same oil. Ask if that matters to you.
- Not vegan. Masala tsot's chutney contains yogurt.
Our guide to vegetarian food in Kashmir covers home-style dishes and how to order in restaurants.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Something sweet
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text:
- Halwa-paratha is the classic sweet street food.
- Phirni in Ramadan. In 2025, Kashmir Life reported on a family in Aali Kadal that sells phirni, a set pudding, only on Ramadan evenings. It dated the tradition back 61 years; a 2022 report in The Kashmir Monitor had put it at 45.
Our guide to Kashmiri sweets and desserts covers the rest.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Eating street food safely
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text:
Street food is part of daily life in Srinagar, but hygiene varies. ETV Bharat reported in February 2025 that:
- Police booked a vendor outside the Hazratbal shrine after a dead mouse was found floating in cooking oil at the stall.
- The J&K Drug and Food Control Organisation had imposed more than Rs 42 lakh in fines in 2024, for offences ranging from adulteration to unsafe hygiene.
That's a reason to choose carefully, not to stay away:
- Pick stalls with a steady crowd, where food is cooked in front of you and doesn't sit around.
- Eat fried food hot, straight from the pan.
- Go easy on raw chutneys and uncooked garnishes if your stomach is sensitive.
- Drink bottled water or tea. Noon chai and kahwa are both made with boiled water.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: A street-food day in Srinagar
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text:
To try it all, plan your day by the clock:
1. Early morning (winter only): harissa in the old city.
2. Morning: masala tsot near a shrine or college, before sellers finish in the early afternoon.
3. Midday: a rice plate at Batte Gali.
4. Afternoon: noon chai with bread from a neighbourhood bakery.
5. Evening: tujji and seekh kebabs at Khayam Chowk.
6. On a Friday: swap one stop for the stalls outside Hazratbal.
Our 4-day Kashmir Food Trail itinerary builds street food into a longer route with Wazwan and bakery visits. New to the Valley's food? Start with what to eat in Kashmir.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Frequently asked questions: What is the most famous street food in Kashmir?
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Frequently asked questions: Where can I find the best street food in Srinagar?
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text:
"Best" depends on what you want to eat, but some places are known for particular foods:
- Khayam Chowk is the evening kebab street.
- The stalls outside Hazratbal shrine are known for halwa-paratha, fried fish and nadur monji, especially on Fridays.
- Masala tsot is sold outside shrines, colleges and courts in the morning.
- Harissa shops are in the old city, around Aali Kadal, Nawakadal and Fateh Kadal.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Frequently asked questions: What time does Khayam Chowk get busy?
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text: Khayam Chowk is an evening destination. The grills are busiest after sunset and, during Ramadan, around iftar. Hours vary from stall to stall, so ask locally.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Frequently asked questions: Is Kashmiri street food vegetarian-friendly?
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text:
Yes. These are all vegetarian:
- masala tsot
- nadur monji
- aloo monji
- halwa-paratha
Batte Gali also serves vegetarian rice plates. If it matters to you, ask whether fryers are shared with fish or meat. Masala tsot contains yogurt, so it isn't vegan.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Frequently asked questions: When can I eat harissa in Srinagar?
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When
chunks.text: Harissa is a winter breakfast. The shops PARI reported on serve it from about October to March, roughly 7 to 10am, and it often sells out early. Months and hours vary from shop to shop.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When: Frequently asked questions: Is street food in Srinagar safe to eat?
chunks.page: Kashmiri Street Food: What to Eat in Srinagar, Where and When

chunks.title: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan
chunks.page: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan
chunks.text: Kashmiri winter food: harissa at dawn, hokh syun sun-dried vegetables, turnip and fish dishes, plus Chillai Kalan dates and when harissa is served.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan
chunks.page: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan
chunks.text:
Kashmiri winter food is built for the cold:
- Harissa is the dish most people know. It's mutton and rice slow-cooked into a smooth paste and eaten for breakfast in Srinagar's old city, roughly from October to March.
- Hokh syun is winter's home cooking: vegetables dried in the summer sun and cooked into curries when fresh produce runs short.
- Turnip dishes, fish, corn bread and endless cups of noon chai complete the Valley's winter table.
This guide explains each of them and when to find them. It also covers how Kashmir's coldest 40 days, Chillai Kalan, shape what people eat.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan: Kashmir's winter, in three chillas
chunks.page: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan
chunks.text:
Kashmiris divide the deepest part of winter into three periods, known as chillas.
| Period | Dates (Wikipedia) | Length |
| Chillai Kalan | 21 December – 29 January | 40 days |
| Chill-i-Khurd | 30 January – 18 February | 20 days |
| Chill-i-Bachha | 19–28 February | 10 days |
Chillai Kalan is the "major cold", and sources differ slightly on when it ends: Kashmir Life gives 31 January. Wikipedia describes these weeks as a time of:
- nights below freezing;
- frequent, heavy snow that lies for a long time.
The two later chillas are shorter and milder.
This is the season of the pheran, the long woollen cloak (21 December is marked as Pheran Day). It's also the season of the kangri (kanger): an earthen pot in a wicker casing, filled with hot embers and carried inside the pheran.
Wikipedia's article on Chillai Kalan notes that harissa and other high-calorie foods are eaten for warmth and energy. The rest of this guide is about those foods.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan: Harissa: winter's breakfast
chunks.page: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan
chunks.text:
What it is. Harissa is mutton and rice cooked for hours with spices until the meat falls apart, then stirred into a smooth, sticky paste. Methods vary:
- Overnight over a wood fire. In the Srinagar shops PARI visited, it cooks overnight in a mathh heated with firewood.
- An underground oven. Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes describes a version cooked for 24 hours in an underground oven and stirred by hand.
- Chicken. Kashmir Life notes that harissa can be made with chicken as well as mutton.
How it's served. PARI describes harissa served hot with:
- methi (minced intestines);
- a kebab;
- hot oil poured over the top;
- kander czot, round bread from the neighbourhood bakery.
When and where.
- Season: PARI's reporting puts it at October to March.
- Hours: served from about 7 to 10am.
- Earlier openings: GOYA's 2021 visit found one shop opening at 4am between December and February.
- Where: the shops are in the old city, including around Aali Kadal and Nawakadal (PARI) and Fateh Kadal (ETV Bharat).
Service ends by mid-morning, and popular shops sell out, so go early.
Where it comes from. No one knows for certain:
- A harissa maker told PARI that the dish arrived with the Sufi saint Shah-i-Hamdan.
- GOYA credits the Mughals.
- Some shops say they are 150 to 350 years old. Those figures come from the shops' own family histories and haven't been independently checked.
Treat all of these as tradition rather than recorded history.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan: Harissa: winter's breakfast: Harissa vs haleem
chunks.page: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan
chunks.text:
They're relatives, not twins:
- Haleem. Wikipedia says haleem is eaten across West, Central and South Asia, and is especially popular during Ramadan and Muharram. It almost always contains wheat or barley, often with lentils, and developed from harees, an Arab dish that spread through Persia, Central Asia and the subcontinent.
- Kashmiri harissa. As Srinagar's shops make it, it's built on mutton and rice instead.
- What they share. Both are slow-cooked and stirred until the meat and grain turn smooth.
For a closer look at the dish, see our harissa dish page. For the rest of Srinagar's early-morning and evening food, see Kashmiri street food in Srinagar.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan: Hokh syun: summer's sun, saved for winter
chunks.page: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan
chunks.text:
For generations, Kashmiri households prepared for winter in the summer. Vegetables were dried in the sun and stored for the months when fresh produce ran short. These dried vegetables are called hokh syun. Kashmir Life lists the most familiar:
| Kashmiri name | What it is |
| Ruvaganhachi | Dried tomatoes |
| Waganhachi | Dried brinjal (aubergine) |
| Alle hachi | Dried bottle gourd |
| Gogjar | Dried turnip |
| Hokhgaad | Dried fish |
Wikipedia adds:
- fenugreek leaves, lotus stem, shallot leaves and mint;
- quince, collard greens and spinach;
- tang haech, dried pears from Charar-i-Sharief. When it's dried. Sources disagree, which likely reflects different vegetables ripening at different times:
- Kashmir Life gives August and September in one report, and April to October in another.
- GOYA gives May and June. How it's eaten. The dried vegetables are cooked into winter curries. Writing in the Daily Excelsior in 2026, Dr Rekha Jad:
- lists curries of dried pumpkin, brinjal, tomato and turnip among traditional Kashmiri Pandit dishes;
- warns that such preparations are now "on the verge of extinction" in homes and restaurants. A tradition in decline. Kashmir Life reported in November 2024 that fewer households now dry their own vegetables.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan: Hokh syun: summer's sun, saved for winter
chunks.page: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan

chunks.title: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan: More Kashmiri winter food
chunks.page: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan
chunks.text:
- Rajma gogji. Kidney beans cooked with turnip, which Wikipedia calls a winter staple. The version described by Incredible India, drawn from Kashmiri Pandit cooking, uses no onion, tomato or garlic.
- Turnip in other forms. Wikipedia's list of Kashmiri dishes notes that turnip (gogji) thrives in winter conditions and becomes a key ingredient, including its greens cooked with a pinch of asafoetida.
- Fish. Dried fish (hokhgaad) is part of the hokh syun store. Fresh fish is cooked with lotus stem in dishes such as nadru gaad.
- Corn bread with salt tea. Kashmir Life lists corn bread eaten with nun chai among winter's comforts. Sahapedia describes makai tschot, made from corn flour, as one of Kashmir's rural breads. For the morning table of tea and bread, see our guide to Kashmiri breakfast.
- Noon chai. Kashmir's salted pink tea is drunk morning and afternoon with bakery bread all year. Read the science and ritual of noon chai.
- **Pickles (anchaar). Kashmir Life lists them among the season's foods.
- Lotus stem (nadru).** The harvest begins in September, and dried lotus stem is also one of the hokh syun vegetables. Read the story of nadru.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan: Winter food and festivals
chunks.page: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan
chunks.text:
Some of the season's food is tied to ritual, especially in Kashmiri Pandit homes. Customs vary between families and places, so treat these as broad outlines.
- Gaad Batt. Usually in December, Kashmiri Pandit families offer fish and rice to the household's guardian deity, according to the Free Press Journal.
- Khetsimavas. By tradition, on the new moon of the month of Pausha (December–January), khichri is offered to Kubera and the Yakshas.
- Herath. The Kashmiri Pandit celebration of Shivratri falls in February or March, following the lunar calendar.
- Soaked walnuts are shared as a religious offering (Daily Excelsior).
- Many families cook meat, fish and cheese dishes.
- ETV Bharat reported in 2025 that some families living outside Kashmir now avoid meat at Herath.
Our guide to Kashmiri Pandit food covers these customs in more detail.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan: Visiting Kashmir in winter: how to eat well
chunks.page: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan
chunks.text:
- Plan one early morning for harissa. Service in the shops PARI visited ran from about 7 to 10am, and popular shops sell out.
- Expect restaurant Wazwan, not wedding Wazwan. The wedding season generally falls outside the coldest months; in 2015, The Tribune reported it running from mid-April to October. Winter visitors are most likely to taste Wazwan at a restaurant. Our comparison of restaurant, wedding and home Wazwan explains the differences.
- Ask for home-style dishes. Hokh syun curries and rajma gogji are home food and rarely appear on tourist menus. Ask your guesthouse or host whether they can cook one for you.
- Buy hokh syun to take home. It's light and made to keep. Check that it's dry and free of mould.
- Plan the rest of your trip. If you're coming for the snow, our Kashmir winter itinerary covers routes and timing.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan: Frequently asked questions: What food is Kashmir famous for in winter?
chunks.page: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan

chunks.title: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan: Frequently asked questions: When is harissa season in Srinagar?
chunks.page: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan
chunks.text: Roughly October to March. The shops PARI reported on serve harissa from about 7 to 10am. Seasons and hours vary between shops: GOYA found one that opened at 4am from December to February.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan: Frequently asked questions: What is the difference between harissa and haleem?
chunks.page: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan
chunks.text:
Both are slow-cooked dishes of meat and grain, stirred until smooth. They differ in two ways:
- Grain. Haleem is made with wheat or barley and often lentils. Kashmiri harissa is made with mutton and rice.
- When it's eaten. Haleem is eaten across South and West Asia, especially during Ramadan and Muharram. Kashmiri harissa is a winter breakfast, served with toppings such as a kebab and hot oil.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan: Frequently asked questions: What is hokh syun?
chunks.page: Kashmiri Winter Food: Harissa, Hokh Syun and Eating Through Chillai Kalan
chunks.text: Hokh syun is the Kashmiri name for sun-dried vegetables, such as tomatoes, brinjal, bottle gourd and turnip, along with dried fish. They're dried in the warmer months and cooked into curries in winter. Fewer households dry their own now, but hokh syun is still sold in Srinagar's markets.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Cuisine Explained: Two Kitchens, Everyday Food and the Wazwan Feast
chunks.page: Kashmiri Cuisine Explained: Two Kitchens, Everyday Food and the Wazwan Feast
chunks.text: Kashmiri cuisine explained: Pandit and Muslim kitchens, rice and haakh, the spices behind the red colour, bakery and tea culture, and where Wazwan fits in.

chunks.title: Kashmiri Cuisine Explained: Two Kitchens, Everyday Food and the Wazwan Feast
chunks.page: Kashmiri Cuisine Explained: Two Kitchens, Everyday Food and the Wazwan Feast

chunks.title: Kashmiri Cuisine Explained: Two Kitchens, Everyday Food and the Wazwan Feast: Kashmiri cuisine at a glance
chunks.page: Kashmiri Cuisine Explained: Two Kitchens, Everyday Food and the Wazwan Feast
chunks.text:
| Element | In Kashmiri cuisine |
| Staple | Rice, at lunch and dinner |
| Signature green | Haakh (collard greens) |
| Cooking fat | Mustard oil |
| Core flavours | Fennel, dry ginger, Kashmiri chilli and cardamom; asafoetida in Pandit kitchens, shallots and garlic in Muslim kitchens |
| Dairy | Thick yogurt in gravies; paneer (tschaman) |
| Meat and fish | Mutton is the main meat; fish comes from the Valley's lakes and rivers |
| Bread | From the neighbourhood bakery (kandur), eaten with tea |
| Tea | Salted pink noon chai; saffron kahwa |
| Feast | Wazwan, cooked by professional chefs called wazas |

chunks.title: Kashmiri Cuisine Explained: Two Kitchens, Everyday Food and the Wazwan Feast: Where Kashmiri cuisine comes from
chunks.page: Kashmiri Cuisine Explained: Two Kitchens, Everyday Food and the Wazwan Feast
chunks.text:
Kashmir's food has deep local roots and a long history of outside influence.
- A rice culture. Rice has been the Valley's staple since ancient times, according to Wikipedia. The everyday phrase haakh-batte, "greens and rice", plays the role that "bread and butter" does in English.
- Persian and Central Asian connections. Wikipedia traces the cuisine to South Asian, Persian and Central Asian influences, alongside local innovation. The dish names reflect this. According to the same article:
- kabab is Arabic in origin;
- korma has Turkish roots;
- rogan josh, yakhni, aab gosht, rista and gushtaba come from Persian.
- The sultans' court. Sultan Sikandar, who ruled Kashmir at the end of the 14th century, hosted scholars and Sufis from Isfahan, Bukhara and Balkh (Wikipedia).
- A legend, not a record. A popular story says Wazwan began when Timur invaded and cooks from Samarkand settled in Kashmir. History doesn't support it:
- According to Wikipedia, Timur was camped on the Indus in 1398 when he demanded tribute from Sultan Sikandar, and the two never met.
- J&K's tourism corporation presents the Samarkand origin as the wazas' own tradition.
- Treat it as a story the cooks tell, not an established fact.
