chunks.page: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order
chunks.text:
A wedding Wazwan is cooked for the whole guest list at once, so the vegetarian dishes are the ones the host has ordered. Two things help. First, the vegetable dishes above are on the wazas' list. Second, in February 2017 the then state government announced an order capping wedding menus at seven non-vegetarian and seven vegetarian dishes plus two sweets (Gulf News/IANS); whatever its effect on menus since, it counted vegetarian dishes as a normal part of the spread. If you don't eat mutton but do eat chicken, the trami usually arrives with two chickens, one in a white sauce and one in saffron (Wikipedia); see waza kokur.
What a vegetarian guest will not get is the thing itself: the rista, the gushtaba, the sequence. The seating, the shared copper trami, the washing of hands and the kahwa at the end are open to everyone; our serving guide covers them.

chunks.title: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order: In a Srinagar restaurant
chunks.page: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order
chunks.text: Restaurants sell Wazwan dishes by the plate (Wikipedia) and as set thalis, Outlook Traveller's word for Kareema's (Outlook Traveller), so a vegetarian can order the vegetable dishes on their own. From the same kitchens, look for ruwangan chaman, dum aloo, nadru yakhni and haakh. Our Srinagar guide lists the restaurants and what each has been recommended for, and vegetarian food in Kashmir covers the wider city, including the Pandit dishes below.

chunks.title: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order: Not vegan: curd, ghee and mustard oil
chunks.page: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order
chunks.text: Vegetarian is not vegan here. J&K Tourism's description of Kashmiri cooking says that no vegetarian or non-vegetarian dish, except certain kababs, is cooked without curd (J&K Tourism). A Kashmiri restaurateur says an authentic Wazwan can only be cooked with ghee, while mustard oil is preferred for home-cooked food (Asia Media Centre), and Sahapedia has the paneer for tamatar chaman fried in mustard oil (Sahapedia). Ask before you assume.

chunks.title: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order: The Kashmiri Pandit kitchen
chunks.page: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order
chunks.text:
Wazwan, as J&K Tourism presents it, is a Kashmiri Muslim banquet (J&K Tourism). Kashmiri Pandits are not vegetarian: they eat mutton and fish but not beef (Wikipedia), and one Pandit writer insists that "it's always lamb meat and not goat" (Outlook India). What differs is the seasoning. Pandit cooking uses asafoetida and curd where Muslim cooking uses onions, garlic and shallots (Wikipedia), with dry ginger and fennel powder as the aromatics (Outlook India). Wikipedia's list even records a name for the Pandits who were fully vegetarian and ate neither onions nor tomatoes: dal battas (Wikipedia).
From that kitchen come the vegetarian dishes with the most depth: nadir yakhni; lyader tsaman, paneer turned yellow with turmeric; razma gogji, kidney beans with turnips; al yakhni, bottle gourd in a yogurt gravy; and tsaman monje kaliya, kohlrabi with paneer, which Wikipedia's list says used to be made in big pots on the mehndi night before a wedding (Wikipedia). "Paneer, collard greens, lotus stem and Kashmiri turnips all contribute to the colour in our thali," a Pandit writer puts it (Outlook India). Our guide to Kashmiri Pandit food goes further.

chunks.title: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order: Frequently asked questions: Is there a fully vegetarian Wazwan?
chunks.page: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order
chunks.text: Not as a tradition. Wazwan is defined by its mutton dishes and the order they are served in. Vegetarian dishes are served alongside them, and more have been added in recent years, but a Wazwan without rista and gushtaba is not what the word means.

chunks.title: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order: Frequently asked questions: Which Wazwan dishes are vegetarian?
chunks.page: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order
chunks.text: Ruwangan chaman (paneer in tomato gravy), waza hedar (mushrooms), waza palak and waza haakh (spinach and collards), dum aloo, the nadru dishes, a vegetarian pulao, and the chutneys and yogurt. Wikipedia lists the greens and mushrooms among the main dishes and calls dum aloo rare at a Wazwan.

chunks.title: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order: Frequently asked questions: Can a vegetarian go to a Kashmiri wedding?
chunks.page: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order
chunks.text: Yes. The vegetable dishes, rice, chutneys, yogurt and kahwa are all there, and a 2017 government order counted seven vegetarian dishes as a normal part of a wedding menu. The mutton dishes that define the feast are not for you, and that is the honest picture.

chunks.title: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order: Frequently asked questions: Are the vegetarian dishes vegan?
chunks.page: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order
chunks.text: Usually not. J&K Tourism says almost every Kashmiri dish is cooked with curd, and a restaurateur says an authentic Wazwan is cooked in ghee. Ask the restaurant.

chunks.title: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order: Frequently asked questions: What is the most Kashmiri vegetarian ingredient?
chunks.page: Vegetarian Wazwan: The Vegetable Dishes at the Feast, and What to Order
chunks.text: Nadru, lotus stem, which Sahapedia calls a staple of Kashmiri households. It is cooked in yogurt as nadir yakhni, with spinach as nadir palak, and fried as the street snack nadur monji.

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text: The same dishes, three different meals. What a wedding Wazwan involves, from the vur to the last gushtaba; what a Srinagar restaurant can and can't reproduce; and why what Kashmiris cook at home isn't Wazwan at all.

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text: People who have eaten Wazwan at a Kashmiri wedding and people who have eaten it at a Srinagar restaurant have, in a real sense, eaten different meals. The dishes carry the same names. The cooks, the fire, the quantities, the order of service and the occasion are not the same, and what Kashmiris cook at home on an ordinary evening is different again. This guide sets out the three, with what the sources record about each. For the dishes themselves, see Traditional Wazwan.

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan: The wedding: the feast the tradition was built for
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text: Wikipedia puts Wazwan where it belongs, among dishes "prepared for weddings and special occasions like Eid" (Wikipedia). It is cooked at the family's home, in the open, not brought in. A waza quoted by Sahapedia describes work "with fire, smoke, and heavy copper daigs, starting at dawn" (Sahapedia); Asia Media Centre describes logs of wood lined up in the courtyard with copper degs mounted on top (Asia Media Centre). A Gulf News writer at a wedding watched the wazas arrive around evening in two red wagons, "carrying the cooking weaponry: ladles, pestles, knives and the army", and cook at the vur, an open kitchen, "the old fusty way with firewood" (Gulf News). Who cooks. A head cook, the vasta waza (Sahapedia spells it wasta), oversees the preparation; a typical wedding needing 200 to 300 kg of meat takes three or four wazas with their assistants (Sahapedia). Many of the dishes are cooked through the entire night under the vasta waza's supervision (J&K Tourism); Wikipedia likewise has the meal cooked overnight (Wikipedia). Wazas are paid by skill, from 700 rupees a day for beginners to 2,000 to 3,000 for trained wazas (Sahapedia). Our guide to what a waza is covers the trade. The fire and the pots.

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan: The wedding: the feast the tradition was built for
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text: The wood is from fruit trees, apple, walnut or plum, with acacia and willow occasionally used, and the cooking is done in large copper cauldrons, daigs (Sahapedia). Reuters' 2026 photo essay from a Srinagar wedding shows the same: meat "still pounded by hand and slow-cooked over wood fires, giving Wazwan its distinct texture and smoky flavour", in heavy-bottomed copper pots (Reuters). How much. A 74-year-old waza, Ghulam Nabi Baba, told Reuters that "at an average marriage we cook 200kg" of meat; forty years ago, at one wedding in Delina, he cooked 4,500 kg (Reuters). Sahapedia's figure is 200 to 300 kg (Sahapedia), and Asia Media Centre puts the food served at around 2.5 kg a person (Asia Media Centre). An opinion piece in Kashmir Reader in October 2026 did the arithmetic for a typical wedding: a saal traem, the meat platter for four, at 5,000 to 7,000 rupees; 500 to 600 guests, so 125 to 150 tramis and 300 to 500 kg of mutton; between 6.25 and 10.5 lakh rupees on the Wazwan alone (Kashmir Reader). Those are one writer's estimates, not a survey, but they show the scale. Kashmir Life put a whole multi-day wedding at 20 to 40 lakh rupees or more in 2025 (Kashmir Life). The ingredients.

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan: The wedding: the feast the tradition was built for
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text: Praan, the Kashmiri shallot, is the allium of the feast; the restaurateur Azmat Ali Mir calls it "the life of Wazwan", available only once a year and difficult to source (Asia Media Centre). Sahapedia gives the quantities: 7 to 10 kg of praan paste for every 100 kg of Wazwan, at 500 to 1,000 rupees a kilogram (Sahapedia). The rice is Mushqbudji, a short-grained aromatic variety from the higher reaches of the Valley, traditionally served at marriages and festivals and given a geographical indication on 31 July 2023 (Wikipedia); it "takes centre stage in Wazwan" (Asia Media Centre). And the fat is ghee: an authentic Wazwan "can only be cooked with ghee" (Asia Media Centre). How it is served. Four guests share one copper trami (Wikipedia), topped with "hot rice enough for eight people" (Gulf News). The wazas bring each course from the cauldron, "exactly four pieces" at a time, and guests have less than ten minutes before the next dish appears (Gulf News). The order is "set in stone", and the meal must end with gushtaba (Asia Media Centre). Guests take the leftovers home in bags the host provides (Asia Media Centre). Our serving guide walks through it. How many dishes. The sources disagree, because weddings differ.

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan: The wedding: the feast the tradition was built for
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text: A waza told Reuters there were seven mutton dishes in his forefathers' time and around 20 now (Reuters); Sahapedia says 12 to 24 (Sahapedia); Wikipedia and J&K Tourism give 36 courses, 15 to 30 of them meat (Wikipedia; J&K Tourism); Asia Media Centre says a wedding can run to 72 dishes, while a funeral Wazwan usually has at least seven (Asia Media Centre). The Kashmir Walla reported in 2022 that Wazwan "used to be a measured eight meal course" and that wazas had cooked 21 on demand, which Ashraf Waza, cooking for five decades, called "nothing but a show off and an entire waste of money and food" (The Kashmir Walla). Kashmir Life reported 30 to 40 dishes at wedding feasts in 2025, and a shift from four guests a trami to two (Kashmir Life). In February 2017 the state government announced a cap of seven non-vegetarian and seven vegetarian dishes plus two sweets (Gulf News/IANS); our history guide covers the attempts to limit the feast. When. The marriage season runs from mid-April to the end of October, with a break during Ramadan, by The Tribune's 2015 account (The Tribune). Sahapedia adds that Wazwan, once reserved for weddings, is now served at other family functions too (Sahapedia).

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan: The restaurant: the same dishes, by the plate
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text:
Restaurants serving the Wazwan dishes "by the plate" have sprung up (Wikipedia), and for visitors they are the way in, because weddings are private.
What changes. The fire, first of all. Azmat Ali Mir, whose Bangalore restaurant Sarposh is built around Kashmiri food, says that restaurants like his come "tantalizingly close", but "replicating this experience within their walls is challenging, especially since firewood cooking isn't feasible in a restaurant" (Asia Media Centre). The format, second: a restaurant sells a set thali or platter, or single dishes. Outlook Traveller's word for Kareema's offering is a "Wazwan thali" (Outlook Traveller), and no restaurant serves the wedding sequence course by course to a trami of four. The scale, third: a kitchen cooking for a dining room is not a team cooking 200 kg through the night.
What a restaurant can do. Serve the dishes well, at a known price, on any day of the year. In January 2024 Outlook Traveller's Srinagar guide put a meal for two at about ₹1,500 at Ahdoos, ₹1,000 at Mughal Darbar and ₹800 at Shamyana (Outlook Traveller). Ahdoos, which began as a bakery on Residency Road in 1918 (WION), is called the first restaurant in the Valley to serve Kashmiri Wazwan (Kashmir Life). The restaurant trade is also where some of the craft is going: Reuters reports that the son of the waza it interviewed chose to open a restaurant rather than work weddings, and that some younger chefs have moved from wedding catering into restaurant work (Reuters).
Our Srinagar guide compares the restaurants from dated sources, and the cost guide covers prices across the three settings.

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan: Home: Kashmiri cooking, which is not Wazwan
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text: The commonest confusion is to call any Kashmiri mutton dish a Wazwan. Wazwan is the feast. The everyday food of Kashmiri homes is something else, with its own logic. Rice, greens and mustard oil. Rice has been the staple since ancient times, and bread is generally eaten only with tea (Wikipedia). Mustard oil "is used extensively in Kashmiri cuisine" (Wikipedia), and the restaurateur Azmat Ali Mir draws the line exactly there: "while mustard oil is preferred for home-cooked food, an authentic Wazwan meal can only be cooked with ghee" (Asia Media Centre). In Kashmiri Muslim homes vegetable curries are common, "with meat traditionally considered an expensive indulgence" (Wikipedia); the everyday phrase haakh-batte, greens and rice, does the work that "bread and butter" does in English (Wikipedia), and nadru, lotus stem, is "a staple in Kashmiri households" (Sahapedia). The home rogan josh. One dish name hides two methods. The wazas' rogan josh, as Sahapedia records it, simmers the meat with garlic, ginger, red chilli powder, clove, cardamom, cinnamon and praan paste (Sahapedia).

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan: Home: Kashmiri cooking, which is not Wazwan
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text: The 1988 Pandit cookbook Culinary Art of Kashmir makes its home rogan josh with mustard oil, curd, dry ginger and asafoetida, and nothing from the onion family (Kilam and Kilam); a Pandit writer in Outlook fries the mutton "in mustard oil in a heavy pan or a pressure cooker", then adds asafoetida, dry ginger and fennel (Outlook India). Wikipedia's rogan josh article records both strands, praan and mawal petals for some cooks, yogurt and asafoetida for others, with Brahmin versions leaving out onions, ginger and garlic (Wikipedia). Our rogan josh story follows the dish through both. What home cooking is not. It is one or two dishes with rice, not a sequence; it is cooked by the family, not by wazas; and it is not pounded, portioned and served four pieces at a time to a trami. When a family hosts a Wazwan at home, for a wedding or another function, it is the wazas who cook it, in the courtyard, as above. The difference is the cook and the occasion, not the address.

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan: Which one to seek out
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text: If you are visiting Srinagar, the restaurant version is what is open to you, and at the right places it is very good; go with others so you can share a platter. If you are invited to a wedding, go: the fire, the sequence and the scale cannot be bought. And if you eat in a Kashmiri home, enjoy it as the cooking it is, and don't measure it against the feast.

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: Is restaurant Wazwan authentic?
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text: The dishes are real and often well made, but the setting changes the meal. A restaurant cooks indoors, without the wood fire that one restaurateur says can't be replicated within its walls; it serves a thali or single dishes rather than the full sequence; and it cooks for a dining room rather than for hundreds of guests at once.

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: How many dishes does a wedding Wazwan have?
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text: It depends on the wedding. Sources give 12 to 24, around 20, 36 and even 72; a waza told Reuters his forefathers served seven mutton dishes, and in 2017 the government tried to cap menus at seven meat and seven vegetarian dishes.

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: How much meat does a wedding Wazwan use?
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text: About 200 kg at an average wedding, a veteran waza told Reuters in 2026. Sahapedia gives 200 to 300 kg, and a 2026 estimate for a wedding of 500 to 600 guests runs to 300 to 500 kg.

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: Does the wood fire really change the taste?
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text: Reuters describes the slow cooking over wood fires as giving Wazwan "its distinct texture and smoky flavour", and a restaurateur devoted to the cuisine says firewood cooking is the part a restaurant can't replicate. Whether a first-time visitor would notice is another question.

chunks.title: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: What do Kashmiris eat at home?
chunks.page: Wedding, Restaurant and Home: What Changes in a Wazwan
chunks.text: Rice with greens, vegetable curries and, less often, meat, cooked in mustard oil rather than the ghee of a Wazwan. Haakh-batte, greens and rice, is the everyday meal, and lotus stem is a household staple.

chunks.title: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir
chunks.page: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir
chunks.text: Rista and gushtaba compared: the same hand-pounded mutton, two sizes, a red gravy and a white one, and where each comes in a Wazwan.

chunks.title: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir
chunks.page: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir
chunks.text: Rista and gushtaba are the two meatball dishes of a Wazwan. They start from the same pounded mutton and become different dishes: rista small, in a red gravy, early in the meal; gushtaba large, in a white yogurt gravy, at the end of it. Each has its own page with a recipe: rista and gushtaba.

chunks.title: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir: At a glance
chunks.page: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir
chunks.text:
| | Rista | Gushtaba |
| Meat | Mutton pounded with fat | The same, shaped into larger balls |
| Size | About 80 to 100 g, one for each diner | One large ball, shared by the four at a trami: 200 to 400 g, or 500 to 750 g in one 2012 account |
| Gravy | Red: Kashmiri chilli, coloured with mawal or alkanet, with saffron and fennel | White: yakhni, made with yogurt and mutton broth and topped with cumin and dried mint |
| When it comes | Early, soon after the trami's first dishes | Last in the main meal, before dessert and kahwa |
The sources for each row are in the sections below.

chunks.title: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir: The same meat
chunks.page: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir
chunks.text:
For both dishes the mutton is pounded straight after slaughter with a wooden mallet on a flat stone. Fresh sheep fat is worked in until the paste turns light pink, then black cardamom seeds and salt. The paste is shaped into larger balls for gushtaba and smaller ones for rista, and both are boiled in water until soft and expanded before they go into their gravies (Sahapedia).
Wikipedia adds that the meat has to be pounded before rigor mortis sets in, and that it is folded as it is beaten to keep the balls light. The texture is so hard to achieve that both dishes are rarely found outside the valley (Wikipedia). At weddings the meat is still pounded by hand (Reuters).

chunks.title: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir: Two gravies
chunks.page: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir
chunks.text:
- Rista is cooked in a red gravy. Wikipedia describes it as a paprika, saffron and fennel gravy coloured with alkanet (Wikipedia). Azmat Ali Mir, a Kashmiri restaurateur interviewed by Asia Media Centre, credits mawal, dried cockscomb flowers, with the red of Wazwan dishes, and the article calls rista's gravy saffron-based (Asia Media Centre).
- Gushtaba is cooked in yakhni: yogurt and mutton broth with shallots, ginger, garlic and spices such as cinnamon and cardamom, topped with cumin and dried mint (Sahapedia). Onmanorama names curd, cardamom, dry ginger and fennel (Onmanorama). Neither lists chilli, though Wikipedia's Wazwan article calls the gravy "spicy" (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir: Where each comes in the meal
chunks.page: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir
chunks.text:
Rista comes early. Gulf News calls it the second course, and Outlook India lists it straight after methi maaz, near the start of the meal (Gulf News; Outlook India).
Gushtaba comes last. "As a rule, the meal must end with gushtaba" (Asia Media Centre), and its arrival signals that the main course is over (Wikipedia; Reuters). Desserts follow (Wikipedia), and kahwa closes the feast (Sahapedia).
At the trami each diner gets a rista of their own, while a single gushtaba is shared by the four and divided by the eldest (Sahapedia). Sahapedia gives about 80 to 100 g for a rista and 200 to 400 g for the gushtaba; the researchers who recorded the dishes at a Srinagar wedding in 2012 gave the gushtaba as 500 to 750 g (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, JMS SKIMS, 2012). For the rest of the order and the manners at the trami, see How Wazwan Is Served.

sources.label: Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, JMS SKIMS, 2012

chunks.title: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir: Frequently asked questions: What is the difference between rista and gushtaba?
chunks.page: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir
chunks.text: Both are balls of hand-pounded mutton. Rista is small, one for each diner, cooked in a red gravy and served early; gushtaba is large, one shared by the four at a trami, cooked in a white yogurt gravy and served last.

chunks.title: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir: Frequently asked questions: Are rista and gushtaba made from the same meat?
chunks.page: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir
chunks.text: Yes. The same paste of mutton pounded with fresh sheep fat, black cardamom and salt is shaped into small balls for rista and larger ones for gushtaba, and both are boiled before they go into their gravies.

chunks.title: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir: Frequently asked questions: Which comes first, rista or gushtaba?
chunks.page: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir
chunks.text: Rista, early in the meal. Gushtaba is served last, and its arrival signals that the main course is over.

chunks.title: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir: Frequently asked questions: How big are rista and gushtaba?
chunks.page: Rista vs Gushtaba: The Twin Meatballs of Kashmir
chunks.text: Sahapedia gives about 80 to 100 g for a rista and 200 to 400 g for the gushtaba that serves a trami of four. A 2012 study of a Srinagar wedding recorded a gushtaba of 500 to 750 g.

chunks.title: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand
chunks.page: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand
chunks.text: Do gushtaba and tabak maaz have a GI tag? Not yet: applications for both were filed in August 2024, and the register still lists them at pre-examination.

chunks.title: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand
chunks.page: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand
chunks.text: Gushtaba and tabak maaz, two of the seven dishes Wikipedia lists as a must at a Wazwan, are not registered as geographical indications (GIs). Applications to register both were filed with India's Geographical Indications Registry in August 2024. On 15 October 2026 the registry listed both at "Pre Examination": neither had been accepted, advertised in the GI Journal or registered (GI Registry, application 1336; application 1337).

chunks.title: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand: The two applications
chunks.page: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand
chunks.text:
| | Tabak maaz | Gushtaba |
| Name as filed | Tabakmaaz (Meat Products) of Kashmir | Goshtaba (Meat Products) of Kashmir |
| Application number | 1336 | 1337 |
| Applicant | The Kashmir Wazwan Cooperative Limited, Chatterhama, Srinagar | The same |
| Filed | 8 August 2024 | 8 August 2024 |
| Class | 29, foodstuffs | 29, foodstuffs |
| Status on 15 October 2026 | Pre Examination | Pre Examination |
| GI Journal and certificate | None yet | None yet |
The register spells the dishes "Tabakmaaz" and "Goshtaba". This site writes tabak maaz and gushtaba, and Wikipedia writes tabakh maaz and gushtaba.

chunks.title: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand: What has happened so far
chunks.page: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand
chunks.text:
The register lists the same papers, on the same dates, for both applications:
- 8 August 2024: the application, on Form GI-1, with five annexures: the specification and description of the product, its historical background and origin, the geographical area, the method of production, and what makes it unique. An affidavit, the details of the applicant association, and a gazetteer with supporting documents were filed with it.
- 22 August 2024: the registry's formality check report.
- 27 October 2025: the applicant's reply to that report.
Nothing later appears on either record. This page reports the register's entries only. The annexures, which set out the applicant's own case for each dish, are listed on the register, and we haven't summarised them here.

chunks.title: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand: How a GI is registered in India
chunks.page: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand
chunks.text:
Under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, a geographical indication identifies goods as coming from a particular territory, region or locality, where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods is essentially due to that origin (Wikipedia).
Only an association of producers, or an organisation or authority representing their interests, can apply. The application sets out the product's characteristics and how they come from its place of origin, with a map of the area and a list of producers. The registry first checks it for deficiencies. The registrar can then accept, partly accept or refuse it. An accepted application is advertised in the GI Journal, and if no one opposes it, a certificate of registration is issued to the applicant and its authorised users. A registration lasts ten years and can be renewed (Wikipedia).
Both Wazwan applications have been through the registry's formality check, which the applicant answered in October 2025. The register now lists them at "Pre Examination": before acceptance, advertisement or registration.

chunks.title: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand: What registration would mean
chunks.page: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand
chunks.text: A registered GI gives its owner and its authorised users the exclusive right to use the indication on the goods it is registered for, and the right to sue for infringement (Wikipedia). How that would apply to these two dishes depends on what, if anything, is registered and how it is worded. The names filed are "Tabakmaaz (Meat Products) of Kashmir" and "Goshtaba (Meat Products) of Kashmir".

chunks.title: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand: The two dishes
chunks.page: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand
chunks.text: Tabak maaz is lamb ribs cooked twice: braised with ground spices, then browned in ghee (Wikipedia). Gushtaba is large balls of hand-pounded mutton in a yogurt gravy (Sahapedia; Wikipedia), and the main course of a Wazwan usually ends with it (Wikipedia). Each has its own page: tabak maaz and gushtaba. For how gushtaba compares with rista, which starts from the same pounded meat, see Rista vs Gushtaba.

chunks.title: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand: Frequently asked questions: Does gushtaba have a GI tag?
chunks.page: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand
chunks.text: Not yet. An application for "Goshtaba (Meat Products) of Kashmir", number 1337, was filed on 8 August 2024. On 15 October 2026 the register listed it at "Pre Examination".

chunks.title: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand: Frequently asked questions: Does tabak maaz have a GI tag?
chunks.page: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand
chunks.text: Not yet. An application for "Tabakmaaz (Meat Products) of Kashmir", number 1336, was filed on 8 August 2024. On 15 October 2026 the register listed it at "Pre Examination".

chunks.title: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand: Frequently asked questions: What happens next?
chunks.page: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand
chunks.text: An application has to be accepted by the registrar and advertised in the GI Journal, where it can be opposed, before a certificate of registration is issued.

chunks.title: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand: Frequently asked questions: How can I check the status myself?
chunks.page: Gushtaba and Tabak Maaz GI Tags: Where the Applications Stand
chunks.text: Open the two records on the GI Registry's public search: application 1336 and application 1337. The register shows the status on the day you look; this page was last checked on 15 October 2026.

chunks.title: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures
chunks.page: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures
chunks.text: About 5,500 calories a guest in the one published count, a 2012 Srinagar wedding where a trami for four held 21,933 with rice. Dish by dish, with sources.

chunks.title: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures
chunks.page: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures
chunks.text:
A Wazwan came to about 5,500 calories a guest in the only published count we know of. At a Srinagar wedding in the autumn of 2012, three researchers from the Sher-i-Kashmir Institute of Medical Sciences (SKIMS) had the vasta waza record every ingredient he used, and worked out that a trami for four carried 18,484 calories in its eleven dishes and about 3,450 in rice: 21,933 in all, or 5,483 for each guest (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, JMS SKIMS, 2012). A 2026 health advisory in Srinagar estimated less, 6,000 to 9,000 calories a trami, or 1,500 to 2,250 a person (Kashmir Reader, 2026).
This page sets out what was counted, dish by dish, and why the two figures differ. It reports published figures; it isn't dietary or medical advice.

sources.label: Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi, JMS SKIMS, 2012

chunks.title: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures: How the feast was counted
chunks.page: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures
chunks.text:
The three were Mushtaq Ahmad, of the SKIMS department of medicine, and Sakina Akhter and Shariq R. Masoodi, of its department of endocrinology. They chose one wedding at random, with the consent of the host and of the vasta waza, the head cook, and the waza was asked "to keep a record of every ingredient used and the number of servings prepared". The calories were worked out from those lists with the reference tables for Indian foods published by the National Institute of Nutrition in Hyderabad. Because the meat on a trami "varies greatly (usually from 3 kg to 5 kg)", they repeated the exercise three times and averaged the results (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi).
It is a two-page brief report, and it is open about its limits: one wedding, calories estimated from the ingredients rather than measured in a laboratory, and no count of any nutrient but calories, which the authors call "beyond the scope of this study". Its text also has a slip, giving the highest figure, 3,597 calories, to rista; the paper's own table gives that figure to the chicken, and the table is what this page uses.

chunks.title: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures: The dishes, in serving order
chunks.page: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures
chunks.text:
The paper lists the eleven dishes it counted "in the order in which they are served". Per trami is the platter four guests share; per guest is the paper's own division by four. Where the paper spells a dish differently, its spelling is in brackets.
| | Dish | Calories per trami | Per guest |
| 1 | Methi maaz (meethi), sheep's intestine and omentum | 1,356 | 339 |
| 2 | Whole chicken, fried in ghee (waza kokur) | 3,597 | 899 |
| 3 | Seekh kebab (kabab) | 2,960 | 740 |
| 4 | Tabak maaz (tabakmaaz) | 1,470 | 367 |
| 5 | Dani, a single piece of meat on the bone | 709 | 177 |
| 6 | Rista | 1,814 | 454 |
| 7 | Rogan josh (roganjosh) | 1,322 | 331 |
| 8 | Tamatar paneer, paneer in tomato gravy (ruwangan chaman) | 1,475 | 369 |
| 9 | Aab gosht (aab ghosh) | 934 | 234 |
| 10 | Marchwangan korma (marchawangan korma) | 1,059 | 265 |
| 11 | Gushtaba (goshtaba) | 1,787 | 447 |
| | The eleven dishes | 18,484 | 4,621 |
| | Rice, 1 to 2 kg a trami | about 3,450 | |
| | With the rice | 21,933 | 5,483 |
Each figure is the average of the three counts, and the paper gives the spread for each, from 60 calories either way for the dani to 1,348 either way for the chicken. Daniwal korma and yakhni were not among the dishes counted, and the total leaves out the spinach and the fruit and vegetable dishes that the paper lists as also served.

chunks.title: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures: Where the calories come from
chunks.page: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures
chunks.text:
The chicken. The whole chicken, one or two to a trami and fried in ghee, carried the most of any dish: 899 calories a guest, with the ghee counted in. The authors called it "the biggest surprise of the study", against "the popular belief that chicken is better than mutton dishes" (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi).
The kebabs. Two to four seekh kebabs, each 20 to 30 cm long, came next, at 740 calories a guest.
The pounded meatballs. Of the dishes served in a gravy, rista, four balls to a trami, carried the most, 454 calories a guest, just ahead of gushtaba, one ball of 500 to 750 g for the four, at 447. Fat is pounded into both. In a university study of gushtaba, the recipe adds a "considerable amount of animal fat (20 %)" to hold the emulsion, and the traditional batch measured 17 per cent fat and 15.4 per cent protein once cooked (Rather and others, 2015). A study at SKUAST-Kashmir notes that traditional gushtaba "with an average fat content of 15–25% is having a high sensory appeal" (Jalal and others, 2015). Those were batches made for research, not a wedding's, but they show where the calories sit. The craft behind both is in the stories of rista and gushtaba.
The lightest dishes. The single piece of meat called dani carried 177 calories a guest, aab gosht, cooked in milk, 234, and marchwangan korma 265.
The rice. One to two kilograms of rice went on each trami, about 3,450 calories: on its own, about as much as the chicken.

chunks.title: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures: The 2026 estimate
chunks.page: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures
chunks.text:
In June 2026 Kashmir Reader published a health advisory by Dr S. Muhammad Salim Khan. It estimated that a trami for four "may contain between 6,000 and 9,000 calories", about 1,500 to 2,250 a person, or "80 to 125 per cent" of an adult's daily need, which it put at 2,300 to 2,700 calories for a moderately active man and 1,800 to 2,200 for a woman. It named large portions of rice, red meat, "meatballs such as Rista and Gushtaba", kebabs, tabak maaz and gravies rich in fats and oils as the main sources, and it closed: "Wazwan is a celebration, not an everyday meal" (Kashmir Reader).
The two figures differ by a factor of two or more. The 2012 count is of one wedding's actual ingredients, ghee and rice included. The 2026 article doesn't say how its estimate was made, only that the total depends on the quantity and preparation of the dishes. Trami differ, too: the 2012 authors found 3 to 5 kg of meat on one. What the two agree on is where the calories come from: the rice, the meatballs and the fat.

chunks.title: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures: What the 2012 authors concluded
chunks.page: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures
chunks.text:
The study was written with obesity and diabetes in mind, both "now very common" in Kashmir, the authors noted, and with ready-made Wazwan making it easier to eat the feast more often. They didn't suggest giving it up. Being "rich in protein, calories, iron and vitamin B12", they wrote, it can be useful for growing children and for pregnant and breastfeeding women. Their suggestion was to "reduce the amount served per person" (Ahmad, Akhter and Masoodi). The 2026 advisory makes the same point.
For how the dishes come to the trami, and in what order, see how Wazwan is served and the full feast, dish by dish.

chunks.title: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures: Frequently asked questions: How many calories are in a Wazwan?
chunks.page: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures
chunks.text: About 5,500 a guest in the only published count we know of, at a Srinagar wedding in 2012: a trami for four held 18,484 calories in its eleven dishes and 21,933 with the rice. A 2026 health advisory estimated 1,500 to 2,250 a person.

chunks.title: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures: Frequently asked questions: Which Wazwan dish has the most calories?
chunks.page: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures
chunks.text: The whole chicken fried in ghee, at 899 calories a guest in the 2012 count, then the seekh kebabs at 740. Of the dishes served in a gravy, rista carried the most, 454 a guest, just ahead of gushtaba at 447.

chunks.title: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures: Frequently asked questions: How many calories are in rista and gushtaba?
chunks.page: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures
chunks.text: In the 2012 count, rista carried 454 calories a guest (1,814 for the four balls on a trami) and gushtaba 447 (1,787 for the one large ball). Both are made from mutton pounded with fat.

chunks.title: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures: Frequently asked questions: Which Wazwan dishes are the lightest?
chunks.page: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures
chunks.text: Dani, a single piece of meat on the bone, at 177 calories a guest, then aab gosht, cooked in milk, at 234, and marchwangan korma at 265.

chunks.title: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures: Frequently asked questions: What did the researchers recommend?
chunks.page: How Many Calories Are in a Wazwan? The Dish-by-Dish Figures
chunks.text: Eating less of it rather than giving it up: the 2012 study suggested reducing "the amount served per person", and the 2026 advisory called Wazwan "a celebration, not an everyday meal".

chunks.title: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan
chunks.page: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan
chunks.text: A waza is a professional Wazwan cook, led by a vasta waza. What the word means, how the teams work, where wazas come from and how the craft is passed on.

chunks.title: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan
chunks.page: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan
chunks.text: A waza is a professional Wazwan cook. The word means cook, and it gives the feast its name: waz, cook, and wan, usually glossed as shop (District Budgam; Sahapedia). The head cook is the vasta waza, also written wasta or wouste waze.

chunks.title: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan: What the vasta waza does
chunks.page: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan
chunks.text:
The vasta waza leads the team and supervises rather than doing the heavy work himself (JK Arts Foundation). Asia Media Centre describes a vasta waza keeping watch over roughly 15 to 20 degs, the large cooking pots, at once (Asia Media Centre).
Families book their waza first and often fix the wedding date around him (JK Arts Foundation). In 2015 The Tribune reported that a wedding Wazwan takes at least six to eight wazas, and one waza said his bookings had started six months ahead (The Tribune). Sahapedia describes three or four wazas with assistants for 200 to 300 kg of meat, and working days of 18 to 20 hours in the wedding season (Sahapedia). The cooking often starts before dawn or runs through the night (JK Arts Foundation; J&K Tourism).

chunks.title: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan: Where wazas come from
chunks.page: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan
chunks.text: Most wazas are based in Srinagar's old city (The Tribune), and many belong to Wazpora, the community of cooks there (Reuters; JK Arts Foundation). Their own tradition traces the craft to cooks from Samarkand in Timur's time, as J&K Tourism presents it; no document records when or how they came (J&K Tourism). The history of Wazwan sets out what is known.

chunks.title: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan: How the craft is passed on
chunks.page: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan
chunks.text: Recipes pass mostly through apprenticeship, often from father to son. Ghulam Nabi Baba, a 74-year-old waza, told Reuters in 2026 that he joined his father as a cook at 15 (Reuters). Much of the knowledge is oral, and wazas are said to talk in a code of their own in the kitchen (JK Arts Foundation). It isn't entirely unwritten: one waza family has published its recipes (Sharief Waza, Waza Shafi and Rocky Mohan, Wazwaan: Traditional Kashmiri Cuisine, Roli Books).

sources.label: Sharief Waza, Waza Shafi and Rocky Mohan, Wazwaan: Traditional Kashmiri Cuisine, Roli Books

chunks.title: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan: The work
chunks.page: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan
chunks.text: At a wedding the wazas set up a temporary kitchen at the host's home and cook in large copper pots, degs, over fires of fruit-tree wood such as apple, walnut or plum (Sahapedia). The meat for rista and gushtaba is still pounded by hand (Reuters); see the dishes in serving order on Traditional Wazwan.

chunks.title: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan: A trade under pressure
chunks.page: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan
chunks.text: Younger men are leaving the trade (Sahapedia). The son of the waza Reuters interviewed opened a restaurant instead of cooking at weddings, saying the round-the-clock demands were too exhausting (Reuters).

chunks.title: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: What is a vasta waza?
chunks.page: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan
chunks.text: The head cook of a Wazwan, also written wasta or wouste waze, who leads the team of wazas and supervises rather than doing the heavy work.

chunks.title: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: How many wazas cook a wedding Wazwan?
chunks.page: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan
chunks.text: In 2015 The Tribune reported that a wedding takes at least six to eight wazas. Sahapedia describes three or four wazas, with assistants, for 200 to 300 kg of meat.

chunks.title: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: Where do wazas come from?
chunks.page: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan
chunks.text: Most are based in Srinagar's old city, and many belong to Wazpora, the community of cooks there. Their own tradition traces the craft to cooks from Samarkand in Timur's time, but no document records when or how they came.

chunks.title: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan: Frequently asked questions: How do wazas learn the craft?
chunks.page: What Does Waza Mean? The Cooks Behind Wazwan
chunks.text: Mostly by apprenticeship, often from father to son, and much of the knowledge is oral. One waza family has also published its recipes, in Wazwaan: Traditional Kashmiri Cuisine (Roli Books).

chunks.title: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.page: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.text: How a Wazwan is served: the hand-washing, the shared copper trami, the serving order from the first dishes to gushtaba, and the manners at the trami.

chunks.title: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.page: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.text: A Wazwan is served in a set order, from a shared copper platter, by the cooks themselves. This guide covers what happens at the trami, from the hand-washing to the last course, and the manners that go with it. For the dishes themselves, see Traditional Wazwan.

chunks.title: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette: Where you sit
chunks.page: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.text: Guests traditionally sit cross-legged on a dastarkhwan, a long white cloth spread over carpets (JK Arts Foundation). They are grouped in fours, and each group shares one trami (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette: Washing hands: the tash-t-naer
chunks.page: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.text: Before the food arrives, attendants bring round the tash-t-naer, a copper basin and ewer, and pour water over each guest's hands; it comes round again when the meal is over (Wikipedia; JK Arts Foundation). Traditionally no spoons, forks or knives are used (J&K Tourism): Wazwan is eaten by hand, by custom the right hand. Hosts now usually provide napkins (Asia Media Centre).

chunks.title: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette: What is a trami?
chunks.page: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.text:
The trami (also written traem or tarami) is a large copper platter. Copperware like it has been made in downtown Srinagar, around Zaina Kadal, since the 19th century, engraved with chinar, almond and arch motifs, and everyday copper is lined with tin, known as kalai (JK Arts Foundation). The trami usually arrives under a copper cover, the sarposh (Outlook India).
When the cover comes off, the trami holds a mound of rice with the first dishes laid on it. Wikipedia and the Budgam district administration list two seekh kebabs crossing the rice to divide it into quarters, four pieces of methi maaz, two of tabak maaz, and two chickens, one white (safed kokur) and one saffron-coloured (zafran kokur) (Wikipedia; District Budgam). Outlook India describes two halves or two whole chickens. Chutneys and yogurt usually come separately, in small bowls (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette: The serving order
chunks.page: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.text:
After the first dishes, the wazas bring the gravies to each trami one course at a time and serve them onto the rice, usually four pieces at a time, one for each diner (Gulf News). The exact dishes vary from cook to cook, and Outlook India notes there are no set rules about which are served. A common sequence starts with rista and rogan josh, moves through the other meat dishes, and ends with yakhni and then gushtaba (Asia Media Centre; Outlook India).
Gushtaba closes the main meal: a large ball of pounded mutton in a yogurt gravy. Sahapedia records that one gushtaba of 200 to 400 g serves the four at a trami, and that the eldest of them portions it (Sahapedia). A dessert such as phirni and then kahwa usually follow (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette: Manners at the trami
chunks.page: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.text:
- Start together. Wait until all four are seated; the eldest usually says the opening prayer and begins (Onmanorama; Asia Media Centre).
- Eat from your own quarter of the trami (Asia Media Centre).
- Let the eldest share out the pieces meant for the whole trami, such as the gushtaba (Sahapedia).
- Expect to be pressed to eat more. Hosts often urge extra helpings on their guests (Onmanorama).
- Finish together, as a group of four (Asia Media Centre).
- Leftovers go home. Guests are usually given bags for what's left; one restaurateur says the custom became accepted only in recent decades and was once thought shameful (Asia Media Centre; Sahapedia).

chunks.title: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette: In a restaurant
chunks.page: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.text: Restaurants serve Wazwan as set menus or as single dishes, so not every part of the ritual applies. Our guide to restaurant, wedding and home Wazwan explains what changes, and where to eat in Srinagar lists places to try it.

chunks.title: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette: Frequently asked questions: How many people share a trami?
chunks.page: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.text: Four. Guests are grouped in fours, each group shares one trami, and each diner eats from their own quarter of it.

chunks.title: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette: Frequently asked questions: What is the tash-t-naer?
chunks.page: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.text: A copper basin and ewer. Attendants bring it round so each guest can wash their hands before the food arrives, and again when the meal is over.

chunks.title: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette: Frequently asked questions: Is Wazwan eaten with the hands?
chunks.page: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.text: Yes. Traditionally no spoons, forks or knives are used, and the food is eaten by hand, by custom the right hand. Hosts now usually provide napkins.

chunks.title: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette: Frequently asked questions: What is served first at a Wazwan?
chunks.page: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.text: The trami arrives with a mound of rice and the first dishes laid on it: seekh kebabs, methi maaz, tabak maaz and chicken. The gravies follow one course at a time, commonly starting with rista and rogan josh.

chunks.title: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette: Frequently asked questions: Do guests take leftovers home?
chunks.page: How Wazwan Is Served: The Trami, Serving Order and Etiquette
chunks.text: Usually. Guests are given bags for what is left on the trami, a custom one restaurateur says became accepted only in recent decades.

chunks.title: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.page: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.text: Where Wazwan comes from: the Timur story the wazas tell, what the historical record shows, the earliest descriptions of Kashmiri feasts, and how the menu changed.

chunks.title: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.page: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.text:
Ask where Wazwan comes from and you will usually hear one story: that Timur brought cooks from Samarkand. The written record tells a slower and less certain one. This page sets out what is documented, what is told, and where the two part ways. The short version is on our Traditional Wazwan page.
"Wazwan is not food. It is a covenant between a host and a guest, sealed with thirty-six courses and broken with the washing of hands."

chunks.title: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape: The story that is usually told
chunks.page: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.text: The wazas' own account, as J&K Tourism presents it, traces their craft to cooks from Samarkand in Timur's time (J&K Tourism). Many writers repeat it, some as fact: Reuters described Wazwan in 2026 as arriving from Central Asia in the 14th century (Reuters), and Sahapedia dates its arrival to about 600 years ago (Sahapedia). None of them cites a document, and no document is known: accounts of Wazwan's origin rest on word of mouth (JK Arts Foundation).

chunks.title: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape: What the record shows about Timur
chunks.page: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.text: Timur's army crossed the Indus on 30 September 1398 and sacked Delhi that December (Wikipedia)). He never entered Kashmir. From his camp on the Indus he demanded tribute from Kashmir's ruler, Sultan Sikandar, and the two never met (Wikipedia). So the story can't be true as usually told: Timur's army never reached the valley.

chunks.title: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape: Persian influence came by other routes
chunks.page: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.text:
What is documented is a steady flow of people and ideas from Persia and Central Asia into Kashmir under its sultans, who ruled from 1339 to 1586 (Wikipedia). Sikandar's court hosted scholars and Sufis from Isfahan, Bukhara and Balkh (Wikipedia). His son Zain-ul-Abidin, remembered as Budshah, who ruled from 1420 to 1470, had spent years at Timur's court in Samarkand. The craftsmen later accounts say he brought back were paper-makers, bookbinders, carpet weavers and saddle makers; cooks are not among those named (Wikipedia). The names of many Kashmiri dishes come from Persian (Wikipedia).
Outlook India lists several competing theories, including a link to Zain-ul-Abidin's reign, which it notes is contested, and the view of INTACH's Saleem Beg that the feast grew out of the caravans of merchants, saints and travellers that reached Kashmir from the Sultanate period on (Outlook India).

chunks.title: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape: The earliest descriptions
chunks.page: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.text: The closest thing to early evidence is a Persian work completed in the early 17th century, the Tuhfat-ul-Ahbab. As Kashmir Life summarises it, the book describes 16th-century feasts given by nobles and at Sufi lodges with kabab, pulao and yakhni; cooks hired for weddings, whom the writer only ventures may have been forerunners of the wazas; and food served on a dastarkhwan in a copper dish under a cover, perhaps an ancestor of the trami (Kashmir Life). Kashmir Life argues that Wazwan has no single starting point and took roughly its present form by the late Afghan period.

chunks.title: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape: Under the Mughals and after
chunks.page: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.text: Kashmir came under Mughal rule in 1586 (Wikipedia), and by Kashmir Life's reading the feast went on taking shape under the Mughals and then the Afghans. One thing the early feast could not have had is tomato, which came into Indian cooking only after Europeans introduced it (Wikipedia). Wazwan's red dishes take their colour from Kashmiri chilli and from mawal (cockscomb) flowers instead (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape: How many courses
chunks.page: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.text: Thirty-six is the number most often given for a full royal Wazwan, with 15 to 30 of the dishes meat (J&K Tourism). A 2016 review in the Journal of Ethnic Foods gives seven to 36 (Rather, Masoodi and Akhter). No source records when the 36-course ideal arose. Sahapedia describes the feast growing from a seven-dish meal to 12 to 24 dishes (Sahapedia), and in 2026 a 74-year-old waza, Ghulam Nabi Baba, told Reuters there were seven mutton dishes in his forefathers' time and about 20 now (Reuters).

chunks.title: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape: Attempts to limit the feast
chunks.page: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.text: Governments have tried more than once to rein in wedding feasts. In the 1960s G. M. Sadiq, then head of the state government, tried to phase Wazwan out and then limited guest numbers (Outlook India). In February 2017 the state government announced an order capping weddings at seven non-vegetarian and seven vegetarian dishes plus two sweets, with up to 500 guests for a daughter's wedding and 400 for a son's (Gulf News/IANS).

chunks.title: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape: Wazwan today
chunks.page: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.text:
The core techniques continue: meat is still pounded by hand and cooked over wood fires at weddings (Reuters). The trade is under pressure, though. Younger men are leaving it (Sahapedia), and the son of the waza Reuters interviewed opened a restaurant rather than cook at weddings. In August 2024 The Kashmir Wazwan Cooperative Limited applied for geographical indications for two dishes, Goshtaba and Tabakmaaz; when we checked the registry in October 2026, both applications were still at the pre-examination stage (IP India, application 1337; application 1336).
"When the last Waza puts down his copper ladle, it will not be a recipe that is lost. It will be a language."

chunks.title: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape: Frequently asked questions: How old is Wazwan?
chunks.page: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.text: No document dates it. Reuters puts its arrival from Central Asia in the 14th century and Sahapedia about 600 years ago, but neither cites a source. The earliest description of feasts like it is in the Tuhfat-ul-Ahbab, a Persian work completed in the early 17th century.

chunks.title: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape: Frequently asked questions: When did the 36-course Wazwan begin?
chunks.page: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.text: No source records it. Thirty-six is the number most often given for a full royal Wazwan, a 2016 review gives seven to 36 dishes, and a waza told Reuters in 2026 that his forefathers served seven mutton dishes where about 20 are served now.

chunks.title: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape: Frequently asked questions: Has the government ever limited Wazwan?
chunks.page: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
chunks.text: Yes. In the 1960s G. M. Sadiq, then head of the state government, tried to phase it out and then limited guest numbers. In February 2017 the state government announced an order capping weddings at seven non-vegetarian and seven vegetarian dishes plus two sweets.

chunks.title: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape: Frequently asked questions: What makes Wazwan's red dishes red?
chunks.page: History of Wazwan: Legends, Evidence and How the Feast Took Shape
