chunks.title: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.page: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.text: Both have Persian roots, both are famous for meat, and menus mix them up. What Mughlai cuisine is, what Wazwan is, where the two met under Mughal rule, and the differences you can taste: praan, curd, Kashmiri chilli, the wood fire and the trami.

chunks.title: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.page: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.text: Kashmiri Wazwan and Mughlai cuisine get confused for understandable reasons. Both descend in part from Persian cooking, both are famous for meat, and both use the words korma, kebab and rogan josh. Even the names on the street mislead: Mughal Darbar, upstairs on Residency Road in Srinagar since 1984 by its own account, sells a Wazwan trami, plate and majma, and Outlook Traveller recommended Mughal Darbar for its rista and gushtaba (Mughal Darbar; Outlook Traveller). Sahapedia puts the difference in one ingredient: praan, the Kashmiri shallot, "distinguishes wazwan from its Mughlai counterparts" (Sahapedia). This guide sets out what each cuisine is, where they met, and what separates them at the table. For Wazwan's dishes, see Traditional Wazwan.

chunks.title: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India: What Mughlai cuisine is
chunks.page: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.text:
Wikipedia defines Mughlai cuisine as "delicately-spiced dishes developed or popularised in the early-modern Indo-Persian cultural centres of the Mughal Empire", a combination of the subcontinent's cooking with "the cooking styles and recipes of Persian cuisine", created for the Mughal court (Wikipedia). Its tastes "vary from extremely mild to spicy", and it is associated with "a distinctive aroma and the use of ground and whole spices" (Wikipedia). The Mughals "brought cooking methods including the tandoor clay oven"; kebabs had been introduced earlier, under the Delhi Sultanate (Wikipedia). The representative dishes are biryani, kebabs, korma, murgh musallam, pasanda, "marinated meat in a creamy sauce with yoghurt, nuts, and mild spices", Mughlai paratha and shahi tukra, a rich bread pudding (Wikipedia). The cuisine "has been adapted by restaurants and roadside food stalls for a mass market", where its dishes are commonly "cooked in a thick sauce based on tomato or cream" (Wikipedia).
The korma shows the lineage. Kormas "were prepared in the Mughal court kitchens", first mentioned in cookery books from the reign of Shah Alam (1643–1712); in the 18th century court cooks "enriched the Persian-style stew with almonds, garlic, spices, and yoghurt", and a 19th-century Lucknow quarama held ghee, yoghurt, cream, crushed almonds, cloves, cardamom and saffron (Wikipedia). The curry-house korma that descends from it is "a mildly spiced dish with a thick sauce", often with almonds, cashews or coconut (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India: What Wazwan is
chunks.page: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.text: Wazwan is the multi-course feast of Kashmiri cuisine, cooked overnight under a master cook, the vasta waza, and eaten by groups of four from a large copper plate, the trami (Wikipedia). Of its thirty-six courses, fifteen to thirty can be meat (Wikipedia; J&K Tourism). It is cooked for weddings and special occasions, not every day (Wikipedia), over wood from fruit trees in copper cauldrons (Sahapedia), with the meat "pounded by hand and slow-cooked over wood fires" (Reuters). Its allium is praan, its fat ghee, its rice the short-grained Mushqbudji, and its dishes come in a set order that ends with gushtaba (Asia Media Centre). The wazas who cook it are a trade with their own training and hierarchy (Sahapedia); see what a waza is.

chunks.title: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India: Where the two met
chunks.page: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.text:
Kashmir came under Mughal rule in 1586 (Wikipedia), and Kashmir Life's reading of the earliest Persian sources is that the feast went on taking shape under the Mughals and then the Afghans (Kashmir Life); our history guide sets out the evidence. The names of many Kashmiri dishes are Persian: rogan josh, yakhni, aab gosht, rista and gushtaba "stem from Persian sources", while kabab is Arabic in origin and korma has Turkish roots (Wikipedia). Dum cooking, the slow sealed cooking behind Kashmir's dum aloo, "was made popular by the Mughal courts around the 16th century" (Wikipedia; Wikipedia).
Rogan josh is the dish on both lists. Wikipedia's Mughlai article includes it, as "Kashmiri red meat in an aromatic sauce" (Wikipedia); the dish's own article calls it a Kashmiri dish "from the time of the Mughal Empire", with a Persian antecedent of meat fried in hot butter, brought to North India by the Mughals and later "a staple of Kashmiri cuisine" (Wikipedia). The food writer Vir Sanghvi tells the same story with its hedges left in: it "came to India with the Mughals (we think) perhaps from Persia" (Vir Sanghvi), and a 2016 review calls the traditional knowledge behind Wazwan's meat dishes "poorly documented" (Rather, Masoodi and Akhter). Our rogan josh story follows the evidence.
So the two cuisines share ancestors and a few names. What they don't share is the kitchen.

chunks.title: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India: The differences you can taste
chunks.page: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.text: The base of the gravy. In Wazwan it is curd and stock. "No vegetarian or non-vegetarian dish, except certain kababs, is cooked without curd" (J&K Tourism); "the main skill of a wazwan lies in the preparation of this stock made of onions and shallots", in which the rista and gushtaba are poached (Wikipedia); Sahapedia's gushtaba gravy is yogurt, mutton broth, shallots, ginger and garlic paste with cinnamon and cardamom (Sahapedia). In Mughlai cooking the richness comes from cream and nuts, the pasanda's "creamy sauce with yoghurt, nuts, and mild spices", the korma's almonds and cream (Wikipedia; Wikipedia), and in mass-market versions from a thick sauce "based on tomato or cream" (Wikipedia). The allium. Praan, the Kashmiri shallot, "the life of Wazwan" (Asia Media Centre): 7 to 10 kg of praan paste go into every 100 kg of Wazwan, and Sahapedia makes it the ingredient that separates Wazwan from Mughlai cooking (Sahapedia). The colour. Wazwan's red is Kashmiri chilli, mawal, the dried cockscomb flower, and, in rogan josh, the root of ratanjot (Wikipedia).

chunks.title: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India: The differences you can taste
chunks.page: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.text:
Tomato "is incorrectly used as a substitute when mawal and rattanjot are not available" (Wikipedia): it reached Indian cooking only after Europeans introduced it (Wikipedia), and it is Western and British versions of rogan josh that add tomatoes, and sometimes red peppers, for the colour (Wikipedia). The spices. Kashmiri cooking seasons with fennel and dry ginger. A Pandit cook adds "shonth (dry ginger powder) and badiyan (fennel powder)" (Outlook India); Wikipedia's Wazwan has lamb "cooked with a fennel-based spice mixture, cardamom and partially evaporated milk" (Wikipedia), and dum aloo "cooked with ginger powder, fennel and other hot spices" (Wikipedia). Mughlai cooking is known for "ground and whole spices", and its kormas for cloves, cardamom and saffron (Wikipedia; Wikipedia). The technique. Wazwan's signature work is pounding: meat beaten by hand before it is simmered (Reuters), the rista and gushtaba poached in stock (Wikipedia), the tabak maaz ribs cooked and then fried in ghee (Sahapedia). Its one grill is the seekh kebab, "minced meat roasted on skewers over hot coals" (Wikipedia). The Mughals' method was the tandoor (Wikipedia); in Kashmir, bread is the baker's trade, brought fresh from the kandur to be eaten with tea (Wikipedia). See our guide to the Kashmiri bakery. The fire.
Wood from fruit trees at a wedding (Sahapedia; Reuters), which a restaurateur says can't be replicated within a restaurant's walls (Asia Media Centre). Mughlai cuisine went from the court to "restaurants and roadside food stalls" (Wikipedia). Rice, not bread. Wazwan is served on a mound of rice (Wikipedia), and in most Kashmiri cooking "bread is not part of the meal" (Wikipedia). Mughlai meals have their breads, the Mughlai paratha among them (Wikipedia). The table. Four to a trami, a fixed order, gushtaba last (Wikipedia; Asia Media Centre). Our serving guide covers the manners.

chunks.title: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India: One word, two dishes: korma
chunks.page: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.text: Kashmir's daniwal korma is mutton in a gravy of yogurt and stock with praan, garlic and fresh coriander; the Mughlai korma is the court stew enriched with almonds, garlic and yoghurt, and in Lucknow with cream and saffron (Wikipedia). They share the word, from the Turkic qawirma, "a fried thing" (Wikipedia), and the braising, and little in the pot. Our daniwal korma story makes the comparison in full.

chunks.title: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India: Frequently asked questions: Is Wazwan a kind of Mughlai cuisine?
chunks.page: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.text: No. Mughlai cuisine is the cooking developed for the Mughal court and spread by restaurants and street stalls across North India; Wazwan is the feast of Kashmiri cuisine, cooked by a guild of wazas over wood fires for weddings and other occasions. They share Persian ancestors and a few dish names, and Sahapedia names praan, the Kashmiri shallot, as the ingredient that separates them.

chunks.title: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India: Frequently asked questions: Is rogan josh Kashmiri or Mughlai?
chunks.page: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.text: Wikipedia's Mughlai article lists it as a Kashmiri dish, and the dish's own article dates it to the Mughal era, with a Persian antecedent and a later home in Kashmiri cuisine. The documentation is thin: a food writer hedges the Mughal story with "we think", and a 2016 review calls the tradition poorly documented.

chunks.title: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India: Frequently asked questions: Why are Wazwan gravies red without tomato?
chunks.page: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.text: The red comes from Kashmiri chilli, mawal (cockscomb flower) and, in rogan josh, ratanjot. Tomato reached Indian cooking only after Europeans introduced it, and Wikipedia calls it an incorrect substitute for mawal and ratanjot.

chunks.title: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India: Frequently asked questions: Does Wazwan use a tandoor?
chunks.page: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.text: No. The tandoor came to North India with the Mughals. Wazwan's only grilled dish is the seekh kebab, cooked over coals; the rest is simmered, poached or fried in copper pots over a wood fire. In Kashmir, bread comes from the kandur, the neighbourhood baker, not from the waza.

chunks.title: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India: Frequently asked questions: What single ingredient separates Wazwan from Mughlai food?
chunks.page: Wazwan vs Mughlai: How Kashmir's Feast Differs from the Court Cooking of North India
chunks.text: Praan, the Kashmiri shallot, which Sahapedia says distinguishes Wazwan from its Mughlai counterparts and which a restaurateur calls the life of Wazwan.

chunks.title: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food
chunks.page: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food
chunks.text: Where to eat Wazwan, bakery goods, noon chai and street food in Srinagar, with the published sources and dates behind every place we name.

chunks.title: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food
chunks.page: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food
chunks.text:
Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food
Srinagar's food goes well beyond the Wazwan. The city has a restaurant that began as a bakery in 1918, a shop that has sold walnut fudge since 1896, a tea room serving noon chai and kahwa, an evening kebab street, and harissa shops that open on winter mornings.
Every place in this guide has been written about by independent publications, and each section says who reported what and when. Prices and opening details change, so check before you go. The last section explains how we chose these places.

chunks.title: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food: Wazwan: Ahdoos, Mughal Darbar and Shamyana
chunks.page: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food
chunks.text: These three were the only restaurants named on all five Srinagar restaurant lists we compared (see how we chose, below). They're listed by area, not ranked. Ahdoos, Residency Road. Ahdoos started as a bakery in 1918 (WION, 2018; Kashmir Life, 2025) and had become a restaurant by the 1920s (The Tribune, 2018). Kashmir Life calls it the first restaurant in the Valley to serve Kashmiri Wazwan, and WION reported that tourists travel from around the world to eat its Wazwan. In January 2024, Outlook Traveller put a meal for two at about ₹1,500. Mughal Darbar, Residency Road. Two businesses use the name a few steps apart: the upstairs restaurant, which dates itself to 1984 on its own website, and a ground-floor one near the GPO. Outlook Traveller recommended Mughal Darbar for Wazwan in 2022, naming its rista and gushtaba, and in January 2024 put a meal for two at about ₹1,000, without saying which floor. The upstairs restaurant's own website sells a full Wazwan trami for four at ₹6,200 (17 November 2026). Shamyana, Boulevard Road. Shamyana is at Ghat No. 2 on Boulevard Road, beside Dal Lake. The city guide so.city recommended it for Wazwan in 2018, as did Outlook Traveller in 2022.

chunks.title: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food: Wazwan: Ahdoos, Mughal Darbar and Shamyana
chunks.page: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food
chunks.text:
Outlook's January 2024 guide put a meal for two at about ₹800. Also named on published lists. Outlook Traveller's 2022 Wazwan guide calls Kareema "popular for its authentic Wazwan thali at reasonable prices". TravelTriangle's Srinagar list (updated December 2024) includes Stream, on Boulevard Road at Dalgate, for Indian, Chinese and Kashmiri food at about ₹800 for two; it doesn't single out Wazwan there. Each appears on some of the published lists we checked, not all five. Every Wazwan restaurant we found. Our Srinagar Wazwan directory goes wider than this guide: 29 places with evidence that they serve Wazwan, from the restaurants' own menus, the press, Google listings and delivery apps, each with its address, phone, dishes and dated prices. Courses, and ordering for two. A full wedding feast "can have as many as 36 courses" (Outlook Traveller, 2022), and no restaurant serves that: restaurants sell Wazwan as a set thali or platter — Outlook Traveller's word for Kareema's is "Wazwan thali" — or as single dishes. The trami itself is a four-person format, and one gushtaba is shared by the four at it (Sahapedia). The meal-for-two prices above are from January 2024, the trami price from November 2026; the Wazwan cost guide has the rest.
Restaurant vs wedding vs home explains what else changes, and how many calories a feast carries is its own guide. What to order. If you only try two dishes, make them rista and gushtaba, the two Wazwan meatballs made from pounded mutton. Rista vs Gushtaba explains how they differ, and Traditional Wazwan covers the rest of the feast.

chunks.title: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food: Bakeries: Ahdoos, Jan Bakery and Moonlight
chunks.page: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food
chunks.text:
There are two kinds of bakery to know in Srinagar. The kandur, the neighbourhood baker, makes everyday breads such as girda and lavasa; our Kashmiri breakfast guide covers those. The city also has bakeries in a European style, selling cakes, biscuits and pastries.
Ahdoos. Before it served Wazwan, Ahdoos was a bakery. Its founder, Mohammad Sultan, learned baking at a foreign bakery in Calcutta (The Tribune, 2018). Kashmir Life's 2025 history of the valley's bakeries says Michael Adam Nedou, founder of Nedou's Hotel, encouraged Sultan's father to send him there.
Jan Bakery, Maharaja Bazaar. Three brothers founded Jan Bakery in Maharaja Bazaar in 1965. By 2025 it had three shops, two in Maharaja Bazaar and one in Chanapora (Kashmir Life, 2025).
Moonlight, outside the University of Kashmir. Moonlight has sold a single product, walnut fudge, since 1896, according to Kashmir Life. It started near Dal Lake in Dalgate and moved in the 1990s to a complex outside the University of Kashmir.

chunks.title: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food: Tea: Chai Jaai
chunks.page: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food
chunks.text:
Chai Jaai, on the Bund. Chai Jaai is a first-floor tea room in the Mahatta & Co. photo studio building on the Bund, the embankment along the Jhelum. Roohi Nazki opened it in 2016 (Greater Kashmir; Kashmir Life, 2016). The rooms are decorated in a Victorian style, with a wall of papier-mâché work, and the menu includes noon chai, kahwa and sheermal (Kashmir Life, 2016; Curly Tales, 2018).
Noon chai is Kashmir's salted pink tea; kahwa is green tea brewed with saffron and spices. Kahwa vs. Noon Chai compares the two.

chunks.title: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food: Street food: Khayam Chowk, Hazratbal and harissa
chunks.page: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food
chunks.text:
Khayam Chowk, in the evening. Khayam Chowk is Srinagar's kebab street. The Kashmir Monitor reported in 2022 that it had grown from a single seekh kebab shop into more than a dozen eateries; the area's cinema had shut in the early 1990s. A shopkeeper told NotInTown in 2022 that hundreds of local and visiting food lovers come every evening, and Rising Kashmir described it in 2025 as a popular place for families and friends to eat after iftar during Ramadan.
- What to eat: seekh kebab, mutton kanti and tujji, which is cubes of marinated mutton grilled on skewers over hot coals (Outlook Traveller, 2017).
- Which stall: stalls change, so ask locally. Outlook Traveller's 2024 city guide names Imran Barbeque Cafeteria and Sher Barbeque Cafeteria, and a 2018 so.city guide credits Mustafa, owner of Gareeb Nawaz, with bringing tujji into the mainstream. Hazratbal, especially on Fridays. Stalls outside the Hazratbal shrine sell nadur monji (lotus stem dipped in rice flour and gram flour, then deep-fried), fried fish, poori with halwa, and masala tsot, bread wrapped around boiled chickpeas and radish chutney. Slurrp reported in 2023 that the bazaar is busiest on Fridays, and Outlook Traveller's 2024 guide also lists sheermal and tandoori roti.

chunks.title: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food: Street food: Khayam Chowk, Hazratbal and harissa
chunks.page: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food
chunks.text: Hazratbal is a working shrine, so dress and behave as you would at any place of worship. Harissa, on winter mornings. Harissa is mutton and rice cooked slowly overnight into a smooth paste, and it's only made in the cold months: October to March, according to PARI in 2024. The shops are in the old city. PARI reported from Nawakadal and Aali Kadal, and ETV Bharat from Fateh Kadal in 2023. It's breakfast food: the Nawakadal shop PARI visited starts serving at 7am and its pot is empty by 10am. It's eaten with kander czot, a wheat bread from the kandur. For more, see Kashmiri street food in Srinagar and Kashmiri winter food. For what a Wazwan costs, see the Wazwan Cost Guide.

chunks.title: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food: How we chose these places
chunks.page: Where to Eat Kashmiri Food in Srinagar: Wazwan, Bakeries, Tea and Street Food
chunks.text:
We only name places that independent publications have written about. Here's how we checked:
- Published sources. Every place is covered by at least one newspaper, magazine or city guide. Review sites, listings and a business's own website don't count.
- Wazwan restaurants. In September 2026 we compared five published lists of Srinagar restaurants, from TravelTriangle, Cliffhangers India, Kashmir Travelport, so.city and Outlook Traveller. Ahdoos, Mughal Darbar and Shamyana were the only restaurants on all five.
- Dated facts. Every price and detail comes with the year it was reported. Prices change, so treat them as a guide.
- Unsourced claims left out. If we couldn't find a published source for something, such as today's plate prices at Khayam Chowk, we didn't include it.
- No ranking. Places are grouped by what they serve, not placed in order.
We last checked these sources on September 15, 2026, the Outlook Traveller and TravelTriangle lists again on October 21, 2026, and the two Mughal Darbars' websites on November 17, 2026. If something has changed, let us know.

chunks.title: Achabal, South Kashmir, Anantnag
chunks.text:
Achabal, South Kashmir, Anantnag.
Best time to visit, as the site gives it: April to September.
A town in Anantnag district known for its Mughal garden, laid out around a spring by the empress Nur Jahan.
Achabal Gardens is a small Mughal garden at the south-eastern end of the Kashmir valley, about 8 km from Anantnag. Nur Jahan laid it out in the early 17th century; Shah Jahan's daughter Jahanara remodelled it between about 1634 and 1640, and after it decayed Gulab Singh rebuilt it on a smaller scale. It is now a public garden. Its main feature is a waterfall from the spring into a pool, and local tradition holds that the spring is the river Bringhi reappearing after it vanishes into a fissure upstream.
Things to see: Achabal Gardens; The Achabal spring and its waterfall.

chunks.title: Aharbal Waterfall, South Kashmir
chunks.text:
Aharbal Waterfall, South Kashmir.
Best time to visit, as the site gives it: May to September.
Known as the Niagara Falls of Kashmir, it is a stunning waterfall in Kulgam district.
Aharbal is renowned for its spectacular waterfall where the Veshu River falls noisily 25 meters down a narrow gorge. It is also a base for trekking to high altitude lakes.
Things to see: Aharbal Waterfall; Veshu River; Kounsarnag Trek.

Astanmarg, Srinagar.
Best time to visit, as the site gives it: Year-round.
A beautiful viewpoint overlooking Srinagar city and Dal Lake.
Astanmarg is a high altitude meadow offering panoramic views of Srinagar, Dal Lake, and the surrounding mountains. It's a favorite among locals for sunset views.
Things to see: Sunset View; Paragliding; City View.

chunks.text:
Chatpal, South Kashmir.
Best time to visit, as the site gives it: April to October.
A completely offbeat hidden gem surrounded by lush green forests and streams.
Chatpal is one of the most beautiful and untouched tourist destinations in South Kashmir. Ideal for travelers seeking solitude, it offers pristine nature without the commercialization of popular spots.
Things to see: Pine Forests; Water Streams; Meadows.

chunks.title: Daksum, Anantnag District
chunks.text:
Daksum, Anantnag District.
Best time to visit, as the site gives it: April to October.
A scenic stop at about 2,438 m in Anantnag district, on the road over the Sinthan pass to Kishtwar.
Daksum is in the Larnoo tehsil of Anantnag district, on the Anantnag–Sinthan–Kishtwar road (NH 244), about 42 km from Anantnag and 100 km from Srinagar, on the trekking route to Kishtwar. Kokernag's springs and botanical garden are on the way, and beyond Daksum the road climbs to Sinthan Top.

Best time to visit, as the site gives it: April to October.
A serene garden and historic site nestled in the Zabarwan range.
Harwan features lush green lawns, majestic Chinar trees, and the ancient Buddhist ruins nearby. It's a perfect spot for family picnics and peaceful retreats away from the city noise.
Things to see: Harwan Garden; Buddhist Ruins; Chinar Trees.

chunks.title: Kokernag, South Kashmir, Anantnag
chunks.text:
Kokernag, South Kashmir, Anantnag.
Best time to visit, as the site gives it: April to October.
A town in the Breng valley of Anantnag district, known for its freshwater springs, botanical garden and trout farm.
Kokernag lies at about 2,000 m, some 25 km from Anantnag on NH 244. Its springs gush from the foot of a wooded hill; Wikipedia describes them as the largest freshwater springs in Kashmir, and the Ain-i-Akbari praised their water. A trout farm set up in 1984 with European Economic Community support rears rainbow and brown trout. The poet Sheikh-ul-Alam called Kokernag "a crown of gold".
Things to see: Kokernag springs; Kokernag botanical garden; Kokernag trout farm.

chunks.title: Lolab Valley, North Kashmir, Kupwara
chunks.text:
Lolab Valley, North Kashmir, Kupwara.

chunks.title: Pari Mahal, Zabarwan Range, Srinagar
chunks.text:
Pari Mahal, Zabarwan Range, Srinagar.
Best time to visit, as the site gives it: April to October.
A seven-terraced Mughal garden on the Zabarwan range above Srinagar, looking out over Dal Lake and the city.
Dara Shikoh, the eldest son of the emperor Shah Jahan, built it in the mid-1600s on the ruins of an old Buddhist monastery, and it served as a library and a place of learning, including astrology and astronomy. It is now owned by the Government of Jammu and Kashmir. Its terraces, arched doorways and water channels look out over Dal Lake.

chunks.title: Shalimar Bagh, Dal Lake front, Srinagar
chunks.text:
Shalimar Bagh, Dal Lake front, Srinagar.
Best time to visit, as the site gives it: April to October.
A Mughal garden on the north-east shore of Dal Lake in Srinagar, built by the emperor Jahangir in 1619.
Jahangir enlarged an older garden here into a royal garden in 1619, and in 1630 Zafar Khan, Shah Jahan's governor of Kashmir, extended it. It covers about 12.4 hectares on three terraces, with fountains, a long central water channel and chinar-lined walks; a canal about 1.6 km long once linked it to the open water of Dal Lake. Jahangir and Nur Jahan used it as their summer residence and court. It is now a public park.
Things to see: Diwan-e-Aam, the public audience hall on the first terrace; Nishat Bagh, a Mughal garden on the same shore.

chunks.title: Sinthan Top, Kishtwar-Anantnag Border
chunks.text:
Sinthan Top, Kishtwar-Anantnag Border.
Best time to visit, as the site gives it: April to September.
A mountain pass at about 3,800 m (12,500 ft) on the road between Anantnag and Kishtwar, snow-covered for most of the year.
The pass is on the Anantnag–Kokernag–Kishtwar stretch of NH 244, 48 km from Kokernag and 73 km from Anantnag, and most of the area lies on the Kishtwar side. It is the only road linking Warwan and Marwah with Kishtwar town. No one lives at the top: shepherds and people working in tourism stay overnight in tents, and the nearest hotels are at Kokernag and Daksum. From the spot called "360 Degree View" you can see parts of both the Kashmir and Jammu divisions.
Things to see: The "360 Degree View" point.

chunks.title: Tarsar Marsar, Pahalgam
chunks.text:
Tarsar Marsar, Pahalgam.
Best time to visit, as the site gives it: July to September.
Twin alpine lakes famous for their breathtaking high-altitude trek.
The Tarsar Marsar trek is one of the most beautiful treks in Kashmir, taking you through pristine alpine meadows to two stunning oligotrophic lakes.
Things to see: Tarsar Lake; Marsar Lake; Alpine Meadows.

chunks.title: Verinag, South Kashmir, Anantnag
chunks.text:
Verinag, South Kashmir, Anantnag.
Best time to visit, as the site gives it: April to October.
A spring in Anantnag district, regarded as the source of the Jhelum, that the emperor Jahangir enclosed in an octagonal stone basin in 1620.
The spring rises at the foot of a pine-covered hill about 26 km from Anantnag. Jahangir enclosed it in an octagonal stone tank with an arcade around it, dated 1620 by an inscription in its southern wall, and his son Shah Jahan later laid out a garden in front of it with cascades and channels. The spring and its Mughal arcade are protected by the Archaeological Survey of India as a monument of national importance. On the road from Jammu, Verinag is the first sight in the valley.
Things to see: Verinag spring, its octagonal tank and arcade (1620); The Mughal garden laid out by Shah Jahan.

chunks.title: About Wazwan Way and Waza AI

Waza AI is its assistant; it answers from the site's own pages. Wazwan Way was founded by Nasir Kirmani, who also founded ORL Media, a tourism marketing agency. The stories and guides say how they were researched and list their sources; the restaurant directory was compiled from published sources and listings, and no restaurant was phoned or visited.

What a journey includes: Private car & chauffeur (Your own car and chauffeur for the whole journey, on your schedule.); Private concierge (One dedicated concierge from arrival to departure, reachable day and night.); Handpicked stays (Hotels, heritage houses and lakeside suites, each inspected by our team.); Every detail arranged (Transfers, permits and reservations handled before you land.).
